Oral Answers to Questions
FRIDAY, 17 JUNE 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 9 a.m.
Prayers.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): I thought it would be useful to give
the House an indication of the work set down for next week. The House will be asked to
consider legislation, and it will be much the same as set out on the Order Paper. The second
reading debate on the Shop Trading Hours Bill will be continued, notices of motion will be
taken on Wednesday afternoon, and local Bills will be taken on Thursday-if there are any
available, and I am not certain about that at the moment. It is hoped that there will also be
reports of select committees.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Home Guidance Bureau, Auckland
1. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Housing, What is the present
position regarding the Home Guidance Bureau recently piloted in Auckland, and, in
particular, how is it staffed and what numbers of inquiries are being received on a weekly
basis?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Housing. A home guidance bureau was opened in Auckland on 13 May representing a first
step in the Government's policy of providing an information service to people seeking
homes. The bureau is currently staffed by two officers, with provision for one other, and
inquiries have so far averaged 55 personal, and 80 telephone per week. The bureau is clearly
already filling a definite need in the Auckland community. The Auckland scheme is of a pilot
nature, and the intention is to review progress after 6 months with a view to the scheme's
extension to other centres.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: What advice can the officers give to people having difficulty with
refinance?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Quite obviously this would depend on the individual circumstances of
each applicant. The member will be interested to know the degree to which refinance does or
does not feature as a major item in the inquiries received. I have an analysis of the 55
personal and 80 telephone inquiries, and refinance is an important element, but by no means
the only element.
Mr Wellington: Is it the corporation's intention, because of the success of the pilot
scheme, to develop greater flexibility and mobility, and to provide guidance and advice to
people living in the outer suburbs of the larger cities?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: That is the Government's intention. This bureau was set up on a trial
basis, because the type of staff needed and the type of inquiry made to the bureau had to be
found by experience. Indications are that the bureau is doing a good job, and in due course
the Minister will no doubt be recommending to the Government that the service be extended
to other parts of the country.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Would the Minister agree that people with refinancing problems
do not want another house-they want to stay in their own houses-and would not be
attracted to the bureau for the solution to their problem?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The bureau is available for all inquiries relating to housing, including
refinancing, and the officers are not interested only in those who have requests for a new
house.
Mr McLay: Could the Minister confirm that the establishment of this pilot scheme
represents the implementation of a specific plank in the National Party's 1975 manifesto, and
that it also results from an excellent report prepared for the Minister by the member for
Manurewa, and the committee he chaired?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I am pleased to confirm that, and I should make the point that the
member for Manurewa was chairman of a caucus subcommittee, which made extensive
inquiries to find out the best format for the bureau.

Oral Answers to Questions
Mr Rogers: Could the Minister tell us the estimated cost of running this bureau for 12
months?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: No, I cannot, but the cost is very reasonable. At the moment there
are only two officers on the staff, both seconded from the Housing Corporation, and there is
provision for a third. The bureau is located in the Auckland Building Centre, and, of course,
some costs are incurred there, but it is ideally situated to meet the maximum interest of
people.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Mortgages Interest Rates
2. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Finance, Can he confirm that new
mortgages with interest rates of 12 percent or more have climbed from 15.5 percent of all
new mortgages registered in the 1975-76 March year to 26.5 percent of all mortgages
registered in February 1977?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Acting
Minister of Finance. New mortgages with interest rates of 12 percent or more were 10.7
percent of new mortgage registrations in 1975-76. The comparable figure for February 1977
was 26.5 percent. It should be noted, however, that over this period the average interest rate
for new mortgages was 10.3 percent, an increase of only 1.7 percent over the 1975-76 year.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Farm Purchase Assistance, Wairarapa
3. Mr COOPER (Otago Central), on behalf of Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), asked the
Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation, How many farmers were
assisted to gain their farms in the Wairarapa area from December 1975 to date?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corpora-
ton): Separate figures for the Wairarapa area are not kept by the Rural Bank, but loans for
farm settlement through its Masterton office from December 1975 to 31 March 1977 totalled
46 for $2.5 million.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Housing Corporation Loans
4. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Housing, Can he confirm that the
number of Housing Corporation loans, including low income supplements, fell from 7172 in
the March year 1976 to 3905 in the March year 1977, and can he confirm that this means a
drop of 45.6 percent?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Housing. "I confirm that the honourable member's figures are correct, except that the drop
was 46 percent. The budget in the past year was 3500, and the honourable member will not
overlook that the gross overrun permitted by the Labour Government in 1975-76 was a
major factor in overheating demand well beyond the Government's capacity to sustain and
so contributing to many of the problems currently affecting the country and bedevilling the
housing market in particular."
Mr Wellington: Is it true that the income limits under the National Government have
been substantially increased, that the emphasis of the Government's housing policy remains
on housing those on the low, and indeed the lowest, incomes, and that the purchase of State
houses which has been implemented by the National Government is a substantial means by
which such persons are at present being housed?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I can confirm that the points made by the honourable member are
prominent features of the thrust in the Government's housing policy.
Mr O'Brien: Can I take it from the Minister's replies that the next time members receive
approaches from disappointed home seekers they should quote statistics so that while home
seekers will not have a house they will at least have a set of statistics?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I think that next time the honourable member is approached by
someone who seeks a house and who complains about the price of houses he should be frank
enough to explain why the present cost of houses is as high as it is, and he should admit the
Labour Government's contribution to the problem which, not least, included a policy that

Oral Answers to Questions
would have meant an overspending of $70 million if it had been allowed to continue to
March 1976, an implied commitment for the following year's lending of $136 million, and
5000 unsatisfied loan applications at 31 March.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Will the Minister confirm that the figures set out in the question
illustrate not a fall in housing demand but a reduction in the Government's willingness to
service that demand?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I think that the significant point shown by the figures in the question
is that the move from an almost total obsession with Government finance for housing to a
more balanced finance for housing, part Government and part private sector, is in the
process of being followed through.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that the National Party's propaganda during the
1975 election campaign implied that it would be easier to secure home finance under a
National Government, but that is not so?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: It is a fact that the emphasis in the National Government's housing
policy drew attention to the need to make finance available for those who were willing to
earn and save for a home of their own. It is also a fact that a major preamble to all the
National Government's policy proposals was that the state of the economy had to be
repaired as a first consideration. That is what we are now in the process of doing.
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the Minister's claims relating to the expenditure on housing
under the third Labour Government, will he now say why it was possible for him, as housing
spokesman during that period, to recommend strongly to the Government that a further
$200 million should be made available at that time for refinancing homes?
Mr SPEAKER: It is extremely difficult to find the remotest connection between
elucidation of an answer given and this question, which, like so many others, is just part of
the sort of parry and thrust business that pretends it is elucidatory in accordance with our
Standing Orders. However, I shall not stop it. I merely mention that we are so far abusing
our question procedure that yesterday 7 questions out of 32 on the Order Paper were
answered. Today we have 30 questions. If we carry on with this sort of nonsense of ostensible
elucidation the same sort of thing will apply. I can do no more than point out what the House
is doing. It is for the House to make its own rules.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The member for Northern Maori has completely misunderstood my
reference to $200 million. It was not a suggestion that the Government itself should find that
money, but an accusation against the Labour Government that the state of overheating it
had permitted in the housing market and in housing finance had resulted in $200 million
worth of unsatisfactory mortgages being written in the last 18 months of the third Labour
Government. That problem was inherited by the National Government, and some of it is still
with us.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Magistrate's Court Cases in Masterton and Featherston
5. Mr COOPER (Otago Central), on behalf of Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), asked the
Minister of Justice, How many civil and criminal cases are awaiting hearing at Masterton and
Featherston and is he satisfied that these courts are adequately served; if not, does he intend
to take the necessary steps to overcome the situation?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): There were 10 civil, including domestic,
proceedings, and 25 defended criminal cases awaiting hearing at Masterton on 13 June, and 1
civil and 3 defended criminal cases at Featherston. These figures represent a considerable
improvement on the situation late last year. Proposals are in hand to increase the number of
sitting days in the Wairarapa and I am confident that this will ensure that the courts are able
to administer justice promptly.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Do the local practitioners still intend to continue with their
proposals for setting up an arbitration scheme in order to overtake the arrears before the
magistrate's court?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No, they made no mention of such an arbitration scheme to
me when the member for Wairarapa arranged for me to discuss the matter with them, both
here in Wellington and again in Masterton when I went to speak to them there. I am told
there was an article in the Wairarapa Times-Age last Saturday, including an item on the
efforts made to clear the arrears, in which the local law society is reported to have been most
complimentary to the department over the efforts made. I hope they extend their compli-

Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Wanganui Hospital Board-Criticism of Minister
6. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Health, Has he seen a report in
the Wanganui Herald of 21 April in which a member of the Wanganui Hospital Board, Mrs
Lysbeth Noble, criticised him for not allowing money for cars necessary to provide
extramural health services, and, if so, can he indicate what action he is prepared to take to
meet the objection raised by members of the Wanganui Hospital Board?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have seen the article referred to. There is no
basis for any criticism of the Government about the supply of vehicles for the Wanganui
Hospital Board. With the exception of one car, all the vehicles requested in the current
year's programme by the Wanganui Hospital Board were approved for purchase. The
exception was an old Vauxhall that had already been replaced in the 1975-76 programme,
and quite correctly its replacement was declined when it was submitted for the second time in
the 1977-78 programme. If the Wanganui Hospital Board is still short of vehicles for
extramural services the responsibility lies with the board, as it did not have the foresight to
apply so that its request could be considered.
Mr Downie: Are there no administrative procedures which would have prevented the
board from putting up a vehicle that had already been replaced?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Apparently the administrative procedures do not stop the board from
putting up a vehicle for a second time, having already had a replacement. The administrative
procedures in Wellington are satisfactory to cope with the situation. It is not the hospital
board or the hospital board's staff that has been inefficient. Only one member of the hospital
board described the Minister as hypocritical, because he had not provided twice for a worn
out motorcar.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Consumer Price Index
7. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Statistics, Can he indicate how the
consumer price index is arrived at and to what extent it is an accurate reflection of changes in
the living costs of the average New Zealand family?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Statistics. The consumer price index is arrived at by the regular pricing of 565 items, either
weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annually at a variety of retail stores and service establish-
ments throughout the 25 main centres of New Zealand and eight smaller towns. The pattern
of expenditure used in this index has been established from a survey of the factual situation
of households throughout New Zealand. The Government Statistician believes that at
present the index is a reasonably accurate reflection of changes in prices of goods and
services pujchased by the average New Zealand family.
Mr Malcolm: Is there any validity in the recent claims of the Leader of the Opposition,
quoted in Trade Report of 18 April, that the overall consumer price statistics understate the
position as it applies to the ordinary wage and salary earner?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: There is no validity in that belief. The Government Statistician
believes that the index at present is a reasonably accurate reflection of changes in prices of
goods and services purchased by the average New Zealand family.
Mr O'Brien: Will the Minister admit that there is no such thing as an average New
Zealand family, and as increases in food prices under this Government have outstripped
rises in other groups of the consumer price index and families on lower or single incomes
spend a higher proportion of their income on food than other earners, will he confirm that
the consumer price index understates the effect of inflation on these families?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: In establishing a New Zealand pattern an averaging process must be
followed. The honourable member is aware of the great care and attention, and input of
observation and experience that was made in the last revision procedure. I cannot accept the
honourable member's contention that the position is distorted, or that it is not a reasonable
and fairly accurate reflection of the true position.
Mr Downie: Can the Minister indicate by how much the percentage of increase in the
consumer price index is affected by tobacco and alcohol, and beer in particular?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: No, I do not have those details with me at the moment. It would need

Oral Answers to Questions
to be put forward as a separate question.
Mr Prebble: If the Department of Statistics is satisfied with the consumer price index,
are Treasury and the Government completely satisfied that the consumer price index gives
accurate reflection of changes in the living costs of the average New Zealand family?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: From time to time I have heard comment about the degree to which a
delay factor follows in some categories of expenditure from one period into the next. There
must be some delay factor, but it does not necessarily work to the disadvantage of the people
whose circumstances are related to the consumer price index. It will tend to smooth out the
movements rather than magnify them. Earlier I made the point that some of the pricing
procedures are adopted on a weekly basis, some on a monthly basis, some on a quarterly
basis, and some on an annual basis.
Mr Prebble: Is Treasury satisfied?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Treasury advice helped in the development of the procedure.
Mr Prebble: Can we take it that the answer is no?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! We cannot have a running conversation across the House. A
question has been asked and it is being answered. We cannot have three or four little
questions being thrown in the middle by way of interjection. The question may be answered,
and then we shall proceed in accordance with normal practice.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: If there was any serious objection to the present situation it would be
changed.
Mr O'Brien: In light of the Minister's reply to my previous question, can he confirm that
the food group of the consumer price index has risen by 45.8 percent since the index was last
revised, and that when wages are restrained householders spend a higher proportion of their
income on food, and the large increases in food costs are therefore understated in the index?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: In posing that question the honourable member is being selective
about the time in history he takes between the 1974 change and the present. If he were to
take the whole period, and I believe it is proper that he should, I could quote the information
provided by the Minister of Statistics: "If the rates for housing and food had been transposed
over the first year of the life of the index there would have been no change in the percentage
movement of the all-groups index, as both food and housing price increases were much the
same." Over a short period there can be some change, but in the long sweep of history this
matter rectifies itself.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Housing Corporation Lending
8. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Housing, Can he confirm that the
total Housing Corporation lending fell from $249.01 million in the year ended 31 March 1976
to $169.48 million in the year ended 31 March 1977, and can he confirm that that represents a
drop of 32 percent?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Housing. His answer is as follows: "I can confirm the honourable member's figures. As he is
well aware, the Government's policy is to avoid being the biggest client of the housing
industry or supplier of mortgage funds. I reiterate that the Government believes the private
and institutional sector should be restored to its traditional and major role in housing, and
the 1976-77 figures reflect the Government's intentions. Consequently, a proper considera-
tion of the Government's efforts will extend to the introduction of supplementary policies
designed to strengthen the private sector, an enhanced guarantee scheme, relaxed security
ratios, the introduction of a housing bond, and similar matters."
Mr Bell: Can the acting Minister confirm that the number of completions of new houses
in the years in question was down by a mere 10 percent, and because of the Government's
immigration policy the number of New Zealanders housed in the year ended 31 March 1977
actually increased?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I do not have the specific figures in front of me. I can confirm that the
supply of houses relative to the number of persons seeking houses has improved under the
National Government. I can also confirm that the immigration figures have helped ease the

FOREST AND RURAL FIRES BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): I move, That the Forest and Rural Fires Bill be
introduced. This Bill updates and clarifies the Forest and Rural Fires Act 1955, and follows
an unsuccessful attempt in 1967 to make some minor machinery adjustments to the 1955 Act.
Since then, my department has discussed the question of fire control in vegetation with all
the parties concerned, and the efforts the Forest Service has taken to reconcile the interests
of those involved provides an object lesson in open government.
Following wide distribution of the new draft Bill the Forest Service organised a series of
meetings to discuss improvements to the present Act. These meetings were held in Rotorua,
Nelson, Christchurch, Masterton, and Wellington. At each of these meetings were represen-
tatives of county and district councils, Federated Farmers, forest companies, farm forest
associations, catchment boards, other authorities, and Government departments. I have a
letter from Federated Farmers which states: "The preparation of this measure has been
legislative consultation at its best." The federation certainly appreciated the opportunities
for involvement provided by the Forest Service and the draftsmen, but is not the only
organisation impressed by the Forest Service's attempts to increase public participation. I am
confident that the present Bill will accommodate the interests of all parties as far as it is
possible to do so.
Honourable members will appreciate that this legislation is aimed at combating the
spread of fire. Its provisions are not restricted to forest fires, but relate also to fires in tussock
land, scrub, stubble, and even pastures and peat lands in drought conditions. In general, the
Bill preserves the main features of the present Act. Areas of New Zealand not served by the
New Zealand Fire Service Commission are divided into fire districts, which comprise the


## p. 778 (#20) #############################################

778
17 June
Forest and Rural Fires Bill
counties, the rural fire districts, and the State areas, as before. However, the Bill introduces
two new concepts-forest areas, and specially protected property, to which I shall refer
later. As the long title indicates, the Bill is concerned with the safeguarding of life and
property by the prevention, detection, and control of fires in forest and rural areas and other
areas of vegetation. This is a wider range than the 1955 Act, which related only to the
prevention and suppression of forest and rural fires. Where there is fire, the first aim should
be to safeguard life and property, and this is now made clear. Furthermore, the Bill is
concerned with fire control in vegetation, which may be a fire hazard in urban parks and
reserves, and on large scrub-covered building development lots. The Bill contains provisions
whereby the special powers it contains for fire control of any vegetation are available to
protect these areas, and thereby assist the New Zealand Fire Service Commission.
At this early stage I want to correct a fairly widespread misconception. A short while
ago I referred to tussock, stubble, and grasslands fires. I also pointed out that the
counties are fire authorities, and under this legislation are the basic unit of fire control. In
other words, this is not a Bill to advance the interests of forestry alone. There has been some
misunderstanding over this, and I should like to have it corrected. In 1969, one of my
predecessors, the present Minister of Agriculture, convened, as Minister of Lands, what is
known as the Lincoln conference, which was a conference of farmers and farming interests,
as well as soil conservation and county representatives. One of the main concerns of this
gathering of farm interests was fire control in high country pastoral runs. This Bill deals with
the problems of those farmers just as much as it deals with the fire risks at Tokoroa or
Golden Downs, or in farm woodlots, and provides county councils with ways and means of
dealing with all such cases. Perhaps it would have been given the right emphasis if the
original statute had been called "The Rural and Forest Fires Act", but the present name is
well established.
During discussions by my department it was realised that some properties need unusual
fire control measures, for example, peat areas, private scenic areas, coal outcrops, historic
sites located amidst flammable vegetation, and other similar areas. It was not possible to
cover such a variety of cases by any specific legislation. Accordingly, clause 6 empowers the
Minister, after consulting with the property owner and the fire authority, to gazette
provisions appropriate to protect that particular property against fire risk. This is available as
a specific environmental or conservation measure.
The Bill is divided into four parts: fire control organisation, fire control operations, fire
control finance, and general provisions. Part I preserves the existing organisation of fire
control. I have already pointed out that the counties have the main jurisdiction, that there
are a few rural fire districts, and that the balance comprises the State areas, defined in clause
2(1). Part II brings us to the fire control operations, the field work. Part III deals with
finance. Clauses 41 to 54 are largely as at present except that costs are defined in clause 41,
and appeals are to a rural fire mediator. Fire authorities have two main classes of
expenditure: ordinary routine expenditure such as purchase and upkeep of equipment, and
special occasion expenditure in fighting specific fires.
I remind the House that there are three main classes of fire authority: the county
council, the rural fire committee, and the Minister of Forests. For routine expenditure the
county strikes rates, as mentioned in clause 50; the rural fire committees strike levies, as
mentioned in clauses 44 and 45; and the Minister seeks an appropriation, where necessary,
for his department. For expenditure in fighting a specific fire, counties and rural fire
committees can impose levies under clause 46, while the Minister can impose levies under
clause 47. However, all of these levies are reviewable by the rural fire mediator, and take
into account benefits and risks. Farmland is not normally levied for fire control measures
affecting forests; the details are set out in the clauses I have listed. Furthermore, under
clause 43, which is new, a fire authority should try to recover its fire fighting costs from the
person responsible for a fire before it imposes a levy. The only other new item is clause 42,
which enables the various brigades to recover costs for mutual assistance. This clause is
needed because there is no other authority for payments of this kind. Clause 51 is enlarged
so that the Forest Service can further assist fire authorities in fire control measures.
Part IV is general, and I shall comment only on alterations to the 1955 provisions, where
these are substantial. Clause 64 provides for rural fire mediators. There will not be any
permanent appointment. Anything like that would defeat the object of the scheme. A
permanent man would have to travel, and this would lose time. We must keep in mind the
farmer or forester who wants to catch a favourable weather break, and get his burning done.
In such a case, an independent disinterested check-up may be of little use unless it is almost


## p. 779 (#21) #############################################

17 June
779
Forest and Rural Fires Bill
immediate. There will need to be plenty of common-sense flexibility here. All decisions of
the mediator will be subject to appeal, and if any party disagrees with the mediator the
decision may be taken to the magistrate's court. My department has devised ways and means
of very rapid action when forest diseases are discovered, and I hope that any problems or
injustices that arise, or are thought to arise, in respect of fire control measures can likewise
be cleared up by immediate action. The Forest Service has spent much time and has had
many meetings and discussions to try to produce a draft Bill that meets the needs of the day.
I am glad that, during their investigations, my officers have found increased concern for
common action. I have pleasure in moving the introduction of the Forest and Rural Fires
Bill, with a view to its being referred in due course to the Lands and Agriculture Committee.

Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): I thought I had given the member that
information. I repeat, the members of the Fire Service Commission have been consulted and
are happy with the provisions in the Bill. It ties in with their own legislation.
Bill introduced and read a first time, and referred to the Lands and Agriculture

FREEDOM OF INFORMATION BILL
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. I
thank Parliament for allowing the Bill to be given a second reading, if somewhat belatedly.
This is an important Bill about democracy, and about the public's right to know what the
Government is doing. I believe deeply in democracy. To believe in democracy, one has to
believe in people, and that when the issues are put before them, people will decide to do the
right thing, not only for themselves, but for their neighbourhood and their country.
Today, democracy is under threat, not from extremists of the far left and far right—
because they are of small number and easily identifiable, and we can protect democracy
against them-but from the pressures and changes of modern life. It was simply not possible,
10 years ago, for the Government and the Executive branch of the Government to collect,
collate, and sort the enormous amount of information that the Government is now
collecting. With its space-age computers, the Government collects, collates, and uses more
information in a single day than the Seddon Government, less than 80 years ago, collected in
a year. This is a threat to democracy, because knowledge is power, and unshared knowledge
is extremely undemocratic. How can the ordinary citizen enter into a dialogue or discussion
with his Government when, for example, the Prime Minister has a department comprising
more than 78 people, and access to computers, libraries, lawyers, accountants, thousands of
civil servants, and literally tens of thousands of files, which are not available to the ordinary
citizen? In Dick Seddon's day, the Prime Minister did not have a department; I understand
that he had only a secretary.
Eighty years ago a well-informed citizen probably knew as much about the Government
and the issues facing it as any Government member. Then the citizen could enter into a
discussion and meaningful dialogue with the Government. Today that is not possible.
Abraham Lincoln, one of democracy's greatest advocates, put forward a definition of
democratic government with which I personally agree: "Government of the people, by the
people, for the people." None of those things are true of our system of Government today. I
say that not as a criticism of the National Government but as a criticism of our Westminster
style of parliamentary government, which was designed for a country of landed gentry. The
Westminster style of parliamentary government was not designed for an industrialised and
mixed economy such as we have in New Zealand today. The fact that we do as well as we do
is a reflection of the inherent strength of democracy, and not a defence of our system of
government.
There is no justification for most of the information the Government collects not being
freely made available to all citizens. The fact that most of the Government's actions are
secret cannot be disputed; it is irrefutable. In the first reading I gave examples of facts that
are not available from the Immigration Division and the Electricity Department. I draw the
attention of members to the fact that the Frank Holmes committee, set up by the National
Government to look into government affairs, said in the book New Zealand At The Turning
Point that there is so much secrecy in Government today that the left hand of Government
does not know what the right hand is doing.
This Bill is a first step towards freeing information. It will open Government doors that
at present are closed but will not open the floodgates. Indeed, I freely concede that the Bill
does not go as far as I believe we, in Parliament, will eventually have to go in freeing
information if we want a fully participatory democracy, but it is a useful first step. I assure
members that the exemptions set out in the Bill will not prevent the Government from
making information freely available. The exemptions are set out with a view to preventing an
individual from literally forcing the Government to reveal information in certain exempted
areas such as New Zealand security, trade secrets, and so on. However, if the Government
wishes to make that information available nothing in the Bill will prevent it from doing so. I
believe that the Bill is basically sound. My fellow lawyers who helped me draft the measure
also believe it is basically sound. Most of the criticism levelled at it in the first reading was
either the result of misunderstanding, such as the false belief that the Bill will close doors, or

Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West): I have listened with interest to what has been said. An
expression I used in a previous debate when I referred to intellectual virginity has apparently
caused some offence, and I should like to give the origins of that expression. It emanated
from a Canadian debate on the freedom of information. Under cross-examination a witness
was asked to give an illustration of something that had been kept secret, by a certain Dr
Railton. The Chairman asked, "How can he give an instance of something that has been
kept secret if it has been kept secret?" The chairman then intervened again and said, “I wish
I had the intellectual virginity of Dr Railton. I have been here for so long and have been
violated so many times."
That cautionary tale has been worth explaining at some length. I do not intend to
elaborate upon the extent to which I have been violated. Suffice to say the truth has been
violated. On the question of motive, I rest on the old legal axiom that the devil himself
knoweth not the mind of man. That is all that needs to be said about motivation, except for
the fact that I know this measure has been discussed in secret in the Opposition caucus for
the last 2 months by people who ostensibly favour freedom of information. I am at a loss to
understand why it should have been kept so secret and at a loss to know why it should have
been dropped on the House at such short notice. The devil indeed knoweth not the mind of
man.
The need for freer public access to information about the affairs of the Government is
not in question in this debate. The present law, which has been with us for 66 years, is
thoroughly negative and restrictive and centres around section 6 of the Official Secrets Act,
which is a duplicate of section 2 of the United Kingdom Act. This was not considered
legislation passed as a constitutional measure to preserve democracy, but was in fact passed
through the House of Commons in about 3 hours, because a Cabinet Minister was annoyed
that information had been leaked by a departmental official. In the 66 years since the Act
was passed much has changed, as the member for Auckland Central has pointed out. The
flow of information has increased, the powers of Government have increased, and
technology-particularly computer technology-has expanded enormously. The European
Commission believes that by 1980 the computer industry will be the third largest industry in
the world after the automobile and oil industries.
Sir Guy Powles has commented of section 6 of the Official Secrets Act that a section
ostensibly designed to protect democracy can in fact be turned against it. Section 6 must be
replaced, but how is the necessary reform to be achieved? Reform efforts in other countries
indicate that freedom of information legislation is no magic wand solution to the problem.
Indeed, such legislation has been used to close more doors than it opens. This was the initial
experience in the United States. The 1966 Act was a failure because of the difficulty in
understanding the workings of the bureaucracy, and the ramifications of very general
statements of exemption. Rigorous study of the Act's weaknesses resulted in amendments
being passed in 1974. The original Act has been improved, but nobody would be deluded
enough to believe that there is a full and free flow of information, as envisaged by the
authors of the legislation.
Nobody can legislate attitudes, and the attitudes of the civil servants are crucial. It is
absolutely vital that any measures passed by the House are passed after adequate consulta-
tion with the people who will be required to administer the legislation. The Whitlam
Government in Australia made a commitment to introduce legislation which was in line with
the American Freedom of Information Act, and a departmental committee was set up. The
recommendations made by that committee are revealing, and were in fact more restrictive
than the present law in Australia, which has its own version of the Official Secrets Act. I do


## p. 787 (#29) #############################################

17 June
787
Freedom of Information Bill
not believe a departmental committee can investigate measures to make information more
freely available, because it is in the nature of the departmental creation that secrecy can be
convenient, and it can cloak imcompetence and inaction. Such action must come from the
House, but it must come in a calculated way and be formulated in such a fashion that the
administration is in sympathy with the aims and objects, because otherwise the legislation
would not work. I believe there should be more public discussion, because the more the
public and civil servants know about this legislation, the better are the chances of success.
Legislative forms will achieve nothing.
What is in the minds and hearts of men is what matters. While legislative reform is
necessary no legislative reform will work unless we bring to bear the attitudes, and the
understanding of the attitudes that are so vital to people. Experience abroad has shown that
freedom of information legislation can be, and is, widely abused and misused, and is an
avenue for closing doors rather than opening them. There is a great need for responsibility in
what the House does in undertaking reform. Experience suggests that successful freedom of
information legislation must have a number of essential features. The first and most vital is
that exemptions from disclosure must be precisely defined. General exemptions from
disclosure are a disaster and a means of closing doors. I shall refer to some of the blanket
exemptions of clause 6 of the Bill. There is a blanket exclusion to the Cabinet and about
matters concerning security and economic questions. These exemptions are too wide, and
anyone with an elementary knowledge of the difficulties experienced overseas would know
that you cannot incorporate any blanket or wide exemptions in freedom of information
legislation. This Bill in failing to define the exemptions strictly and precisely, breaches the
first rule of those seeking freedom of information.
Secondly, those with experience of what has happened overseas know that freedom of
legislation that creates massive administrative problems is futile. The administrative arrange-
ments suggested in the Bill envisage the establishment of a new bureaucracy. Mr Speaker,
you have rightly pointed out that the Bill involves appropriations. It envisages unacceptable
costs, and an administrative entanglement that no sane and responsible person would
contemplate. The next requirement is that freedom of information legislation should be
enforced as cheaply and expeditiously as possible. The Bill provides that every recourse goes
through the Supreme Court, but it makes no mention of who will pay the costs, or if it does,
it does obliquely. What is needed for run of the mill freedom of information cases is cheap
and expeditious recourse to an ombudsman, who could resolve the minor difficulties without
any problems at all. Forcing recourse in every instance through the Supreme Court will
defeat the little people without means, whose problem may be minor, and could be resolved
through the Ombudsman with very little cost without facing the formidable barrier of court
hearings. That would preclude the little man, for whom the Opposition expresses concern. If
that is what democratic socialism means I do not want to hear any more about it.
To those who know what they are talking about freedom of information legislation must
be linked with the right to privacy. There is no mention of the protection of privacy in the
Bill, except in an inverted and half baked way. In the age of the computer it is essential that
these two matters are married effectively. Many people are fearful when they hear freedom
of information discussed, because they think it means freedom for other people to know
about them. One of the first requirements is reassurance on this score. An individual's
privacy and its protection is as much a matter for concern as the disclosure of information
about the affairs of Government. The Bill under consideration fails to define exceptions
narrowly and precisely. The definitions are broad and will close more doors than they open.
The Bill displays a lack of knowledge of the experience that has blighted efforts in other
countries. It envisages administrative and financial arrangements that, in the experience of
other countries, would be totally unacceptable. It envisages costly and cumbersome enforce-
ment procedures that would bar ordinary men and women from effective recourse to
freedom of information legislation. It ignores the issues of privacy and the right of
individuals to protection consistent with the public's right to know, and these are vital
defects.
I am indeed pleased that the Opposition is committed now, firmly and openly, to the
passage of freedom of information legislation. I anticipate that the campaign will continue,
and that discussions scheduled to take place at my own party's conference will lead to the
introduction of a Government measure that removes most of the defects and that takes
positive note of most of the requirements I have mentioned. I remind the House again that
we do not wish to be concerned with opening doors into futility. We are concerned with
producing practical measures that take account of the real experience of people overseas.


## p. 788 (#30) #############################################

788
17 June
Freedom of Information Bill
May I conclude the discussion of freedom of information on my part by referring to a
matter that is vital to the information flow to all members of Parliament. I refer to the
General Assembly Library which, as a source of information for members, requires much to
be done. This will involve not merely the amendment of the Official Secrets Act, but the
amendment of other legislation as well. Before I go to that, though, I should like to bring to
the attention of the House the impact of replacing clause 6. This would involve much more
than the Official Secrets Act. We would have to look at section 78 of the Crimes Act, at
regulation 42 of the Public Service Regulations, at section 56 of the State Services Act, and
at section 19 of the Oaths and Declarations Act. In addition, we would have to look at the
Statistics Act and other enactments that give a statutory right to secrecy. We would have to
deal with the problem of document classification. This is not mentioned in the Bill, nor does
the Bill display a knowledge of the other enactments that would be affected by the
replacement of clause 6. The devil himself knoweth not the mind of man. I do not know why
this half-baked and ill-conceived Bill has been dropped before the House. I am content that
it has been, and that people are now committed to freedom of information legislation.
I now wish to return to the parliamentary library. I compliment the staff of that library.
They are first class, and they do an excellent job. But I know from discussions with them that
there is much information they do not receive-that should be in store, and that should be
able to be retrieved for members at quick notice. At present the library is deficient in this
and whatever we do about freedom of information, we have to improve the information
sources available to members on both sides of the House. This would probably mean the
introduction of some computer technique into the General Assembly Library such as has
been done in the parliamentary library in Canada. It also means that Government depart-
ments and all State agencies, even the universities in some instances, need to be more
forthcoming and open about the information they possess, and in making it available to the
General Assembly Library. In this way, the disadvantages from which all members suffer in
terms of availability of information could be remedied, in substantial measure at least. Such
a measure would facilitate the research operations of both parties, as well as those of
individual members, and would be invaluable as an adjunct to freedom of information
legislation. All the information in the world will be of little avail if attitudes run counter to it,
whether they be in the administration or in the House. Freedom of information legislation by
itself will be of little advantage to members if we spend so much of our time in time-
consuming futility. The proposed Bill is so deficient in vital matters that it does not provide a
basis for intelligent bi-partisan consideration, such as it requires.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 1 p.m.

Social Welfare Beneficiaries-Rent Increases
1. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Housing, How many
beneficiaries (including age beneficiaries who have been subsequently transferred to
national superannuation) who occupied Government-owned premises have had their rent
increased since the Government took office, and what was the total amount per week of such
increases?


## p. 791 (#33) #############################################

Oral Answers to Questions
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): In 1973 the then Labour Government
introduced income-related rents with annual reviews. As a result of this policy, rents for all
Housing Corporation tenants, including beneficiaries and former age beneficiaries now in
receipt of national superannuation, have been reviewed since this Government took office.
The Housing Corporation is unable to supply details of the total amount per week of such
increases, but in the case of former age beneficiaries whose sole income is national
superannuation increases are limited to a maximum of $2 per week per year.
Mr Wellington: Can the Minister confirm that whereas the ordinary minimum rent is
$10 a week, the minimum rent for social welfare beneficiaries, including the superannuitants
to which the original question refers, is $7.50 a week—a reasonable proportion in view of the
considerably better deal that superannuitants are receiving under the new superannuation
scheme?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I can confirm that the minimum rent for beneficiaries is $7.50
provided their sole source of income is national superannuation. The rents charged are not
related simply to the fact that they are beneficiaries, but to the income they earn. If they are
beneficiaries or national superannuitants with a large income they will pay the same rent as
anybody else, but if their income is solely from national superannuation their rent is
calculated at one-sixth of their income, as with everyone else, and in order to get to that
point the maximum increase in any one year in any review is $2 a week.

superannuitants in corporation houses while there is a rent freeze in progress?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: The member should know that there has been no rent freeze
since 1 January this year.

Immunisation Programme
2. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Health, In view of the world
interest in immunisation in the interests of better health, can he indicate how effective the
programme in New Zealand is, and what figures has he available to indicate the trends in
immunisation over recent years?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The present immunisation programme underta-
ken by general practitioners and departmental staff has been shown to be effective by the
extremely low incidence of diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, and poliomyelitis in the
community. As immunisation of children is not compulsory, complete statistics are not
available. Medical officers of health in districts are responsible for ensuring that adequate
immunity is maintained in the community, and where this falls below a satisfactory level they
will take the necessary steps to remedy the position. Figures available from the general
medical services benefit claims by general practitioners indicate that there is an overall
increase in the number of immunisations, but the department is not satisfied with the
immunisation levels for measles, and this is at present under action.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Geneva Conference on Rules of War
3. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs, (1) Was
New Zealand represented at the recent Geneva conference on the rules of war, (2) if so, did
we vote for and/or sign the protocols agreeing to extend to guerrillas the same prisoner-of-
war status as is required to be given to regular soldiers, and (3) will this protection cover
"urban guerrillas" or is it to be confined to para-military groups such as the Yugoslav
Partisans?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): New Zealand was represented
at the conference. It supported the adoption of the protocol providing for guerrillas to be
entitled to prisoner-of-war status. We were not prepared, however, to accept provisions that
would have placed guerrillas in a better position than regular soldiers. Urban guerrillas are


## p. 792 (#34) #############################################

792
21 June
Oral Answers to Questions
unlikely to qualify for the protection of the protocol unless they were part of a larger group
of dissident armed forces under responsible command that occupied part of the state's
territory and was able to carry out sustained and concerted military operations. The protocol
is not yet open for signature.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Does the extension cover only those who wear uniforms or
otherwise distinguish themselves, and openly bear arms?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Yes. There was a move by some countries that a guerrilla
indistinguishable from a civilian should be given the right of prisoner-of-war status, and New
Zealand, along with a considerable part of the Western World, was against that.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Some press reports seem to indicate that the protection would
also cover guerrillas with no distinguishing marks, so long as they exhibited their arms before
discharging them, which of course is a very narrow distinction. Is this correct?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Urban guerrillas would be unlikely to qualify for the
protection of the protocol unless they were part of a larger organisation that met the criteria
of a dissident armed force, organised and under responsible command, that occupied part of
the state's territory, and was able to carry out sustained and concerted military operations.
Those were the three criteria laid down.

Social Welfare Beneficiaries-Costs
4. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson), on behalf of Mr BRILL (Kapiti), asked the Minister of
Social Welfare, What is the basis of calculation of the difference between the amount paid to
a single beneficiary and that paid to a married beneficiary, and does the difference of $25.60
represent the cost of maintaining the additonal adult in the house?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Under present benefit levels a
married couple receives $64 a week, or $32 a week each. A single person receives $38.40 a
week, which represents 60 percent of the married couple rate. Single persons receive more
than half the married couple rate because they are not able to share expenses in the way that
married couples can.

Native Trees at Karioi Pulp and Paper Mill
6. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Forests, In view of the reports
that native trees are being felled by the company building the Karioi pulp and paper mill
(Dominion, 9 June 1977), can he tell the House what action he intends to take on the matter?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The afforestation programme of the company
building the pulp mill at Karioi involved land of various ownerships but predominantly of
Maori tenure. No State forest land is involved in the afforestation programme. The
company, Winstone Afforestation Ltd, proposes to commence planting radiata pine on this
land, which it could either lease or buy. The land on which planting will take place is largely
scrub covered, but it also includes some areas of cut-over indigenous forest and virgin bush.
The revised policy for State indigenous forests does not apply to private landowners,
although private landowners are, of course, subject to the constraints of the normal town
and country planning and water and soil conservation procedures. If it is the private
landholders' wish to remove indigenous forest for farm or plantation forest development,
they are free to do so within these constraints. In this case, the Rangitikei-Wanganui
Catchment Board proposes to use the forest operations guidelines and land use capability
assessments as a basis for exercising its statutory role in protecting soil and water values.
Dr Shearer: How much Maori land is involved?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: It is not possible at present to indicate exactly how much Maori
land is involved, because negotiations are still proceeding with the owners. However, I do
have with me a report from the Taranaki Herald of 18 June, which states that the Maori
owners of 5600 hectares of land between Raetihi and the Wanganui River will be asked to
lease their land to Winstone Afforestation Ltd for planting in pine forest. I understand that
this could perhaps be only part of the land involved in the final afforestation programme.
Mr Prebble: In light of the Minister's answer and his reference to press statements, I
wonder if he could clarify the statement appearing in the Waikato Times on 2 June 1977
stating that: "Claims that native forests will be felled to make way for pine forests in the King
Country were denied today by the Minister of Forests", and that appearing 2 days later in
the same newpaper that: "The company building the Karioi pulp and paper mill admitted
that native trees will be felled to make way for its pine plantations."?


## p. 794 (#36) #############################################

794

Hon. V. S. YOUNG: In the original agreement entered into between Winstone's and, I
think, Samsung Industries, and the Crown, the basis was the use of wood from the Karioi
exotic forest for the pulp mill. Waste from mills in the southern half of the North Island was
also involved. In my first press statement dated 9 December 1976 I said: "The original
offering from Karioi was an annual volume of approximately 45 000 cubic metres of wood for

Chemosterilants-Evaluation
8. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Agriculture, What progress has
been made in the evaluation of chemosterilants such as diethylsthibestrol and BDH 10131
for the control of rabbits, opossums, and goats?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The use of chemosterilants for the
control of rabbits, opposums, and goats does not appear promising at present. Some
chemicals, such as diethysthibestrol and BDH 10131, were evaluated by Dr Godfrey, a
ministry scientist, while in America, and showed considerable potential. However, all
chemicals evaluated were unsatisfactory for reasons of cost, availability, or effectiveness. At
present there is little likelihood of suitable chemicals being developed by the pharmaceutical
companies because of the high development costs and the limited markets. Dr Godfrey, who
is now at Invermay Research Centre, is keeping in touch with the companies, and if a
suitable chemical is produced it will be followed up.

BUILDING INDUSTRY CRISIS—NOTICE UNDER STANDING ORDER 89
Mr SPEAKER: I have to inform the House that I have received a request from the
member for Manukau to move the adjournment of the House to discuss a definite matter of
urgent public importance, in terms of Standing Orders 89 and 90. Actually, the wrong
Standing Orders have been given, presumably because an earlier edition was used. The first
paragraph of the letter from the member for Manukau reads: "In terms of Standing
Orders"—and, as I have mentioned, they should be 89 and 90—“I wish to give notice of my
intention to move the adjournment of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public
importance, namely, the rapidly deteriorating conditions in the building industry as set out in
the special report No. 93 into the crisis carried out by the Building Industry Advisory
Council, a copy of which is attached hereto." I have looked at the copy, and it seems to me
that the nature of the "special report", as it is termed, has been rather overstated. In fact, it
is the June newsletter of the Building Industry Advisory Council, and the caption is "Recent
building trends of concern to the industry". The copy I have is date-stamped 13 June-8 days
ago. It is a copy from the General Assembly Library, and therefore the newsletter was
probably issued a little earlier than that.
The opening sentence of the report itself states: "It was the Council's intention to await
the outcome of the 1977 Budget before reviewing building industry prospects for 1977-78,
but at the council's meeting on 18 May it was apparent that conditions within the industry
were deteriorating rapidly and an interim report on current trends would serve a useful
purpose." At the end of the newsletter it is stated that the association would support the
council's view. I shall read that part: "Recent meetings of the Building Industry Confedera-
tion and Material Supply Council of the New Zealand Manufacturers Association give
support to the council's view that conditions in the building industry have deteriorated since
March, but, because of regional differences and the 2 or 3 months' delay with official
building statistics, the seriousness of the current situation is not entirely clear. The council is
seeking clarification through surveys of the forward workloads of builders and the profes-
sional groups in the regions most affected, and hopes to be in a position to report in more
detail by the end of June."
The limitations on the type of subject for a debate of the sort desired are set out in
Standing Order 90, which commences: "The statement of the matter proposed to be
discussed on a motion for the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 89 shall not
be framed in general terms but shall deal with a particular case of recent occurrence which
requires the immediate attention of the House and the Government. . ." The remainder of
the Standing Order does not apply. It seems to me that the suggested subject, the rapidly
deteriorating conditions in the building industry as set out in what is called "the special
report No. 93" into the crisis, does not amount to “a particular case of recent occurrence" of
the sort contemplated by the Standing Orders. Therefore, I am unable to grant leave to
move the motion.

FREEDOM OF INFORMATION BILL
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West): The House may recall that, when we adjourned on
Friday, there had been some discussion of the essential features of freedom of information
legislation, as revealed by the experience of other countries. I had drawn the attention of the
House to the need to ensure that the proposals could be expeditiously and cheaply
administered, and also readily enforced, without necessarily involving recourse to the
Supreme Court. I stressed the need to protect privacy, because of the concern of ordinary
people that greater freedom of information could, in fact, mean greater access to informa-
tion about them and their private affairs. It is necessary, therefore, to marry the public right
to know to the effective protection of the privacy of the individual.
Over the weekend, I took the opportunity to re-read the debates that preceded the first
freedom of information Act in America, as well as the debates amending that legislation. I
am more than satisfied that the passage of this legislation would produce precisely the
dilemma that arose in America-that is to say, a freedom of information Act that is called


## p. 800 (#42) #############################################

800
21 June
Freedom of Information Bill
into operation without adequate consultation invariably runs into a barrier of adverse
attitudes. Years of foot dragging, as it was described, in the federal bureaucracy frustrated
the very good intentions behind the first freedom of information legislation in the United
States, and the same could happen here, which is something to be avoided. That is why I
have always argued that, rather than suddenly present a draft measure-which, following
overseas precedent, could be done at any time—the ground has to be carefully prepared; not
only public discussion, but discussion with the officials who would be called upon to
administer such an Act is essential. I am more than ever persuaded that the action envisaged
would not have the required effect. However well intentioned such legislation may be, its
effect on people's minds would be adverse.
It is not enough to be well intentioned. We have to learn from the experience of others,
and apply that experience in this country. Progress in the United Kingdom has been
inordinately slow. It can be attributed to the reluctance of either the present Government or
the bureaucracy to come up with firm proposals, but what is envisaged there is far more
liberal than anything in the present Bill, particularly the blanket exemption that this Bill
gives to any document that has been before the Cabinet. That exemption is so wide that, as
happened in Sweden, I have no doubt that devices would be employed somehow to bring
almost any paper to the attention of the Cabinet, thereby excluding it. The blanket
exemption of a document on the grounds of an adverse effect on the economic interests of
New Zealand could be exploited to exempt any document. Therefore, the draft Bill repeats
the fundamental errors that have so frustrated the advance of freedom of information
legislation in other countries.
I applaud the author's intention, but I cannot regard this Bill as providing a satisfactory
foundation for legislation, or even as providing the basis for the kind of discussion in which
we must all be involved if we are to make any advance in this field. I applaud the bipartisan
approach; that is absolutely essential. I repeat that I applaud the author's intention, but let
us get to the point where a Government measure can be introduced that takes full account of
the matters I have mentioned. On that sound foundation, let us proceed to the deliberation,
which I believe will last for some time. None of us should be so deluded as to believe that the
mere passage of any kind of legislation ensures our objectives. The only effect of passing the
freedom of information legislation would be to reverse the present, totally negative,
approach of the restrictive section 6 of the Official Secrets Act, and to substitute for that
provision more positive provisions stating that information that is not included in one or two
well defined exemptions should be available. All we are doing is beginning the process of
evolution.
There is no revolutionary answer to the problem. The real answer lies in the hearts and
minds of men, and in their attitudes. This evolutionary process is certainly a beginning, but it
must begin with a Bill that is firmly founded on experience overseas. We must not be led into
the mire of the American experience by making exemptions that are too broad, and we must
not act too hastily. If we do, we produce legislation that is nothing but an exercise in
frustration, and, like the Americans,we would find ourselves, 4 or 5 years from now, forced
into a fundamental review because the legislation did not work. So, while I applaud the
intention, and commend the necessity for a bipartisan approach, I cannot regard the Bill
before us as providing the necessary foundation. For that reason, I urge those concerned to
consider that it is quite evident, as I have detected in the discussion already, that the
majority of members favours an advance on this front. I am concerned with the most
effective mode of advance; and I say that the most effective mode is a Government measure.

This Bill could be used as a basis for discussion in a committee, for bipartisan examination of

As I have indicated, the matters raised by the member for Hamilton West on Friday

but retrieval of information becomes important only when the information is available. This
Bill is concerned with the freedom to get information; it is not concerned with the practical
problem of retrieving something that is already stored in our library, or any other. That
could be a practical problem, but the real problem is whether our library should be entitled
to get the material from the Government, and whether the public, members of Parliament,
or anyone who wishes to serve the public should have the right to get information from the
Government at a time when it can be used.
In the United States, this question has gone another way and there is pretty well open
slather for the press, which has almost complete exemption from the laws of libel by being
able to claim it is acting in the public interest. That is not what we want. We have seen today
yet another intrusion into the private affairs of a public figure by members of the press, who
claim to act in the public interest but who are, in fact, only seeking sensationalism. Because
the United States legislation took a few years to perfect and a draft Bill in Britain has not
been acted upon, that is no reason for us to sit back meekly and say that, as those places face
difficulties, so it is too difficult for us. We should look at the problem in the light of New
Zealand experience, and decide what we are trying to protect and ensure that other
information is freely available. We could do that better by making a detailed examination of
the exemptions in clause 6 and the following clauses, to see what we want to protect and
what we want to make available, and devise a formula that makes it possible.

drafting a private member's Bill, because I have been through the same tortures, and
particularly as his Bill is considerably longer, and, inevitably, more wide-ranging. The Bill
that I introduced contained concepts accepted by the British House of Commons, and
ultimately accepted by this House after the draft Bill was changed in the select committee.

the United Kingdom. In other words, the Bill as it came back to the House, emasculated
though it may have seemed on the face of it, was changed only during the natural
evolutionary process of that legislation—a process that was followed not only in the United
Kingdom, but also in Canada, Australia, and in some American states. This Freedom of
Information Bill does not, and cannot, lend itself to this same evolutionary process. I
therefore suggest that it is neither appropriate that it be given a second reading, nor that it be
sent to a select committee.

If the Freedom of Information Bill were to be viewed as an assurance to people that
they have access to the information on which decisions about their rights are made, that
would give a greater degree of security to and confidence in our system of government. In
respect of matters which transcend the individual citizen, but which are of great public
moment, people are not now justified in concluding that any statement made by a
Government is necessarily correct for all purposes; they need the assurance that they can go
to the basic data upon which the Government or the department is working, so that they can
challenge assumptions that are being made, correct that which is wrongly recorded, and so
give us a better and a better informed Government.
There is a variety of ways of introducing legal change. One is for a member of the House
to present a Bill for consideration. That has an element of urgency that is appropriate at a

even though we have the assurance of the member for Birkenhead that he is convinced that
the whole question can be solved administratively, and not legislatively. I regard such a view

administrative means. It is a fact of life that an administrator tends to want secrecy, because

mistakes-although that should be done-but that we on this side of the House believe that
decisions made in public, with the public's interest being taken into consideration, are far
more likely in the long run to be better decisions. We believe that if you involve people in


## p. 809 (#51) #############################################

21 June
809
Freedom of Information Bill
decisions, and give them the reasons and the bases on which decisions are made, you make
for better government. The resolution of difficulties of secrecy in administrative decisions
has failed in the past; it failed with the Whitlam Government in Australia, and it will fail with
this Government.
I thank the member for Hamilton West for making yet a further change in his attitude
today. His stance on Friday was different from his attitude on the introduction of the Bill. He
raised the only basic argument, that of whether an appeal should go to the courts-as put
forward by me-or to the Ombudsman. I believe that the Ombudsman is a commendable
concept. He is Parliament's man, and is a man to check ordinary administrative errors. He is
not an appeal authority or a court, and he has no authority to force the Government to do
anything. I looked carefully at the idea of the Ombudsman, because it appealed to me. I
thought that it would be a way whereby information could be readily obtained; but I realised
that the concept of an ombudsman was fundamentally different from what is needed here.
We need a system of checks and balances.
We have the Executive, Parliament, and the courts. I believe that history, and
particularly recent history, has clearly shown that only the courts are, in fact, the bastions of
freedom. Only the courts can say to the administrative wing of Government, “You have
gone too far. You must stop." If we in Parliament wish information to be made available, we
must pass a law to that effect, and then entrust it to the highest courts in the land. We muşt
say to those courts, "We want you to uphold this legislation, as you have upheld legal rights
in the past. We believe you have not only the authority and the public support, but you have
also the precedents of the past in other fields to enable you to uphold the concept of freedom
of information." I envisage that the legislation would be subject to a series of test cases, as is
other legislation, and that the Supreme Court would make very clear, not only to every
Cabinet Minister at present, but also to all those in the future, the proper requirements to be
set before the public.
That is the way all legislation should be designed. I do not believe that Parliament
should dot every i and cross every t in a Bill. I do not agree with the tremendous number of
tribunals we have at present, and I do not consider that the Ombudsman should be
overloaded. I draw the attention of the member for Hamilton West to the statements already
attributed to the Ombudsman that show his concern about the Human Rights
Commission-we can kill a good idea by thrashing it to death. Only the courts can ensure
that the law is carried out properly. I also point out to the member for Hamilton West that,
as shown in the measure he circulated, although there is an Ombudsman in England the
courts are being used as the appeal authority. I emphasise that it is the courts that uphold the
law; and we all know that the Chief Justice has shown that he is only too willing to do so.
I also wish to mention briefly some other contributions to the debate. The member for
Hamilton East asked if I had approached his scientific friends, or some other people. I am
well aware from the press statements I have read—and I have one in my hand-that "there is
an expressed need for the present archaic Official Secrets Act to be replaced by more
positive legislation such as a Freedom of Information Act. That point was brought out
clearly at a forum on secrecy in science held in Dunedin at the weekend." Indeed, that was
one of the reasons I brought the Bill forward.
The member for Hamilton East put a most interesting concept to me. He said that,
before a properly elected member of Parliament-and I was properly elected by the people
of Auckland Central-can bring forward an idea to be voted on by the House, he should
approach some unelected bodies for their views. I strongly believe that, if Parliament is to be
retained as a place for the consideration of law and government, we should be able to bring a
Bill before the House and then invite the friends of the member for Hamilton East to come
forward and give their views. If the member for Hamilton East, even at this stage, can
persuade the Government to send this Bill to a select oommittee, all his friends will be able
to present their views. I am sure, because many scientists have contacted me, that he would
then discover they are in favour of my Bill.
I thank the member for Wanganui for his very thoughtful speech. He put all the issues
very clearly, and I shall summarise briefly what he said. The rapid growth of knowledge is
presenting a real threat. For example, 10 years ago the Wanganui Computer Centre was a
scientific impossibility; today it is a reality. We also have other Government computers. If
we wish to provide protection by sharing knowledge, which is the basis of democracy, we
must have legislation such as the Bill I have brought forward.
I shall also comment briefly on the statements made by the member for Birkenhead. At
least one of his arguments should be mentioned. He said he had produced a Bill for the

The Bill contains no provision that will prevent unions from negotiating the conditions
they want, and it does not provide for the removal of the penalty payment provisions or any
changes to overtime provisions. Retail outlets will not be able to open on Saturdays,
Sundays, or statutory holidays without the specific approval of the Shop Trading Hours
Commission.
Mr SPEAKER: Is the honourable member reading outside comments on the Bill?
Mr LUXTON: Yes, I was.
Mr SPEAKER: He must know that is out of order, and that it must not be done.
Mr LUXTON: The award covering employees in grocery stores and supermarkets
allows a 51 1/2 hour week in cities and boroughs, and in country areas these shops are
permitted to open for 53 hours a week, but that does not mean that they are open for more
than 40 hours. This Bill should win approval throughout New Zealand. There is no doubt
that it is good legislation, and will enable better law enforcement than at present. It provides
for an absolute freedom of choice between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. during the week. Clause 19 sets
out the very rigid requirements that must be met before any extension into Saturday and
weekend trading is approved. The Bill does not provide for a relaxation of the present
position, but will meet today's conditions much better. In the past we have had a one-man
tribunal, which is to be replaced by a three-man commission.
The provision for filing an application in the magistrate's court remains, but provides for
wider notification so that more people will know of the proposed changes. The Bill also
contains provision for group application, but requires that the majority of shops in a
particular area must file the application. Before granting an extension the commission must
take into account the interests of other affected parties. It must also look at the best interests
of the public, public demand, the effect on retail prices, the effect on the family-and other
social patterns-the district in which the shops are situated, and the class of customer to be
served. The commission can also vary the type of extension it approves. A group application
may be for only a year, so the conditions for that extension can be determined and laid down
by the commission. This will result in greater variation than we had in the past when an
exemption was given, which meant an absolute extension.
This is good legislation, and I believe it should be welcomed. I am sure that once it
becomes law it will be only a matter of a few months before it settles in and works in the way
we feel it should work. I am sure there will be no great changes, but, rather, machinery that
will enable the legislation to be well enacted.

opposite has suggested that retail shop staff will be seriously affected in one way or another
