The union's claim that a change of hours by one or two shops will cause extended hours
to spread like a gorse fire is unjustified. It is the kind of statement that has come from the
Socialist Unity Party and the group that is trying to influence thousands of retail employees.
There has been a continual attack on the Bill and the use of fear tactics on issues that are not
in the Bill. Clauses 18 and 19 cover aspects of the criteria to be used in determining whether
or not an alteration to hours should be approved. There is a similarity in the attempts to
mislead the public on a Bill that will in no way disadvantage employees, or affect overtime
they would normally receive.
Good sales people are hard to come by, and any group of shops, in deciding whether or
not to change hours, will obviously take that into account, because without the support of
employees and the public there cannot be a viable retail industry. A retailer will bear in mind
the question of costs when he considers whether or not to work outside normal hours,
between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. For instance, hardware shops might find it convenient, as
butchers have done for many years, to open at an early hour, but to close earlier, or make
provision for extended hours by way of overtime. Most tradesmen start work at 7.30 a.m. or
8 a.m., and hardware shops might like to have that flexibility. Conditions change over the
years, as do buying habits. Retailers in areas where there are mostly two-income families will
have an opportunity to consider adjusting their opening hours to suit local needs.
New Brighton was mentioned a little earlier, and it was suggested that people went
down there because of the beach. Not much swimming is done at this time of the year, yet
those shops still cater for the public demand. We have to have flexibility. It is needed and
demanded, and it is right and proper that the Government saw fit to introduce a Bill and to
send it to a select committee so that people affected by it could make submissions. Many of
those who made submissions had little understanding of the purport of the Bill, often they
had been influenced by prejudices and ideas gathered from various quarters. But the
opportunity for them to come forward to voice their opinions, and for their objections to be
met by the committee, and carefully sorted out and examined, has resulted in very much
improved legislation.
The Bill will be a great asset, not only to the retail industry, but to the public. I
challenge the next Opposition speaker to say how he sees the Bill will encroach on the rights
of individuals. How will people be disadvantaged? We have heard generalities tonight, but
no details of how the public will suffer, or how large firms will walk over the smaller ones. I
do not believe that will be the case. The Bill can only improve conditions in the retail
industry.

concentrate the greatest degree of its turnover in the shortest possible time, because thus it is
possible to minimise overheads and get a better unit margin in return. This Bill will militate
against that. Most submissions were strongly opposed to the Bill. Under its provisions,
retailers will be compelled to compete with Woolworths, in particular, and other similar
businesses, which are enthusiastically in favour of the Bill. Other businesses will have to
compete against them, opening their stores for longer hours with greater overheads to meet.

the economy tightens. There will be less impulse buying. Therefore the same quantity of
food will be bought, irrespective of the hours that shops are open; the same quantity of
clothing, footwear, and other essentials will be bought, irrespective of the hours of opening.
But the costs of keeping open and maintaining those retail premises will be substantially
higher, and the consumer, as is usual under a National Government, will pay more.

that "protect the 40-hour week" was said, and that is exactly what we have done. I shall not
keep on with history, but that was said in 1955 too. Do you know what a Labour member
said in reply? He said, "Perhaps all those little shops do want to open, but there are some
people who have to be protected against themselves." That is very interesting.
We can go back to 1892, and the first amendments in 1894. We can look at the 1922
amendments, and the amendments to the Police Act in 1927 that took most of the policing of
the Act away from the Police and gave it to the Department of Labour-except for Sunday
trading. We can go to the 1952 amendments, and to the 1955 amendment, and ask what
Labour did about the legislation. The answer is, nothing. We have had some reference to the
committee's report as a starting point. That report to the Minister of Labour in the Labour
Government was made in June 1975. There is another piece of background that has not been
mentioned tonight, and I refer to the 1971 private member's Bill of Mr Tolhurst, the
National member for Wanganui. The Minister of Labour at that time was Sir John Marshall,
and he asked the commission to furnish him with a report. The report was given to the
Labour Government in May 1973, and I cannot find it. I rather wonder what that report said.
I should like the Minister of that time to tell the House what was in that report.
This move is not new. For a long time many people have been asking for more sense in
the legislation governing weekend trading and trading hours. On 13 December 1974 the
Labour Government did something. It appointed a committee. The Acting Prime Minister
spoke of the composition of that committee, and reminded the House that it included a
representative of the Federation of Labour. I believe the member for Roskill, who was
Minister of Labour in the Labour Government, implied afterwards that the report was not
unanimous. I have had a copy on my files for a year, and I challenge his statement, because if
you read it through and read the dissenting opinion by Mr Brosnahan of the Federation of
Labour you will see he does not in any way mention the overall recommendation at the end
of the report; paragraph 19.
He gives his point of view, quite correctly, on the extended hours, but paragraph 19
states: "The committee is of a firm opinion that the law in this sphere is overdue for a
complete review." This is what was said to the Labour Government on 13 June 1975, and it
did nothing about it. "At present the law is obscure and is to be found in the Act"—and this

The member for Mt. Albert has drawn the attention of the House to the type of lease
used in some malls; not in all of them, but in those whose owners did not appear before the

sales of the shop owners in the mall includes all sorts of noxious provisions, including very
strong rights of inspection of books and turnover, and of the businesses, by the management.

the key to this Bill. The retailers have given ample evidence-and have not been

shopping patterns to increase their gross turnover. I do not think anyone could reasonably
dispute that. No one has given any evidence that retailers' profits will increase because of

NOTICE OF MOTION-ADMISSIBILITY
Mr SPEAKER: This might be a convenient moment for me to deal with a matter that
was raised some days ago. I am sorry I have omitted to give my ruling sooner. It was
suggested that notice of motion No. 15 on today's Order Paper was out of order on the
grounds that it contained statements of fact that were not, in terms of Standing Order 103,
necessary to render the notice intelligible, or that could not be authenticated. I want to avoid
a situation in which a preliminary debate on fistfuls of notices of motion is held and
adjudicated on by the Speaker. On the other hand, clearly inaccurate statements should not
appear in or be implied in notices of motion-in other words, statements that cannot be
authenticated.
Three matters were objected to. One was the suggestion in the notices of motion that
only 19 percent of those employed in the retail trade in the area voted to disrupt the lives of
the people of that area. I understand from information submitted to me that the expression
"of those employed in the retail trade" included self-employed persons. The inconsistency
between the number of members of the appropriate union on the one hand, and the number
of those engaged in or employed in the retail trade on the other hand, this figure having been
obtained from the Department of Labour, does not invalidate the notice of motion because
the two figures are not ad idem and refer to different groups.
Later in his notice of motion, the member congratulated 297 responsible members of
the union who had voted against illegal strike action. The seeming authority for this appears
in the Evening Standard, a Palmerston North publication, of 10 June. The article is headed,
"Some Strike Victim Firms Paying Wages", and states in the third paragraph, “The strike
started yesterday when a Palmerston North meeting of shopkeepers voted 711 to 297 to stop
work." Later the article states, "The Secretary of the Wellington Shop Employees Union,
Mr G. D. Kelly, said from Wellington that the 711-to-297 vote proved. . ." and so on. There
does seem to be some substantiation of the figure used.
Finally, objection was taken to the words, "and further commends and assures full
support against any such reported intimidation methods as used in Wellington", and so on.
The authority for that suggestion is a report in the Evening Post of 3 June headed,
"Intimidation tactics during shop strike denounced by angry Trades Council." The article
commences, "Confirmed and unconfirmed threats of intimidation and violence following
yesterday's strike action..." In the third paragraph it is stated: "A good many of the
threatening reports phoned into the Evening Post this morning were by other parties, but
some proprietors confirmed that they had pressure put on them allegedly by union
members."
It is not for me to enter into the discussion on the correctness of the suggestion in the
notice of motion, except to say that, when reported intimidation methods are mentioned, it

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Industrial Stoppages-Days Lost
1. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Labour, What percentage of days
lost through industrial actions, over the most recent surveyed period, has been the result of
stoppages on conditions, stoppages on wage claims, stoppages on relativity claims, or other
causes?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The detailed statistics requested on the
causes of industrial stoppages have yet to be compiled for 1976 and the March quarter 1977.
However, there were 67,541 working days lost recorded in the March quarter 1977,
compared with 94,809 for the same period in 1976. This represents a 40.37 percent decrease
in the number of working days lost between the two March quarters. In 1975, the latest
period for which detailed statistics are available, disputes over basic wages and special
payments accounted for 27 percent of working days lost, disputes over work allocation and
manning levels for 17.5 percent of working days lost, and dismissals for 10 percent of
working days lost.
Mr Isbey: How do those figures for 1976 and 1977 compare with the figures for 1975?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I would require notice of that question, so that the figures for the
right quarter can be obtained.
Mr Falloon: Why has the downward trend occurred during the last 12 months?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The general trend has been downward, particularly in the last
quarter. The Economic News Bulletin gives an unbiased view of the reason for the downward
trend.

Mortgagee Sales-Public Trust Refinance Facility
2. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) asked the Minister of Housing, Is he aware of a report in
the Evening Post of 2 June 1977 in which the Minister of Justice confirmed that there had

Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I am aware of the report. The

Office facility. In future, any Government assistance with mortgage refinance will be funded
solely through the Housing Corporation as a lender of last resort, and under strict criteria.

information in front of me. It is not generally regarded as the function of the Housing
Corporation to provide refinance. The corporation's function, and it is not a new function, is
to provide first loans for first homes.
Mr Wellington: Where there are extenuating circumstances, especially those involving a
couple with dependent children, will cases for refinance be considered sympathetically by
the Housing Corporation?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: In the original answer I said that in future any Government
assistance with mortgage refinance will be funded solely through the Housing Corporation as
a lender of last resort; and I emphasise that a criterion will be that the family home is at risk.

6. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Railways, How many persons were

cars-1949, 1484; 1977, 357. Wagons-1949, 34 429; 1977, 30 379. The 1977 figure of 35
railcars was made up of 3 Silver Ferns, 23 Twinsets, 7 Vulcans, and 2 permanent way
railcars. Of the 30 Twinset and Vulcan-type railcars shown on the books at 31 March 1977,
only 11 are at present operational. Much more detail could be given in answer to the
question, and if the honourable member cares to submit a written question I shall answer it
fully for him.

Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: It means that the increase in heavy industry development
in New Zealand has resulted in workers being taken away from the railway workshops. As

BUILDING PERFORMANCE GUARANTEE CORPORATION BILL
Mr ALLEN (Tauranga): I am directed by the Commerce and Mining Committee to
present the report of the committee on the Building Performance Guarantee Corporation
Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move,
That the report do lie upon the table.
I remind members that the Bill fulfils a promise made in the National Party's 1975
manifesto. The evidence produced to the committee further established the real need for the
Bill to proceed. For example, the Consumer Council said that it received more than 600
complaints a year about building and there are other complaints made to the Department of
Trade and Industry. The National Council of Women reported complaints, and the submis-
sions of individuals and associations underlined the problem.
Building a house is probably one of the biggest investments people make, and there is a
need for protection against poor work, poor material, and other problems arising out of the
contract. It must be remembered that not all faulty workmanship shows up immediately, or
within the very short servicing period normally allowed-that is, the first few months after
the house is completed. It often shows up many years later when the house owner might have
difficulty getting the faults remedied. There is no problem with a reputable master builder,
but if the builder is deceased, or has gone out of business, or moved out of the country there
would be a real problem. The Bill is being brought back into the House to meet that
problem. Where there is an argument about the terms of the contract between the builder
and the house owner, and providing an indemnity has been taken out, the corporation will
negotiate on behalf of the home owner and have the fault fixed if the fault shows up during
the period of the indemnity, which would normally be 6 years.
The evidence proved that this is a very timely Bill, because it offers protection to the
home owner. It was clear from the submissions that a couple building a house is almost
always inexperienced in building, planning, or recognising the proper materials that should
be used. Such people are obviously at a disadvantage, and would rely on the builder for
advice and guidance. Most couples receive sound advice and guidance and the Bill poses no
threat to the ethical builder; but if there is misunderstanding and a difference of opinion the
corporation will not only help the owner, but will protect the builder by relieving him of
improper and frivolous complaints. So the Bill works both ways.
The Bill provides for the establishment of a corporation to indemnify the home builder
against poor performance. It does not require the registration of builders, and the indemnity
is not compulsory. The person building can have the builder of his choice, and he is free to
take out the indemnity or not, as he wishes. The lack of compulsion might be interpreted as
letting the deliberately bad builder off the hook-the fly-by-night builder who lacks proper
skills and experience. If the person building wants a cheap job at a cheap price, that is what
he will get, and he must accept that risk. If a builder refuses to contract under an indemnity it
is a warning to the home builder, and he should heed that warning and proceed with caution.
The functions of the corporation will be to issue an indemnity, to administrate it, to
supervise, to arbitrate, and, where necessary, to take legal proceedings.
Opposition members adopted a peculiar stance-perhaps weird is a better word-and
chose not to participate in the committee's deliberations. I think the statement made by the
senior Opposition member was that, while Opposition members of the committee agreed in
principle with the Bill, they thought that the Master Builders Federation should be given
time to put forward a redrafted Bill. I wonder why, because up to that time very little interest
had been shown in the Bill. Although the Master Builders Federation said it would produce
a redrafted Bill, nothing has yet been received by the Government. I draw the House's
attention to the fact that the Master Builders Federation has been saying this for 10 years,
but it has produced nothing. Perhaps it will produce a redrafted Bill, or perhaps the
Opposition has been misled in thinking that a redrafted Bill will come from the Master
Builders Federation. If it is produced the Minister would give it serious consideration, and if
the suggestions made are worthy of the Minister's attention he will give them that attention.
Contrary to what might be said later, the select committee heard 24 submissions, and
only 4 were against the Bill. Of those four against the Bill, two were very halfhearted. The
submission of the Master Builders Federation states: "This federation is substantially in


## p. 849 (#91) #############################################

849
Building Performance Guarantee Corporation Bill
agreement with the principle of providing warranties for newly constructed residential family
home units, subject to them being equitable to both parties." That is slightly qualified, but it
is in support. The second line of the Consumer Council's submission states that the Bill is a
step in the right direction. The council does not think the Bill goes far enough. The House
should understand that, of the 24 submissions heard, 20 were in support of the Bill, and 4
might be construed as being against it. I therefore recommend this Bill to the House.

Government and another when it is in Opposition. A few years ago, on the reporting back of

got together and decided what their function really is at a select committee. In Hansard,
Volume 402, at page 5216, the member for Porirua is reported as having said: "The purpose
of the select committee system, as you, Mr Speaker, and the House know, is to act in an
advisory capacity for this Chamber." The present Opposition acts in an advisory capacity for
this Chamber by going on strike. Opposition members simply say, "We will have nothing to
do with it. If it is a National Party proposal we are against it." I wonder why this does not
happen at all the committees? I wonder what the effect would be if that attitude were
adopted in the Statutes Revision Committee?
Let us take a further look at what the member for Porirua said, because he obviously
thinks about these things-something that I am afraid the member for Mt. Albert does not
do. The member for Porirua said: "Over recent years this system, because it has been used
more and more frequently, is becoming wrongly interpreted by members of the public as
being a forum in which groups may protest their interest concerning measures coming before
the House." Later on he said, "The committee invites people to give advice, but it is not the
right of the public to protest . . . It would very much encourage the popular misconception
that select committees are a proper forum for protests that the public may feel disposed to
make."
Last Wednesday we had another example of the Opposition's simply throwing up its
hands and saying, "We don't approve of this. We are going on strike. We will not have
anything to do with it." The Bill that is reported back today is a better Bill than the one that
went to the select committee, and I believe that the hearing of evidence was worth while.
Mr Rogers: It's a disaster, and the Minister knows it. It's a complete disaster.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: Here is another one of those Auckland strikers having a word
to say. He wants to speak on the Bill now, but his colleagues did not want to speak last
Wednesday. When they get into the House they sit in the front row, where they do not
belong, and are very fond of chipping in. They are very quiet when there is any business to
be transacted, but very chatty when it is simply a matter of interjecting. I am totally against
the Bill's going back to the committee. If the Master Builders Federation has any proposals
the Government will consider them, but it is not prepared to hold up its legislation if the
federation really does not want to do anything about it. The Bill is a good Bill, aimed at
protecting the interests of prospective home owners. I am sure this will become manifest
when we come to the second reading.
The House divided on the question, That the amendment be agreed to.

DISCUSSION OF MOTIONS
Migration Loss
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): I move, That this House notes with considerable interest
the claim of the Deputy Prime Minister that there was a net outflow of 13 000 New Zealanders
in 1974 in an apparent attempt to divert attention from the all-time record net loss of departing
New Zealand citizens and long-term residents, and contrasts this with the repeated claims of
the National Party in the past that so much of the economic difficulties experienced in 1974 and
1975 were the result of excessive net inflows of 33 576 in the year ended March 1974, and 22 477
in the year ended March 1975.
This motion draws attention to the Government's efforts over recent months, and in the
last few weeks in particular, to try to cloud the issue about the all-time record outflow of
people from New Zealand. One can well understand the Government's wanting to divert
attention from that aspect of its economic policy. The National Party's tactic in 1975, the
year of the election, was to blame the then Labour Government for all the economic
problems it alleged were confronting New Zealand because of the high level of migration to
this country. The present Prime Minister, and almost every other member opposite,
deployed this tactic in an endeavour to whip up public feeling and opposition to migration to
New Zealand. The extravagant statements of some National members knew no bounds. A
typical statement, made by the present Prime Minister in 1975, was: "In the last 2 years we
have brought in 60 000 immigrants that we cannot absorb. National will cut immigration to
the smallest possible number. Our target is no more than 5000, and this includes returning
New Zealanders and relatives of people already in this country. This would be the largest
initial step towards living within our income."
If a person could not get a house, members opposite said it was because of the number
of immigrants. If health, education, or other Government or local body services could not be
provided, it was because of the pressure from migrants to New Zealand. The lack of job
opportunities, the balance of payments, or anything else, was blamed on immigration.
However, it is very interesting, now there is an all-time record outflow from New Zealand,
that all the problems that were supposed to have been brought about because of the
excessively high levels of migration to New Zealand are just as chronic, if not more so, than
they have ever been. Now that we have a record outflow of 17 000-odd people from New
Zealand, I ask members opposite whether it is any easier to get a house. Is it any easier to
refinance a mortgage? Is it any easier to obtain the level of health services that the National
Party promised the National Government would provide? Is employment any easier to find?
What is the level of unemployment, and how many people are working on Government
assisted schemes? Is the balance of payments any better because we have an all-time record
outflow from New Zealand? The answer to each question is, of course, no, which underlines
the fact that the present Government was making immigration a propaganda tool for its re-
election to office.
One can well recall the National Party's propaganda in November 1975, and especially
its television cartoons. Migrants were made the scapegoats by the National Party for no
other reason than political gain. However, the position has now reversed, and boomeranged
on the present Government, which is endeavouring to divert attention from what is
happening. In its first 12 months in office, the National Government neglected to control
immigration as it should have been controlled, even though the Labour Government's policy
had been working at the time of the change of Government. Remember the present


## p. 852 (#94) #############################################

852
22 June
Discussion of Motions
Government's target of a net gain of 5000 people? Within 3 months of the change of
Government that target was achieved, not because of any action by the National Govern-
ment, but because of the efforts of the previous Labour Government. Members opposite
were so taken in by their propaganda that they decided to shut their eyes completely for 12
months. As a consequence, immigration has got out of hand.
The immigration statistics are open to wide interpretation. I have never known statistics
to be more incorrectly analysed. Perhaps I could quote from an official document, which I
am prepared to table if any member so wishes, that indicates what was happening 12 months
after the Labour Government brought in the controls that had operated from April 1974.
The paper, by Mr P. D. Jones, Director of Research and Planning for the Department of
Labour, analyses the position very effectively: "The main reasons for the relatively high rate
of immigration is not so much the inflow from controlled areas, but the high inflow of
returning New Zealanders, Australians, and family reunification cases”—and I draw this to
the attention of members opposite-"and the relatively low proportion of persons leaving
this country." That is an official interpretation of the statistics. The Minister, or any other
member opposite, could check that with Mr Jones, who is now the Director of Immigration.
As I said earlier, I am prepared to table that paper, which states: "The main reasons for the
relatively high rate of immigration is not so much the inflow from controlled areas, but the
high inflow of returning New Zealanders", because that is exactly what was happening
during the first 2 years of the Labour Government.
New Zealanders left, because under the National Government there was no opportunity
to use their skills, and they took up positions overseas. With the change of Government and
the improved economic climate, with opportunities available to them in New Zealand, a
great many came back. In 1974-75 we actively recruited carpenters, engineers, and trades-
men generally, overseas, so that we could build more houses and provide much needed
services. After only 18 months, the National Government has dramatically reversed the
position. There is now a net outflow from New Zealand, on a permanent or long-term basis,
of 17 124 a year. That is the biggest loss ever recorded, and far exceeds 1967 and 1968
figures, when there were net outflows of 10 000 and 11 000 people respectively. In 1974-75
New Zealand was a desirable place in which to live, not only for New Zealanders, but for
would-be immigrants. The National Party set a target of 5000.
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): The member for Petone referred to the
high outflow of New Zealanders in 1967 and 1968. The net outflow in 1967 was 4000, and in
1968 it was 5000. The net outflow in 1973, under the Labour Government, was 8000; in 1974
it was 12 000; and in 1975 it was 11 000. Let the member compare those figures with the net
outflow for 1967-68. He talked about an official paper that he was prepared to table, and
about the number of New Zealanders fleeing the country. How many New Zealanders are
returning?
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Read the heading at the top of the page.
Hon. T. F. GILL: The heading on this page is, "Permanent and long-term arrivals and
departures of persons whose country of birth was New Zealand". The Leader of the
Opposition talked about New Zealanders born and bred. To answer the charges he made
about New Zealanders born and bred, I have had the figures extracted. The member for
Petone knows that in 1974, 69 815 permanent and long-term immigrants arrived in New
Zealand; and in the following year there were 65 900. That was the problem. It is all very
well to talk about net figures of 35 000 or 40 000, but every member of the House knows that
a New Zealander who leaves this country may have been living in his own home, or in his
parents' home. If he has children, he takes them away from their school. A migrant does not
take that New Zealander's job, or have accommodation with that man's parents; he does not
send his children to the same school. The inflow of 69 815 permanent and long-term arrivals
in 1974, and 65 900 in 1975 placed a strain on the economy that was difficult to absorb.
Nobody has suggested that it was the only strain. The malfunctioning of the Treasury
benches at that time had a great deal to do with it.
Labour made a lot of other very silly mistakes. It spent the $1,000 million in reserve
when it came into power, and borrowed another $2,000 million. We know the troubles it
caused, and included among them were problems with schools, hospitals, and buses. It
would not have been so difficult if every migrant rode to work in the same bus that a
departing New Zealander had used, or lived in the same house, or his children attended the
same school. In that case, it would be reasonable to quote the net figure of 30 000. What
caused the trouble were the 69 815 permanent and long-term arrivals in 1974 and the 65 900
in 1975, for whom accommodation, transport, and hospital services had to be found. If they

had gone to some of the smaller centres where the hospital services existed it would not have

In 1 year, the population of Auckland increased by about the number of people living

Mr Jones, the head of the planning division, who was mentioned by the member for
Petone and who is a very zealous and capable officer, is now head of the immigration
division of the Department of Labour. He produced the figures I quoted. They are very
illuminating. The Deputy Leader of the Opposition wanted to query them. He said, "Read
the top of the page". I have read the top of it, and I am reading the top on this one:
"Permanent and long-term arrivals and departures", and the permanent arrivals in 1974
were 69 000-odd, and in 1974 were 65 000-odd. The then Government did nothing about it,
but now that it is the Opposition it tries to pretend that that sort of inflow caused no
problems. It caused great problems. I would be concerned if young New Zealanders were
leaving the country because of any sort of pressure-psychological or otherwise-about job
opportunities and training, or financial and economic problems. I would want to know about
it, and would try hard to put right whatever was wrong. But I have had no indication that
young New Zealanders are doing anything other than follow what has been the normal
pattern since the days when I went overseas, about 40 years ago.
I have heard of people among the 69 000 who had sold a house in their own country and
were told they could refinance in a couple of years. Having been assisted to come here, after
a couple of years-and some of them have had problems of refinancing and that kind-they
have decided to go-no skin off their noses; the New Zealand Government had paid their
fare. I do not blame them. I know that every New Zealander who leaves the country to go
overseas has it in the back of his mind-and they all tell their mothers and fathers this to be
back in 2 or 3 years. Indeed, the majority of them do come back within that time. I should
certainly like to see any evidence--and I have asked for it several times-to show that New
Zealanders are leaving the country other than as an expression of individual freedom to
travel around the world, perhaps to gain wider experience in their work, training in industry,
or just to enjoy life in a different society.
For whatever reason they go, good luck to them. If they are under any pressure,
psychologically or in any other way, or if they are not finding suitable job opportunities or
believe that life in New Zealand is not agreeable to them, I should like to hear all about it.
Many who have lived in England for a couple of years and then returned have come to me
and said, "Of course, the atmosphere in Paris on a Sunday is wonderful; the atmosphere in
London, where you can go shopping in the markets on a Saturday morning is great, but when
we came back to New Zealand we found the whole country closed down on a Saturday and
Sunday." As young people they object to that, but a little later, when they are married and
have gardening to do on Saturday morning and a football match to watch or golf to play in
the afternoon, they change their minds. As youngsters, they may believe that some of the
things I have mentioned are wrong with New Zealand. That is of concern to us, and we
intend to put things right.

continuing. The tragedy is that great numbers of those leaving are the young and able bodied

Gleneagles Agreement
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): I move, That this House records its pleasure at the
outcome of the heads of government discussions on sporting links with countries where racial
discrimination in sport is practised and congratulates the Government in adopting Labour Party
policy. At the outset let me state that members on this side of the House were very sincere in
expressing congratulations to the Government in the fond hope that the decision reached at
Gleneagles would be implemented to the full, and to the letter, by the Government, and by
the Prime Minister when he returns, because it is one thing to sign an agreement and another
to honour it.
This is just the beginning of a real testing time for New Zealand. It is essential that New
Zealand, and principally the Prime Minister and the Government, prove by their actions that
what they agreed to in Gleneagles will now be put into effect. We are well aware that,
although this agreement was reached within the Commonwealth, members of the Common-
wealth are a very small minority in the Organisation of African Unity, an organisation which
would still be in a position to cause considerable embarrassment to this country if it believed
there was a need to continue with some form of sporting embargo. The only way to avoid
such a situation developing is to make sure that the decision to which the Prime Minister put
his signature is implemented by this Government. We must act in accordance with that
agreement or New Zealand's international standing will fall to a lower than ever level.
There can be no possibility of the Government going back on this agreement, and yet
already we see signs of disagreement within the Government itself. The Prime Minister, on
television in New Zealand and in press statements from London, has intimated that there has
been "a shift", according to one term he used-"a change in policy" was another term he
used-and yet the member for Hastings has denied that this has happened, and, if I may use
the term he did, he expressed the "hope that nothing has changed". A great deal has
changed. It has changed on the admission of the Prime Minister himself. The member for
Wairarapa has gone further. In the Christchurch Star of 18 June we read this excerpt:
"Returning to the possibility of several All Blacks going to South Africa later this year, Mr
Couch said he doubted this would contravene the spirit of the Gleneagles agreement by
Commonwealth heads earlier this week." That agreement spelt out "contact" as well as
"competition". This position must be clarified very quickly before members of the OAU
meet to decide the sincerity of the statement made on behalf of this Government.
We are reminded that many conflicting statements have been made on this issue in this
calendar year. I am certain that the Acting Prime Minister, who no doubt will follow me in
this debate, will be aware that many people took heart at some of the statements made by
him and by the former Minister of State, whom his Government has since honoured. Many
people have been disturbed that those encouraging signs from the Government were
destroyed overnight by a varied approach to the issue by the Prime Minister. However, we
take comfort from the fact that the Prime Minister reached agreement at the Commonwealth
meeting, an agreement which, if implemented, can do nothing but good.
Hon. David Thomson: Then why try to put it down.

the Acting Prime Minister replies, will he answer these three questions? Will the Govern-

Trade Unions and the Law
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I move, That this House notes with approval the remarks by
the editor of the New Zealand Law Journal, Mr A. Black, in the 17 May 1977 issue of that
journal, that, even if unions do not like the law, they could live with the law better than
individuals could live without it, and that it was hard to believe that the sentiments expressed by
Mr H. B. Stubbs, Secretary of the New Zealand Tramways Union (that there were areas of the
law that unions were entitled to disregard) were widely held within the trade union movement;
and this House confirms its determination to uphold the rule of law and afford the protection of
the law to all citizens whether or not they be members of trade unions or any other body.
This motion is of particular importance and topicality because only recently the
Tramways Union announced that it would disobey the court order made last month, and
specifically will not pay the costs awarded against it. It is not my intention to outline the
history of the case, but merely to draw the House's attention to the three fundamental issues
that arise from that history. First, we have an order of the court made on legal principles that
date back to 1592; principles that protect all citizens, all individuals, all unions, all
companies, everybody under the law. Secondly, we have that order being disobeyed by a
union, and as a result of that disobedience the court imposed a punishment that has been met
not by the union but by somebody else, although the court made an order that the costs were
to be paid by the union itself. It was claimed at the time that it was done by agreement, but
there seems since to have been some confusion on that point. Thirdly, we have the union
now saying that it is taking unto itself the power to decide which laws it will obey and which it
will disobey, and it has decided on the basis of that assumption of its authority that it will not


## p. 859 (#101) ############################################

22 June
859
Discussion of Motions
pay the costs that have been awarded against it.
I believe I speak on behalf of every member on this side of the House when I say that no
person, no union, no company, no private individual has a right to determine which laws he
or it will choose to obey and which laws he or it will choose to disobey. Laws are passed by
the Government, and laws evolve through the common law. Each is binding on all.
Mr Prebble: Why doesn't the Government obey them?
Mr McLAY: I shall answer the question raised by the member for Auckland Central.
The Government has obeyed every order in respect of it made by the court. This trade union
is not doing that. It is disobeying an order of the court, whereas the Chief Justice's order was
Complied with in all respects. No person has a right to choose which laws he will be bound
by, and which he will not be bound by.
Mr Prebble: What about the Prime Minister?
Mr McLAY: The Prime Minister obeyed the order of the Chief Justice, and the member
for Auckland Central knows that full well. I believe the principle will be agreed to by
members on both sides of the House. At least, I hope members opposite will agree; I know
the member for Henderson does. I quote from an article in the Dominion of 26 May 1974 in
which the member for Henderson said: "On one point I am utterly firm. The same rules of
law enforcement must apply equally to all. To assert the right for one affected party to
decide for itself which laws are approved and will be obeyed is to call into question our whole
legal and constitutional heritage." I am happy to tell the member for Henderson, and I am
sure he will not be surprised to hear this, that I agree entirely with what he said on that
occasion.
I also agree with something else he said-something that was reported in the New
Zealand Herald on 26 June 1974, just 3 years ago. He said: "Generally speaking an
injunction is available to any party who suffers loss as a result of a breach of the law. The use
of injunctions has been and is equally open to use by employers, employers' associations, or
unions. That law is available to protect all citizens. It is available to ensure that legal rights
are protected, and if need be enforced by the courts." I have no doubt that those sentiments
will be endorsed at least by members on this side of the House, and I hope by members on
the other side as well.
The live issue in this debate arises from the Labour Party conference in May of this year,
as reported in a number of newspapers. A remit was passed at the conference agreeing that
laws that the unions do not like will be repealed by a future Labour Government. I put three
questions to the next Opposition speaker, who I perceive may well be the member for
Mangere; and I hope he is noting my questions. First, in the light of the Labour Party
conference decision that laws need not apply to unions, which laws will the Labour Party
exempt unions from, and which laws will remain applicable? Secondly, if all the laws of the
land are not to apply to all citizens, will any other groups be exempt from the law? Thirdly, if
any group-trade union or otherwise-is to be exempted from certain laws, how will that
attitude be justified in the light of the long-standing legal principle that all citizens are equal
before the law?
Finally, I address a question specifically to the member for Henderson. If the Labour
Party does adopt such a policy of inequality before the law, will he fulfil the pledge he made
to the 1974 Labour Party conference and sever his ties with the Labour movement? I ask that
last question because I believe the member for Henderson shares my views on the need for
the law to be enforced-the same views that were expressed by Mr Black in the New
Zealand Law Journal article, in which he says: "It is worth remembering that people are still
suffering for principles and beliefs. These include that no one shall be above the law, that the
rights of the individual are important, that the rule of law is fundamental to human liberty,
that independent judges whose orders are respected and obeyed"—and I hope the member
for Auckland Central is listening-"are essential to the rule of law. If the law is unsatisfac-
tory let it be changed by Parliament, not ignored." The unions might not like injunctions,
they might not like the content of the law, but the unions can live with the law better than we
as individuals can live without the law.

Dr WALL (Porirua): Unfortunately, the argument we have been listening to has the

Hon. Members: Sure.
Dr WALL: The chorus of "Sure" from Government members indicates how little they
have thought about the position. The provision of labour is treated differently from the
provision of goods or other services. Restrictions on the way in which a person who contracts
to supply his labour may opt out do not apply, in the ordinary law, to people who are giving
other types of services and supplying goods. If the law applied equally firmly across the
board, with absolute equality, then on this side of the House there would be no dispute. If
the argument in the notice of motion is accepted, the two parties in the failure to keep
Auckland's transport services operating were the employing authority and the union. Yet
the injunction was taken only against the union. Why could an injunction not have been
taken against the employers? They should have been told, "Until a decision is made about
this mess, you will keep the transport services operating according to the employees' terms."
Hon. Members: Ha, ha!
Dr WALL: Government members think that is funny; they are not used to thinking of
trade unionists in terms of equality. Instead, the courts ordered the workers to give way to
the bosses, temporarily, and keep the services going; the dispute to be sorted out later. The
court's authority was not applied equally across the board. It was applied heavily against
those supplying the labour, and not equally heavily against those employing the labour. I see
no reason in natural justice why that injunction should not have been directed at the
employing authorities. Had they pleaded that they were incapable of complying without
giving in to the workers, they should have been told, "Right, give in to the workers until this
matter is decided, and then you can go back again."
Always, in these disputes, the workers are told they must give in to the employers.
Whenever an injunction is applied, it is never ordered that the employers must side with the
workers until the matter is decided, but simply that the workers must agree to the
unacceptable conditions imposed by the employers. The argument may be raised that it is
uneconomic, but again this is always looked at from the employer's point of view, and it may
be increasingly uneconomic for the worker to continue his employment, because his family is
getting further and further into debt. He can be compelled to carry on working in a totally
uneconomic circumstance, which the employer, the supplier of services, never is. The
employer's plea would be, "It is uneconomic for me to continue as I am going into debt”,
and relief would immediately be given.

whatever in the Shops and Offices Act, part of which is being repealed by this Bill, to make it
any more difficult for a person to open his shop on a Sunday than on a Saturday. This Bill
will make it a little more difficult, and once more bears out the point stressed by the member
for Eden in his very fine speech last week-that we were relying upon legislation half a
century out of date to stem the present commercial pressures for more trading on weekends.
In this effort to shore up that legislation we find opposition from Labour members, who
are not prepared to tell us what it is in the Bill that they find objectionable. They merely talk
in broad generalities about the likelihood of weekend trading. During the debate when the

Mr Courtney: It is of the retailers.

The Bill does achieve a number of important fine-tuning changes to the present system
of determining shop hours. In my view, these are the only major matters it deals with. First,
it replaces an ad hoc review committee by a standing committee known as the Shop Trading
Hours Commission, to advise the Minister on extensions to the exempted goods list. This is a
very real improvement. Previously, committees set up from time to time invariably recom-
mended extensions to the exempted goods list, until the point was reached where weekend
trading and, indeed, 24-hour trading, 7 days a week, would have been upon us without any
decision having been taken by Parliament. The Bill grants recommendatory powers to the
Shop Trading Hours Commission, which will comprise three persons skilled in the issues
who will hear cases presented by union representatives, employer representatives, and
retailers generally. The commission will also have a thorough understanding of what is
involved in any extensions to the exempted goods list, now called the approved goods list.
This was the principal reason why the Bill had to be introduced, following the strong
criticism of the present law contained in the report of the latest review committee set up by


## p. 864 (#106) ############################################

864
22 June
Shop Trading Hours Bill
the then Minister of Labour, the member for Roskill.
The second matter that the Bill attends to is the extension, to a minor degree, of the
present exempted goods list. Of the 135 items on the list, only a few have appeared since the
introduction of the Bill, and they are almost exclusively home handyman items, or items sold
in garden centres. There was virtually no criticism before the select committee over the
addition of that narrow band of exempted goods to the first schedule. The third provision
introduced by the Bill is a schedule of special goods, which represents an eminently sensible
halfway-house approach. Instead of making it legal to sell goods at any time of the day or
night, or on any day of the week, the schedule restricts some items to be sold on Saturday
morning only, outside the normal 5-day week. In the Bill, these items are essentially
confined to motor vehicles, again a matter on which there has been virtually no criticism.
The fourth point is the change in weekend trading hours, for which the Bill not only
applies tighter criteria, but also removes the right of the Industrial Commission to allow
opening on weekends. The current law in the Shops and Offices Act provides not only for an
independent authority-the Shops and Offices Exemption Tribunal-to allow weekend
trading, but also the Industrial Commission. This may be negotiated between the employers
and employees in awards, but if negotiations are not successful, an order can be made by the
Industrial Commission. The Bill has taken that power away. In future, nobody can open on a
weekend to sell any exempted goods without going to the independent authority. Again,
there has been a further tightening of the law.
The next matter is the introduction of area applications, and some sinister confusion has
been read into this provision. Anybody who was involved in any way with the application in
1974 by the 144 shop owners at Paraparaumu for a change in closing day from Wednesday to
Monday would be aware that the present lengthy and expensive procedure serves nobody
but the legal advisers of the people involved. The provision to have an application made on
an area basis streamlines the existing procedure, has little effect on the substantive law
and the point that was most heavily criticised before the select committee-removes the
local authority's right to make application for an area exemption. Again, one of the major
criticisms of the Bill has been taken out by the select committee.
We come then to the question of week days. The hours of opening have been removed
from awards. Until now, the awards have contained both the opening hours and the working
hours of shops. For the first time, prohibition against weekend trading has actually been
written into legislation. The present Shops and Offices Act does not have a prohibition
against trading on Saturday or Sunday. The Bill introduces such a provision for the first time
but, as a corollary, it removes the decision making from the Industrial Courts and from the
provisions of awards. At present, the opening hours on week days are not contained in
awards relating to factories, cinemas, hotels or any concern other than shop opening. There
are nine different industrial awards determining shop hours, and matters can become very
complex, particularly when a Christmas Day falls on a weekend and there is a movement of
opening hours from one day to another, and again on New Years Day. By the time this is
carried out across nine different awards one has a picture of total confusion, and, on the
suggestion of the review committee set up by the member for Roskill, these matters have
now been brought together in one Bill, so that they can be readily understood without cross
reference to a multitude of other documents.
It is now quite clear that opening hours range between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m., but that
employment hours continue to be governed by the awards. This is a point that has been
constantly hammered by the Opposition. Members opposite seem to be under the impres-
sion that there has been a change in the law on employment hours. Lest they continue to
cling to that misapprehension, I draw their attention to the provisions of the Shops and
Offices Act set out in clauses 13 to 17. These are contained in the Act under the heading
"Hours of employment in shops". Earlier sections, 3 to 12, are under the heading "Closing
of shops". Opposition members have conducted this debate on the assumption that the Bill
will repeal not only sections 3 to 12 relating to the closing of shops but also sections 13 to 17
relating to the hours of employment in shops. I invite them therefore to turn to the back of
their copies of the Bill, where they will find very clearly set out in the fourth schedule
"Enactments repealed", "Sections 3 to 12 (inclusive), and section 49, of the Shops and
Offices Act 1955". The Bill contains no reference whatever to sections 13 to 17 inclusive of
the Shops and Offices Act 1955. The existing provisions regarding hours of employment will
be left entirely as they are.
Any doubt Opposition members might have had about the matter could have been
removed if they had taken the trouble to read the Bill in its substantive form. I refer directly


## p. 865 (#107) ############################################

22 June
865
Shop Trading Hours Bill
to clause 23 of the Bill before the House, headed "Effect of Act on awards and agreements":
"(1) Notwithstanding anything in any award or agreement (within the meaning of the
Industrial Relations Act 1973), any shop may be open at any time in accordance with this
Act. (2) Nothing in this Act shall require any employee to work in any shop contrary to any
such award or agreement that applies to him." It could not be stated more plainly. That
being the case, what is the substance of the Opposition's attack on the Bill as abrogating
awards or overriding the present provisions covering the hours of employment? Turning to
the question of weekends, Opposition members have chosen-if they have referred to the
Bill at all rather than to peripheral matters only-to compare the Bill with some ideal which
would presumably provide for a total closedown of New Zealand from Friday evening to
Monday morning. Of course, the comparison to be made is that between the amendments
set out in the Bill and the provisions in the existing law. Under the existing law anyone
applying for an extension to Saturday or Sunday trading must satisfy the authority that such
an extension would be in the public interest. Under the Bill as amended by the select
committee, an applicant must satisfy the independent authority that the extension would be
"in the interests of the public generally", so there has been no substantive change to that
provision.
When the criteria or guidelines set down to assist the commission in deciding whether
the application is in the public interest are considered, only two matters are mentioned under
the existing law. One is the desirability of providing service to the public at all reasonable
times, which is a fairly wide provision. In the new Bill, this has been condensed simply to
public demand. If Opposition members contend that the words "public demand" are wider
than the terms used in the Act, I invite them to explain to the House how this comes about.
The new Bill also provides that the commission-the authority—must now for the first time
have regard to the effect on family and social patterns. This provision is not in the present
law; but is an addition made by the select committee. The authority must also look at the
effect on retail prices. This is not in the existing law either, but will be introduced by the
amendment to the Bill made by the select committee. I should like to refer in particular to
the provision of clause 19(6)(h), which requires the independent authority, the commission,
to take into account the application of the principle of the 40-hour week, as embodied in
sections 93 and 94 of the Industrial Relations Act 1973, and any derogation from that
principle that may be caused by the granting of the order. The significant factor there is that
section 94 of the Industrial Relations Act does not refer specifically to a 40-hour week, but to
a Monday-to-Friday week. In this Bill there is therefore a provision containing the express
requirement that, in addition to the matters already set out in the existing law, the Shop
Trading Hours Commission must take into account the effect on prices, the effect on town
planning matters, the effect on family life, and, in particular, the principle of the 40-hour
week and the Monday-to-Friday week.
Mr Courtney: How will that be gauged?
Mr BRILL: The commission will work on the guidelines set out in the Bill as it does in
the present law, but the guidelines in the Bill are much tighter than those in the present
legislation. It must be assumed that, in the absence of any argument to the contrary,
Opposition members accept that the Bill tightens the provisions for weekend trading.

The Opposition in concerted chorus says the Bill will be the ruination of the 40-hour

Saturday shoppers.

Shops and Offices Act, the principal Act that this Bill also amends. That Government was
proud of its amendments, which made exemptions from the Act possible. The 1959
amendment states: ". . . the tribunal, in its discretion, may refuse any application for
exemption, or may by order grant the application either wholly or in part and either
unconditionally or upon or subject to such conditions as the tribunal thinks fit." The member
for Roskill, who has spoken against the Bill, praised that legislation, yet the tribunal could
make any exemptions it thought fit. In making the order it had to satisfy itself that it was
desirable in the public interest to do so, and it had to have regard to the interests of the
occupier of any other shop affected and to the desirability of providing a service to the public
at all reasonable times, particularly in the case of shops situated in a holiday resort. Labour
members, like the member for Roskill and the member for Mt. Albert, were proud of that
legislation in 1959.
The Bill improves the law, and I am glad to support the passage of this amendment to
the Shops and Offices Act. It is part of our consumer legislation that has been badly in need
of revision for a long time. That need was most succinctly expressed in the unanimous report
of the committee of review on the Act set up in 1975 by the then Minister of Labour, the
member for Roskill. The committee, including the Federation of Labour representative, Mr
Brosnan, was firmly of the opinion that "the law in this sphere is overdue for a complete
review. At the present time the law is obscure and is to be found in the Act, collective
agreements, in awards, decisions of the Shops and Offices Exemption Tribunal and the
exempted goods list." The committee said that even lawyers had difficulty in finding and
understanding the law, so it is no wonder that the member for Grey Lynn, even if he had
read the Bill, would not understand it. The committee urged a complete reappraisal and
clarification of the law, so that it might be easily found and understood by all those affected
by it. That was very good advice, and we now have this Bill to deal with those parts of the
Shops and Offices Act that dealt with shop trading hours.
In their evidence before the select committee, to which the Bill was referred by the
Minister of Labour last December for study, the shop and office employees referred to the
repeal of the Shops and Offices Act. Of course, they were wrong. The Shops and Offices Act

remain in the Shops and Offices Act that deal with the things the socialists opposite are
complaining about.

law. It involves the people much more than did the Labour Government's 1959 legislation.
The criteria laid down substantially restrict the commission, because they insist that the
commission, before making a decision on an application, shall consider much more detailed
and explicit criteria, which were added to the Bill after evidence had been heard by the select
committee. Among these criteria are public demand—and it would be for the applicant to
show that there was a public demand-and any effect the granting of the order might have on
retail prices. The socialists opposite have been saying that retail prices will go up, but the
commission cannot make such an order until it is satisfied as to the effect the granting of the
order will have on retail prices. The commission must also consider the effect on family and
other social patterns in the area concerned. That indicates the Government's concern for the
family and for social patterns. The commission must consider the nature of the area in which
the shops are situated, and that takes into account tourist areas. A special provision in the
Supplementary Order Paper makes it clear that the commission shall consider the nature of
the area in which the shop or shops concerned are situated and the class of patron intended
to be served thereby, having regard in particular to the desirability of providing services to
the public at all reasonable times in tourist and resort areas.
If members opposite read the Bill, they would agree that this is a much tighter and
better way of serving the public interest. The commission has to have regard to stability and
orderly and economic planning and development of any wider area, and of the transport and
other services in any wider area in which the shop or shops concerned are situated. Surely
that is good. It has to have regard to the interests of occupiers of other shops, and the need to
minimise the amount of commercial activity taking place on Sundays. That did not have to
be considered under the Labour Government's legislation, but I think most people would
agree that it is a good thing-certainly, reasonable trade unionists would agree. Finally, the
commission has to consider the application of the principle of the 40-hour week as embodied
in the Industrial Relations Act, and any derogation from that order that might be caused by
the granting of the order. The Minister of Labour would agree that the Bill is very much
better than it was when it was introduced. The Government—almost alone, because Labour
members walked out of the select committee and would not deliberate on it—considered the
evidence given before the committee, and has substantially improved the Bill. The job of all

The Bill proposes to correct what I regard as a serious anomaly—the present trading
hours-by providing that it will be legal for all shops to be open 5 days a week between 7
a.m. and 9 p.m. Inspectors of the Department of Labour will not have to go around finding
out the provisions of the relevant award for any particular shop. They will know that all
shops can be open during those hours. As the Minister of Justice said, the fact that shops will
be entitled to open during those hours will not affect current awards. Clause 23 of the Bill
specifically covers that point: "(1) Notwithstanding anything in any award or agreement
(within the meaning of the Industrial Relations Act 1973) any shop may be open at any time
in accordance with this Act. (2) Nothing in this Act shall require any employee to work in
any shop contrary to any such award or agreement that applies to him." That is eminently
reasonable. It means that unions and employers will be able to negotiate hours in an award,
but if someone wants to work outside those hours-and there is a demand for people who
work outside those hours-he will be able to do so provided he is paid overtime rates.

interested in what the amendments were. The member for Grey Lynn suggested that the Bill
should go back to interested parties for further submissions, but the committee has listened
to submissions for months and the Bill had been amended accordingly.
The member for Southern Maori referred to shop hours for opening and closing during
the week. It is true that the Bill allows a shop to be open between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. during
the week. She talked about the problems for families with young children where mothers are
expected to work inhuman hours, starting at 7 a.m. and working again later in the evening.
What shopkeeper will rush to open his shop at 7 a.m.? Retailers and businessmen know,
even if the member for Southern Maori does not, that customers are not queuing to get into
their shops at 8 a.m., nor even at 9 a.m. So what is all the panic about opening at 7 a.m.? A
few traders are being given the opportunity to provide a service by opening at 7 a.m. if they
so wish, but there will be no rush and no inconvenience will be caused to the thousands of
employees who will be working reasonable hours, rather than starting at 7 a.m.
The member for Southern Maori also talked about employees' being forced to work
longer hours at the other end of the day. Many stores at the moment close at 5 p.m. The
grocers' award provides for 6 p.m. closing, but some grocers close at 5 p.m. and others at
5.30 p.m. In Auckland, Foodtown decided recently to stay open until 6 p.m. on Wednes-


## p. 884 (#126) ############################################

884
22 June
Shop Trading Hours Bill
days, Thursdays, and Fridays. Shortly afterwards, Woolworths decided to remain open until
6 p.m., but after a short time went back to 5.30 p.m. closing. There is flexibility in closing
hours already, and that pattern will continue. In the Johnsonville Mall, Woolworths stays
open until 6 p.m., but Self Help closes at 5.30 p.m. Woolworths also stay open until 6 p.m. in
Kilbirnie, but other traders have not found it necessary to extend their hours. The member
for Southern Maori put forward a fallacious argument when she said that thousands of
women would be going to work in the small hours of the morning and returning home late at
night. The Bill has been surrounded by a number of misconceptions and misunderstandings,
some of them genuine and some of them deliberately engineered.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: What do you mean by that?
Mr ELLIOTT: I am talking about a document of this type, which was handed to shop
assistants in Christchurch. It talks about the fight against the erosion of the 40-hour week. It
also says that workers should develop rank and file activity such as this to build up these
struggles into the final fight against the cause-capitalism. That document was distributed by
the Christchurch branch of the Communist Party of New Zealand; P. O. Box 1000,
Christchurch. That is what I meant by deliberately engineered misunderstandings and
misconceptions.
Theoretically, I could support a trader's opening at whatever time of the day or week he
desires, subject to the demand for his services and consideration for employees. Most New
Zealanders do not want a proliferation of weekend trading, so, in the best interests of
everyone, some control must be exercised. The Bill will not result in an open slather in
trading hours; the present pattern of weekend trading will continue. However, any shop or
group of shops can apply to the Shop Trading Hours Commission for an exemption to open
at the weekend. Applications will be heard by the commission of three people, which must
take into account a number of very carefully constructed criteria before granting an
application.
I point out to the member for Southern Maori that the submissions of interested parties
will be argued for and against and the commission will decide, according to the criteria in the
Bill, whether an extension is justified. Those criteria are very tight. Indeed, it could be said
that they are now too tight, which could result in the granting of fewer exemptions than are
granted at present. The wholesale granting of exemptions will not result. Under the previous
Act, the tribunal had to consider only three criteria when granting exemptions; now, the
commission must take eight criteria into consideration.
I predict that very desirable exemptions may result-and I hope they will result-in
Auckland and other major metropolitan areas, and in tourist areas; but in other areas there
will be very few exemptions, and the Bill will not create the trouble and fuss that the
Opposition says it will.
Debate interrupted.

PRIVILEGE
Mr SPEAKER: This might be a convenient time for me to refer to a question of
privilege that was raised the day before yesterday, and to which there was some reference
yesterday. The matter was raised by the member for New Lynn, who said, on 21 June:
"Under standing Order 428 I raise a matter of privilege. I refer not to the member for
Wairarapa, which matter you properly ruled in the House on Friday was not a breach of
privilege, but to the Minister of Police. On Friday we were told that to the best of his
memory the Minister of Police had not given a police document to the member for
Wairarapa. We have since learned from newspaper reports, which have not been denied,
that the member for Wairarapa said that documents had been given to him, and, alterna-
tively, that information had been given to the member by the Minister.
"I raise the matter for two reasons. First, there is a direct contradiction between what
the Minister of Police said and what the member for Wairarapa said, and, secondly, I should
like to know the status of the remarks passed by the Minister of Police to the member for
Wairarapa. Were the remarks passed as a result of something that happened in the Cabinet
room, or were they from a police report? It they were from a police report, the Minister had
no right to say what he did to the member for Wairarapa, because previously he had told the
member for Northern Maori he was not able to supply details. I say that prima facie there
has been a breach of privilege."


## p. 886 (#128) ############################################

886
23 June
Privilege
The Minister of Police said: "I was not in the House when this matter was brought up,
but I have caught up with it since. My recollection of it is that the member for Wairarapa
mentioned it to me. I gave him some verbal information. I would not have shown him or
given him a police report. I wrote to the member for Northern Maori in the same strain. I
should like to see"-this is an unrevised Hansard report and the word "see" is perhaps
inaccurate “a discussion with the member for Wairarapa on just what the position was.
Certainly, the police report that came to me would be for my information only."
I have since received a letter from the member for Northern Maori, and some
newspaper excerpts from the member for New Lynn. It seems to me that the only two ways
in which a matter of privilege could arise would be if there had been circulated a document,
that was, in a parliamentary sense, a privileged document, such as a committee report that
had not yet been presented to the House. There is no evidence of any sort to suggest that a
document, privileged as a parliamentary document, was circulated, so in that respect there is
no occasion at all to suggest a breach of parliamentary privilege.
The second question is, was there an indication that the member complained of was
wilfully misleading the House? If that were so, there would be a prima facie case of privilege.
But when one bears in mind that the matter raised alluded to an incident that happened last
September, and then looks again at what the Minister said "I was not in the House when
this matter was brought up, but I have caught up with it since. My recollection of it is that the
member for Wairarapa mentioned it to me. I gave him some verbal information. I would not
have shown him or given him a police report. I wrote to the member for Northern Maori in
the same strain”—it is not surprising that his recollection at the time was not accurate, if it
were inaccurate.
There is reference in some newspaper excerpts to a document, and the member for
Wairarapa is quoted as saying that he had been given a summary of the police report by the
Minister of Police during a caucus meeting. Elsewhere it was stated that a caucus report had
been shown to the Maori Council. There is no question but that the preparation of a report
to caucus, which would be interested in the incident in question and about which there was
considerable emotional discussion at the time, would not be surprising. It may well be that
the member inferred that the information came from a police source, as it almost certainly
and quite properly would. However, a report to caucus of an incident very much in the
public eye is quite a different matter from a police report, so there is no indication of the
Minister in question taking any step wilfully to mislead the House.
When he said he mentioned the matter verbally to the member for Wairarapa it seems
at that point, if a caucus paper was supplied, that he did not give the full information. But, as
it was off the cuff, that, to me, is not an instance of wilfully misleading the House. The
circulation of a paper to caucus-and I am sure many a paper circulated in both parties'
caucuses is not for public consumption—is no doubt what the member for Wairarapa had in
mind when he said it was a privileged paper, a paper not for general circulation. I find, in the
circumstances, that there is no prima facie breach of privilege.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I
raise a question that ranges outside the ruling you have just given, but certainly relates to a
comment made by the member for New Lynn when the matter was raised on Friday last. I
refer to the status of the remarks made by the Minister of Police to the member for
Wairarapa, remarks which are evidently contained in some kind of report, and to the fact
that another member of Parliament-in this case the member for Northern Maori, and I
think also the member for Western Maori-asked for the same, or similar, information, but
was refused. You have indicated that the report was not a police report. In that case, I
suggest it would be quite proper for us to request the tabling of the report which was
apparently given to some members of Parliament, but refused others.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): I simply make the observation that
on Tuesday when we were discussing a private member's Bill relating to information, the

that documents circulated in caucus would not be documents that would be made public.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): Speaking to the point of order—

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Hospital Facilities in Provincial Towns
1. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Health, Having regard to
prolonged and difficult staffing problems at the Oamaru Hospital, can he give an assurance
that it is the announced policy and the firm intention of the National Government to foster
and encourage the full use of facilities in hospitals in provincial towns in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I appreciate the difficulties that the Waitaki
Hospital Board has encountered in staffing Oamaru Hospital, particularly with medical staff.
A meeting was held recently between the chairman and officers of the board, the director of
the division of hospitals, Department of Health, and a representative of the Otago Hospital
Board. Agreement was reached on measures to improve the level of the junior medical
staffing of the hospital. The department has also given an assurance that it will refer any
suitable applicants for senior positions to the board. One of the Government's stated policy
aims is the marshalling of all public, private, and voluntary agencies in the fight to prevent
sickness, accidents, and ill health. In doing so, the Government will foster the best possible
use of hospitals serving provincial communities. The Waitaki Hospital Board has already, in
consultation with departmental officers, adopted a development plan which will make
maximum use of the existing Oamaru Hospital resources, and provide a sound basis for
future services. It is understood that the board's consultants are working on the practical
implementation of this plan.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Traffic Officer Safety
2. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Transport, In view of the tragic
death of the New Plymouth traffic inspector, the attack made on a traffic officer in
Wellington, and the effect such incidents are having on the men and their families, will he
give urgent consideration to ensuring that during the hours of darkness traffic inspectors,
like the police, work only in pairs?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): When answering a similar
question last week, the Acting Minister of Transport assured the House that both the
ministry and myself shared the concern of the member for Wanganui. He also said that
discussions were being held with the Public Service Association and the traffic officers'
group, in order to examine acceptable ways of minimising the risks inherent in the traffic
officers' occupation. These discussions are continuing, and will do so over the next few
weeks. I am satisfied that every effort is being made to reach a satisfactory solution to the
problem.
Mr Marshall: I thank the Minister for his answer. That question, in fact, was not asked
last week, as it transpired. Could the Minister give any indication as to how long the
negotiations might take, and when they might come to some sort of fruition?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: The negotiations are taking place as quickly as possible.
As I have said, I share the honourable member's concern about what has happened. We did
have a back-up system, as he probably knows, but I am satisfied that it is not sufficient in
certain areas at night, and we are discussing this with the Public Service Association at
present. In my opinion, the sooner the matter is resolved, the better.
Mr Wellington: Bearing in mind the gravity with which the Minister has treated the
case-as he should-can he advise which groups are involved in the negotiations in an
attempt to find a solution to the difficulties traffic officers are encountering?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: The groups are, the traffic officers themselves and the
Public Service Association, and I have talked to the Minister of Police. That is about as far as
I can go at present, but I feel that the police could have a part in the proceedings which may
help the traffic officers.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: In view of the Minister's reply, how does he reconcile the
statement made by Superintendent S. L. Young, Officer in Charge of the Wellington
