National Superannuitants-Telephone Concession
4. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Social Welfare, How
many age beneficiaries, following transfer to national superannuation, have so far lost their
half telephone-rental concession?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Of the 194 557 age beneficiaries
transferred to national superannuation, 11 932, or 6.1 percent, have had their telephone
concession withdrawn. This is for the reason that their other or private income added to the
full national superannuation benefit gives them a total income in excess of the statutory limit
for concession purposes.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Will the Minister confirm that next year, when the Govern-
ment's policy is fully effective, all those receiving a half telephone-rental concession will lose
it?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, I can confirm that. The reason is that when national
superannuation reaches 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage and is in fact
greater than the take-home pay of many in our work force, the relationship between national
superannuitants and wage earners will be such that concessions will no longer be considered
necessary or justifiable.
Mr Bell: How much is the concession worth to the national superannuitant, in terms of
dollars and cents per week?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The value of the concession for both the telephone rental and the
television licence fee is assessed to be about $1.27 a week.
Hon. Michael Connelly: To those who have already lost it, does it not represent a loss of
$360,000 a year?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: As I pointed out previously, the reason 6.1 percent of national
superannuitants have lost the concession is that their other income, over and above their full
superannuation payment, takes them above the statutory limit which bars concessions.
Mr Wellington: Can the Minister confirm that under national superannuation superan-
nuitants will be far better off than they would have been under the old system, receiving an
age benefit plus the telephone and other concessions?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, I can confirm that. I recommend that Opposition members
again read the report of the Royal Commission on Social Security, which sat between 1970
and 1972. In that report they will see factual evidence to show that under the national
superannuation scheme beneficiaries will receive more than they would have received if their
benefits were tied to the consumer price index, as has been the case in the past.
Mr Hunt: Can the Minister indicate in which part of the royal commission's report the
recommendations he has just referred to are made?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: If I remember correctly, it is chapter 8, and about page 72.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Will the Minister confirm that the loss to those who have lost
this half telephone concession is worth about $360,000 a year?

and economics in form V. In form VI, with the growth of school-based sixth-form certificate
courses, there is increasing scope for liberal, general, and political studies in which
controversial subjects and propaganda, and their effects, can be analysed. Schools them-
selves organise liberal studies programmes for students in form VII who may also opt into
subjects in the formal curriculum, like English and history, where propaganda is examined
through historical and literary materials.

More New Zealand-born persons returned to this country after absences of at least 12
months during the year ended March 1976 than during the year ended March 1974.

number coming to New Zealand. They were good citizens, good immigrants, skilled people,
and those who came for humanitarian purposes, but there were more than the country could
absorb. We have cut back on that. The number of people going overseas has been a
continuing trend since statistics were kept in 1950. More go each year as permanent
departures, which means that they are away for a year or more.

Mr SPEAKER: Order! There must be no reference to past debates in the same session.

SHOP TRADING HOURS BILL
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei): Before I continue from where I left off last night, I report
that the Minister of Labour has given me a letter he has just received from Mr Kelly of the
shop employees' union claiming that members continue to quote from an article about him in
the Evening Post that he now informs us is incorrect. That is the first information the
Government has received denying the tenor of the article. I repeat what I said last
night—that too many people, consciously or unconsciously, have been confusing the public
about the Bill. Many Opposition members have not debated the Bill.
Most New Zealanders do not want a proliferation of weekend trading, and it will not
eventuate from the Bill. Lengthened weekday hours will not result, either. If anything, the
Bill will tighten the Act and make exemptions more difficult to obtain. A New Zealand
Retailers Federation press statement of 21 June states: "Saturday shopping will be every bit
as difficult to obtain as under the present Act." The Bill provides for trading hours from 7
a.m. to 9 p.m., but it does not cover working conditions. Hours of work, penal rates, and


## p. 897 (#139) ############################################

23 June
897
Shop Trading Hours Bill
overtime provisions will remain unchanged. They are provided for in the collective agree-
ments or awards. Those subjects are covered in the New Zealand retail grocery and
supermarket collective agreements, and have nothing to do with the opening hours of shops,
or the Bill.
Conditions will continue to be negotiated between the union and the employers. The
press statement from the New Zealand Retailers Federation states: "Because of the nine
retail awards covering sections of the industry, and allowing for different opening and closing
hours, particularly over holiday periods, there is no other logical way of catering for the
situation other than a 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. opening provision." Intensive inquiries indicate that
very little change will be likely. The statement quite correctly continues that retailers will not
be forced into uneconomic trading hours as a result of some isolated competitor's action, and
that this should allay one of the union's greatest fears. The hours of work clause in the
awards is not interfered with by this Bill, therefore any changes in working conditions
affecting the 40-hour week, penalty payments, and so on, can be made only with the union's
consent in conciliation or by the Industrial Commission. The Retailers Federation states—
and I believe this is true-"Union members' working conditions are fully protected". The
Bill is permissive, but not mandatory, about weekday hours. Despite the protestations
of the Opposition, there are people in some areas who do want extended shopping hours.
They find it convenient to shop, particularly on Saturday mornings, in the east coast bays in
Auckland, at Coastlands, and at New Brighton; these are examples of Saturday trading. I
now quote from a recent letter from Mr Purdie, Executive Director of the New Zealand
Retailers Federation, to the Minister: "I think I have checked with the top management of
virtually all the major chains, and nobody is currently interested in any significant change.
Furthermore, nobody is going to rush into any alteration from the current hours. Of 150-odd
retailers in Wellington last night, very few indeed left the meeting still concerned about the
possibility of a grass-fire situation of extended shopping hours."
Mr Lange: Does that include Woolworths?
Mr ELLIOTT: Yes, it includes Woolworths, which has no present plans for extension.
Mr Purdie says that the matter has been under continuous discussion in all parts of the
country for 3 weeks, and as a result of those discussions he does not see any possibility of
widespread changes in shopping hours. He believes that there will be very little change in the
foreseeable future. So much for the fears and concerns of the Opposition. I remind members
that we do not have a factories working hours Act, and quite rightly so. Employees are not
abused by unscrupulous employers in factories.
There is no doubt that the suggested extension of Saturday trading has produced
different responses from different communities, ranging from "Let's get into it" in Parnell,
to "We don't want it in any circumstances" in Invercargill and several other places. There
will be different reactions in different parts of the country to applications for exemption.
There has been very little reaction in my home town of Whangarei. I do not think the Bill
will create any enthusiasm, although the opportunity will be there, as it is in the present Act,
for applications for exemptions. If applicants satisfy all the criteria, exemptions will be
granted. I have not had one letter opposing the Bill from anybody in my electorate.
Retailers will adjust their trading hours gradually to suit the requirements of local
communities. Members should remember that New Zealand is made up of many types of
community, large and small. The problem will be better met and solved at a local level than
by a bureaucratic system of licensing. There is some demand in some areas for weekend
services, and the Bill offers the chance of some extended hours. People may make
application to the commission, but the Bill does not compel them to do so; there will be no
change in the status quo.
Opponents of the Bill seem to think it is a cut and dried device paying no heed to the
fact that hours of work are regulated by working conditions and awards and agreements. It is
not. It is an attempt to meet a public demand by considering the interests of all parties. The
opening hours from Monday to Friday are between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. These times are the
outer limits; it is not obligatory for shops to be open. Demand will be the controlling factor.
In gearing themselves to that demand the parties will naturally be governed by what the
awards allow, and in the case of retailers by what profitability is feasible.

apologise to the House. I thought perhaps there would have been one, but there have been
no letters in favour of the Bill. That sums up the position of the member for Whangarei, who

Let us look briefly at the three major claims the Labour Opposition has made about this
Bill. First, it is claimed that widespread Saturday trading will result. Clause 19(6) requires
the commission to take certain factors into account in determining whether or not it is in the
best interests of the public that an application for extended hours be granted. The criteria
are: public demand; any effect the granting of the order would have on retail prices; the
effect on family and other social patterns; the nature of the area in which the shops are
situated; the stability, and orderly and economic planning, of the area, including transport
patterns; the interests of occupiers of other shops; the need to minimise the amount of
commercial activity taking place on Sundays; and the application of the principle of the 40-
hour week as embodied in the Industrial Relations Act, and any derogation from that
principle that may be caused by the granting of the order.
The Government has stated on many occasions that the legislation is not intended to
introduce widespread Saturday trading, and I believe that the comprehensive list of criteria
that I have just read out confirms the Government's intention. The Opposition claims that
these criteria represent a substantial easing of the law and that, whereas the present law
prevents the introduction of Saturday trading, the Bill will introduce it. Let us do what


## p. 902 (#144) ############################################

902
23 June
Shop Trading Hours Bill
Opposition speakers have failed to do: look at the legal detail of the Bill. I particularly note
the absence of contributions on legal questions from lawyer members of the Opposition; I
can only conclude that they have read the Bill carefully, that they understand it, and that
they will not make claims about its legal effects, as some of their colleagues have done.
Section 10B of the Shops and Offices Act 1955, which is the present law, says nothing
more than that the tribunal may make an order granting an exemption if it is satisfied that it
is in the public interest, having regard, first, to the interests of the occupier of any other shop
and, secondly, to the desirability of providing a service to the public at all reasonable times,
particularly in the case of a holiday resort. Those alone are the criteria. There is no
prohibition against Saturday trading and, what is more important, under the 1955
Act-which the Opposition criticised when it was passed, but which certainly has not
resulted in widespread Saturday trading—the tribunal is not obliged to take into account the
effect on retail prices, as the commission is under this Bill. It is not obliged to take into
account the effect on family and social patterns, as it is in this measure. It is not obliged to
take into account the nature of the area, as it is under this legislation. It is not obliged to take
into account the stability and orderly economic planning of the area, as it is under this Bill.
Nor is it obliged to take into account the need to minimise the amount of commercial activity
on Sundays, as it is under this Bill-but the member for New Lynn did not think that was so.
Most important of all, the 1955 Act made no reference to the need to protect the 40-hour
week, and there is specific provision in this Bill.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: No, there is not.
Mr McLAY: I refer the member for Timaru to clause 19(6)(h). If it does not refer to the
protection of the 40-hour week, I do not know what does. In other words, we have in the
new Bill a considerable extension, not a derogation, of the criteria that would protect the
general public and prevent widespread Saturday trading. I can deal very briefly with the
second Opposition claim-that the Bill spells the end of the 40-hour week-by again
referring to clause 19(6)(h), which states that in satisfying itself that the granting of an
application is in the best public interest, the commission must have regard to the principle of
the 40-hour week as embodied in the Industrial Relations Act, and any derogation from that
principle that may be caused by the granting of the order. I challenge any Opposition
speaker who has claimed, either during the debate or in much less temperate terms outside
the House, that the 40-hour week is in jeopardy to show me where there is a similar
provision protecting the 40-hour week in the 1955 legislation, which Opposition members
praise so highly; or where there is provision anywhere in any other previous legislation. The
Opposition knows that it is not there. It also knows that the fact that it was not in the 1955
Act did not lead to a derogation of the 40-hour week.
The third Opposition claim is that, as a result of the Bill, shop assistants will be forced to
work one extra late night a week. The Opposition knows that is simply not so. The Minister
has given an assurance that it is not the case, and the employers have given an assurance that
they have no intention of seeking such a change in awards. It is perhaps appropriate that I
should explain briefly to the House-as has been explained before, but apparently ignored
by the Opposition-the reason it is necessary to provide that retail stores can remain open
from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. on each working day. This is in specific answer to the points raised by
the member for New Lynn. The Opposition has, I suggest deliberately, misunderstood this
clause, and it is hardly surprising, therefore, that people outside the House should also be
confused. At present the opening and closing hours of retail stores are defined in nine
separate retail awards. For instance, butchers can open at 7 a.m. On the other hand, non-
food retail stores can open at 8 a.m. and remain open until 5.30 p.m.
The late night of the New Year week has now been transferred to the week preceding
Christmas. Christmas falls on a different day each year, so it is logical, even for members
opposite, that the night of Christmas Eve late night shopping also changes. Easter is a
movable feast, and no specific date for that can be included in the legislation. The
combination of all these different factors operating each year means that a late shopping
night can quite legally fall on any night of the week during a 12-month period. Christmas Eve
late night shopping may be on a Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, or Friday, and
therefore opening hours must be any time between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. on any day of the
week. The alternative would be to spell out separately all the different circumstances that
can occur at Christmas, Easter, the movable feasts, and all other holidays that are preceded
by a late shopping night. The Bill is drafted in its present form to overcome that situation,
nothing more and nothing less, and it is irresponsible for the Opposition to claim that it is
intended that workers will be obliged to work more than one late night a week. That is not

accordingly, the cost of the same would necessarily have to be passed on to the consumer."

legislation will affect organised sport and recreational activities. Everyone knows that sport
and recreation is healthy and beneficial to young children and teenagers, and that most
sporting activities take place at the weekends. Frequently it is the mother or father who take
the children to tennis, football, basketball, or another sport on a Saturday morning. If the
Bill is enacted, one or both parents could be away at work, and children who might
otherwise make their own way to the sporting activity will have to stay home to look after the

Despite what the Opposition says, the Bill has protective clauses, which I promised my
constituents I would ensure were in the Bill, or vote against it. The first of these refers to the
opening of shops. Clause 6 (1) states that: “Subject to the provisions of this Act, no shop
shall be open between the hours of 9 p.m. and 7 a.m., or on any day that is a Saturday, a
Sunday, New Years Day. . ." and then it goes on to mention a number of holidays. I think
most reasonable people would have to agree that the inclusion of Saturday among the
prescribed days on which shops may not be open effectively rebuts any argument that the
Bill will encourage general Saturday trading. We go through the Bill from that point,
omitting only those clauses that have been struck out, and come to new clause 17 (2), which
states: "The occupiers of the majority of the shops in any area may apply to the commission
for an order that all the shops in that area be authorised to open at specified times on
specified days." That clause spells out to everyone, except the Labour Opposition-which
would not participate in any select committee discussions of any merit—that an area
application has to have consensus support from the retailers, and that the majority of the
occupiers of shops in any area, not a minority, may apply to the commission.
We turn now to clause 19, dealing with hearings and orders, subclause (1) of which
states: "At the hearing of an application under section 17 of this Act, any of the following
persons may appear and be heard, in person or by counsel: (a) the applicant; (b) any
inspector; (c) the occupier of any shop that may be affected by the result of the application;
(d) any person or organisation specified in section 18 (2) of this Act; (e) any other
organisation that, or any of whose members may, in the opinion of the commission, be
affected by the result of the application." Surely this provision must refute the distortions
and deliberate misrepresentations presented to shop assistants, which have advanced the
spurious claim that the Bill will force them to submit, without right of objection, to an
employer's whim to open on Saturdays.
The proposed new subsection (5) of clause 19 is of the utmost significance, in the
avoidance of which the Opposition has been most conscientious. I do not think for one

and rugged individuals. How often we hear National members talking about New Zealan-

number of hours (exclusive of overtime) to be worked in any week by any worker bound by

the Industrial Relations Act could become an escape clause for the commission.
Section 94 of the Industrial Relations Act, which is referred to in the Bill, states: "In any
award made by the commission fixing at not more than 40 the maximum weekly working
hours, the commission shall endeavour to fix the daily working hours so that no part of the
working period falls on a Saturday." That does not mean that the commission must do this, it
means simply that the commission shall endeavour to do it. Clause 19 of the Bill, leaves the

Thursday night shopping, or encourage it to continue.

there is no guarantee of increased income; and, if their costs go up and their income does not

submissions, because the new subclause (6) (b) of clause 19 provides that, before any orders
are granted, the commission shall have regard to any effect the granting of the order would

grant? It is obvious that, almost without exception, any orders that it does grant will increase
costs and therefore increase prices. The inclusion of that provision shows that members
opposite recognise that factor, and salved their consciences by making that provision.

Subclause (6) (g) of clause 19 provides that the commission shall have regard to the need
to minimise the amount of commercial activity taking place on Sundays. Government
members have said that there will be no increase in Saturday trading. In the Wairarapa
Times-Age of 18 November 1975, the Minister of Trade and Industry is reported as
saying—and he was challenged on this point during the election campaign: "National will not
introduce large-scale Saturday trading." However, that clause makes no reference to
Saturday trading or to any increase in Saturday trading, no reference to public holidays, no
reference to statutory holidays or religious occasions; it refers only to Sunday. No review of
the present level of activity is proposed; there is reference only to applications for new
activity on Sundays, and the Saturday extension that the Minister of Trade and Industry
spoke about before the election has faded out of sight.
The member for Hastings, the member for Wairarapa, and the member for Kapiti were
terribly concerned about any extension of hours, but somehow they managed to salve their
consciences by this ineffectual reference to minimising trade on Sunday. As Sunday alone is
mentioned, the clear implication is that the commission does not have to take into account
any need to minimise the amount of commercial activity on Saturdays or public holidays. If
the Government had intended that those days should be included, they would have been


## p. 925 (#167) ############################################

23 June
925
Shop Trading Hours Bill
mentioned together with Sundays. That point has led shop assistants and their union
representatives to see this Bill as a real threat to the New Zealand way of life.
Most members on this side of the House would accept the need for a review from time
to time. There may be a need for some goods to be available on Sunday. Changes are always
taking place, and not everything is covered in present legislation. O.K.-let us extend the
principle of exempted goods. Let us have a tribunal or council-call it what you like—that
acts coherently and directly. But how are we to interpret the new subclause (9) of clause 19?
It reads: "Subject to subsection (7) of this section, an order made under this section that
applies to all the shops in an area shall also apply to every shop that may be built or opened
in that area during the currency of the order." So there is provision for a considerable
extension of the principle. There might be a dairy-the only shop in an area-which has an
exemption, but under that subclause a developer can move in and with the right to open at
the same time as the dairy. It is that kind of insidious attack on the principle of the 40-hour
week and limited weekend trading that members on this side of the House are really
concerned about.
Many members opposite quite conscientiously stated their position before the election.
In considering the Bill, none of them seem to have lived up to what they proferred then.
There has been some window dressing; some notice was taken of the submissions, but

cost of retail trading, can members opposite say that it is part of their overall programme,
when their leader has said that part of his purpose is to cut the real incomes of New
Zealanders? If people cannot buy the same quantity of goods at the same price, on the way
incomes are held today that is tantamount to cutting the real incomes of New Zealanders.
That is what this Bill does..

When pressed-and I stress that-companies say that they could be interested in a second
late night, but that they would probably not want to remain open until 9 p.m. The crux of
that is that the companies would have to negotiate with the union, and would have to pay
penal rates and double time. Retailers in Dannevirke have expressed concern, through the

North might extend their opening hours, thereby taking business away from Dannevirke.
The Bill, as amended, covers the public interest, the people who can make submissions,
and the unions. It is much better than the present law. The commission will consist of three
people, and, before granting an order, it must study these criteria: the public demand; any
effect the granting of an order would have on retail prices; the nature of the area in which the

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Secondary School, Eastern Beach, Auckland
1. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Education, Can he state when work
will be commenced on the proposed secondary school which is to be built on the Crown Land
at the back of Eastern Beach, and when is the school expected to be opened?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): This site is a Crown-owned public
reserve, and its proposed use for a secondary school is being opposed by the Eastern Beach
action group. Objections under the Town and Country Planning Act concerning the use of
the land for a secondary school must be lodged by 30 August 1977. Detailed planning of the
school must be delayed until a decision on these objections is available. It is unlikely that the
secondary school will open before February 1980.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
National Superannuitants-Supplementary Benefits
2. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Social Welfare, How
many age beneficiaries, following transfer to national superannuation, have had additional
benefits reduced in accordance with Government policy to phase out additional benefits, and
what is the total value per week and per annum of such reductions to date?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): A total of 47 808 former age
beneficiaries had their grants of additional benefit reduced from 9 February 1977 following
their transfer to national superannuation. These grants were reduced by a uniform amount
of 50c a week, and will be phased out over a period of 5 to 6 years. The amount of the initial
deduction from additional benefit grants was decided bearing in mind the increases in cash in
hand payments that superannuitants received under the new scheme while ensuring that
even after the deductions, national superannuitants would be significantly better off than if
age benefits had been retained. When national superannuation reaches 80 percent of the
average ordinary-time weekly wage it is considered the relationship between wage earners
and superannuitants will be such that an additional benefit will no longer be justifiable.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Will the Minister answer the question and tell me the total value
per week and per annum of the deductions to date? The amount, of course, is about $1.25
million, but will he state a figure?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: No, I cannot give the honourable member the actual figure.
However, I can say that although the benefits were reduced by 50c, there was still more cash
in hand than previously. All those beneficiaries received a substantial tax refund at the end
of March, and they will also get an increase as a result of the Department of Labour's survey
of April last. The income test has been done away with so that beneficiaries can earn money
if they wish, and the benefit will be increased to 80 percent of the average ordinary-time
weekly wage from 31 August next year.
Mr Comber: On the information available to him, can the Minister indicate whether

Oral Answers to Questions
Maori Council-Right to Attend Meetings
9. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa) asked the Minister of Maori Affairs, Will he advise the
House by what right the four members representing the Maori electorates attend meetings of
the New Zealand Maori Council?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): There is no statutory provision for
the attendance of the four members for Maori electorates to attend meetings of the New
Zealand Maori Council. There is nothing to prevent the council from seeking advice
wherever it wishes or from inviting whomsoever it wishes to attend its meetings.
Mr Couch: Do the four Maori members receive the minutes from the New Zealand
Maori Council?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: I have no idea. I have no close connection with the council. If it
wishes to invite me to a meeting, I go. If it wishes to correspond, it sends correspondence.
Hon. M. Rata: Will the Minister confirm that at the last meeting of the New Zealand
Maori Council held in this building last weekend, the council affirmed the right of members
to attend as a standing invitation to Maori members of Parliament as published in the
Dominion of 17 June, but then went on to say that in order to prevent any further dangerous
interference as a result of the circulation of a police report by the member for Wairarapa, the
members will have a standing invitation to council meetings but will not have the right to
vote?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: The council has not informed me of the decision it made, and I
did not see the article in the Dominion.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: Has the Minister any objection to the Maori
members of Parliament receiving minutes from the New Zealand Maori Council or from any
of its components such as the executives within the members' electorates?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: I have no objection at all to the New Zealand Maori Council
doing whatever it likes with its minutes. It can send them to anyone it likes. It is none of my
business.
Hon. M. Rata: Will the Minister confirm that the relationship between the Maori
members of Parliament and the New Zealand Maori Council and its affiliated councils since
the inception of the council has been relatively good, and that this is threatened by the
inopportune action of one of his colleagues.
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: I will not confirm that.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Rural Bank Assistance to Maori Incorporations
10. Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori), on behalf of Mr WETERE (Western Maori), asked
the Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation, Could he indicate
how many Maori incorporations and Maori farmers were assisted by way of loans for the
March years of 1975, 1976, and 1977 in the eight Maori Land Court areas?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corpora-
tion): The Rural Banking and Finance Corporation does not keep a record of the nationality
of the farmers it lends to and I am therefore unable to give the honourable member the
number of Maori farmers the Rural Bank has assisted. Furthermore, all statistical informa-
tion available from the Rural Bank can only be given as it relates to its branch office areas
rather than the Maori district areas. With regard to Maori incorporations, as I advised in a
recent answer to a question from my colleague the member for Gisborne, the policy of
providing development assistance to Maori land incorporations through the Rural Bank was
only introduced late in 1976. For the year ended 31 March 1977 the bank authorised six loans
to incorporations for a total of $293,760.
Mr Reweti: Are the interest rates charged greater or lesser than when the incorporations
were receiving loans from the Department of Maori Affairs under section 460 of the Act?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Offhand I cannot be absolutely certain on that. The member
should ask a separate question.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

FISHERIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. The Bill provides for the declaration of controlled fisheries and for a new Part III in the
Fisheries Act 1908. As such it is a major step in the conservation of New Zealand's fish
resources. We all want correct management and proper utilisation of our resources. At
present great attention is being paid to the possible overexploitation of our deep-water
resources, but this Bill looks much closer inshore, at the conservation of the very valuable
inshore species, such as rock lobster, paua, eels, oysters, scallops, and the like, that are
harvested exclusively by New Zealand fishermen. This has nothing to do with the operations
of foreign nations that fish in our waters. This Bill empowers the Minister of Fisheries to
declare any fishery listed in the schedule to the Bill-and there are six-to be a controlled
fishery for the conservation of the resource and for the economic stability of the industry.
It has been argued that certain fisheries are self-regulatory; that is, once the fishing is no
longer a commercial proposition the fishermen will leave, and the fishery will recover. That
may be true in some areas and of some species, and in those instances no controls will be
imposed. I remind the House that the legislation is empowering legislation only, and will be
used only as the Minister considers necessary for the conservation or management of the
fishery, and for the economic stability of the industry or those engaged in that particular
sector of it. There are situations, however, where, from a conservation point of view, it is
necessary to apply controls to avoid overexploitation. With a resource that is limited and
definable, and especially if the financial return is high-as with scallops and rock
lobsters-people are encouraged to stay longer in the fishery than the resource can sustain.
Good returns from the fishery may mean the maximum economic yield is not reached until
well after the optimum sustainable yield is passed; accordingly, the fishery is damaged by
being overfished, and is reduced for a very considerable time.
This legislation arose from requests expressed by the Fishing Industry Board and the
fishermen's associations at their annual conferences for legislation to control the type of
fisheries listed in the second schedule. From my discussions with the industry, I believe there
is wide acceptance of the proposals from those engaged in the fisheries that are likely to be
controlled. I am sure that is a statement with which the member for Nelson will agree,
particularly as it pertains to the scallop industry. I believe the member for Marlborough will
agree, also. The legislation is similar to that which has been operating successfully in some
Australian states, for similar types of fisheries.
I shall now look at some of the major provisions in the Bill. The proposed new sections
101 to 116 provide for the establishment of a Fisheries Licensing Authority, which shall
consist of an independent chairman, one member appointed after consultation with the
Fishing Industry Board, and one other member. None of the members would be from the
Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. The select committee recommended that the authority
have the power to co-opt an extra member with specialist or local knowledge, or who has
some particular skill that would be of value to the authority in considering the control of any
particular fishery. This is an important amendment to the Bill. Such a person would have full
rights as a member of the authority, but would not be entitled to vote.


## p. 941 (#183) ############################################

24 June
941
Fisheries Amendment Bill
The principal functions of the authority are to sit as a licensing authority to consider
applications for licences to fish in a controlled fishery, and to grant, renew, revoke, or
amend such licences as it determines. The authority will have the power to hold hearings, to
receive evidence on applications from interested persons, and to establish a register of
controlled fishery licences. The proposed new sections 117 to 119 provide for the Minister of
Fisheries to declare controlled fisheries within which all fishing will be specially licensed.
Generally, a controlled fishery would be defined by reference to the species, quality,
quantity, or size of fish that may be taken; the methods of fishing that may be employed; the
areas that may by fished; and the number of fishing units that may be engaged in the
industry. Before declaring any particular fishery to be a controlled fishery, the Minister must
consult the Fishing Industry Board. That maintains the concept of the legislation—to be in
accord with the wishes of the industry, or those who represent the industry.
Under the proposed new section 118 the Minister may also restrict the number of
licences or permits issued under Part I of the Act before declaring a controlled fishery. That
is to prevent excessive overfishing, which would happen if the number of ordinary fishing
licences or permits issued was higher than would be considered desirable if the fishery was
controlled. The proposed new sections 120 and 121 detail the procedures for obtaining
controlled fishery fishing licences, and those the authority will follow in granting licences.
Applications for licences may be made personally, or, if on behalf of a company, shall give
the name or names of the masters who will be in command of the boats intended to be used,
and shall set out in writing the grounds on which the application is made.
The authority is empowered to and shall refer applications to the director-general for a
report. This report would then be given to the authority, which would hold a hearing and
may grant a licence. I propose to introduce a Supplementary Order Paper further amending
section 120 to provide that a copy of the report shall also go to the applicant. This was
discussed by the select committee, but was not included in the Bill as reported back. On
reflection, I consider it is important that the applicant be aware of the contents of the
director-general's report before the authority hears the application.
The proposed new sections 122 to 125 provide, in considerable detail, for matters to be
considered in determining an application for a licence, the classification and duration of
licences, the terms and conditions of those licences, and the renewal of licences. In
determining applications the authority is to consider the desirability of giving preference to
fishermen from a community within the area of the controlled fishery. This would allow
applications from fishermen in small coastal communities to be considered favourably by the
authority. The New Zealand Maori Council raised this point at the select committee, and
provisions have been made in the amended Bill to meet what the committee considered to be
a legitimate request.
The proposed new sections 126 and 127 provide for temporary licences, appointment of
temporary masters, and for boat authorities, which are abbreviated versions of a licence,
held on each licensed boat. The temporary licences allow a person other than the licensee to
operate the licence if the licensee is unable to do so for a variety of reasons. These licences
are effective for only 1 month. The temporary master's provision was inserted by the select
committee, and allows another master to take a licensed boat to sea in urgent
circumstances-for example, when the regular master has been taken ill. This is designed to
permit the continuation of the fishery, and to ensure that it is not hamstrung by excessive
legislation.
The proposed new section 128 states that licences or boat authorities are not transfer-
able, and there shall be no goodwill attached to any licence or boat authority. Goodwill is
not to form part of the purchase price of any boat that has been issued with a boat authority,
or of any shares in a licensee company other than companies listed on the Stock Exchange.
The provision for companies listed on the Stock Exchange is needed, because it would be
impossible to determine the value that might be attributed to the shares of a large company
with licensed boats. The authority must also approve the purchase price of any such boat.
This section is intended to eliminate the possibility of goodwill accruing to licences, which is
a failing in many licensing systems. The select committee spent considerable time studying
the proposed new section, and it meets the intention to prevent value accruing to licences so
that they can be traded.
The proposed new sections 128 to 135 contain provisions on the suspension of fishing by
the licence holder, revocation or suspension of licences by the authority, and reviews of
licences. The Minister is also empowered, in urgent circumstances, to restrict licences in
certain areas after informing the authority and consulting the Fishing Industry Board if

24 June
Fisheries Amendment Bill
practicable. The circumstances in which this provision would be used are, for example, the
pollution of a shellfish bed by sewage discharge where public health was in danger by
continuous fishing. This is purely an emergency procedure, but it was necessary to include it
in the legislation.
The proposed new sections 136 to 142 provide for an effective appeal system. Appeals
can be made to the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court, and these sections outline
the grounds on which a decision by the authority may be appealed, and list the persons
entitled to appeal. The proposed new sections 143 and 144 relate to offences, penalties, and
evidence and proof in court proceedings, and the proposed new section 145 prescribes
regulation-making powers. Regulations made under this Part of the Act shall have prece-
dence over regulations made pursuant to Part I and Part II of the Act, except that nothing
shall derogate from anything relating to Maori fishing rights in Part I or Part II of the Act.
That is a major proviso.
The proposed new section 146 allows the Governor-General to extend the second
schedule, which specifies the fisheries that may be controlled. Other species considered to be
endangered by overfishing can be included in the schedule, but the Governor-General must
be satisfied that the Fishing Industry Board has been consulted about any additions. It is the
Minister's responsibility to consult the industry before any additional species are added to
the schedule. The schedule provides that scallops in the Nelson area and the Bay of Plenty-
Coromandel Peninsular, rock lobsters, paua, eels, and mussels in the New Zealand fisheries
waters, and oysters in the Foveaux Strait oyster fishery are the fisheries that may be
controlled. Those are the main provisions in the Bill.
I consider that the Bill will be widely accepted by the industry. It will be welcomed by
the people in the industry, because they see it as being necessary to preserve the valuable fish
species. One does not need a long memory to recall the boom and bust situation that
occurred on the Chatham Islands crayfish beds 3 or 4 years ago.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Eight years ago.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: Eight years ago-I stand corrected. One recalls the concern
expressed at that time because there was no provision within the Fisheries Act to prevent the
mad scramble to the Chathams to take part in that fishing. I recently visited the Chatham
Islands and saw the now derelict fish processing factories that were set up during the boom.
The Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Local Government was with me, and
he saw the aftermath of the boom. The Bill before the House is designed to prevent a
repetition of that type of fishing, which does no good to anyone, but considerable harm to
the long-term nature of the fishery concerned.
Some reservations have been expressed about the licensing system, stemming in the
main from the concern felt by people within the industry when they operated under a
licensing system from 1945 to 1964. That system controlled the fisheries in a rather strict and
harsh manner. The Bill will not allow that situation to recur. The legislation is selective in the
fisheries that will be or can be controlled. At present only six fisheries are listed. It is up to
the Minister to determine how many of those six fisheries should be controlled, or if any
other fisheries should be controlled. That provision will be implemented only after full
consultation with the industry. I commend the Bill.
As I said when the Bill was reported back from the select committee, evidence was
heard from 10 or 12 groups, and the committee deliberated in a harmonious and constructive
manner. I thank the members of the committee for their work. The Government has
introduced a Bill that will control selected fisheries, and as set out the Bill will do that in a
proper manner. It is my intention to have the Bill passed through all its stages as soon as
possible, because I know there is some anxiety, particularly in the Nelson area where the
scallop season will open shortly. I hope the House will co-operate so that the Bill can be
passed through all its stages as quickly as possible.

shellfish, a traditional source of food for the Maori people. The New Zealand Maori
Council's submissions to the select committee stated: "The New Zealand Maori Council has
for some considerable time been concerned for the commercial exploitation of the country's
fisheries. Particular concern was focused on the council's 1971 submissions on the exploita-
tion of the natural stock of shellfish. The council's view was that the shore fishing licences
were too readily obtained to the detriment of Maori communities living on the coasts who
derived a considerable part of their subsistence from the sea." The coastline of my electorate
stretches from the south of Gisborne to the Thames Bight, and is probably one of the only
places in the country where one can harvest all the various types of shellfish important to the
Maori way of life.

to operate in a controlled fishery should know the department's views about him and his
operations. The committee discussed this at some length. There were reservations, but I am
pleased that the Minister has come round to the view that the Supplementary Order Paper
should be introduced, and it will have the support of the Opposition.
Some reservations were expressed about section 146, which allows other species to be
added to the schedule in future, particularly in respect of wet fish. This section now reads,

schedule to this Act by adding the description of fisheries that may be declared to be
controlled fisheries if the Governor-General in Council is satisfied that the Fishing Industry
Board has been consulted in respect of this addition." That was as far as we could go at this
stage to ensure consideration other than just Government consideration if it were deemed
advisable to add other species to the second schedule. In practice, this section may well need
to be tightened up, but at this stage I am prepared to go along with the belief that inclusion of
the Fishing Industry Board is desirable. Perhaps it is wise at this stage not to prejudge the
situation. We shall let the authority operate and watch results.

Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson): I agree with the Minister that the Bill is supported by both
sides of the House. I was a little disappointed that the member for Nelson tried to make

position on the Order Paper. I am not interested in which Government first floated the idea
of the Bill. I know it was brought in because of a request by the industry—the board and the
fishermen's associations. This is empowering legislation only. It is locking the stable door
before the horse has bolted, or, to put it another way, lifting the net or drawing up the
lobster pot before it is too late and while there are still some fish for future generations. In
the past we have seen fish stocks being wiped out, or at least so badly depleted that special
prohibitions on the fishing of the species concerned have had to be applied.
This Bill has only two purposes: to husband and control fish resources so that there is an
industry for fishermen to work in the future, and to ensure that future generations of New
Zealanders can enjoy the succulence of any of the six species named in the second schedule.
It is vital that the legislation be implemented to conserve those species. There is no fence
around a fish resource, nor is there any way in which the rate of depletion of the resource can
be determined other than by actually going down and examining the fishing ground or
gauging the lessening of the take.
I recall the fate of some of our fish resources. Mention has been made of the Chatham
Islands crayfishing industry and its virtual disappearance. In my electorate there was a
toheroa processing factory, which no longer operates. I can recall the times I have taken my
family to the toheroa beds on Ninety Mile Beach and, as of right, been allowed to gather as
many toheroas as I wished. Now, because of the greediness of our people, only one area was
opened last year for the taking of toheroa. That was at Bailey's Beach in the south of my
electorate. The toheroas were very badly exploited, and it is timely that the Bill be passed to
ensure that such a thing does not happen again.
A Fisheries Licensing Authority of three members, one being chairman, is to be
established. It is worth noting that no member of the authority shall be from the ministry.
The industry will be largely represented by the common sense of the Government in
appointing the members of that authority. All through the provisions of the Bill the key note
is common sense. In addition to its three members, if it thinks it is necessary the authority
will have the right to co-opt another member, who will have no voting power. That will be to
facilitate proceedings if certain expertise or local knowledge is required. The member for
Eastern Maori expressed concern that no Maori viewpoint would be available to the
authority. The Bill does not stipulate that persons of any particular ethnic origin are to be
appointed to the authority. If one of the three members is not a Maori, then under the
proposed new section 103A provision is made to co-opt a member because of his particular
expertise or local knowledge. That could well be a member of the Maori race.
I welcome the provision that, except in certain circumstances, the hearings will be in
public. It is most desirable that we all know what is going on. It will be a process of open
government in that everybody will be able to hear what is happening, to hear the decision
and the way in which it was arrived at by the authority. The authority has the right to refer
applications for a licence to the director-general for a report. As further evidence of the
openness and common-sense approach being taken by the Government, an applicant will be
supplied with a copy of that report. The Minister has already said he proposes to introduce a
Supplementary Order Paper to deal with that. By his being furnished with a copy of the
report an applicant can be sure that the evidence presented to the authority is all the
evidence and that no other evidence will be slipped in in a sealed envelope. He will know
fully what is happening. That is most essential, and it will ensure that not only an applicant
but those who oppose an application will know the background of any decision the authority
makes.
I mentioned earlier that some people have been rather greedy in the taking of certain

the penalty provisions might seem substantial, but if we are to protect our resources then
they must be substantial. At the moment, only six species are mentioned. The Bill is a
common-sense approach to the problem and will not necessarily impose blanket control on
any controlled fishery. It will be flexible and the provisions will vary from area to area.

Minister, but the authority will allocate the licences, and for this reason I believe that the
Fishing Industry Board should remain independent of any arguments that might arise.
The simple objective of the Bill is to conserve threatened fish species. These species are
not being conserved from foreign boats, but, whether we like it or not, from New
Zealanders. The intention of the legislation is not to lock up the resource, but to maintain it
at its maximum sustainable level so that New Zealanders will be able to harvest and enjoy a
particular food, and also to maintain a valuable export earner.

CIVIL LIST AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The main purpose of this amendment to the Civil List Act is to provide for the
payment of an annuity to a retired Governor-General who was domiciled in New Zealand at
the time of his appointment, and who continues to reside here after his retirement. Over the
years, New Zealand has had Governors-General who have served the country and the
Crown with great capacity, and it has been the established tradition, of course, that they
return to their homeland. A New Zealander has now been appointed to the position, and it is
likely that there will be other New Zealand Governors-General.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Just a faint possibility.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The present Governor-General is a New Zealander, his
successor is a New Zealander, and it is my guess that other New Zealanders will be
appointed. We now face the possibility that a New Zealander who retires from that high
office continues to live here.
I shall now refer to the clauses. Clause 1 is, of course, the short title. Clause 2 provides
for the payment of such annuity to a Governor-General who continues to reside in this
country after his retirement. The payment of an annuity is necessary, because it is most likely
that those New Zealanders who held that office would retire in this country. The annuity
recognises the continuing status in the community of a retired Governor-General, and will
help him maintain an appropriate standard of living as befits his position. It is considered
that the annuity should be equal at least to that paid to a former Prime Minister, which is
$5,000 a year at present.
The Bill provides that any person eligible also for an annuity as a former Prime Minister
would receive only the higher of the annuities payable. This provides for a former Prime
Minister, or a former Prime Minister's widow, who could in the fullness of time become
Governor-General of this country. Provision has also been made for the widow of a retired
Governor-General to receive half the annuity payable to the retired Governor-General. The
sum paid is equal to the amount paid to the widow of a former Prime Minister. Clause 3 is a
machinery provision adding a former Governor-General to the classes of persons to whom
benefits and privileges apply, as well as clarifying the group. It is a simple measure to meet a
significant change in the persons likely to occupy the high office of Governor-General.

Civil List Amendment Bill
disrespect of any kind of a personal nature-the Opposition believes the appointment has set
an undesirable precedent, which it certainly has no intention of following.
A question that has seemed academic until quite recently is how powerful or, as it is
more often put, how powerless is the Governor-General. Is his office just a vestigial and
ceremonial remainder, or does it have some residue of executive power? Is his hand merely
that which signs documents-that of Jacob acting out the voice of Esau-or has it the power
to strike and, in particular, the power to strike down, as well as meekly obeying directions to
sign? Events in Australia in 1975, when Sir John Kerr dismissed the Whitlam Government,
suggested that the office is not just the toothless, docile, and house-broken tiger that it has
been generally imagined to be. It is suggested, of course, that what happened there in the
dismissal of a Prime Minister and his Government was out of character, and was due entirely
to the srcial features of the Australian constitution and, in particular, its federal system. It
is true at there is no possibility of the events of November 1975 being exactly reproduced
here, but the events of April 1977 in Fiji could very well arise here, as they have very nearly
happened in the past.
The constitutional questions arising out of the Australian affair have recently been
interestingly and, I suggest, illuminatingly analysed in the Parliamentarian, the journal of
the Parliaments of the Commonwealth, by a number of constitutional experts, including our
own Sir John Marshall. I propose to quote from some of the extracts appearing in that
journal. I turn first to the contribution of Sir John Marshall, because he refers to the incident
I have mentioned. At page 15 of the January issue of that periodical I find this statement: "In
1957 the newly arrived Governor-General, Lord Cobham, found himself in a situation where
he had to contemplate the possibility that following the election, which was due to take place
at the end of November in that year, there might be an equal number of parliamentary seats
held by both the National Party, then in Government, and the Labour Party, then in
Opposition. I was the Attorney-General at that time, and I had a number of discussions with
Lord Cobham on the constitutional problems which he was anticipating. These discussions
were not formal consultations, because we were dealing with a hypothetical situation, which
in fact did not arise. The Labour Party won the election by two seats. If there had been a
draw, my opinion, and one which I would have given to Cabinet, would have been that l
Prime Minister should have advised the Governor-General that as the National Government
had not been defeated in the country it should continue in office until it was defeated in
Parliament. This defeat would have been inevitable, but could have been delayed for as long
as 7 months, since Parliament need not be summoned before the end of June in any year. On
the election of a Speaker, who is traditionally selected from the governing party in N *
Zealand, the Government would have been in the minority of one, since the Speaker while
he is presiding only has a casting vote. The Government would have been defeated on the
first majority matter of confidence to come before the House. My opinion for Cabinet would
then have been that the Prime Minister should advise the Governor-General to dissolve
Parliament, and if that advice had been given I believe it should have been taken as there
was no other alternative Government.” As I have said, the very circumstance that arose in
Fiji was one of which we were on the threshold in 1957, 20 years ago.
But in any period such as the 7-month period Sir John refers to, the Government, given
the wide regulation-making powers now available to it, could completely undermine
Parliament and negate the electoral mandate of the people. I accept Sir John's analysis, and
his assessment of the constitutional practice in that case, although I believe he is too
sweeping in stating as a general principle, again on page 15 of the Parliamentarian, that “a
request for a dissolution in order to appeal to the people through a general election would
not be refused to a Prime Minister who still retained the support of a majority of the House".
The point is, however, that a Governor-General in New Zealand may well have to make an
intensely political decision, and his instructions explicitly free him from slavish acceptance of
ministerial advice.
I quote from the Letters Patent issued to a Governor-General, which go back to 1917
but still appear in the same form. Clause 5(a) states: "In the execution of the powers and
authorities vested in him, the Governor-General shall be guided by the advice of the
Executive Council, but if in any case he shall see sufficient cause to dissent from the opinion
of the said council he may act in the exercise of his said powers and authorities in opposition
to the opinion of the council, reporting the matter to us"—that is, to Her Majesty "without
delay with the reasons for his so acting." That is an authority seldom invoked, I concede, but
far from atrophied and undoubtedly still in being.
The position is, I believe, aptly and correctly summarised in the same publication by Sir


## p. 954 (#196) ############################################

954
24 June
Civil List Amendment Bill
Peter Rawlinson, a former Conservative Attorney-General in Britain. He said: “There does
exist a limited personal prerogative in the Sovereign"—and, of course, in her representative
in New Zealand, the Governor-General-"to dismiss her Government and to dissolve
Parliament without or against the advice of her Ministers who are presently sustained by a
majority of the House of Commons, but the exercise of such power would be contrary to
convention and unconstitutional.” It goes without saying that such circumstances as Sir Peter
Rawlinson adverts to would be not only very exceptional, but inevitably embedded in a
highly controversial situation, in which the Governor-General must not only be independent
but also free of any suspicion to the contrary. If such suspicion existed, his decision, even if
correct and fully supportable by precedent, would continue to be questioned. The
appointee-designate would not be free of the taint of dependence, as he should be in the
circumstances.
Sir Peter Rawlinson gives an example of the very exceptional circumstances that would
warrant the exercise of this residual power: "the introduction of Bills for the unnecessary or
indefinite prolongation of the life of Parliament". The need for an extension for a year was
asserted in New Zealand, and was questioned, in 1934. There have been other occasions
when the life of Parliament has been extended by consent-twice during war periods—but in
1934 this power was again invoked and exercised against the sustained opposition of the then
Labour Opposition in Parliament. As Sir John Marshall himself says in his article: "The
Governor-General must not take into consideration the political advantage of either party.”
In acceding to the request for a prolongation of the Government's term of office in 1934, the
then Governor-General very definitely advantaged one political party, as was dramatically
shown in the election the following year when the Labour Party swept into power. That is an
example of the--I shall not say improper, but-unwise exercise of a gubernatorial decision
to act on the ministerial advice of the Government then in power; in line with Sir Peter
Rawlinson's statement of the limits of the office, the Governor-General should have resisted
the desire of the then Government to prolong its life.
Equally, as well as favouring the position of the party in power, a Governor-General
could be moved to disfavour one party at the expense of another. The authorities suggest
that a revolutionary situation could justify the dismissal of a Government. But what is, after
all, a revolutionary situation? One can look back, for example, to the time when Opposition
members, including the future Governor-General, condemned and excoriated the New
Zealand Export-Import Corporation Act 1974. It was hard to believe, from the way they
talked and behaved then, that the revolution was not just a day or two away. The then
Opposition, including Sir Keith Holyoake, presented that as an act by the then Labour
Government that was likely to induce a revolutionary situation in the country.
That Act remains on the statute book, and the achievements of the corporation are now
cited with almost paternal pride by the present Government; but emotional exaggerations of
this kind can easily translate benign intentions into harbingers of doom. The National Party,
and indeed any other political party, is prone to exaggeration. It is not immune from panic,
and anyone who has led its ranks for as long, and who has been as intimately involved in its
affairs, as has Sir Keith must be less open to inoculation from such emotional responses than
someone who has been less closely involved. Try as he may-and I am sure he will try, and I
give him the deepest and most profound credit for that—to disengage, he will never be seen
to have achieved total detachment, and that is the point. And let us remember that he is to
be appointed for a shorter time than is normal; this, again, will arouse suspicion as to his
total disengagement from the governing party. There should be no need for clause 2(4). It is
an excrescence on an otherwise admirable Bill, and we deplore the circumstances that make
it necessary.
We have significantly fewer safeguards against absolute power than other Western
democracies. We have a one-chamber, not the typical two-chamber, Parliament. We have an
unwritten, and therefore flexible, constitution, not a written one. We have regulation-
making powers that far exceed those of other governments; for instance, the regulations that
froze wages and prices. Things that Australia could not do even by legislation we can do, and
have done, by regulation. We are not so generously endowed with constitutional backstops
that we can afford to jettison even one of them, however residual it may be and however
occasional may be the times upon which it can be invoked.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Educational Policies Consultation
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education, What consultations
are taking place, and with whom, on the drafting of future educational policies?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Consultations leading to future educa-
tional policies are undertaken by myself and by the director-general at my request. These
consultations often extend over a long period of time, and may take the form of discussions
with statutory bodies and organisations in the education system which could be affected, or
which have views that need to be considered; with persons and organisations whose expert
knowledge may have a bearing on the subject; and through committees, working parties,
conferences, and officials of other departments. Future policies of the National Party are
evolved from the democratic process of remits passed by any of the more than 1000
branches, followed by divisional and dominion conference endorsement, together with
consultations within the party caucus. From the lack of knowledge of this method of policy
formation, as displayed by the honourable member's question, I assume that such democra-
tic procedures do not apply to the Labour Party.
Mr Marshall: In view of the Minister's last comment, I wonder if he is aware that a
former Labour Minister of Education, Hon. Sir Terence McCombs, has been asked by
Christchurch National Party members to help in the formation of National Party education
policies?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I am not aware of that, but if it is a fact, that is true democracy at
work.
Mr Wellington: Can the Minister confirm that, as part of the consideration of future
educational policy, he is about to establish a review of the training college procedures and
mechanisms in relation to the training of students?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Yes, I can confirm that. I have already been in touch with and
have written to all the bodies that might be interested, and I hope that a lot of lay people and
other interested people will attend the conference to be held later this year to review and
consider the whole question of teacher training.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Does the Minister propose to write directly to Sir Terence
McCombs, asking for assistance in writing the 1978 policy?
Mr SPEAKER: Question 2.

House Rentals
4. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Statistics, What has been the percentage
increase in private sector rentals over each of the past 5 years, and how frequently have such
rental increases exceeded the increase in the urban housing index for the corresponding
year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): There are no statistics available that
would give the required information for all private sector rentals over each of the past 5
years. A partial indication can be obtained from the rental section of the consumer price
index. That covers unfurnished dwellings only and it subdivides into Housing Corporation
and other dwellings. Over the 5-year period 1971 to 1976 the urban house property index of
residential properties increased by 131.4 percent, while the rental section index of other than
Housing Corporation rental dwellings increased by 79.1 percent over the same period. In
that time the latter index in general stayed fairly constant, although in a couple of years its
figures exceeded the urban house property index.
Mr Brill: Can the Minister confirm that the figures he has given establish that the
increase in accommodation costs has been considerably lower than the increase in ownership
costs over the past 5 years?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Yes, the percentages do confirm that-79.1 percent as
against 131.4 percent—although I should note that the urban house property index has
dropped markedly in the last 2 years.

at Lake Manapouri. The future of all indigenous forests in Westland, and in particular South

Hokitika this week. The member will undoubtedly be aware that remnant stands of
kahikatea can still be found on the Hauraki Plains and in the Waikato, where it was the
dominant forest type on some of this country before the land was cleared for farming.

existing?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: No, I do not know whether the member is referring to pure
kahikatea or to kahikatea in association with other forest types, but I do know that at Bruce
Bay, down in the Manapouri area, there are 9000 ha of unlogged kahikatea in fairly pure
stands.

Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The drug praziquantel, which is
registered under the trade name Droncit, has been extensively tested for efficiency and
safety prior to its registration under the Animal Remedies Act and approved by the National
Hydatids Council for use in hydatids control programmes.

administering the Act have assured me that they have checked it out and have carried out

had preliminary field trials with over 100 dogs in which the details were recorded of age,
breed, stage of gestation, lactation in bitches, weight, condition, appetite, whether in work
or not, type of food, time since last fed, temperature, pulse, respiration rate, and degree of
dehydration. Then 900 dogs were tested, including between 50 and 60 pet dogs. Then 1400
dogs were tested under working conditions in the Gisborne and East Coast areas. Those
dogs have been on the drug for 18 months, and the only recorded case of any condition which
might be put down to the use of Droncit related to a 14-year-old dog which took a wee heart
turn, but was quite all right next morning.

CARTER OBSERVATORY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology): I move, That the Carter
Observatory Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill's main feature is that it recognises the
Carter Observatory as the national astronomical observatory. We owe the foundation of the
Carter Observatory to the philanthropy of a Wellington settler, Charles Rooking Carter. At
his death in 1896 Carter left the nucleus of a fund to build an observatory for "the public use
and benefit". This project did not bear fruit until it was adopted as a 1940 New Zealand
centennial project through the enthusiasm of the Royal Society of New Zealand and the
Wellington City Council. The observatory was officially opened in 1941, and since then its
activities have expanded to the point where it has, in fact, taken on the role of a national
observatory.
The importance of a national observatory lies first in providing a source of reliable
astronomical information which has, for example, practical use in time and tide calculations,
navigation, and surveying. A national observatory is also a focus for the encouragement of
astronomy, and is an important link in the international network of astronomical obser-
vatories. Many problems of astronomy can be solved only by observations from widely
scattered places throughout the world. Because of its isolated geographical position and high
mountain peaks New Zealand is specially favoured in this regard and scientific work in
astronomy done in New Zealand is of worldwide importance. Referring to the Bill, the main
provisions explicitly declare the Carter Observatory to be the national observatory. The
Carter Observatory Board is authorised to establish observatory outstations at sites more

Bill introduced and read a first time.
PRIVATE SCHOOLS CONDITIONAL INTEGRATION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Private Schools Conditional Integration Act 1975, which the present Bill
amends, is a significant and complex piece of legislation. It provides an opportunity for
private schools, should they so wish, to join into a partnership with the State. The Act
resulted largely from deliberations of the State aid conference held in 1973, established by
the previous Administration, during which all parties, State and private, had the opportunity
to put forward their views on conditional integration. The Act could be called a remarkable
compromise. However, I believe that the Act is based on sound principles, and that any
move to amend it needs most careful consideration.
The amendments that are now proposed have been carefully considered by the
Government and by private and State school interests. The amendments are essentially of a
technical nature, and clarify particularly the role of proprietors of private schools, which I
understand caused them some concern, and which it was thought would lead to legal
argument if they were challenged. Not one of the amendments in the Bill before the House
varies or departs from the principles of the original Act in any way. A full review of the Act
will be undertaken only when integration can be seen to be fully operative, but, because of
the degree of interest shown by private schools in integrating, I believe that the points
covered in the Bill should be resolved at this stage.


## p. 976 (#218) ############################################

976
28 June
Private Schools Conditional Integration Amt Bill
The integration programme provides for Catholic schools to integrate at the end of a 5-
year period. During this time grant integration will be made available to integrating Catholic
schools so that, where appropriate, they may be brought up to State standards, and the grant
may be expended solely on items for which the Government will ultimately be responsible
when the schools are fully integrated. The Catholic bishops drew my attention to the
difficulty they would have in accepting grant integration and undertaking at the same time to
repay the grant should any of their schools not integrate, as the legislation now stands. I
therefore authorised negotiations on possible amendments to the Act, and I know that those
now before the House have the complete support of the Catholic bishops.
Additionally, the Integration Advisory Committee, which I set up last year, supports
the amendments. On that committee there are representatives of both the integrating and
the integrated schools, people nominated by the Interdenominational Committee of Inde-
pendent Schools, the PPTA, the NZEI, the Education Boards Association, and the
Secondary School Boards Association. The advisory committee endorses the proposals in
the Bill. I have also been advised by the Interdenominational Committee of Independent
Schools that the committee "fully supports the proposed amendments". I am thus assured
that the major interests in both State and private education support the present Bill as one
which, while making the legislation clear, does not in any way depart from the principles of
the Act.
Clause 2 of the Bill provides that the Act shall bind the Crown. This is put in merely to
remove any legal doubt. Similarly, an amendment to section 7 of the principal Act provides
that an integration agreement between the Crown and the proprietors of an integrating
school shall be binding. Again this makes the Government's intention clear. The proprietors'
responsibilities about the preservation of the special character of their school were originally
set down in the definition section of the Act alone. It could be construed from this that, while
the responsibilities are spelt out, the Act confers no legal powers upon the proprietors to
fulfil their obligations. This situation is remedied by incorporation in the Bill of an
amendment to section 3 of the Act, which details quite clearly that the proprietors, subject to
the provisions of any integration agreement, continue to have responsibility to supervise the
maintenance and preservation of the education with the special character provided by the
school, and that they have the right to determine from time to time what is necessary to
preserve and safeguard it.
Because the very composition of the Integration Standing Committee requires the
existence of a number of integrated schools before it can be established there is, as I
mentioned earlier, an Integration Advisory Committee that will perform similar functions in
the meantime, but it is, of course, purely advisory. The standing committee, when estab-
lished, is empowered to recommend solutions to problems of any aspect of integration. The
agencies to which these recommendations may be made were spelt out in the original Act,
and included, for example, the Minister of Education and controlling authorities of schools.
An important omission was the enrolment review committees, both primary and secondary,
which can be established in terms of the Act. The amendment now enables the Integration
Standing Committee to make recommendations to the enrolment review committees, but
does not take away the power of decision from those committees. Provision is also made for
the proprietors to consult before any advice or recommendation is implemented.
Some time ago, the Education Boards Association drew my attention to an anomaly in
the existing Act, which provides for small school committees at integrated schools to have
one more member than comparable State schools. The Bill ensures that school committees
at integrated schools will be the same size as those at comparable State schools. I hope it will
also resolve the doubts of proprietors of private schools. I regard the Bill as important
because it will facilitate the implementation of the integration programme. By clarifying the
integration Act, it will assist schools now considering integration to assess more readily
whether they wish to participate in the programme. However, I repeat that this is not the
review of the integration Act which the Government said it would undertake. I think it has
been accepted that such a review is not possible until sufficient experience of integration and
its problems has been obtained. There is no intention of going back on that promise.
