Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I thank the member for Wanganui for
his comments. As he quite rightly said, there appears to be no objection from any quarter to
the amendments in the Bill. When he said that integration brings in a new era he was, to a
certain extent, correct. It has also brought in a new and forward commitment from the
Government, in that we have undertaken a declared policy of commitment to make
provision for integration by way of grants over the next 5 years. That represents a sum rising
from $1 million last year to about $17 million 5 years hence, a total of $44 million. That is
unusual, in that it has already been committed and published in the Gazette to signify the
Government's intention.
The member pointed out that we have created machinery that removes the need for
State aid. The National Party does not go along with that. When the original Bill was
introduced in 1975, we said that we supported the principle of integration, but over and over
again I made the point that it was only one leg of the treble; that, in addition to integration,
we should, at the same time, make certain that no school was forced to integrate as a result
of financial stringencies or its inability to carry on under what was the then level of grant. We
made it clear in our policy that we would introduce immediately 50 percent aid to schools,
based on the pupil-teacher cost. That was only the second leg.
The third very important leg was the status of teachers—the ability of teachers to move
freely through the total education system, consisting of integrated schools, State schools, and
private schools. We have carried out that policy plank by setting up a committee under the
Rt. Hon. Sir John Marshall, and I hope that it will report back to me fairly soon. As a result
of its deliberations, I suspect that we will have legislation to enable the free flow of teachers,
which involves status, registration and deregistration, and discipline. That would make a
complete picture, and integration is an important step in the general movement.
At the time of the original discussions the then Labour Government had the support of
the National Party Opposition, although we were concerned at the speed with which the Bill
was introduced. However, in retrospect, one must acknowledge that the legislation was
satisfactory, and that within its general outline we were able to move forward towards
integration. But one would expect a few amendments of this sort fairly early in the life of
totally new legislation. I understand the points raised by the member for Wanganui about
the concern of education boards that the 1975 Act might appear to give advantages to certain
schools. I am sure that should come into the total review we have spoken about, and it would
be most unwise, in the meantime, to make any great moves. I refer to matters such as
householder elections, and so on.
The member asked if education boards would be consulted on the drawing up of
agreements. Primary school education boards will be involved, but the involvement of
secondary school boards will not be so direct. Section 6(2) of the principal Act provides for
the forms of consultation. I do not expect that the form of integration agreed to by the
Roman Catholic bishops will be substantially altered. It would require them to incorporate
all their schools into the system at the one time, and this would require a steady movement
forward towards an integration programme-bringing the schools up to standard—and then,
at some stage towards the end of the period, integrating all the schools together.
We have a problem in ascertaining the difficulties, and where the snags will arise, so I
have set up a model of an integration system, and I have asked the department to take an
appropriate number and variety of schools-and Wellington has been chosen simply because
of convenience. The department will take all those schools right through the integration
procedures the setting up of an integration agreement, the requirement to bring the school
up to State standard-except for the signing of the agreement. In that way, the department
and the Catholic Education Council will be able to find out what is involved in integrating
the large number of schools in that category. It seems rather an ad hoc way of approaching
the problems, but it is necessary, because we have not had this kind of experience, and we
will learn a lot from it.
The member mentioned one college that might want to integrate, but has a difficulty
because it does not own the land; it merely leases it. I am not certain what the present
position is. We are exploring to see if the integration procedure can go ahead. Maybe it is not
possible, although it would in no way alter the principles of the Act to introduce another

979
Private Schools Conditional Integration Amt Bill
minor amendment to solve a problem like that, or any others that may reveal themselves as
we proceed through the integration process. I do not think it is necessary to hold up the

sorting them out. We are in a totally new field, and it is not always possible to foresee the
various arrangements that private schools have entered into. Many of them would be known

I believe that the Bill will do what it sets out to do, that it will give confidence to schools
that are contemplating integration, and that it will provide a reasonable and businesslike
method of integration for those schools that wish to integrate. There is no intention, and
never has been, that all schools should integrate. A private school still has the right to
continue to operate, but if it decides to integrate, it should be done freely. An agreement will
have so much more authority and strength if both parties-the Crown on the one hand, and
the integrating school on the other enter into it freely and of their own volition without any
sort of compulsion.

and should be recognised in the pension paid to him. If Government members need to be
convinced that the position of Governor-General is of real constitutional importance, I
would point out that he has a royal prerogative.
Mr Allen: Another personal attack.

Minister, can dissolve this House, as history confirms. He can decide who is to form a
Government. His position is no rubber stamp, as has been shown recently in both Australia
and Fiji. While a Prime Minister cannot issue regulations, a Governor-General in Council
can: indeed, he can refuse to issue a regulation. Rumour has it that that power is very much
alive today.

appointed as Governors-General, the provisions should be made more comprehensive so

the public about the position of the Governor-General. It will also be difficult for a former

and for that reason I believe the Bill is very badly thought through, and very badly drafted.
Because of the constitutional issues raised in the provision of a pension, and because of
the importance of ensuring that the Governor-General is the Queen's man and not
Parliament's man, the Bill should go to a select committee. The committee could then
consider what would be an appropriate amount of money to be paid, rather than the
arbitrary amount set out in the Bill. No Government speaker has given any justification for
the amount set out in the Bill. If the Government analysed the Bill it would realise that the
way in which it is written demeans the position of Governor-General, and reveals very
graphically that the Government has confused the constitutional significance of the positions
of Governor-General and Prime Minister. For that reason, I hope the Government will
reconsider its decision, and will send the Bill to a select committee.

Mr LANGE (Mangere): I take issue with the apparent conflict in the Bill over the use of
the concepts of “domicile” and “residence”. I submit that the Bill in effect pays people to
stay in New Zealand after they have fulfilled a term in office as Governor-General. Clause 2
provides that where a person who was domiciled in New Zealand at the time of his
appointment has vacated the office of Governor-General, certain benefits shall flow to him.
I take exception to the use of the word "domicile". There is a conflict between the use of that
word and the use of the alternatives of "domicile” or “residence" in respect of the actual
payment of an annuity after the period of office has expired. The member for Birkenhead
used the expression "domiciled within this country". The test of domicile is the test that
could have arisen in the case of Sir Bernard Fergusson, who, throughout his life, expressed
considerable affection for New Zealand, to the point where it could have been claimed that
he considered New Zealand to be his emotional home. It is possible for a person to be absent
from New Zealand for many years, but to claim that he is domiciled in New Zealand
although he may not have been here for 40 years. If the test is to be that this should be for the
benefit of someone so closely identified with New Zealand as not to qualify for the label
"expatriate New Zealander", then the use of the word "domicile" is unsatisfactory.
Some people would superficially disagree with this definition of the word "domicile",
which has been a principle of law for many years, and the subject of determination, for
instance, in estate and probate cases. It is possible to retain one's domicile while not visiting
the country for 60 years. This is a confusing principle within the legislation, because if one
moves to the point where the annuity is actually being paid it can terminate on two
principles; first, that a person is not resident, and, secondly, that he is not domiciled in New
Zealand. Again, it is theoretically possible for a person to be resident in New Zealand, but to
be domiciled abroad. In the absence of any machinery, who is to determine that issue? One
presumes it is within the exclusive province of the Minister of Finance to make such a
determination, and it would have been easier to give the Minister of Finance carte blanche to
do whatever he liked in interpreting these matters, rather than engage in words such as
these.
The second aspect that I should raise relates to whether the annuity afforded by the Bill
will attract taxation. This would be fundamental to the issue of the quantum of annuity. In
the Civil List Act there is power to exempt a Governor-General, or any member of his
family, or in some circumstances his entourage, from any of the provisions of taxation,
irrespective of its source. I suggest that it would be perfectly competent for a Governor-
General to assert that an annuity afforded by the legislation did not attract taxation. If that is
so the passing of the legislation is more advantageous at this stage than we would believe.
I draw attention to the question of the need for the legislation. In the Civil List Act
there is provision for the Governor-General on retirement to receive a terminal gratuity of 3
months' salary and allowances, which are historically tax-free. If what is being presented is
the new position for the Governor-Generalship, and legislation is proposed enabling New
Zealanders to hold that office, why does this legislation not amend the Civil List Act to take
away the provision of 3 months' income and allowances? This provision is a manifest relic of
the days when, before the new appointee arrived in the country, his predecessor hopped on a
ship and spent his 3 months getting to the United Kingdom. If a change in constitutional and
conventional patterns in the office of Governor-General in New Zealand is to be achieved,
this measure is inadequate.
Why, in 1977, should a Governor-General of New Zealand origin be entitled to the
exemptions afforded by the Civil List Act? I do not deny the right of a Governor-General to
be given consideration after the period of his service in office, but more information is
needed as to how this will be furnished. Are we to live for ever with the concept that
Governors-General will come from abroad, or are we to move towards a new order? If we
are moving towards a new order, this legislation is inadequate. Why should a Minister of
Finance have power to exempt a Governor-General from estate duty? If ever there was a
historical absurdity in 1977, it is the fact that under this legislation a Governor-General, a
robust New Zealander, and his family can, by the action of the Minister of Finance, avoid
paying any estate duty.
The role of Governors-General in New Zealand must be considered properly, not by
legislation that is designed, in my submission, to protect as an ad hoc amendment to bad law.
Notwithstanding the fact that the Bill provides that a retired Governor-General cannot hold
two annuities from two sources, one political and one by virtue of his office under the
Crown, does a Governor-General, if he is a political successor to a previous Governor-
General, forgo his Prime Ministerial annuity during the period of his incumbency? This point

he is relevant; but I draw attention to Speaker's ruling 83/1, which states: "It is usual to allow
a member to reply to statements made by a preceding speaker even though that speaker was
not called to order for going outside the debate; or if the preceding speaker was so called to
order, to reply to the extent that such preceding speaker had been allowed to speak.” We are
at the stage of reply, and I thought it was reasonable to allow the Acting Prime Minister an
opportunity, in his speech in reply to the debate, to reply to the matters raised in the debate,
whether or not they were strictly relevant. Were I not to allow him to do that, I think he
would have little opportunity to make any speech at all, because there was very little raised
in the debate that was relevant to the Bill. I am sure that the honourable member will soon
terminate the matters that he was referring to, and come back to the other matters raised
during the course of the debate.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: It is important to note that the idea of the annuity is
introduced, not because it reflects the need but because it reflects the continuing status of the
former Governor-General. An annuity for a former Governor-General is a reasonable
provision, by the same arguments as those brought forward in support of an annuity for a
former Prime Minister, if the individual continues to reside in New Zealand, and he receives
the annuity only if he does. The provision introduced in 1973 of a 2-year qualifying period for
a former Prime Minister was discussed, and the argument advanced that there should not be
this qualifying period for a former Governor-General. What should the qualifying period
be? It is not inconceivable that there might be an interim Prime Minister for a brief period,
and the question would arise as to whether this would constitute a qualifying period. The
suggestion was made that a New Zealander-I think that this was directed at a specific
individual-would have social and political contacts that would make it difficult for him as
Governor-General to be truly dispassionate. This argument, put forward by the member for
Porirua and supported by the member for New Lynn, could well rule out many New
Zealanders. Most people likely to be appointed would have played some part in the life of
New Zealand, and would obviously have social, and possibly political, contacts. That is not a
disqualification, but a measure of a man's capacity to perform the job. The Bill marks a most
interesting step forward in the development of this country's history.

Income Tax (Compensatory Export Incentive Allowance) Bill 28 June
INCOME TAX (COMPENSATORY EXPORT INCENTIVE ALLOWANCE) BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. As I said when introducing the Bill, it gives effect to the Government's
announcement late in 1976, following the Australian devaluation of the dollar, that help
would be given to exporters to sustain their export sales. I need hardly remind the House of
the importance of that. The measure has helped exporters, and has met the Government's
objectives. As I made clear during the introduction, the allowance is available for those
export sales eligible also for the increased exports taxation incentive. In effect, the general
qualifying conditions that apply for the purposes of that incentive apply also to the
compensatory allowance.
If we examine the March quarter figures on export performance since the compensatory
measure was introduced in December 1976, the measure has been successful. The March
figures show that both manufactured and qualifying exports have sustained growth for that
period considerably above the total average export performance for the previous March
quarter. Compared with the average growth figure of 27.5 percent, it is estimated that the
increases for manufactures have reached 45 percent, and qualifying exports 57 percent-a
very successful effort by those concerned.
Clause 1 relates to the short title and the commencement. The Bill is deemed to have
come into force on 1 April 1976. Clause 2 sets out the general application provision, making
it clear that the Bill will apply to tax on income derived in the income years that began on 1
April 1976 and 1 April 1977. Clause 3 is the usual provision to cover those taxpayers whose
balance dates are other than 31 March. Clause 4 provides for the additional concession from
taxable incomes at the rate of 3 percent of the total qualifying export sales for both the 1977
and 1978 income years. As I mentioned when introducing the Bill, the 3 percent rate for the
1976-77 income year is calculated on the basis of 9 percent but restricted to one-third of the
total export sales, thus covering the remaining 4 months of that year, and giving an effective
rate of 3 percent for the full year.
Provision is made for the commissioner to make any necessary adjustments where the
taxpayer, because of a change in balance date, furnishes a return of income for a period
greater or less than 12 months, and is thereby at either an unfair advantage or disadvantage
for the purposes of the concession. There is also the normal provision allowing an
adjustment to be made where arrangements have been entered into to gain an undue
advantage under the scheme. The additional concession will not be available to firms which
ceased trading on or after the devaluation date, and which had no further export sales on or
after that date. Nor is it available to those companies to which the main increased export
incentive deduction does not apply.
Clause 5 provides that the Bill will automatically expire on 1 October 1978, because, as I
mentioned during the introductory debate, 30 September is the last effective balance date in
the tax year. That means that 30 September 1978 will be the latest balance date for the 1978
income year. This small Bill is confirmation of the Government's recognition of the
importance of exports. I mentioned last week that an expert in this field, Dr Ojala, now of
Massey University but formerly of the FAO, was emphasising that New Zealand's future
depends on its capacity to export. He coined the slogan "trade or fade"-one that members
might wish to remember.
The Government's policy is to build on the success of exporters in developing sales and
markets. That certainly applies in this instance, particularly to manufacturers who export to
Australia. Last year's Australian devaluation made it essential that the Government take
this compensatory measure. It shows the difficulties New Zealand faces in developing
exports in the face of changes in the international economy and monetary system. I believe it
requires direct national understanding of the difficulties our exporters face, a major desire to
help, and Government support of the kind embodied in this measure. We have increasingly
to recognise that New Zealand's small size and its vulnerability as a trading nation mean that
considerable Government action is needed to support our exporters. But, even if we are
small and vulnerable, we know we have great resources and skills, and that more and more
New Zealanders engaged in production and manufacturing are looking at export develop-
ment. The opportunities for trade are there, and the Government-and I hope the
community-will stand ready to assist our exporters in the difficult years ahead. The Bill is
designed to provide help for more than just the Australian market; it applies to all areas, and
provides confirmation by the Government that we must focus more and more on the
importance of exports to the New Zealand economy. The Government believes there is no
other way of breaking out of our economic strait-jacket and moving ahead as a major trading
nation in a competitive world, despite our size. If, over the next few years, New Zealand


## p. 989 (#231) ############################################

28 June
989
Income Tax (Compensatory Export Incentive Allowance) Bill
could develop an export growth rate of 2 percent a year or the equivalent in import
substitution-it would go a long way, in the medium term, to break the economic strait-
jacket we face because of limited primary prices, overseas protectionism, and high import
costs. It is a simple fact that a growth rate of 2 percent a year would enable us to hold our
place among the developed countries.
It is in this economic climate that the Government reiterates its belief that economic
incentives are so vital to New Zealand and its economy. It should be emphasised that our
living standards depend on our exporters. The Government will do all it can to help New
Zealand producers and manufacturers to export in the years ahead.

Marine Pollution Amendment Bill
PERSONAL EXPLANATION
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Attorney-General): With the leave of the House, I wish to
make a personal explanation of a statement made in the House this afternoon. In the course
of answering a supplementary question, I said that since becoming Attorney-General I had
not been approached to exercise my power in a prosecution under section 25 of the Race
Relations Act 1971. While this statement is correct, the House might nonetheless have been
misled, because a few cases have been referred directly to the Solicitor-General. This is
pursuant to a well established practice, under past Administrations as well as under this
Administration, whereby the Solicitor-General acts under statutory authority in place of the
Attorney-General in criminal prosecutions generally where consent is required.
MARINE POLLUTION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. I said during the introductory debate on the Bill that it was for the general
purposes of strengthening the enforcement provisions of an Act that penalises and deters all
types of marine pollution, and controls the dumping of waste at sea. Clause 2 of the Bill adds
a number of new definitions designed to clarify what is meant in the principal Act. "Court" is
defined so as to make it clear that a magistrate's court will have civil jurisdiction up to the
usual limit of $3,000. The use of magistrate's courts is advantageous because many coastal
towns have a magistrate's court but not a Supreme Court. That is the reason for this part of
the Bill. The definition of "harbourmaster" has been extended to include deputies.
Clause 3 provides for the making of regulations dealing with the carrying of equipment
for reducing or preventing pollution on board ships servicing pipelines or offshore installa-
tions, and thereby remedies an omission in section 9 of the principal Act. I should add that
when the principal Act was before Parliament, the need for this provision was not as great as
it is now. Clause 4 deals with certificates of insurance to be carried by oil tankers. A
requirement of the International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage
1969 is that certificates be carried proving that certain ships are insured against the cost of
repairing any oil pollution they might cause. However, as some countries have not signed
that convention, their certificates might be valueless. Clause 4 substitutes a new paragraph
dealing with ships registered in non-convention countries, and provides for recognition of
their certificates either by the Minister, or automatically, as long as the certificate is given by
a country whose certificates are recognised by regulations. This will enable New Zealand to
ensure that those ships are effectively insured.
Clause 5 makes it clear that the Admiralty jurisdiction of the New Zealand Supreme
Court, along with all its features, applies to a civil claim in respect of liability for pollution
damage. With these few words it is being made clear that a plaintiff in a civil claim can arrest
the offending ship. A feature of the Admiralty jurisdiction is that a writ can name not only
the offending ship, but also her sister ships. Therefore, even if the polluting ship has left New
Zealand's territorial waters, the plaintiff is not without effective means of redress. Clause 6
enables regulations to be made prescribing a method of calculating currency conversions for
the purpose of the Act, rather than the conversion rate itself, which will save making a new
Order in Council each time the conversion rate changes.
Clause 7, which is highly significant, requires some explanation. The principal Act
provides that New Zealand agents who act on behalf of shipowners can, in some circumst-
ances, be prosecuted instead of the owners. Sometimes it is impossible to prosecute the
owner, which might be a foreign company with no office in New Zealand. It is regrettable
that such provision has to be made, because agents are not usually those at fault. However, a
ship is a mobile object, and after it has left, the agent might well be the only person within
the New Zealand jurisdiction who has any connection with it. The agent's position is
improved if, when he agrees to act as the ship's agent, he can stipulate an indemnity from the
owner, or a reliable security, to cover him against the costs and fines of any prosecution.
However, a long-established principle of common law-and I am sure the lawyers in the
House will know what I am referring to is that the courts will not enforce agreements in
which one party agrees in advance to pay the fines and costs imposed on the other party if
that other party happens to break the law. I am sure that members on both sides of the
House will see the fundamental wisdom of that principle.


## p. 1001 (#243) ###########################################

28 June
1001
Marine Pollution Amendment Bill
It would clearly be against public policy if the deterrent effect of a criminal prosecution
could be removed in an advance contract. For a small fee, citizens would then be able to
commit offences safe in the knowledge that they were covered for the costs and fines by
somebody else. The common law judges who established the principle could not foresee the
Marine Pollution Act and the need to prosecute agents in certain circumstances.
Consequently, clause 7 creates a statutory exception to what we know as the common law
principle. It strengthens the position of an agent, and enables him to place the burden of
liability where it belongs-on the shoulders of the shipowner at fault.
Finally, clause 8 cures an anomaly existing in the present Act. At present, if a water
right is granted under the Water and Soil Conservation Act, a dumping permit under the
Marine Pollution Act is not required. However, the two Acts are quite different. The Marine
Pollution Act deals specifically with dumping at sea, whereas the Water and Soil Conserva-
tion Act is aimed at controlling the discharge of wastes from the land into the water. Clause 8
makes it clear that dumping at sea is controlled by the Marine Pollution Act whether or not
the water right has been granted. I have taken some moments to explain the principle behind
the Bill, but I believe that a detailed explanation was required because of the legal
technicalities of most of its provisions.

The Marine Pollution Act 1974 replaced the Oil in Navigable Waters Act 1965, and
expressed New Zealand's general compliance with five international conventions prompted
by IMCO. The Act's primary focus is on the internal waters of New Zealand, including the
territorial sea, harbours, estuaries, rivers, and all inland waters navigable by ships. There is
no need for me to say that New Zealand is an island nation. However, we cannot stress that
too often when we talk about the possible effect of marine pollution and the reasons for this
country's concern about it. We must always be conscious of our vulnerability to potential
marine pollution, and we should ensure that the best possible practical marine environmen-
tal legislation is in force in our waters. We have made great progress with this in recent years.

Our coastline extends for more than 3000 miles, and is subject to prevailing off-shore
winds and considerable sea action. Our extensive coastal interests, such as fisheries, must
have as much protection as possible from potential marine pollution. What might be
considered a minimal spillage overseas could, in our isolated situation, be of disastrous
proportions. Most overseas tankers that call at Marsden Point-and this should interest the
member for Whangarei-are chartered and the owners do not have New Zealand agents.
For that reason, the Marine Pollution Act 1974 specifically named the charterer's agent,
manager, or operator of the ship; the agents were specifically named and linked with the
owner, because we wanted to ensure that whenever possible somebody could be held
responsible, and a charge could be made to stick in the event of a spillage. That was done to
ensure that there was no loophole, and that all ships operating in New Zealand waters were
liable-not only those operated by owners who had agents in New Zealand, but all ships
coming to New Zealand.

Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): As the member for Timaru pointed out, we on this

roughest in the world.

for instance, there is no way of getting compensation from a tramp tanker that spills oil after
leaving port. As the Minister said, a ship is a mobile object. I point out to him that a ship's
agent can be a mobile object, one of straw, not worth suing.
Clause 7 contains an amazing provision, such as I have never seen in a Bill, whereby the
common law principle that one cannot indemnify another person against a possible crime is
abrogated and an agent can demand that a ship owner indemnify him, in the hope that he can
insist that the shipping company take out an insurance policy or pay for him to take out an
insurance policy. Presumably the clause is intended to pin down irresponsible shipping
companies, but, on a brief perusal of the Bill, the loophole stands out a mile. It is this: an
agent does not have to be a person, but can be a company. I have looked through the main
Act, and can see nothing to prevent an agent from being a company. An agent could decide
to act for some flag of convenience company that has an appalling history of spilling oil. He
could set up a company with a nominal capital of $25 and dissolve it when the ship left port.
So, a tanker could come to New Zealand and appoint as its agent a company that will be
dissolved the moment it leaves port. If the ship spilt an enormous quantity of oil a couple of
miles out, the harbour board would not be protected by anything in the Bill. Nothing in the
Bill provides any method of financing an action against the agent, because he would no
longer legally exist.
Why is there no provision to ensure that the agent must file some sort of indemnity or
pay into some fund so that if he does turn out to be a legal fiction-something that does not
exist-the harbour board or the Government will not be left lamenting? History has shown
that there are always some rogue shipping companies, which would deliberately waltz their
way through a Bill such as this. The ships of some of those companies visit New Zealand
occasionally and offer cut rates, because they have no intention of being bound by our laws.
Responsible companies would be covered by insurance, but, as I read the Bill, a
deliberately irresponsible company can make certain it will not be covered. A shipping
company might have been warned by a ship's engineer of the possibility of an oil spill, but it
could instruct agents in New Zealand to set up a company to act as an agent so that, if the
worst occurred and there was an oil spill, the company would not be caught by our laws. The

spillages are likely to occur, but they can be flown to any district in a matter of hours. The
member for Timaru mentioned the report of the Commission for the Environment. That
report did not contain specific recommendations for amendments, but its main thrust was
financial. He also raised the question of an indemnity fund, and mentioned how this could be
financed. An oil pollution levy is at present under consideration, and this would be used to
deal with the problem that the member mentioned. As I have already said, further
legislation will be introduced, possibly next year, to implement the recommendations of the
1973 Marine Pollution Convention. I thank those who took part in the debate, and 1
commend the Bill to the House.
Bill read a second time.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Fire Code-Rating of Structurally Engineered Timber
1. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry, Can the Minister
explain why chapter 5 of the 1900 standard relating to fire codes refers to "incombustible
material" thereby excluding timber, when it could refer to "fire rated material", which is
what it means, thereby permitting greater use of locally grown and manufactured structurally
engineered timber which has superior fire rating to steel?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): As far as I am
aware, chapter 5 of the 1900 standard does not in fact specify either the use of "incombust-
ible material" or exclude the use of structurally engineered timber in the construction
industry. This matter is, however, extremely complex, and it is not possible for me here to
give a complete answer covering all aspects of the fire safety regulations which govern
building construction. Information concerning technical details could be supplied by the
Standards Association of New Zealand, the independent body responsible for drawing up
the code.
Mr Malcolm: Can the Minister confirm that, while timber is a combustible material, it
has a superior fire rating to steel, and is therefore better used in many fire risk commercial
building situations?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I think that is generally so, but standard 5/1900 deals
also with areas, and it is possible within a confined area that the timber mentioned may in
fact be marginally more combustible than steel. This is a very technical and complex matter,
and I offer two alternatives to the honourable gentleman: he may like to discuss this with Dr
Pinfold, Director of the Standards Association of New Zealand, who has technical expertise
at his command, or he may like to submit a question for written answer, when I could give
him a much more comprehensive reply than I can in this session of questions for oral answer.
Mr Malcolm: If it could be shown to the Minister that the wording of the fire code was
encouraging the use of imported steel, whereas locally produced and manufactured structur-
ally engineered timber could be used, would he support moves to change the fire code to
encourage the use of locally grown timber?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Undoubtedly, the answer is yes. However, it would
involve consultations with the Standards Association of New Zealand, which body has drawn
up the present specifications.
Mr Hunt: As the Minister's answer was "undoubtedly yes", would he be prepared to
put this standard to the Statutes Revision Committee, invite representatives of the Standards
Association of New Zealand and the member for Eden to a meeting of that committee, and
then, if a change were considered desirable, make it?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Before giving a positive answer to that question I
would have to consider the implications. I have offered to have consultations with the
member for Eden and to arrange for him-or any other member-to consult with the
Standards Association of New Zealand.
Mr Hunt: No open government.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: It is all very well for the member to talk about “open
government". I have offered members the chance of consulting with an independent body,
the Standards Association of New Zealand—and I would think independent by the support
of both parties in this House. After we had heard the result of such consultation, we could
make a decision on the question raised by the member for New Lynn.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Coal Miners-No-replacement Policy
2. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), on behalf of Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone), asked the
Minister of Mines, How does he justify his department operating a no-replacement policy for
underground coal miners in certain mining districts at a time when the department is either


## p. 1010 (#252) ###########################################

1010
29 June
Oral Answers to Questions
rationing or refusing to accept new customers?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines): The only places where the Mines Department
operates a no-replacement policy for underground coal miners are in Greymouth and the
Buller. The Liverpool mine at Greymouth exists only to supply coal to South Island
gasworks, and it will have to close when these plants go off coal and on to other feedstocks
for gas making. In anticipation of this, the Mines Department operates a no-replacement
rule at both the Liverpool and Strongman mines in the hope that, when Liverpool has to
close, it will still be possible to employ all the remaining miners at Strongman. The
department is not taking any new orders for Strongman industrial coal, but ample supplies of
an alternative coal are available from the Island Block mine at Reefton. There is no shortage
of coal from the Buller.
Mr T. J. Young: In view of recent television news that Dunedin is facing a serious coal
shortage this winter, and that domestic orders cannot be fulfilled, what steps is the Minister
taking to ensure that adequate coal supplies are available to that city and to other areas?
How does this comply with his no-replacement policy for miners?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The honourable member would do well to look at a map of the South
Island when he would realise that his last question was rather unrelated to his first. However,
I am pleased to give this information about the Ohai district, which bears directly on the
second question asked. No new orders are being accepted for the industrial grade of peas.
This grade, sized between 3/4 in. and 1 in., is both difficult to make and represents a
relatively small fraction of coal produced. If more peas were produced, then a surplus of
other grades, mainly fines, would result. The restriction does not prevent new customers
from obtaining Ohai coal, but they are required to install boilers capable of burning the
other grades that are available. There has been a shortage of domestic coal this year from
Ohai. It is expected that this shortage is temporary and will be overcome when the No. 3
opencast can resume production. This mine was closed last year because of a major slip
which has been very difficult to stabilise. It is now expected that production from this mine
can be resumed within 3 or 4 weeks. Coal is readily available from both a State and a private
mine at Kaitangata, but this coal is not as acceptable to the market because of its lower heat
value and higher sulphur content. A good deal of the answer to the honourable member's
question lies in the types of coal to which he is referring.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Will the Minister give the House an assurance that the shortage of
coal will not be used to follow the procedure which caused the shortage of briquettes earlier
this year, when the briquetting plant, under Government instruction, stockpiled to increase
prices?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: That question completely misleads as to the real nature of the
situation. What happened was that the cost of making carbonetts had so far exceeded the
then approved price that they could not be taken outside the door without incurring a loss.
Those who were making them were, quite responsibly, requesting a price adjustment. The
honourable member, who himself was a former Minister of Energy Resources, will
appreciate that the State coal mines set and control their own prices, and have done so very
responsibly. The private mines are on a different price control arrangement, and it would be
most improper for the State mines to sell at an advantage over the private mines. The
situation to which the honourable member alluded but did not accurately interpret, has been
resolved.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In view of the Minister's lengthy explanation, which amounted to a
Government admission that costs could be recouped only by delaying production, will this
procedure continue in future?
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: A point of order, Mr Speaker. I draw your attention to the
fact that, while ostensibly asking a question, the honourable member was delivering himself
of a considerable statement before getting around to asking his question. I suggest that that
is out of order, and that, incidentally, the member himself knows it.
Mr SPEAKER: There is a problem with these questions. I try to allow honourable
members asking supplementary questions a reasonable measure of freedom. The position as
I saw it was that the previous question made a postulation that seemed highly suspect. The
Minister gave what would normally be considered a long reply, but he was dealing with the

postulated an admission which may or may not be a correct interpretation of what was said.

voluntarily, and 170 were cancelled following discussions with the department. This invita-

who had been receiving the benefit illegally or were not entitled to it came in and discussed
their position they would not be prosecuted. I also gave an undertaking that during a limited
period those receiving the benefit illegally would not be asked to refund the amount that

were kept.

Hon. H. J. WALKER: I said that the review committee recommended that additional

Mr Hunt: How many?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The recommendation was for 188 additional staff, and I have

4. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Postmaster-General, How is he

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): Allocation for second mortgage finance
from the Post Office Savings Bank will be made by the personal loans board at Post Office
headquarters. The maximum loan will be $10,000, and applications are to be lodged through
solicitors, not individual post offices.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Do I take it that no person can go direct to the Post Office and
make application for a loan and that the only people able to handle the application will be
solicitors; and what will be the likely cost to an applicant because of this procedure?

but the application must go to the personal loans board by way of a solicitor. The honourable
member should weigh up the solicitor's fees against an extremely good loan of the sort an
applicant is unlikely to obtain on better terms anywhere else on today's market.
Mr Bruce Barclay: In view of the statement that any of the $5.2 million not used would
be available for refinancing existing homes, how much does the Minister expect of the $5.2
million to be available for that purpose?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: This will depend entirely on demand, and that cannot be
gauged by existing Post Office membership, because we made provision that people who
have not previously been depositors in the Post Office may present a case. Therefore, we
cannot predict for the future, but preference is being given to those seeking money for a new
home.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Could the Postmaster-General advise how many forms each post
office will have, because will it not be a fact that if more than one form is taken from each
Post Office the second person in the queue will have no show of getting a loan?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: I will hazard a guess and say that four and three-quarter forms
will be available at each post office. I may be wrong, and if the member considers this
question is of any real importance he can put it to me again and I will take up the valuable
time of Post Office employees and ask them to count up each individual batch of forms that
goes to each individual post office.

Drugs-Cost of Packaging
5. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of Mr COOPER (Otago Central), asked the
Minister of Health, What will be the additional cost to the taxpayer following the direction
that drugs previously loose-packed should now be strip packaged?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): As manufacturers have at least till 1 September
1977, and retail pharmacies have at least till 1 December 1977, to implement strip packaging
of the six groups of medicines covered by the regulations, it is not possible to indicate what
the total additional cost will be. The Department of Trade and Industry estimates that the
difference in cost between conventional and strip packaging is unlikely to exceed 1c per
tablet. It should be noted that manufacturers of some of the drugs in the groups referred to
had already, of their own volition, strip packaged their products.
Mr Couch: How will the strip packaged drugs affect the elderly?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Last year 1384 children under the age of 5 were poisoned. This will
affect the old people because they are concerned for the safety of children. It has not been
easy to devise an acceptable method of packaging drugs, because a plastic bottle with a top
that is pushed in and turned could defeat some children, but it was also found that elderly
people had trouble opening the bottle. Some old people are at risk, because in the middle of
the night they perhaps do not count the pills, or they take the wrong one. It will be as


## p. 1013 (#255) ###########################################

29 June
1013
Oral Answers to Questions
difficult for some old people to cope with the strip packaging as it is for children. It is thought
that this problem could be overcome if somebody placed the right number of drugs in a
saucer and left it in a convenient place for the elderly person.
Mr Hunt: Did I hear the Minister correctly in his original reply when he said that only
six categories will be strip packed, whereas the original question suggested that all drugs
should be strip packaged?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, the categories are aspirin, paracetemol, iron preparations,
barbiturates, certain tranquillisers, and certain anti-depressants.

Hare Meat Exports

trade issued by the Department of Statistics, and based on customs returns, the following are
the exports of hare meat by volume and f.o.b. value: 1970-71, 25.5 tonnes, $11,200; 1971-72,
10 tonnes, $6,100; 1972-73, 35.9 tonnes, $17,000; 1973-74, 23.2 tonnes, $21,400; 1974-75, 2.6
tonnes, $3,200; and 1975-76, 10.2 tonnes, $13,900. The figures for 1972-73 to 1975-76 are
provisional. Hares are "game" within the provisions of the Game Regulations 1975, and
there are no special restrictions placed on their export compared with other "game" animals.
Hares may be exported provided they are procured, inspected, and processed in compliance
with regulatory requirements. The export of uneviscerated hares, which was permitted until
the promulgation of the current regulations, is now precluded by the requirement that all
carcasses and their accompanying viscera are inspected to comply with overseas veterinary

requirements for game exports.

School Buildings-Comparative Cost of Steel and Structurally Engineered Timber
9. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Education, Can he advise the cost of

Abortions-Rape Pregnancies
11. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Health, From the records available from
the Department of Health, how many cases are known of applications for abortion being
declined when the pregnancy arose from rape?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): Returns are received from hospitals only of
termination of pregnancy and the reasons for the operation. It is not possible to answer the
question from the records available to the department. The law of New Zealand at present is
that rape of itself is not a ground for abortion, although the effect on a woman's health may
be such as to justify termination on medical grounds.
Mr Brill: Are statistics available from the returns from hospitals about the number of
abortions granted on mental health grounds when pregnancy has arisen from rape?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The 1975 Act required returns to be made to the department, and we
have those returns of abortions classified not in terms of rape but in terms of a psychiatric
need. I do not have the figures with me, but a high proportion is for psychiatric reasons. If
the member would like to ask another question I could give him more details.

Maori Education
3. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Education, Would he advise
what specific measures he is taking to close the gap between Maori and non-Maori
educational attainment, and which of these measures were initiated in the calendar years
1973, 1974, and 1975?


## p. 1017 (#259) ###########################################

29 June
1017
Questions and Replies
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, The recommendations of the
report of the National Advisory Committee on Maori Education in 1970 initiated by the
previous National administration have been the basis for most developments in Maori
education since that time. Measures taken to implement recommendations of the report
before 1973 included: (1) the development of English language programmes for Maori
children; (2) a policy for the development of 5-day hostels; extension of the number of
scholarships at secondary school and tertiary levels; (3) the provision of additional staffing in
primary and secondary schools with significant Maori and Pacific Island enrolment; (4) the
extensive provision of in-service training for teachers of Maori children; (5) additional
financial assistance to Maori private schools; (6) special assistance with buildings advisory
service and staffing to improve pre-school education in Maori communities; (7) the
commencement of Maori studies programmes in teachers colleges; (8) the provision of
guidance counsellors in schools with high Maori and Pacific Island enrolment. Since 1975
measures taken to improve Maori educational achievements have included: (1) a substantial
increase in the rates of Maori secondary school scholarships from $450 set in 1974 to $550 in
1976; (2) a programme of marae-based in-service courses for principals and senior teachers
and inspectors of primary and secondary schools and also for Maori language teachers; (3)
the secondment of 30 itinerant teachers of Maori to develop the Maori language and studies
programmes in primary schools; (4) the appointment of five additional advisers on the
education of Maoris and Polynesians; (5) the provision of a course for the diploma of
teaching english as a second language for selected teachers, lecturers and tutors at Victoria
University of Wellington; (6) the provision of working parties to produce resources for
teaching Maori language, Maori studies, and English language programmes for Maori pupils
at both primary and secondary school levels; (7) the formation of a Maori Archives
Committee to co-ordinate the collection and dissemination of Maori music, history, and
literature; (8) the development of a pilot scheme at Opotiki for the co-ordination of guidance
services for families at risk; (9) the development of using Maori as well as English as the
medium of instruction at Ruatoki School as a pilot project; (10) research into the staffing of
schools in areas of special need; (11) a study of truancy and the development of co-operative
efforts to cut down its incidence; (12) measures to improve the recruitment and selection of
more Maoris into teaching, and the continuation of the 1-year course for adult Maori
language teachers; (13) approval for diploma in teaching courses for teaching English as a
second language and issues in Maori education; (14) in 1976 the National Advisory
Committee began an evaluation and review of progress in Maori education since 1971. It will
meet again in 1977 for a week's residential conference, and will bring forward a report and
recommendations as a guide for further developments in Maori education. In particular, it
will study ways of further closing the gap in educational achievement. Of these develop-
ments, the secondment of itinerant teachers of Maori, the diploma course for teaching
English as a second language, and the appointment of additional advisers were initiated
between 1973 and 75, but implemented by the National Government in 1976. Other policies
approved during 1973-75 have been continued and extended by the Department of Educa-
tion since 1975. The present review of Maori education will provide further guidelines and
initiatives to improve the education of Maori children.

Stuart Halls Residence Council
7. Mr N. P. H. JONES (Invercargill) asked the Minister of Education, (1) To what body is
the Stuart Halls Residence Council (Inc.) (the controlling authority of the student residential
colleges in Dunedin known as Carrington and Arana Halls) responsible; (2) who are the
present members of that council, by whom are they appointed, when, and for how long; and
(3) what assets does the council control, are any public moneys from the education vote,
university grants, or otherwise involved, and in what way are its activities subject to public
scrutiny?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, (1) The Stuart Halls Residence
Council was established in 1945 under the Incorporated Societies Act 1908. It was originally
set up to manage a number of halls of residence for the University of Otago and the Otago
Education Board. Its present functions are to act as the agent of the University of Otago for
the administration of Carrington and Arana halls. It operates under delegated authority
from the University of Otago, and is ultimately responsible to the university for the
management of the two halls. (2) The present members of the council and its executive are:
President, the Very Rev. J. M. Bates; Chairman, Mr J. Keith Sinclair; members, the Very
Rev. L. H. Jenkins, Mr F. S. Hanger, Mr R. McNeill, Mr J. Dennison, Mr W. H. Dawson,
Mrs N. Rutledge, Mrs L. Black, Mr A. H. Borick, the Rev. M. Brown, Mr A. E. Wilson;
four members appointed by the university councils-Professor R. E. Corbett, Associate
Professor M. G. Smith, Mr I. W. Lovett, Mr D. W. Girvan; and two student members.
There are also three members of the council who are not members of the executive
committee-Professor F. W. Mitchell, Dr F. G. Soper, and Mrs M. Black. There are no
fixed terms for council membership, and members are admitted by ballot by the executive
committee. (3) The council has very little in assets: it acts as administering agent for the two
halls which are vested in the university council. The two halls were originally built with
Government subsidies towards the capital cost. More recently there have been non-
recurrent grants by the Government of $24,000 at Arana and $45,200 at Carrington for fire
protection in the buildings. There are no grants by the Government or the university towards
the running costs, the halls being expected to pay their own way. An annual report and
audited accounts are submitted to the university.

Benefits Single and Married People
16. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Social Welfare, What is the basis of
calculation of the difference between the amount paid to a single beneficiary with two
children and that paid to a married beneficiary with two children; and does the difference of
$25.60 represent the cost of maintaining an additional adult in the house?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied, There is no such difference
between the benefit received by a solo parent with two children and that received by a
married couple with two children. The solo parent receives $70 a week, including family
benefit, and the married couple $74.25, including family benefit. That is a difference of
$4.25, not $25.60, a week. The Government's policy is to provide for a solo parent with one
child to receive in total benefit, including family benefit, the same as a married couple
without children (currently $64 a week). A solo parent with two children receives the same
as a married couple with one child (currently $70 a week), and so on.

derailments is as follows: accidental causes, 5; natural causes (slips, etc.), 2; pinched off
(train handling), 4; faulty loading/load shifting, 15; vehicle defects, 32; track defects, 30;
staff errors, 6; and (3) four-wheel wagons were involved in 56 of these derailments, and 25
were directly attributable to faults in four-wheel wagons.

South Wairarapa Emergency Services
21. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Police, What does he intend to do to
improve and standardise the emergency facilities and services in the South Wairarapa as
suggested by the Post Office and agreed to by the fire and ambulance services?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied, It is the policy of my depart-
ment to participate wherever possible in the 111 emergency telephone service. However,
there are good reasons why this cannot be done in the South Wairarapa area at the present
time. One of the Post Office conditions that must be complied with by all services
participating in the scheme is that the service guarantees a 24-hour telephone answering
service in addition to the implied assurance that the service will respond to any call
immediately at any time, either day or night. The Police can give no such assurance. Both
the Greytown and Martinborough Police Stations are sole-charge stations, while the
Featherston station is manned by two constables. In this case it would be neither reasonable
nor responsible for my department to make such assurances when it is virtually impossible to
guarantee that such calls for the Police would be answered by and responded to immediately
by the constables. It is not the policy of my department either to arrange for the termination
of 111 calls in private residences where, in the absence of the constable, the responsibility for
the acceptance and actioning of such calls would fall upon his wife and/or family. One
alternative to this is to arrange for the calls to terminate in the Masterton Police Station
watchhouse where a 24-hour service is provided. However, once again it is not possible to
guarantee the Police could provide a prompt response. In fact, should the staff at Masterton
be unable to contact the constables at Greytown, Martinborough, and Featherston it would
become necessary for Masterton staff to respond to the call. An average journey from
Masterton to Greytown takes approximately 20 minutes, and the time is considerably longer
to the other two more southern areas. To assist in overcoming the problems, the telephone
directories for each locality list alternative numbers for the police station concerned, and the
Masterton Police Station number, which should be used in the event of the caller being
unable to contact the local staff. The technical and practical implications of the introduction
of the 111 service to the southern Wairarapa have been carefully evaluated by the
Commissioner of Police, and his decision not to participate in the scheme at this time can
only be regarded as correct. The difficulty is not restricted solely to the Wairarapa, but is
common to many rural areas throughout the country. The honourable member may be
assured the matter will be kept under review in line with departmental policy. Although the
Police are not prepared to take part in the scheme, this should not prohibit its introduction
into the area to embrace other emergency services organisations if they feel able to meet the
prerequisites.
(10/6/77)
Forest Replanting
22. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) asked the Minister of Forests, How many hectares of
formerly productive land does the Government intend to replant this financial year?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied, The area of formerly productive forest
land prepared for replanting is very dependent on the area logged during the preceding 12
months. Fluctuations in levels of industrial activity and natural disasters such as the
Canterbury windblow and the Hanmer fire may result in considerable variation from one
year to the next. The draft estimates for the New Zealand Forest Service, however, include
provision for the replanting of 9300 ha in the 1977-78 financial year. This compares with 6635

Motor Vehicle Imports-Tariff Adjustments
36. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Customs, Is he aware of
widespread rumours to the effect that the Government intends introducing legislation this
year for passage next year adjusting tariff rates on motor vehicles imported from non-
Commonwealth sources, and, if so, are the rumours well based, and, if not, what is the
Government's attitude towards tariff adjustments?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied, No, I am not aware of such
rumours. When Britain joined the EEC it was decided to phase out the British preferences.
The phasing commenced in 1974, but the tariffs on motor vehicles remained unchanged. No
decisions have been taken by the Government on the future tariff policies relating to motor
vehicles, and any rumours to the contrary are groundless. The Government's attitude
towards tariff adjustments on motor vehicles is that, before any changes are made, there will
need to be clear evidence that these are in the interests of our trading relations with other
countries, as well as the motor vehicle and component industry and the public generally.

Palmerston North Technical Institute-Siting
40. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education, Could he explain the
reasoning behind the siting of the Palmerston North Technical Institute at Aokautere in
preference to the Railway land at Fairs Road, in spite of the preference shown for the latter
site by the Palmerston North Ratepayers Association, the majority of Palmerston North
city councillors, a majority of the members of the Technical Institute Council, and a majority
of members of the Association of Technical Tutors?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, I have given full and careful
consideration to all representations concerning the siting of a new technical institute for
Palmerston North. While I am aware that there are very keen advocates for other sites, I am
satisfied, particularly on educational grounds, that the site at Fitzherbert is the best
available. Being located adjacent to Massey University, Palmerston North Teachers
College, and the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, the Fitzherbert site will
enable a unique tertiary educational complex to be developed. There would be the
immediate benefits of shared facilities and the likely interchange of specialist tutors. Such
advantages are more likely to be achieved if the institutions concerned are grouped together.
I should also like to correct the impression that the site at Fairs Road is Railway land. The
property in question is privately owned, and, as it is the only sizable parcel of land
remaining in the industrial area, its acquisition would be extremely expensive. The land at
Fitzherbert is already owned by the Crown, and, while this is not an overriding considera-
tion, it is one which cannot be ignored.

Pilopt Eyedrop Fluid
43. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Health, Is it correct that the eyedrop
fluid Pilopt, which was formerly on the free list, now costs 16c per bottle, and is he aware
that some elderly pensioners need to use this, and, if so, why was the charge made and would
he be prepared to review it?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied, Since 1975 two brands of these eye drops
have been available on the New Zealand market in various strengths. Where more than one
brand of a medicine is available and the prices vary, payment from public funds is based on
the lowest price. If a dearer brand is prescribed, a charge may be made to the patient for the
difference in cost. Because prices fluctuate, the Pilopt brand has been completely free of
charge at times, whilst the alternative brand has been completely free at other times. A
charge to the patient could be avoided if the drops were prescribed by official name rather
than by brand name. Alternatively, the medical practitioner could apply to the Department
of Health for a free supply as a supplementary pharmaceutical benefit if the medical
practitioner is of the opinion that only the more expensive brand is suitable for a particular
patient. I assure the honourable member that any anomalies brought to my notice would be
considered and, if warranted, reviewed.

Banabans-Government Aid
46. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs, What are
the amount and the terms of payment of New Zealand's contribution to the fund of $11.4
million to be set up for the benefit of the Banabans, whose former home of Ocean Island has
been so devastated by phosphate mining as to have become uninhabitable and who are now
residing on an island in the Fiji group?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied, I take it that the
honourable member is referring to my announcement on 28 May that the Government will
contribute to a fund of A$10 million for the Banaban people on Rabi Island. The money for
this purpose will come from the funds which the British Phosphate Commissioners are at
present holding on behalf of the Governments of New Zealand, Australia, and Britain. These
are the three countries which have been involved in the phosphate operations on Ocean
Island. Each partner Government's share of the funds being held by the British Phosphate
Commissioners has yet to be finally determined, and this will probably not be done until
after the mining on Ocean Island has ceased. In the meantime what has been agreed is that a
portion of the funds already in hand should be set aside for the Banabans, on an ex gratia
basis. New Zealand's contribution to the Banaban fund cannot be given precisely, therefore,
but it is unlikely to exceed NZ$2.5 million. The fund's purpose is clear, however; it is to help
to safeguard the Banabans' economic well-being when the mining ends. The three partner
Governments envisage that the fund should be administered in such a way as to constitute a
regular source of income to supplement what the Banabans can provide from their resources
on Rabi. The details of how this can best be done have still to be worked out in consultation
with the leaders of the Banaban people.

Teacher Trainees-Bilateral Aid Scheme
49. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Can he confirm
that there will soon be increases in the stipend paid to teacher trainees on the bilateral aid
scheme so that they will be able to carry out their course of training without suffering
financial hardship?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied, Allowances of all students
and trainees under the bilateral aid programme are reviewed from time to time on the basis
of information contained in the consumer price index. The last two general reviews were in
March 1972 and March 1975. In view of movements in the cost of living over the past 2 years,
my ministry began a further general review of allowances in March this year. It is not
possible to say when the Government's decision will be known. The 43 overseas teacher
trainees financed under aid programmes make up only 6 percent of the total number of aid-
financed foreign students in New Zealand at present, and they receive the same allowances
as all other bilateral aid programme students. It is not intended to treat teacher trainees
separately from those following other courses in New Zealand. In their first 3 years of study
aid-financed students who live in Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch at present receive
$2,055 per year, while those living in other centres receive $1,955. However, because
accommodation in 15 of the 17 hostels used by Government-sponsored students now costs
more than the accommodation allowance built into the above rates, my ministry has, since
February 1977, paid those hostel fees direct, with a consequent change in the monetary
allowance for those students to $1,144 per year. This is an interim measure aimed at
preventing financial hardship. In addition to their annual allowance, aid-financed students
receive, on arrival in New Zealand, an establishment grant of $250 to cover initial
expenditure.

Lubricating Oil-Recycling
50. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources, Has the
Government undertaken any initiative that would lead to the recycling of the 17 000 000
gallons of lubricating oil valued at $13 million per annum over and above the 5 percent
recycled at present?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied, New Zealand imports
75 000 000 litres, or 17 000 000 gallons, of lubricating oil. Of this, about half is lost in use
through friction, spills, and leaks. Approximately 6 000 000 litres of used oil are collected for
rerefining, and it is estimated that a similar amount is collected for burning as fuel. A variety
of lube oils is produced, and some are unsuitable either for rerefining or burning as fuel.
Following consultations with rerefiners and others, the Department of Trade and Industry
has recently completed a survey of the subject. It is hoped that the department's report,
which will be released shortly, will provide a basis for steps to be taken to increase the extent
to which used oils can be reused.

Ruling Rates Surveys
61. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of State Services, How are the surveys for 6-
monthly ruling rates arrived at, and, when actual wages payments of employers are
inspected, is a 40-hour week the basis of ruling rates?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied, There are two main methods of
surveying rates paid in the private sector and used for State pay fixing: the half-yearly
surveys and the ruling rates surveys. The half-yearly survey has been carried out by the
Department of Labour for over 25 years as a means of measuring and monitoring employ-
ment and wage movement trends in the private sector. It is only since 1969 that the survey
results have been used for State pay-fixing. Information is supplied by employers answering
a questionnaire card, which is checked by the Department of Labour and referred back when
necessary. From this data the department calculates, inter alia, the average ordinary-time
weekly and hourly rates in industries (not occupations) outside the State Services. The
provisions in the State Services Remuneration and Conditions of Employment Act 1969 that
the half-yearly surveys-with the public sector excluded-be used as the automatic index of
movement for the adjustment of State rates was suspended by the Wage Adjustment
Regulations, and it is some years since 6-monthly adjustments have been made on this basis.
However, these survey results may still be used, together with any other evidence, in any
negotiations and in proceedings before the State Services Tribunal. The ruling rates survey is
used in fixing the pay rates of tradesmen and manual workers in the State Services. The
Department of Labour surveys ruling rates in two industries (building and engineering) for
seven trades (carpenters, painters, construction electricians, plumbers, fitters, or fitter-
turners, boilermakers, and motor mechanics) and for builders' and engineering labourers, in
eight urban districts (Auckland, Hamilton, Wanganui, Wellington, Lower Hutt,
Christchurch, Dunedin, and Invercargill). A representative sample of firms is chosen by
ballot from each of these districts. Survey results are tabulated and given to State employers
and unions, and form the basis for adjustments of rates for State tradesmen and related
groups. For the purposes of both the half-yearly survey and the ruling rates survey, weekly
pay surveyed is the average gross wage for 40 hours ordinary time excluding special
payments as specified in awards and agreements.
(17/6/77)


## p. 1033 (#275) ###########################################

1033
Questions and Replies
Ruling Rates Surveys
62. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of State Services, What methods are used,
and by whom, to establish the "broadly in line" principle which applies for establishing
ruling rates?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied, The half-yearly and ruling rates
surveys are both attuned to the principle that rewards of employment in the State services
shall be kept broadly in line with those outside the State services. The half-yearly survey is
very widely based, and covers approximately three-quarters of the labour force. The public
sector is then excluded for the purpose of State pay fixing. The trades and localities used in
the ruling rates survey are selected for their relevance to most of the tradesmen employed in
the State services. The Department of Labour consults the Government Statistician about
the soundness of the survey's basis and sampling.
(17/6/77)
Average Wage, State Employees
63. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of State Services, What is the average wage
for all State employees and how does this compare with the private sector, and is he able
further to divide this into male and female ruling rates?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied, The ordinary-time average
weekly wage rates for October 1976 (taken from half-yearly survey figures) were: all
Government sector employees, $120.18; all private sector employees, $104.12; Government
sector male employees, $126.55; private sector male employees, $114.98; Government
sector female employees, $103.32; and private sector female employees, $83.39. The
Government-sector rates reflect the generally higher proportions of professional and techni-
cal staff in State employment such as teachers, engineers, doctors, and lawyers. In the
private sector a large proportion of such professional people and other above-average
income earners would be one-man businesses, and, therefore, not counted in the Depart-
ment of Labour survey on which the information above is based.
(17/6/77)
State Service Salaries Over $8,000
64. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of State Services, How many State employees
are on salaries of over $8,000 a year?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied, The most recent published
figures available are: Public Service (31 March 1976) 11,595; Education service (15 May
1977) 21,877; Post Office (31 March 1977) 3,520; Railways (31 March 1977) 1,638; Defence
Forces (25 June 1976) 4,423; and Health (hospital services) information not available. Here
again the higher rates for professional employees are reflected in the salary levels in the
various services.
(17/6/77)
Ruling Rates Surveys-Comparable State Occupations
65. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of State Services, How many occupations are
surveyed in the private sector which are seen to be comparable to State employees'
occupations?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied, The occupations covered by the
ruling rates survey of tradesmen have been listed in the answer to question 1. As noted in the
answer to question 2, the half-yearly survey covers approximately three-quarters of the
labour force by industry. In addition, under the 1969 Act, where external comparability
exists specific surveys are carried out of comparable positions outside the State services. The
following occupations have recently been surveyed by the State Services Commission or the
Pay Research Unit: accountants, professional enginneers, forest management, sawmilling,
and printing trades and non-trades.
(17/6/77)

Wage-fixing Tribunals, Public Sector
66. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of State Services, How many wage-fixing
tribunals are there in the public sector?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of States Services) replied, There are five wage-fixing
tribunals in the public sector: the State Services Tribunal, the Government Service Tribunal,
the Government Railways Industrial Tribunal, the Hospital Service Tribunal, and the Police
Service Tribunal. By virtue of the Wage Adjustment Regulations, the State Services
Tribunal is at present carrying out the duties of the single-service tribunals.
(17/6/77)
Labour Turnover, Public and Private Sectors
67. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of State Services, What is the labour
turnover in the public sector, and how does this figure compare with the figure for the
private sector?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied, Labour turnover (male and
female combined) for the 6 months ended October 1976 was 10 percent in the Government
sector and 27 percent in the private sector. These figures express terminations as a
percentage of the average pay roll strength, and include workers in all industries except
construction and seasonal workers. This information is supplied by the Department of
Labour.
