Pay Research Unit
70. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of State Services, What difficulties have been
experienced in establishing a pay research unit, and why has there been such delay?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied, The main reason for the delay
until the unit was finally established in 1973 was the belief by the State Services Co-
ordinating Committee that it was essential to the success of the unit that it be established in
co-operation with the employee organisations. From 1962 to 1972 its establishment was
opposed by the Combined State Service Organisations. However, rules for the operation of
the unit were agreed to in 1972, and following its establishment a number of surveys were
completed or partly completed. Unfortunately, since 1973 the unit has not operated


## p. 1035 (#277) ###########################################

29 June
1035
Questions and Replies
effectively, and at the present time no surveys are being undertaken. These difficulties stem
from three main reasons: (1) The Combined State Service Organisations withdrew from the
Pay Research Council during 1973 and until early 1974. The reason given for their action was
the wage freeze regulations applying at the time; (2) the SSCC and CSSO were not able to
agree to a long-term survey programme which is intended to prevent disruptions to the work
of the unit; and (3) the unit had some trouble obtaining the co-operation of employers in the
private sector. The present rules of the unit provide that information cannot be released until
negotiations are completed. This has caused difficulties if one side claims negotiations are
not completed, or if, for one reason or another, there have been delays in negotiations. In
the case of some surveys, delays of over 3 years resulted. The failure to release survey
information expeditiously then caused some private sector employers to refuse to contribute
further information to the unit. This latter difficulty was resolved with the New Zealand
Employers Federation in May 1976, when, following agreement by the Pay Research
Council to release survey information within 6 months, the federation undertook to
recommend to employers that they co-operate fully with the unit. However, the CSSO
advised the Minister of State Services on 19 May 1976 that it would be pointless to undertake
any pay research exercise during a period of wage freeze, and a long-term programme has
yet to be agreed to.
(17/6/77)

State Employees-Discounting of Wage Levels
75. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of State Services, What discounting of wage
levels is made to State employees for permanency of employment, atttractive superannua-
tion, and other fringe benefits, and whose responsibility is it to establish the discounting?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied, By agreement between the State
Services Co-ordinating Committee and the Combined State Service Organisations, a deduc-
tion for alleged "perks" is made for ruling rates survey groups. Since 1 December 1969 the
rate of deduction has been 0.4c an hour. In cases where "perks" can be identified in both the
public and private sectors during specific reviews these are evaluated and balanced against
each other in assessing rates of remuneration for State employees. This information is
available during negotiations and may be used before the State Services Tribunal. In
addition, the Higher Salaries Commission has available to it confidential information from
the private sector when making recommendations for the adjustments of salary rates for
senior civil servants and other public sector positions. This information includes details of
additions to salary in the categories referred to by the honourable member which are not
confidential in the case of the Government sector employees.
(17/6/77)
Hector and Remarkable Mountains-Management Study
76. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Lands, When will the
report "Management Study for the Hector and Remarkable Mountains" be released for
public perusal, and why was the Mt. Cook and Southern Lakes Tourist Company provided
with a copy in advance in view of the fact that it is vitally interested for business reasons in
proposals that were considered by the study group?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied, The management study is due for release
on 18 June 1977. To give interested parties a more complete picture, this release of the
report will be accompanied by a summary of the company's proposals and an assessment by
the Ministry of Works and Development of the company's proposed Rastus Burn access
road. The public will have 28 days from the date of release to comment on the report. An
advance copy of the study was given to the company so that the most up-to-date information
available can be given to the public when the report is released.

Prime Minister's Department-Staff
92. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Prime Minister, In view of his reply of 8
June that 78 people were employed in his department on 1 January 1977 in five sections, will
he advise: (1) how many are employed in (a) the Cabinet office; (b) the external
Intelligence Bureau; (c) the Prime Minister's press office; (d) the Prime Minister's advisory
group; (e) the office of the Prime Minister; (2) what is the range of salaries in each of the five
sections of his department; (3) who are the three senior staff in each division, and what are
the terms of their appointment?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister) replied, (1) I regret I cannot advise the
member for Mt. Albert the number of people employed by each division of the department.
Since its creation by the Labour Government in 1975, and as was indicated in the debate on
the 1976 estimates of the department, the numbers employed by the External Intelligence
Bureau are not made public, and therefore I cannot supply figures for the other divisions. (2)
Just as the Leader of the Opposition considered that it would be "unfair" to reveal the
specific salary of a research officer when he, as Prime Minister, debated his department's
estimates in 1975, and in light of the answer to the following question, I cannot disclose the
required information. I can assure the honourable member, however, that all salary ranges
are consistent with Public Service salary scales. (3) The three senior staff and their terms of
appointment for each division of the Prime Minister's Department are as follows: Cabinet
Office: Messrs Millen, McLeod, and Hill, all career public servants. In addition, although
officially under the Cabinet Office, Mr. D. Williams, a career public servant, is the
Governor-General's secretary. Press Office: Messrs Symmans, Hancock, and Acland, all
under contracts reviewed annually. Prime Minister's Office: Messrs Buckton, Nelson, and
Kerr, all career public servants. Advisory Group: The advisory group has no seniority as
such, but the head of the Prime Minister's Department, Mr B. V. Galvin, heads the group.
Mr Galvin is a career public servant seconded from Treasury. External Intelligence Bureau:
Messrs Jaynes, Clarke, and Lynch, all career public servants.
(21/6/77)
Sheep Numbers
93. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Agriculture, Is
the increase in sheep numbers in any way due to the drop in cattle numbers?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied, After falling to 55 320 000 head
as at 30 June 1975, sheep numbers are now in their second year of recovery. Cattle numbers
on the other hand, after having increased to 9 770 000 as at 31 January 1976, showed a


## p. 1043 (#285) ###########################################

29 June
1043
Questions and Replies
decline of 3.8 percent to 31 January this year. These figures confirm that a recovery in sheep
numbers was already under way prior to the downturn in cattle numbers being recorded. It
could be said, therefore, that the overall carrying capacity released by lower cattle numbers
is being taken up by increasing sheep numbers. The change has been influenced by better
profitability for sheep enterprises relative to beef.
(21/6/77)
Prime Minister's Department-Staff Travelling
94. Hon W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Prime Minister, (1) How many of the staff
of his department have been out of Wellington on official duties; (2) where and for what
purpose; (3) what costs of travel, etc., were involved?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister) replied, As the question does not refer
to any time period it is not possible to provide a full answer. However, I have assumed the
question relates to the period since the National Government took office in 1975. (1) As at
15 June 1977, 25 of the staff had travelled outside of Wellington on official business; (2) the
staff of the department have travelled throughout New Zealand and overseas, either
accompanying the Prime Minister or on his behalf; and (3) the cost of all travel by the staff
for the year ended 31 March 1977 was $37,949.

Fenwick Report-School Librarians
100. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education, When does he intend
implementing the recommendation in the Fenwick report concerning the appointment of
librarians to primary and intermediate schools?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, The Fenwick report was commis-
sioned by the New Zealand Library Association. However, in line with the Government's
policy of promoting the development of school libraries, I approved in February of this year
the setting up of a working party on school libraries. The working party has representatives
from the School Library Service, the New Zealand Library Association, the Post-Primary
Teachers Association, the New Zealand Educational Institute, the New Zealand Teachers
College Association, and the Department of Education. Included in the terms of reference
of the working party is a study of the recommendations of the Fenwick report, and this will
include those dealing with the appointment of librarians to primary and intermediate
schools. The first meeting of the working party is scheduled for early July.

Fenwick Report-School Librarians
102. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education, What provisions are
being made for the professional library education of school librarians, as recommended by
the Fenwick report?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, The Fenwick report was commis-
sioned by the New Zealand Library Association. However, in line with the Government's
policy of promoting the development of school libraries, I approved in February of this year
the setting up of a working party on school libraries. The working party has representatives
from the School Library Service, the New Zealand Library Association, the Post-Primary
Teachers Association, the New Zealand Educational Institute, the New Zealand Teachers
College Association, and the Department of Education. Included in the terms of reference
of the working party is a study of the recommendations of the Fenwick report, and those
dealing with the training of school librarians will be given full consideration. In the meantime
in-service training courses, both national and local, which have been conducted for a number
of years to train school librarians, will continue. The first meeting of the working party is
scheduled for early July.

Ministerial Parties-Overseas Travel
103. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Internal Affairs, (a)
What has been the cost since this Government took office of ministerial parties travelling
overseas; (b) how much of that time has been spent by Ministers "on holiday", in a manner
which has been announced in respect of the Prime Minister's present trip for three occasions,
first in Rarotonga, then in Los Angeles, and later in Yugoslavia?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) replied, For the 1975-76 financial year
the expenditure on ministerial overseas travel was $131,484, of which $17,969 was incurred
by the present Government. For the 1976-77 financial year the expenditure was $287,419, of
which $278,210 was incurred by this Government, and to 31 May this year it was $34,743. All
overseas travel by ministerial parties which is paid for from public funds is for official
purposes, but as I do not have detailed itineraries for the overseas travel of other Ministers I
cannot provide the information sought in part (b) of the question. Such detailed information
should be sought from the Minister concerned in each case.

(22/6/77)
Energy Conservation in Industry
106. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources, In view of
his statement in his reply to my question on 10 June on New Zealand's energy efficiency that
New Zealand's high use of energy is related to the different technologies utilised by
industries, what is he doing to see that the technology used in the steel, cement, and paper
and pulp industries is brought to the same energy efficiency as that in the other OECD
countries?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied, As I mentioned in my answer to
the member's previous question on this topic, energy is but one, albeit an important one, of
the factors which must be taken into account in deciding on the appropriate technology to
use in a particular situation. Other factors are the nature of the raw materials, the type of
product required, and the cost of other inputs. At the same time, however, I also mentioned
in the same reply some of the positive measures the Government has introduced to
encourage the adoption of energy conserving practices in industry, including energy efficient
technologies.
(22/6/77)
Energy Conservation
107. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources, How much
was spent on the promotion of energy conservation during the last financial year, and, in
view of the increasing importance of conservation, what new measures are planned, apart
from further advertising and price increases?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied, In the financial year ended 31
March 1977 $168,521.60 was spent on promoting energy conservation through the publicity
campaign. Over the past 18 months the Government has taken a number of positive steps to
encourage energy conservation, in addition to advertising and price increases, although
these have themselves resulted in very worth-while savings. The Government is also
examining a range of possible new measures, and will make its decisions known at an
appropriate time.
(22/6/77)
Vision-hearing Defects-Schoool Children
108. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt Albert) asked the Minister of Health, In the light of an
Auckland primary school survey recently reported to him which revealed that 33 out of 120
children examined had vision or hearing defects, will he (1) advise whether he has any
information to suggest that this average is higher than usual; (2) appoint additional people to
conduct a thorough or more frequent survey of children; (3) advise whether he has any
information to suggest that this high percentage of defects is likely to be repeated in general
health standards; and (4) advise whether he will give early and favourable consideration to
reintroducing medical examination of primary school children?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied, (1) I am not aware of the criteria used in the
survey which covered children of all age groups in the Auckland primary school involved. I
know, however, that, although results of routine vision hearing tests carried out by the


## p. 1047 (#289) ###########################################

29 June
1047
Questions and Replies
Department of Health on primers in the Auckland region vary considerably, the average is
not significantly different from that found in the school referred to allowing for the fact that
different age groups were screened in that school. (2) Because of the known high incidence
of hearing and vision defects, routine screening with referral to a medical officer or to the
child's medical practitioner, where necessary, is carried out on infants, pre-school children,
and all children in primers and Form I and also on children referred from other classes.
Mobile ear treatment clinics for children suffering from ear conditions are being operated in
Auckland and Whangarei health districts, and a third one will be established this year in the
Auckland region. (3) The reason for the adoption in 1963 of a consultative health service for
other physical defects was the small number of such defects found at routine medical
examinations. Such examinations were thus no longer justified, and it is considered to be
preferable to concentrate on children with a particular need. (4) A detailed study of 5-year-
old children is at present being carried out. The findings will be helpful in deciding whether
or not routine medical examinations need to be reintroduced in some areas.

118. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Police, Has he seen a report on the
front page of the New Zeala rd Herald of 31 May 1977 in which a former policeman, a Mr L.
J. Killkelly, said he "told the police of an alleged plot to oust the Cook Islands Government
led by Sir Albert Henry", that "he considered the discussions he held in Christchurch had

overthrowing the elected Cook Islands Government of Sir Albert Henry. Some proceedings

undesirable for me to comment further.

Nurses Clerical Staff
119. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour, When the practice nurse
subsidy was introduced, was it the intention of the Government to allow replacement of
clerical staff with registered nurses, and does the Government condone this practice?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied, The practice nurse schemes were specifi-
cally designed to provide medical practitioners with professional nursing assistance, and the
thrust of the revised schemes to come into effect on 1 July 1977 is to encourage this further
by the greater use of practice nurses in domiciliary nursing work. It follows that nurses
should not be used to replace clerical staff; their functions are very different, and the
Government certainly does not condone this practice if it is happening. An important
condition of the subsidies is that the services of the practice nurse are to be confined to
professional duties. It is recognised that such duties must include some record keeping and
dealing with some telephone inquiries, but if these functions predominate a full subsidy
would not be payable. I have had no cases drawn to my attention where abuse of the subsidy
has necessitated its withdrawal.

Energy Conservation
123. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources, Is he taking
any corrective action to remedy the situation revealed in the article "Energy, the need for
action", published in the OECD Observer for September-October 1976, which shows in the
countries listed that New Zealand is one of the least efficient users of energy in automobile
transport, that in the production of petroleum products and aluminium New Zealand is the
second least efficient producer, and that in the production of crude steel, cement, and pulp
and paper New Zealand is the heaviest user of energy per ton of product?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied, The OECD Observer article is
based on an International Energy Agency review of the energy conservation programmes in
member countries. This review makes the general comment that New Zealand had "slightly
above average conservation results". A major reason for the varying energy consumption
patterns amongst member countries is the different technologies utilised by their industries.
This reflects the different resource endowments and transportation systems of member
countries. Long-established attitudes to private transportation are also important. Since the
IEA review was written last year, the Government has introduced various measures to
encourage energy conservation. Of these, the major one is the new energy pricing policy.
There is also the introduction of the energy advisory services of the Ministry of Works and
Development, the tax incentive scheme for capital expenditure on energy conservation by
businesses, and the encouragement of energy audits.

Education-Intellectually Handicapped Children
124. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education, What steps are being
taken to ensure that free education is as available to intellectually handicapped children as it
is for other children?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, Except for those children resident
in psychopaedic hospitals, free education is available to intellectually handicapped children
on the same basis as it is to other children. Each intellectually handicapped child of school
age may attend either a special school or school group in his own area, or, if this is not
possible, may be enrolled in the home training section of the department's Correspondence
School. A free teaching service is also provided for those severely handicapped children
attending pre-school and special care centres administered by voluntary agencies which have
requested this service. I recently initiated, with my colleagues the Ministers of Health and
Social Welfare, a review of all existing policies relating to the education of intellectually
handicapped persons, including those in psychopaedic hospitals.

Teachers-Removal Expenses
127. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Education, When was the
"breadwinner" clause added to the education regulations governing removal expenses, who
initiated these additions, and why was this done?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, Amendment No. 14 to the
Education (Salaries and Staffing) Regulations 1957 was promulgated on 6 December 1976.
The provision was initiated by the Department of Education. Under the old regulations
there was no authority to pay removal expenses to teachers transferred in the public interest
or to meet the convenience of the education service when no promotion was involved.
Accordingly, an amendment was made which gave the Director-General of Education the
same discretionary rights in respect of teachers as the State Services Commission has in
regard to the Public Service. The opportunity was taken to include the same provision
regarding a breadwinner as already existed in the Public Service Regulations. I should like to
point out this did not represent a change of policy, however, as State Services policy on
removal expenses has always been administered by my department under the old Salaries
and Staffing Regulations.

Unemployment Statistics
130. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour, Could he confirm that the
combined total of registered unemployed and persons on relief work has risen from 9096 as
at the date of the general election 1975 to 10 385 on 20 May last, and could he also confirm
that this represents a rise of 14 percent in the statistics?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of labour) replied, I can confirm both those points.
However, when considering statistics such as these it is important to ensure that a proper
basis for comparison exists. The member for Grey Lynn has compared a November period
when seasonal work is increasing towards a peak with a May period when seasonal work is
ending. Any comparison on this basis is not valid. Since early 1975 there has been some
pressure on employment, and this Government has put into effect various job-creation
measures to provide additional employment opportunities and keep people in work. As a
result a comparison of unemployment statistics at mid-May 1976 and at mid-May 1977 in fact
shows a reduction in the number registered as unemployed. Twelve-month comparisons
between December 1975 and December 1976, January 1976 and 1977, February 1976 and
1977, March 1976 and 1977, and April 1976 and 1977 all show similar reductions.

Computer Experience
134. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of State Services, Is there a scheme
whereby experience gained in one computer installation may be made available to another,
and, if not, does he intend to implement such a scheme?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied, The State Services Commission
has a statutory responsibility for the co-ordination of and the training for electronic data
processing throughout the Public Service. In addition, through its computer services
division, it provides computer facilities and data-processing services for the majority of
Government departments. The aim of the commission is to use these resources to provide
the best service possible, and it therefore plans the use of its experienced personnel to
achieve this end. The normal method of filling vacancies in the Public Service, usually on
promotion, means that it is possible for staff to move from one computer centre to another.
It should be noted, however, that the operation of the computers in the centres and the
method of designing systems to operate on these computers differ widely, and that expertise
and experience in one centre is not necessarily applicable to another centre or another
computer. The commission appreciates that the work undertaken at some centres is more
sensitive than at others. Apart from experience and technical competence, careful considera-
tion is given to personal characteristics and suitability before appointments are made to
sensitive positions.

East Timor-New Zealand Attitude
135. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Has he seen the
statement issued by Antara, the Indonesian Government News Agency, following official
talks between New Zealand and Indonesia on 5 and 6 May, which claimed that "New
Zealand delegates expressed understanding about the Indonesian view (on the East Timor
issue)"; can he indicate whether this is a fair assessment of the New Zealand position; and, if
so, can it be taken as a denial by New Zealand of the growing evidence that between 10 000
and 100 000 East Timorese have been killed by Indonesian troops?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied, Yes, I have seen the
statement published in the Indonesian press following the recent talks in Jakarta between
senior Indonesian and New Zealand officials. The statement was not seen or approved for
public release by the New Zealand side, and as an interpretation of the New Zealand
position is rather distorted. The New Zealand officials expressed the Government's under-
standing of the sort of security considerations which had led Indonesia to intervene in East
Timor. We have never made any secret of the fact that we consider the original breakdown
of the decolonisation process a key factor determining subsequent events in East Timor. This
does not imply acceptance or approval of Indonesian intervention or the subsequent
integration of East Timor into Indonesia, and this point was made perfectly clear to the
Indonesians. It is nevertheless a fact that, with its formal declaration of the integration of
East Timor into Indonesia, the Indonesian Government considers the issue settled. The
Government continues to view with deep sadness the loss of life that has resulted from the
conflict in East Timor. It is aware of the various estimates of the number of people killed in
the fighting. Many of these estimates are unreliable. What matters, however, is that people
did lose their lives. This concern, too, has been expressed to the Indonesian Government. It
is apparent that the Indonesian Government must bear its share of responsibility for the
casualties of the fighting. I should like to point out to the honourable member, however, that
the Indonesians were not the first, nor the sole, bearers of arms in the East Timor conflict.
(17/6/77)

Phosphate Supplies
143. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Overseas
Trade, Can he tell the House how long our present phosphate supplies can be expected to
last; and what other phosphate deposits does New Zealand hope to use?
Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) replied, New Zealand's supplies of
phosphate rock are at present being obtained from three sources: Nauru. Ocean Island, and
Christmas Island. Depending on the extraction rate, it is estimated that the Nauru deposit
will be available for 15 to 20 years. The Ocean Island deposits are expected to be depleted by
1979. The deposits on Christmas Island will last from 9 to 19 years, depending on whether a
calcination plant for rock phosphate is installed. While there are no problems in the medium
term with phosphate supplies, the Government is taking an interest in possible sources of
future supplies. One possibility is the new discovery of phosphate rock being developed in
North Queensland, where there are deposits of about 2000 million tonnes. Trials are taking
place with this phosphate, and these and other investigations will determine whether
Queensland could be a supplier. There are, of course, more distant sources such as Florida
and Morocco. However, adequate supplies will be available from traditional sources for
many years to come.

Consumer Price Index-1c on Beer and Cigarettes
171. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East),
asked the Minister of Statistics, How much would a lc increase in the price of a glass of beer
and a lc increase in the price of a pack of 20 cigarettes add to the consumer price index?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics) replied, The Government Statistician
has calculated that if lc were to be added to the price of every packet of 20 cigarettes, and
every glass of beer sold in hotels, the consumer price index would rise by 1.03 points. If a lc
per glass increase is applied proportionately to the price of a jug of beer, the resulting
increase of 5c in the price of a jug of beer would add a further 0.41 points to the index. The
consumer price index for the March quarter 1977 stood at 1373. A rise of 1c in the price of 20
cigarettes and a glass of beer would result in an index of 1374 which represents a rise of 0.07
percent. If a proportionate increase in the price of a jug of beer is included, the index would
be 1375, which is an increase of 0.15 percent.

Immigrants-Categories
172. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Immigration, What was the number of
categories of immigrants, both subsidised and non-assisted, acceptable to New Zealand in
October 1972, what changes to this number have occurred between October 1972 and the
present day, and on what dates did these changes occur?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied, There were three commonly used
methods of emigration to New Zealand. Under the first, the subsidy scheme, limits were first
introduced on the number of acceptable occupations in April 1974. The 35 acceptable
occupations at that time were reduced to 8 occupations in April 1975. The second was an
assisted passage scheme under which the New Zealand Government paid the full fare. In
October 1972 approximately 125 occupations were approved under the assisted passage
scheme, which was abolished in April 1975. The third scheme attracted no subsidy. In April
1974, when entry controls were introduced over the previously unrestricted British, an
occupational list dividing occupations into three categories based on demand was developed.
In its final form in December 1974 this list covered 113 occupations. In December 1975 the
list was reduced to 35 occupations. It was raised in September 1976 to 120 occupations and
raised again in May 1977, to 243 occupations.
(14/6/77)

Tuna Fish Industry-200-mile Economic Zone
174. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Fisheries, Has he seen the article on
the tuna fish industry in the New Zealand Herald on 13 May which states that the declaration
of a 200-mile coastal zone around New Zealand may not give local fishermen protection
from big American super seiners, and, if so, does this Government intend to adopt the same
position as the United States has, enabling big American super seiners to work within 12
miles of the coast next season, or will the 200-mile economic zone be fished by New Zealand
owned and operated boats?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied, The Minister of Fisheries replies as
follows: "Yes, I have read the article in the New Zealand Herald of 13 May on tuna fishing
referred to by the member. The American legislation governing its 200-mile fishery zone
does not include highly migratory species such as tuna. However, the Territorial Sea and
Exclusive Economic Zone Bill .which was recently introduced to the House and referred to
the Foreign Affairs Committee will provide for the management of all fisheries resources
within our 200-mile exclusive economic zone. Only New Zealand registered fishing vessels
can fish within 12 miles of our coast. The fishing by American seiners within the proposed
200-mile exclusive economic zone, could, if necessary, be controlled under the interim
provisions in the Bill."

Economic and Financial Restraints
189. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) asked the Minister of
Finance, Why, when he has constantly preached the need for restraint in economic and
financial matters, has he permitted the very considerable increase in the money supply
during the calendar year 1976 referred to on page 18 of the recent report of the New Zealand
Monetary and Economic Council?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied on behalf of the Acting Minister
of Finance. There are two definitions of money supply in New Zealand: first, the money
supply generally known as M1, comprising currency and trading bank demand deposits;
secondly, the money supply and selected liquid assets generally known as M3, comprising
the factors in M1 plus trading bank term deposits, and the total deposits of savings banks,
finance houses, stock firms, and money market dealers. There is always area for argument
on this subject both here and abroad as to the correct level of money supply growth and
which indicator of the money supply is the most important in any particular circumstance.
The Monetary and Economic Council has focused attention on trends in M3. An equally
valid approach would be to note the sharp downward trend in M1, which has decelerated
consistently quarter by quarter from 19.8 percent annual growth in the March 1976 quarter
to 6.3 percent in the March 1977 quarter. The growth rates of M3 have been substantially
affected by the March 1976 monetary measures which greatly increased the deposit effective-
ness of banks, finance companies, and to a lesser extent savings banks. The Holmes task
force was very critical of the massive money supply fluctuations consequent upon Labour
policies. For instance, M1 moved from a 30 percent September 1973 quarter to a 1 percent
December 1974 quarter to a 19.8 percent March 1976 quarter, which, although the
Government had changed by that time, was the effect of the previous Government's policies.
There was a similar wild fluctuation in M3 under the Labour Government. Two factors
emerge since March 1976 which indicate the improving health of the monetary scene. First,
growth in M1 has fallen steadily, and, secondly, there has been a less sharp downward
movement in M3, but an encouraging lack of wild variation from quarter to quarter. Our
money supply growth is on a par with OECD comparisons.
(15/6/77)

Consumer Price Index
206. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Statistics, Can he indicate how the
consumer price index is arrived at and to what extent it is an accurate reflection of changes in
the living costs of the average New Zealand family?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Statistics. The consumer price index is arrived at by the regular pricing of 565 items, either
weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annually at a variety of retail stores and service establish-
ments throughout the 25 main centres of New Zealand and eight smaller towns. The pattern
of expenditure used in this index has been established from a survey of the factual situation
of households throughout New Zealand. The Government Statistician believes that at
present the index is a reasonably accurate reflection of changes in prices of goods and
services purchased by the average New Zealand family.

Partisans?

The revised policy for State indigenous forests does not apply to private landowners,
although private landowners are, of course, subject to the constraints of the normal town
and country planning and water and soil conservation procedures. If it is the private
landholders' wish to remove indigenous forest for farm or plantation forest development,
they are free to do so within these constraints. In this case, the Rangitikei-Wanganui
Catchment Board proposes to use the forest operations guidelines and land use capability
assessments as a basis for exercising its statutory role in protecting soil and water values.
(21/6/77)

216. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Housing, Can he confirm that Housing
Corporation loans for new houses fell from 11 659 in the year ended 31 March 1976 to 8421
in the year ended 31 March 1977, and that this represents a drop of 28 percent in lending for
new houses?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied, I confirm that there was a drop of
28 percent in the number of Housing Corporation loans for new houses between 1976 and
1977. As the member well knows, the 1976 figure reflects a position that was impossible to
sustain within the financial and administrative resources available. The Government's policy
is to avoid such excess levels of demand, and the 1977 outturn for Housing Corporation loans
reflects its considered assessment of that portion of the community's resources that should be
provided in this manner.

Chemosterilants—Evaluation
217. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Agriculture, What progress has
been made in the evaluation of chemosterilants such as diethysthibestrol and BDH 10131 for
the control of rabbits, opossums, and goats?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied, The use of chemosterilants for the
control of rabbits, opossums, and goats does not appear promising at present. Some
chemicals, such as diethysthibestrol and BDH 10131, were evaluated by Dr Godfrey, a
ministry scientist, while in America, and showed considerable potential. However, all
chemicals evaluated were unsatisfactory for reasons of cost, availability, or effectiveness. At
present there is little likelihood of suitable chemicals being developed by the pharmaceutical
companies because of the high development costs and the limited markets. Dr Godfrey, who
is now at Invermay Research Centre, is keeping in touch with the companies, and if a
suitable chemical is produced it will be followed up.

Turning to question 132 about New Zealand's extended 200-mile limit, the Territorial
Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill is at present before a select committee. The Bill is
one of the most momentous developments of recent times in the development of our
potential resources. It increases the breadth of our territorial seas, and establishes for New
Zealand an exclusive economic zone of waters and seabed for 200 miles around our coasts.


## p. 1079 (#321) ###########################################

29 June
1079
Discussion of Questions-Adjournment
The Bill is close to the legislation already put forward by Canada, the United States, the
European Economic Community, and Russia, which have declared their 200-mile territorial
zones. New Zealand's zone is the fourth or fifth largest in the world. It covers 1.5 million
square miles, fourteen times the size of New Zealand's land area, and extends over an
irregularly shaped area of ocean around our coast, 1600 nautical miles in latitude, and 1200
nautical miles in longitude.
Mr Hunt: What's all this got to do with the cost of living?
Mr LAMBERT: It has a lot to do with the cost of living in the future, and I will tell you
how. Within this zone we have sovereign rights for the purposes of exploring, exploiting,
managing, and conserving both living and non-living resources—that is, everything. We have
rights over oil, gas, minerals such as nickel, and copper, and fishing in this area. We could
raise artificial islands or structures. In short, this development will make New Zealand a
martitime power of considerable importance in the Pacific area. Our main interest is in the
immediate fishing resources that this zone offers us. It protects the rights of our fishermen,
and extends their protected area to 12 nautical miles from the coast.

DISCUSSION OF MOTIONS
Economic Predictions
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I move, That this House notes
with deep concern the overall tenor of the report on the state of the economy in the last issue of
Quarterly Predictions of National Income and Expenditure published by the New Zealand
Institute of Economic Research, and urges the Government to take action to offset the trends
apparent in the report. At the outset, I refer members to the words contained at the top of
page 3 in the summary of Quarterly Predictions of National Income and Expenditure: "There
is now little evidence that any overall economic contraction took place during 1976-77.
Nevertheless, the rate of economic growth has slowed palpably. We estimate that real gross
domestic product increased by only 1 percent last year, and forecast a static economy as the
most likely outcome for the coming year. Despite this, the balance of payments will again
begin to deteriorate although the deficit may remain at about the same level relative to gross
national product."
At best, that is a very gloomy forecast; but if we do not even measure up to that the
prospects for the next few years are very poor indeed. Yet one gentleman named Chapman
travels around the country talking about an economic miracle. In the course of this debate I
hope that the Opposition can show some of the facts about New Zealand's economic
situation. The only miracle is that the said Mr Chapman thinks that some people might
believe it. So far, there are no facts to support the contention that a miracle has been
worked. The country has been saved by what the Labour Government anticipated, worked
for, and borrowed for in 1975, which was a significant recovery in New Zealand's export
prices. Just in case members opposite think that that state of affairs will continue, I draw
their attention to a headline in today's New Zealand Herald. Because the export price for
wool has already shown such a downturn, the headline reads, "Wool bales stockpile doubles
to 102,000." Although the spokesman for the marketing corporation makes some hopeful
noises, the recovery that the Labour Government achieved through an increase in overseas
prices has already been dissipated by the action, or the lack of action, of the National
Government.
I shall point out a few facts. The current account deficit on overseas exchange
transactions rose again during May, whether one takes it on a yearly or a monthly basis. This
is normally the time of year when export earnings are fairly high and import payments are
relatively low. It is traditionally a time when our reserves are building up-but not this time.
In the past 15 months, the Government has reduced the balance of payments deficit by less
than the Labour Government did in its last 6 months in office. According to the Institute of
Economic Research, that deficit will worsen. I point out, as I did initially, that this has
occurred at a time of a record boom in export receipts-the boom the Labour Government

worked to achieve, and for which it took the risks of, and the blame for, borrowing.

of net immigration has been the group of those over 60 years; all the productive age groups

economy, and as economic difficulty, is being compounded by the loss in the more efficient
section of our work force. The Government prints a pamphlet to try to take advantage of a
temporary position and to tell people that everything is all right. What it should say is that it
was not true even when it was printed-that it was known then that the later figures would
contradict those set out in the document. Unfortunately, this is typical of the sort of thing put
out by the Government's advertising agents-like the manifesto the Government itself has
disowned on the grounds that it was the work of an advertising man-pretty, glossy, but
misleading.
That is all the Government has to give the public at present, but this publication is the
work of an impartial, independent organisation and makes it quite clear how things are
going. The Minister who was in charge of the Post Office remedied a deficit of about $38
million by increasing charges by $101 million. Is it any wonder that the economy is
floundering? That money has been taken out of the pockets of the lowest income earners.

through the removal of subsidies. When everything is added up, pressure is put on the
spending power of the lower income groups, the economy is depressed, and all the Minister

Discussion of Motions
Regional Development Policies
RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North): I move, That this House notes with considerable
interest the statement by the Leader of the Opposition to the Christchurch Lions Club on 14 June
1977 that a Labour Government would reactivate a town at Rolleston as part of its regional
development policy and sees this as clear evidence that Labour flatly rejects sound population,
land use, regional development, and planning policies that are so necessary to the New
Zealand of the future.
First, I shall quote from the United Nations leaflet, Habitat, which states: "Where and
how do people live? We must accept that the human race is now living in an era of jarring
transition. We are rushing toward the day when the great part of our species will live in a
previously unconceived state of compaction. We must very quickly devise physical, social,
and environmental responses to that condition.”
Let us look at the announcement made on 29 November 1973 about the Rolleston
project, the planning for which was done in a hurried and secretive manner. Why? Because
the then Minister of Works and Development, Hon. Hugh Watt, said that it was a policy in
the best interests of Christchurch and of the South Island. The Christchurch Press stated that
the Minister's announcement came as a bombshell to a meeting of mayors, and to the
chairman and the planning authority itself. It was aptly summarised at the time that one
would expect that the basic research for a decision of such human consequence and historical
impact would be proportional to its social importance and the value of the investment. The
question, did we need Rolleston, was never answered by the Labour Government, which set
up an officials committee after the announcement that there was to be a town. Members
opposite still fail to make a case for a town of 80 000 people at Rolleston. They advocate a
policy that does not even answer any of the questions posed in the Holmes task force report
on our social environment.
We should ask members opposite a few questions. Does this policy take into account
population growth, or population projections of any kind? The answer is no. Does this policy
take into account the need to relate to broad policies for urban and rural development, and
the general use of land and water? The answer is no. Does this policy take into account the
preservation of farmlands, the containment of urban areas, forests, and river estuaries, and
the protection of regional ecology? The answer is no. Does this policy recognise that we have
insufficient information on the attitudes of people to living in cities, the myth of the quarter-
acre section, and their physical, economic, and social needs? The answer is no. Does this
policy take into account the implications for New Zealand of the growth of Auckland? The
answer is no. Does this policy begin to ask questions about what the size of New Zealand
cities should be? The answer is no. Does this policy consider the need to relate to town and
country, to do things on a human scale, and not to let them be swamped by the mass-
produced mediocrity that a socialist Labour Government would give us? The answer is no.
Does this policy take into account the encouragement of alternative population growth in
other regions, which already have a basic and often vastly underutilised infrastructure with
all the necessary services? The answer is no. Does this policy consider what our future
industrial growth pattern might be? The answer is no. Does this policy take into account the
need to process resources for export in the area where those resources are available? Again,
the answer is no. So it goes on.
The policy does not even consider the South Island, the distribution of employment in
New Zealand, or the very vital human resources that make for good industrial development.
The policy does not consider people, the environmental factors of shovelling them into the
inhuman quality of a manufactured town. It does not take into account food, water, waste
disposal, and pollution control, or education, health, and social welfare services. It does not
recognise the problems of housing, that ticky-tacky mass-produced buildings do not produce
communities. It does not take into account communications, the provision of energy, the
need for more pylons to straddle the landscape to bring power from the resources of other
regions, particularly Otago.
This policy was plucked by the socialist Labour Government from the reports of
overseas forums. The proposed town was placed on a convenient spot on the map and
announced without regard to land quality, or the problems of Christchurch, or the people of
the surrounding districts such as Kaiapoi, Rangiora, Amberley, Ashburton, or of Timaru,
Greymouth, Oamaru, Waimate, Dunedin, Balclutha, Gore, and Invercargill, and certainly
without regard to the people of the rest of New Zealand. Rolleston, a socialistic Labour
concept, is a plastic concept conceived by plastic bureaucrats and announced by the plastic
Labour Government then in power. Rolleston was not wanted then, and is not wanted now.
It offends the very basic principle of regional and urban development, and ignores the


## p. 1094 (#336) ###########################################

1094
29 June

available alternatives. It has been correctly described as.the monstrous creation of a few
bureaucrats, a plaything from which they could achieve some sort of satisfaction by having
helped to squander millions of dollars of public money.
The new town of 80 000 people, as announced by the Labour Government and endorsed
by the present Opposition, was infamous in its concept and its intent. It is a bastardised idea
brought back from another country. The Labour Government attempted to give it a cloak of
legitimacy by terming it regional development. That cloak was rejected, especially in the
South Island and by those affected, because of the thinking it reflected. The nightmare of

face against regional development. Until there is a major heavy industrial area in the South
Island to act as a counterbalance to Auckland, regional development will remain just two
words. Ashburton, Timaru, the West Coast, and Dunedin will all have run-on benefits and
advantages from the development of a properly planned heavy industrial area at Rolleston.
Look at the growth in Hamilton, Tauranga, and neighbouring and ancillary areas that results
from the growth in Auckland. The benefits are there for members opposite to see. If they
wake up and make regional development meaningful, that will also happen in the South
Island; but the key is properly planned and developed area in Rolleston. The present
member for Dunedin North will not be there, but the Labour member who represents that
electorate will see the advantages and benefits of the development of Rolleston as part of the
meaningful regional development policies of the Labour Government.

TRADE AND INDUSTRY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I move, That this
Bill be now read a second time. As I said in introducing the Bill, it is simply a machinery
measure comprising the short title and two administrative clauses. Clause 1 relates to the
short title. Clause 2 inserts a new section 2A into the principal Act. The new section provides
that any right, power, or discretion or authority that may be exercised by me under the Act
may also be exercised by the Minister of Overseas Trade or the Minister of Regional
Development.
The Department of Trade and Industry undertakes functions and responsibilities
administratively under the control of three Ministers. Under the Trade and Industry Act
1956, in exercising this control in their respective areas of responsibility the Minister of


## p. 1096 (#338) ###########################################

1096
29 June
Trade and Industry Amendment Bill
Overseas Trade and the Minister of Regional Development act in legal terms on my behalf.
The proposed new section will give those Ministers formal recognition to enable them to act
on matters for which they have administrative responsibilities in their own right. It is an
anomaly that the office of Minister of Overseas Trade is expressly recognised in certain
statutes that confer responsibility on him, yet he is not recognised under the Trade and
Industry Act under which many of the activities of the office are conducted.
It is also important in relation to several of my powers under the Act. There are powers
to establish advisory committees—for example, trade promotion committees and regional
development councils. Those bodies are concerned with the portfolios of Overseas Trade
and Regional Development rather than with the portfolio of Trade and Industry-not
entirely, but mainly. There are also committees of inquiry into trade and industry and
commerce, which are the responsibility of the Minister of Trade and Industry. Again, this
amendment will simply enable my two colleagues, the Minister of Overseas Trade and the
Minister of Regional Development, formally in their own right to exercise the powers
relating to those matters.
Clause 3 is a further machinery measure. It amends section 16A(2) of the principal Act.
The effect of the amendment is that Part X of the Customs Act 1966, which relates to
customs agents and carriers, shall be deemed to form part of those provisions of the principal
Act that relate to the control of imports. Coupled with a proposed consequential amendment
to the Import Control Regulations 1973, this will mean that customs agents as prescribed or
authorised by the Comptroller of Customs under Part X of the Customs Act will be formally
permitted to deal with my department-the Department of Trade and Industry—and the
Customs Department on import licensing matters in the same manner and under the same
conditions of control as apply to other customs matters. The amendment in clause 3 simply
restores the position to that obtaining when the import licensing regime was constituted
under the Customs Act.
Honourable members will recall that when the former Labour Government transferred
the regime to my department in 1973 and re-established it under the Trade and Industry Act,
the connection with Part X of the Customs Act was inadvertently severed. I think that is the
fairest way to state the position. It is a fact that it was severed, and I am sure the member for
Mt. Albert will correct me if it was not severed inadvertently. This is simply a machinery
measure to correct the position so that customs agents can continue with their business as
they have done in the past under Part X of the Customs Act. My department estimates that
about 25 percent of import licence applications are actually being dealt with by customs
agents, and, as colleagues in the House will appreciate, they form an important part of the
importing and commercial community. This amendment will enable them to continue with
the same legal effect as has obtained for many years.
Those are the three clauses in the Bill. One is the formal short title and the other two
make provision for the Minister of Overseas Trade and the Minister of Regional Develop-
ment to have, as it were, legal access to undertake work they are properly doing by virtue of
their portfolios. Clause 3 rectifies the matter as it applies to customs agents.

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I shall reply very
briefly, and thank members for their interesting contributions to the debate. I compliment
the member for Mt. Albert on being relevant at least. I assure you, Mr Speaker, that I intend
to be relevant, just as the Acting Prime Minister was, and to answer the questions raised by
the member for Mt. Albert. He said I had failed to give any reason for the Bill. The Acting
Prime Minister gave the reasons, too. I said that the new provision in clause 2 would give the
two Ministers mentioned-the Minister of Overseas Trade and the Minister of Regional
Development-recognition, and enable them to act in their own right. At present they act
through the Minister of Trade and Industry. They have certain powers and responsibilities
within their portfolios to appoint committees, regional councils, a trade promotion council,
and so on, and when they make a decision to appoint a council the decision is effected
through the Minister of Trade and Industry. With the passing of the Bill, the decision will be
properly taken by the Minister through his own portfolio. It is a technical matter perhaps,
but the member for Henderson, with his great knowledge of the law, will appreciate it.
The member for Mt. Albert asked where we got the Bill from; did somebody with an
axe to grind in overseas trade put the idea to the Government? Did it come from the
Government caucus? I say definitely and clearly that I received advice, as did my colleague,
from my advisers in the Department of Trade and Industry-the legal officer and
others-that I should introduce a simple amendment to the Statutes Amendment Bill to tidy
up the matter. I did as was reported to the House a few moments ago by the Acting Prime
Minister. I approached the member for Mt. Albert to see if this would be suitable, because
successive Governments have been jealous and careful to guard the convention that we do


## p. 1104 (#346) ###########################################

1104
29 June
Trade and Industry Amendment Bill
not introduce controversial clauses into the Statutes Amendment Bill. I simply gave that
courtesy to the member for Mt. Albert, and he said he thought there would be opposition to
that course. I took that as an indication that the Opposition was opposed to approving this
technical amendment, and I said we would drop the proposal.
Tonight the member for Mt. Albert asked why, if the Bill is simply a technical one, we
should have it at all. W ell, we have the Bill because we were advised to clear up this matter
so that Ministers could undertake as of right the formalities attached to their portfolios. We
were advised to put it in the Statutes Amendment Bill, but the member for Mt. Albert said
that was not acceptable as it was controversial. Therefore we dropped it, and I have
introduced it this year. I have also introduced clause 3 in order to clear up this matter of the
customs agents, and give them the right, as they have under the Customs Act, to act on
import licensing matters with my department. That is the reason for the Bill, although an
amendment to the Statutes Amendment Bill last year would have been tidier and neater.
I thank the member for Dunedin North for his contribution, and for reminding the
House that the regional development section was commenced, in a small way admittedly, in
1972 during the administration of the former National Government, and that it was not
established as such by the Labour Government, as claimed by the member for Mt. Albert.
That point has been made, and I will not labour it. The questions raised by the member for
Mt. Albert have been answered by the Acting Prime Minister, but let me make the position
abundantly clear. He said, "Has the Government any intention of establishing a department
of regional development?" I give him the emphatic answer that the Government has no such
intention. He asked if the Government had any intention of establishing a separate
department of overseas trade. The answer is in the negative; that the Government has no
such intention. He asked where the Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade
and Industry would fit into this. The Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade
and Industry will continue to be the Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade
and Industry. He is working full time for me, as did the member for Dunedin Central when
he was Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry in the Labour
Government.
I thank members for taking part in the debate on the Bill. It has been a protracted
debate on a formal measure giving legal authority to the Minister of Regional Development
and the Minister of Overseas Trade to act in their own right and in the law, instead of acting
through me. Instead of appointing a committee and coming to me to sign the documents,
they now sign the documents themselves. I am pleased to support the Bill.

Seddon Shield Districts Trotting Jackpot Empowering Bill
THURSDAY, 30 JUNE 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 0 p.m.
Prayers.
SEDDON SHIELD DISTRICTS TROTTING JACKPOT EMPOWERING BILL
Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. I
point out to the House, and to anybody who may be listening in, that publicity has been
given to this measure as a "private member's Bill", but, as members will know, this is a
"private Bill". A private member's Bill is the brainchild of the member presenting it. I am
putting through this private Bill in my capacity as a good member of Parliament.
Hon. Members: Ha, ha!
Mr BLANCHFIELD: The Bill follows petitions from eminent men in the trotting world
from the Marlborough, Reefton, and Greymouth trotting clubs. I hope approval will be
given by the House, not only to this second reading, but also to the third reading in due
course. I recommend those members who have a copy of the Bill to read the preamble,
which is put more succinctly than I would be able to put it—but perhaps with slightly less
flavour. This Bill reflects the saga of a jackpot that commenced in 1971. It makes a very
interesting story, but the House does not have time to listen to all the details. It involves
people with optimism and pessimism, with hope and disappointment, and even anger.
In 1971, the Marlborough, Reefton, and Greymouth trotting clubs decided to run a
jackpot, to be won by the person who picked five winners. That has not been disputed. If the
five winners were not struck at the first meeting, it was understood the pool was to be carried
on to the next meeting at the next club, and again five winners had to be struck. In 1972,
after 8 days' racing on three different racecourses in three different districts, no one had
struck five winners. And so it came to pass, this historic night of the Greymouth Trotting
Club when still nobody struck five winners.
Nobody was told that the jackpot was non-terminating because, in the first place,
everyone knew it was a non-terminating jackpot. The word "non-terminating" is important,
because on it hinges the four winners or five winners issue. The Greymouth Trotting Club
was not advised that the jackpot had terminated and, consequently, was expecting to run a
further meeting to finalise it. However, the Minister of Internal Affairs said, “Oh, no, we
cannot do that. We can do it under subsection (38), or something or other, but it has to go
through the totalisator." Jackpots were not going through the totalisator and, therefore, the
Government was receiving no revenue from them. The $24,012 accumulated after the 8 days'
racing was held by the trustees and invested. A few thousand dollars have been received
from interest on the investment, and the Minister of Finance has taken out a nice little wad
of tax.
Twelve people—and no one can guarantee that there are not more than twelve; I know
of one or two who, for different reasons, have not come forward-issued writs against the
trustees and the club for a pay-out because they had picked four winners. One gentleman
said that he must win because he had had four wins and a second. Other winners had had two
wins, a miss, and then two more wins. Finally, these 12 people agreed that, if the club paid
out on four wins, there would be no decision on who had the best four wins. The matter went
to the Supreme Court, but one of the judges who came to Greymouth found he could not
take the case because his brother had a ticket in the jackpot. He passed the case over to Mr
Justice Casey. In the meantime, the brother, God bless him, has passed into the silence, and
therefore his estate has an interest in the affair. Well, there is the story. The club is asking for
the legislation. The Minister of Internal Affairs will not touch it. His department dropped it
like a hot spud.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: A hotpot!
Mr BLANCHFIELD: Yes. The three trotting clubs want to run a terminating jackpot. It
would not matter if a person did not have five winners. If a racegoer had only two strikes,
and no one could better that, he would be the winner. I give notice that during the
Committee stage I shall be moving some minor amendments. In the short title, "1976" will
be changed to "1977". Clause 2 deals with interpretation. Mr Justice Casey gave only an
interim judgment, not a final judgment. He told the people who had issued writs that, if they
cared to come again to the court, he would give them all the help he could. No further


## p. 1106 (#348) ###########################################

1106
30 June
Seddon Shield Districts Trotting Jackpot Empowering Bill
approaches to the court have been made. After the words, "Mr Justice Casey in his said
interim judgment", the following words will be deleted: "and payment to the plaintiffs in all
of the writs of summons referred to above of the amounts actually invested by them in the
jackpot conducted by the Greymouth Trotting Club at its trotting meeting on the 20th day of
April 1972". Clause 3 refers to disposal of the jackpot pool. The term "non-contributing",
before the words "terminating jackpot" is to be deleted. Then, at the end of the clause- and
this is very important-after the words "who select", these words are to be deleted: "the
winner of the first jackpot race, and", and, after the words, "the most winners of the", the
words "other 4" are to be deleted. That is the salient point of the Bill. The current
unsatisfactory situation will be terminated, and there will be no more worry.
Clause 4 deals with rules, and states; "Each of the said jackpots shall be conducted
subject to rules consented to by the New Zealand Racing Authority." The Racing Authority
considers these jackpots to be illegal and will not touch them, but, when this legislation is
passed, the racing authority must take over the running of the jackpots. The form used
during the 8 days' racing definitely stated that five winners had to be picked. Those people
who believe, as has been stated on television, it is merely a question of going for your life and
picking five winners, should remember that they will need to be human computers. Every
race on which the jackpot will operate will have at least 14 horses starting, so to have any
certainty of winning the jackpot one would have to multiply 14 by 14 five times. Anyone
wanting to cover the field would have to spend an awful lot of money. As it is, some big
bettors have been trying for the jackpot. One person paid $812, of which $512 was spent on
the last day. Interest in this jackpot is not confined to people living on the West Coast. Some
of the people who went to court came from as far afield as Christchurch, Geraldine,
Ashburton, Nelson, Marlborough, and elsewhere.
Mr LATTER (Marlborough): I have great pleasure in supporting the second reading of
this Bill. It is a very clearly worded and magnificent piece of legislation and I would be a
darned fool if I did not support it. Even the honourable member for Western Hutt must be
able to agree with the wording of the Bill, which states exactly what it means. We were all
delighted with the language used by the member for West Coast. I am only sorry there was
not some poetry. I am glad he mentioned the amendments because I had intended bringing
them to his notice. I am sorry that “non-contributing" will go out. There would have been a
record attendance at the first day of the Marlborough Trotting Club's meeting for that first
jackpot; I know I must not advertise the date.
Finally, on behalf of the Marlborough Trotting Club and my electorate I express thanks
to their colleagues on the West Coast. Probably the total fund could have been kept for one
last jackpot rather than having it split up among Greymouth, Reefton, and Marlborough,
but if that had happened we would have had a fight on our hands. This is called the Seddon
Shield Districts Trotting Jackpot Empowering Bill. The Seddon Shield is not mentioned in
this House very often, but it is a most important football trophy. Marlborough put it up with
the Ranfurly Shield to see if it would breed, but it did not. It is played for mainly in annual
competition between the West Coast and Marlborough, and Tasman and Nelson are allowed
to have a go for practice. I wholeheartedly support the Bill and thank the member for West
Coast for the delightful way in which he moved the second reading.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): There are one or two points I should like to make to
help the honourable member who is promoting the Bill. He may be aware that the Bill has
been the subject of nationwide criticism by members of the racing fraternity because, if the
jackpot were non contributory, every person who attended the meeting could take a ticket
and seek a multiple. There would be no additional cost involved. I am sure that the
honourable member would be the first to agree that all who went to the next meeting would
be entitled to a ticket multiple. The result would be that all would end up with about 56c
each. That was said by a well known racing commentator at the weekend. I hope the Bill will
help the honourable gentleman in dealing with the dilemma in which the clubs find
themselves, but perhaps he will be good enough to have a look at that because it seems futile
to promote such a situation.
I am sure those who attend the meeting will expect to look forward to a small fortune of
about $24,000 because of the way the Bill has been written, but they will be badly mistaken.
As it has been written, everyone attending the course would be entitled to a share in the
appropriation. I am sure that the honourable gentleman will take account of that. I am not
being critical of the way in which the clubs are trying to solve their problem. I am trying to
ensure that the people will benefit because of the changes.
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I suspect that in the the usual colourful contribu-

tion of the member for West Coast, the racing commentator in him was striving to get out
and enter into the real spirit of the debate and deal with the subject in that lighthearted
manner now so rarely heard in the House. Might I suggest that the honourable member
consider changing the short title to the short head, so that it can be dealt with in racing

The subject of this private Bill has been debated at length over the last 6 years; indeed
there has been some litigation. But it should be recorded that no one entrant fulfilled the
conditions of entry for the jackpot. Some people were able to pick four winners, but no one
was able to pick five, hence this Bill. My files testify to the volume of correspondence that
successive Ministers of Internal Affairs have entered into, either directly or through the
department. It is pertinent also to observe that neither the department nor the Minister in
any way signified approval of the type of jackpot betting undertaken by clubs during the
balmy days of the early 1970s when jackpot betting was flourishing on many racecourses.
The clubs acted on the advice of the New Zealand Racing Conference and the New
Zealand Trotting Conference, and it was a rather doubtful interpretation of the then Gaming
Act provisions. The interpretation was not challenged, but the Gaming Act has now been
superseded by the Racing Act 1971, and jackpots must now be authorised by the Minister
under the Racing Act. None has been authorised, and it is unlikely now that one would be
since trebles betting gathers in the high dividend seeking bettor. We may well have seen the
last of the jackpots in New Zealand; this might be the last of an era.
To set the record absolutely straight I should like to explain why the Minister and the
department suggested this course of action as one of the options open to the member for
West Coast, and anyone who might be interested in the outcome of this jackpot and its pool.
I quote from a letter to one of the interested parties from the Minister in September of last
year. This should put the record absolutely straight: "I can, however, advise that following
the receipt of legal advice the Department of Internal Affairs has recently written to the
Greymouth Trotting Club suggesting two courses of action open to it. One would be to adopt
the system of disbursement apparently suggested by Mr Justice Casey in his interim
judgment." That course has already been referred to by the honourable member. "The
other would be to seek the concurrence of the local member of Parliament to the
introduction by him of a Private Member's Bill, seeking statutory authority as a special
instance for the Club to use the accumulated funds as a starting fund for a jackpot to be
conducted and terminated at its October 1976 meeting. Alternatively, if preferred, such a
Private Member's Bill might seek to provide legislative authority for the splitting of the fund
into three equal shares among the three clubs which were involved with the jackpot, each to
use its share as a starting funds for jackpots to be conducted and terminated at the first
available meeting of each of the clubs." That is the course of action that is being followed.
On behalf of the Minister of Internal Affairs I complement the member who has introduced
this private Bill, which is supported by members on this side of the House.
Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast): I thank the members who have spoken in the

Government Printing Office, Masterton
2. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa) asked the Minister in Charge of the Government Printing
Office, What is the total number of persons at present employed at the Government Printing
Office at Masterton, and how many of these workers are claiming a travel allowance under
their awards?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister in Charge of the Government Printing Office): The
total number employed at the Government Printing Office in Masterton is 118, and no
workers are claiming a travelling allowance under their awards.
Mr Kirk: Can the Minister confirm that one of the first actions of the Government was
to defer stage 2 of the transfer of the Government Printing Office to Masterton, and as a
result people are denied employment in that area?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: This question has nothing to do with the first question. It is
correct that the Government has deferred the commencement of stage 2. It will be reviewed
at the end of this year.
Mr Couch: Has a date been set for the official opening of stage 1 of the Government
Printing Office at Masterton?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: The date for the opening has just been set for 2 August. The
honourable member can expect an invitation along with other local dignitaries.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: The Minister mentioned 118 employees. Are there any vacancies for
the 10 printing tradesmen who have been or are about to be dismissed from a private works
in Masterton?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: Of the 118 employees, 79 have been recruited locally. Some
workers from the local works that has just closed have been given employment at the
Government Printing Office in Masterton.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: As the Wairarapa is a designated regional development area with
its own council, is the deferral of stage 2 of the Government Printing Office a reflection of
the Government's regional development policy?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: No, that assumption cannot be taken. Economic circumstances
have caused the 12 months' deferral, and a review will be carried out at the end of the year.

Consumer Price Index-House and Section Prices
8. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Statistics, What time is taken
for increases in house and section prices to be reflected in the consumer price index?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): In the case of existing houses, flats,
and sections, there is approximately 6 to 9 months' lag before market prices appear in the
consumer price index. In the case of building costs for new houses and flats, the delay is 3
months. Similar lags for these components of the index have existed since the consumer price
index was first established in 1949.
Marilyn Waring: Would the Minister confirm that the high rates of inflation in house
and building section prices experienced in the last year of the Labour Government were
reflected in the consumer price index figures in the first 12 months of this National
Government?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Inevitably there would be that overflow into 1976.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: In light of his last comment, could the Minister explain why National
members have been claiming that house prices are at much lower levels under the National
Government than they were under Labour?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: The fact is that the index has come back.

on the figures for 1973, because 6 or 9 months from the start of the financial year in 1973
would take it to about December 1973, so the figures were obviously a reflection of the

Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: My memory is that our dining out was basically on the
figures for 1974 and 1975.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Can the Minister confirm that the movement in existing house
properties for 1975 was lower than it has been during 1976 and 1977?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No, I cannot give the figures offhand.
