Steel-Substitution by Structurally Engineered Timber
10. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry, Can be advise (1)
the value of items imported under tariff codes 73.11.039, 73.11.031, 73.11.021, and
73.11.139 covering steel girders, channels, and joists; (2) the building value of that material
when fabricated; and (3) what steps his department is taking to encourage the substitution of
steel by locally grown and locally manufactured structurally engineered timber?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The total value of
channels, girders, beams, and joists imported under the four tariff items are: 1974-75,
$13,471,760; 1975-76, $6,979,081; and 1976-77, for the 9 months to March 1977, $9,131,661.
No statistics give the building value of these materials when fabricated. As a general policy,
my department encourages the use of New Zealand's indigenous resources. However, no
steps are being taken to promote the substitution of steel by structurally engineered timber
of New Zealand origin, although from time to time the Department of Trade and Industry
has advised the professional people concerned to consider the use of alternative domestic
materials where available. Other materials used in construction also have a high New
Zealand content, for example, pre-cast reinforced concrete beams. The choice of materials
to be used is subject to the expert advice of architects and engineers about the type of
structure required, and other factors.
Mr Malcolm: As the cost of steel is a direct drain on overseas funds, and a large amount
of the fabrication resulting from that imported steel could be carried out on locally grown
timber, and as the use of steel in construction invariably involves the use of the high dispute

consider looking into setting up an active policy of discouraging the importation of steel and
encouraging the use of structurally engineered timber?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: It is difficult to introduce such a policy when most of
the items referred to by the honourable gentleman are exempt from import licensing. I do
not intend introducing import licensing on such items at present. The natural process of
supply and demand is having some considerable effect, as today many people are moving
away from steel because of the problem with the boilermakers, mentioned by the honour-

Union would be re-registered, or that the Wellington Boilermakers Society would be
recognised, or registered. On 11 March I wrote to the Trades Council saying that within 10
days of work resuming on the Bank of New Zealand site under an agreement to be
negotiated between the contractor and the Trades Council representing boilermakers, I
would be prepared to meet representatives of the council to discuss "appropriate union
coverage of those involved". Further discussions took place with the Trades Council, and on
28 April I wrote to it and proffered the advice that the work force and their colleagues doing
similar work in other sections of the industry should apply for registration as an industrial
union of workers as set out in the Industrial Relations Act. This was later done, but was
declined by the Registrar of Industrial Unions. However, instead of using the full procedures
of the law available by appealing to the Industrial Court, the Trades Council commenced
industrial action, which, among other things, has critically affected the two ships mentioned
by the honourable member. There was never any understanding with the Trades Council
other than that the application would stand on its merits as far as the Registrar of Industrial
Unions was concerned, and I would in no way play any role for or against. This is stated

Commonwealth Countries Bill
FRIDAY, 1 JULY 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 9 a.m.
Prayers.
COMMONWEALTH COUNTRIES BILL
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): I move, That the Common-
wealth Countries Bill be introduced. This Bill has a two-fold purpose. First, it creates a system
for ascertaining which countries are Commonwealth countries for the purposes of interpret-
ing New Zealand legislation. Secondly, it repeals 21 existing Acts relating to individual
Commonwealth countries, and enacts an omnibus provision that New Zealand law shall
continue to operate in respect of all Commonwealth countries equally, whether or not Her
Majesty is head of State. In the past, difficulties have occurred in the New Zealand courts,
particularly when the question has been raised whether a certain country was or was not a
Commonwealth country at a specified date.
Members will recall that a number of New Zealand statutes contain provisions relating
to Commonwealth countries, and the first schedule to the Bill sets out all the independent
sovereign States that are members of the Commonwealth at present. Power is given to add to
the first schedule the names of countries that subsequently become members of the
Commonwealth, and to delete from it the names of countries that subsequently leave the
Commonwealth. If the Commonwealth status of the country in question is accurately
reflected in the first schedule, the court will not need to go further than the schedule to settle
the matter. On the other hand, if the first schedule is not accurate in the specific instance
before the court, a certificate setting out the true Commonwealth status of the country at a
particular date may be sought from the Secretary of Foreign Affairs or one of his deputies. In
the event that a certificate is issued, it would be conclusive evidence of the matters stated in
it.
The second purpose is to provide that all existing law shall continue to operate in respect
of those Commonwealth countries that are republics, or have otherwise ceased to recognise
Her Majesty as head of State. As a consequence, we are able to repeal 21 existing Acts that
make the same provision in respect of such Commonwealth countries individually. If we
were not introducing this Bill, we would be introducing three individual Bills, so that a
further consequence of the passing of this Bill is that it will no longer be necessary to pass
such individual Bills. It is a simple measure, which clarifies the question of membership at a
certain date and does away with the need to pass individual Bills as new countries become
members of the Commonwealth.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): This is a practical solution to
what is becoming quite a difficult problem in many cases. To refer to clause 2, I should like
to ask about the basis upon which the Secretary of Foreign Affairs will issue the proposed
certificate. Will this be in line with the decision taken by New Zealand about the status of a
particular territory, or will it be in line with the decision announced by the country
concerned? In other words, will New Zealand be the initiator, or will it be the other way
round, and will we simply react? I am thinking specifically of a country like Uganda, and the
many views that have been expressed about its membership of the Commonwealth. Is it
intended to take the power to say that we do not regard that country as being a Common-
wealth country?
My other point concerns clause 2 (1) (a), which states: "A certificate signed by the
Secretary of Foreign Affairs or a Deputy Secretary of Foreign Affairs that on a date specified
in the certificate a specified country was or was not a Commonwealth country . . ." Does that
mean that we will have a series of certificates in relation to the same country? The court may
seek a certificate in a certain case, but does this mean that, once issued, a certificate is valid
from then onward?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): The question of membership is
one of historical fact. Either a country is a member of the Commonwealth, or it is not. We
are simply recognising an historical fact. As to the issuing of a certificate, the situation can
arise, and indeed has arisen, before the courts that there is uncertainty about whether or not
a country was a member of the Commonwealth at a certain time. This provides that, if
necessary, the court can receive a certificate from the Secretary of Foreign Affairs. It will

simply state that on a certain date that country was a member of the Commonwealth, or that

then have the certificate in front of it to remove any doubt.

Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Yes.

TRUSTEE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Trustee Amendment
Bill be now introduced. This short Bill amends the Trustee Act 1956, as recommended by the
Property Law and Equity Reform Committee. The principal Act contains a number of
monetary limits on a trustee's powers, which, with one exception, have not been altered
since they were fixed in 1956. Even with the exception, which is section 14(6), the limit was
fixed as long ago as 1968. At the time when the values were set in 1956 and 1968, they were
high enough to enable a trustee to sell, without the consent of the Supreme Court, most
family homes or an average farm. With farm prices now nearly 400 percent dearer, and
house values showing much the same increase, the existing limits are hopelessly out of date.
The law reform committee, in reviewing the limits at the request of my predecessor, has
recommended that they be removed, except in one instance.
The present limit for a trustee to purchase adjoining land without recourse to the court
is $2,000. This limit is removed, but as a safeguard the purchase must be for the better
development or use of the existing land, or to facilitate or improve the carrying on by the
trustee of any business that he is authorised to do on the land originally owned. These
safeguards are proper, to enable the trustee to keep within the reasonable limits of the trusts.
It is not intended to enlarge the power of the trustee over land that is not adjoining or
contiguous. In the absence of express provisions in the trust instrument, such a purchase
would require the court's consent.
Under the Act at present the trustee is not permitted, without the consent of the court,
to grant a lease with an optional or compulsory purchasing clause where the value of the land
as determined under section 28, which deals with valuation, exceeds $15,000, or to sell or
exchange any land where the value thereof exceeds $15,000. This monetary limit is removed,
and the power of the trustee is unrestricted. The trustee is not to be liable for any breach of
trust by reason only of any inaccuracy in the amount or value of the sale price or other
consideration, provided that the trustee obtains a trustee valuation under section 28 of the
Trustee Act 1956 and sells at not less than that price. Under section 15 a trustee is
empowered to expend moneys for the improvement of the trust property, provided that, in


## p. 1119 (#361) ###########################################

1 July
1119
Trustee Amendment Bill
the exercise of this power, he does not exceed $10,000 without the consent of the court. This
limit is removed.
A trustee may pay or apply capital for the maintenance, education, advancement, or
benefit of the person entitled to the capital, provided such payments do not exceed half of
the presumptive or vested interest of that person where the value of that share or interest
exceeds $2,000, and, in any other case, altogether such payments do not exceed $1,000. The
Property Law and Equity Reform Committee considered that some measure of control
should be retained, and it therefore recommended not the removal of the limits in toto, but
increases in those amounts to $15,000 and $7,500 respectively. Power is taken to make future
adjustments by way of Orders in Council. In considering the amendments, members will, I
hope, bear in mind that trustees have a duty to act impartially between beneficiaries, and to
exercise care in the administration of the assets entrusted to them. The removal of the
monetary limits is thus not as radical as it may appear at first sight. The proposals have the
approval of those organisations concerned with the drawing of wills and the administration
of estates, and for this reason I do not intend to refer the Bill to a select committee.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): This Bill originated from a request made to me
when I was Minister of Justice. The Public Trustee asked to be relieved of certain monetary
limits imposed on him. I was unwilling to deal with this in isolation, and asked that the
matter be referred to the Property Law and Equity Reform Committee, which has consi-
dered and approved it, and has also produced some other suggestions. The Minister has been
kind enough to let me see a copy of the committee's report, with which I am satisfied, and I
note that it has been referred to the Public Trustee and the trustee companies. As a result,
there will be little opposition to the Bill.
However, it is a fact that people who specialise in trustee law tend to be deeply learned
recluses who find it easy to imagine what to others would be unimaginable. I think there
would be some merit in referring the Bill to the Statutes Revision Committee, although I
shall not make a great issue of it. It is improbable that there would be anything other than a
letter from the Law Society, saying that it has gone into the Bill and agrees with the
committee's report. It is just conceivable that some of those people who spend their lives in
what others consider to be an esoteric branch of the law could detect matters that would call
for some consideration. I do not think the matter would occupy the committee for more than
half an hour at the most, but it might be just as well to invite the committee to cast its eyes
over the Bill.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The New Zealand Law Society has been
approached, and it indicated that it would have no evidence to offer on the Bill. It may be
that some specialist in this area might find some bogy that requires consideration. It would
be better if the Bill had a second reading, and then, if anybody indicated that there was a
matter requiring the attention of the Statutes Revision Committee, I should have no
objection to sending the Bill to the committee.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Livestock Incentive Scheme
1. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister in Charge of the
Rural Banking and Finance Corporation, Is it true that over 95 percent of farmers have not
taken advantage of the livestock incentive scheme?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corpora-
tion): A devious question may receive a devious answer. Over 95 percent can be read as 4
percent or less, and since more than 3000 have applied that could represent 75 000 farmers.
However, if the figure was 3 percent that could represent 100 000 farmers. In the question
the term "farmer" is not defined, so I shall try to answer the question with that background.
The scheme applies only to farms carrying sheep, beef, or dairy cattle, and to commercial
deer farms. It also includes farmers engaged in mixed cropping and livestock
enterprises-other types of farming such as horticulture, poultry, pigs, etc., being excluded
from the scheme. A further requirement is that to be eligible for assistance dairy farmers
must increase their stocking to a minimum of 500 stock units, and other farmers to 1000 stock
units, carried at the completion of a programme. Having regard to these factors, and as the
scheme commenced in late October 1976 and the closing date for applications is 31 March
1979, the more than 3000 applications to date represent a significant proportion of those
eligible farmers the scheme was designed to attract. It was estimated that 16 000 farmers


## p. 1120 (#362) ###########################################

1120
1 July
Oral Answers to Questions
would be eligible, and so 19 percent have applied so far.
Mr Bruce Barclay: I shall not quibble with the percentages, but the Minister managed to
reduce the figures to a very low percentage. Does the Minister disagree with what the
Provincial President of Federated Farmers, Mr Don Middleton, said: "The livestock scheme
has proved too niggardly and restrictive to stimulate more than a token gesture of support."?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Yes, I do disagree with it. It was estimated that the scheme could
apply to 16 000 farmers, and about 19 percent have applied so far. In a recent survey of 3000
farmers just published by Mr Pryde of Lincoln College, he received 2000 replies to the
circulars sent out, and the answer to the question concerning the livestock incentive scheme
showed that 9 percent had joined, 11 percent had not yet decided, 7 percent intended to
apply in the year 1977-78, and 3 percent in the year 1978-79, making a total of 30 percent of
those who answered.
Mr Elworthy: Could the Minister confirm that the applications received represent more
than 2 000 000 increased stock units that in time will earn extra export earnings for New
Zealand, and that this is a very encouraging start to the scheme?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: The figure is actually higher than 2 000 000 at the moment, and
export earnings depend on the day of sale. The figure represents a considerable lift in stock
unit numbers for the country.
Mr Bruce Barclay: As we have over 100 000 000 stock units, does the Minister consider
that 2 000 000 increased stock units constitutes a big percentage increase?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: I think a better word than big is significant.

Telephone Tapping and Mail Interception
7. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General, Has he seen the report in
the Dominion of 24 June 1977, in which the Post Office Association has expressed concern
that Post Office employees might have pressure placed on them to tap telephones or
intercept mail, and, if so, can he give the House his unqualified assurance that this has not
occurred, and that it will not be allowed to occur in the future?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): Yes, I have seen the report referred to,
and I can give an assurance that under this Administration no illegal interference with
telephones or interception of mail has been sanctioned. As Postmaster-General I have no
plans for amendment of any Post Office legislation to allow new grounds for telephone
interference or interception of mail in addition to those which have been specified in the Post
Office Act for many years under both National and Labour Administrations.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Could the Minister indicate the basis of the newspaper article that
gave rise to that speculation?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: It would be more appropriate to ask the Post Office
Association that question.
Mr Quigley: In what circumstances is it legal under the Post Office Act to tap or monitor
telephones and intercept mail?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The tapping of telephones is illegal under the Post Office Act,
and Post Office employees have instructions to report any suspicions of this happening. In
the case of the monitoring of telephones, it is legal for certain prescribed purposes,
particularly for identifying the origin of obscene or other types of offensive calls, or calls of a
suspected illegal nature, but in each case the subscriber must give a written consent for the
interference. Then there is the standard monitoring of telephones, sufficient only to ensure
that the service is properly carried through. In specified circumstances letter mail can be
intercepted: first, where there is a suspected violation of the Post Office Act, the Customs
Act, or any Act that governs the passage of mail of a monetary nature or of a valuable
security nature; secondly, in the undeliverable mail section, where everybody would expect
it; thirdly, when the Governor-General by warrant so directs. Anticipating this question, I
confirmed with the department that the only time the Governor-General's warrant provision
has been used in recent years was during the Administration of the late Rt. Hon. N. E. Kirk,
when the Hon. Mr Douglas was the Postmaster-General, and it concerned the activities of a
suspected terrorist.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Although the Postmaster-General has disclaimed any intention
of amending the Post Office Act to authorise telephone tapping, does he know of any
proposal for legislation of another kind that would have that effect?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: I am not aware of any plans in existence of this nature.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Can the Minister confirm that the Prime Minister has announced
an intention to give effect to a portion of the Ombudsman's report on the Security
Intelligence Service that would authorise the tapping of telephones, and, if so, when are we
likely to see this?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: That question concerns the jurisdiction of an area of the Prime
Minister's concern, not mine, and the question should be addressed to the Prime Minister.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

evaluation of those who have been educated entirely in the traditional type of classroom and
those who have not. There is sufficient evidence to assure us that the use of flexible
classrooms for teaching children is worth continuing.

Farm Leasehold Lands-Rent Increases
11. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Lands, In view
of the policy pledge "National will give priority to controlling farm costs", is it Government
policy to raise rents on Crown 33-year leasehold lands by 600 percent or more when the rents
come up for renewal?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Lands. The rental value of a leasehold property is the value of the land in the lease, and
excludes the value of improvements on the land. Rent is charged upon the rental value. The
present rental rate is 4.5 percent gross and 4 percent net. The rental rate has not been altered
since 1970, when it was reduced from 5.5 percent gross and 5 percent net. The same formula
used by the Labour Government is still in use. The reason rents on 33-year leases expiring
now are showing substantial increases, is only a reflection of the increased land values that
have taken place since the mid-1940s, when the lease commenced or was last renewed. The
increase in rents would have been greater had the rental rate not been reduced.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Does this increase not contribute to the costs of the farmers
concerned, thus putting them in some financial difficulty?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Obviously they would have some difficulty if they have made no
plans for the increase. I remind the questioner that the leases being renewed this year were
first written in 1944, and were probably for rehabilitation farms that have been run for the
past 33 years at a very low rental. The farmers concerned have known that the leases would
be revalued after 33 years, and therefore have had the opportunity to take steps to meet the
conditions.
Mr Friedlander: As the rent of this land is based upon the value of the land, and as land
prices increased more rapidly during the 3 years of the Labour Government than the rest of
the term of the leases in question, could the Minister confirm that that 3-year period is more
responsible than any other 3-year period for the 600 percent increase in land prices, as
mentioned in the original question?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Yes, the statistics show a violent increase in the value of land
between 1973 and 1976, which has contributed to the increase spoken about in the original
question.

Milk Consumption by Children
13. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central), on behalf of Mr HUNT (New
Lynn), asked the Minister of Health, Has he seen the article in Town Milk, May 1977, which
points out that the purchase of milk in households where there are children under the age of
15 years is down 13.2 percent, and, if so, is he concerned at this drop, and what measures
does he propose to take to ensure adequate nutritional standards for children?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Health. His answer is as follows: "I have seen the article in Town Milk, May 1977, referred
to. I am aware of the drop in the purchase of milk where there are children under the age of
15, but it is considered that milk intake is more important during infancy and the pre-school
years. A dietary survey of the pre-school age group made in the early 1970s by the
Department of Health and the epidemiology department of the Wellington Hospital, before
the increased milk prices, showed an average daily consumption of 500 ml of milk per day
per pre-school child. A 13 percent decrease would represent 65 ml a day, and the effect on
the nutrition of a child would be negligible."
Hon. David Thomson: Despite the effect being negligible, does the Department of
Health still send out pamphlets to mothers encouraging them to buy milk rather than things
like Coca-Cola for their children?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I can confirm that those circulars are still published by the
Department of Health. Perhaps it would be helpful to say that considerable research has
been done in recent months into the sale of milk, and it has been found that milk is under
increasing pressure from a range of powdered and vitamin-enriched soft drinks. The
Department of Health proposes to follow a vigorous sales promotion programme to
emphasise the value of milk as a food, rather than as a drink.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Is the Minister aware that I asked a previous question in the House
as to whether there was any Government programme to advertise the consumption of milk,
and that the answer was no, it had been left to the New Zealand Milk Board?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I understand that the Town Milk Federation has been advertis-
ing, but perhaps I could ask the honourable member, by way of reply, has he been able to
reach the figure for solids not fat in his own herd?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! "Perhaps I could ask the honourable member by way of reply"!
So many of our questions are in the form, "Is the Minister aware", after which we have a
little propaganda speech, whereupon the Minister can say, "Yes", if the question happens to
be from his side, or "No", if it happens to be from the other side. But when we get the
Minister asking a question by way of reply, that is carrying things a little too far.

STANDING ORDER 181—ALLEGED BREACH
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister): I raise a question under Standing
Order 181: "Unbecoming references to House, judiciary, etc.-No member shall use
unbecoming words against the House or any member thereof, against any member of the
judiciary, or against any statute unless for the purpose of moving for its repeal or in speaking
to any such motion." I refer to a reported statement in the Christchurch Star of Thursday, 30
June. The headline stated: "Ship of State being steered from gutter." The article contains
the following statement: "The principle of ministerial responsibility is not working in New
Zealand the way it should, Mangere's Labour member of Parliament, Mr D. R. Lange,
believes." The article states: "It was an unusual experience to go from a law practice, from
the bowels of the magistrate's court, to a place like Parliament where the ship of State is
being steered from the gutter." I suggest that that is an unbecoming reference to the House.
I am sorry that I was not able to talk to the honourable member before I raised the point,
because he is absent. I checked with some of his colleagues, and he is not within the precincts
at present. Otherwise, of course, I would have notified him. I suggest that this is a breach of
Standing Order 181.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I understand that the article referred to appears
in the Christchurch Star. That publication has not yet arrived on our side of the House. The
Deputy Prime Minister was good enough to make available to us a copy of the document.
We sought to make a copy, but unfortunately the wrong piece came out of the machine, so
we do not have the article before us. I do not think I need it, because I do not propose to deal
with the merits of the case—that is for you to determine. I simply question the basis on which
the Deputy Prime Minister pitches his case. He cites a Standing Order and claims what
appears to be a breach of that. That is for you to determine, Mr Speaker. I simply suggest
that that is insufficient to found a claim for breach of privilege. Of itself, a mere breach of the
Standing Orders is not necessarily a breach of privilege; there must be something more than


## p. 1128 (#370) ###########################################

1128
1 July
Standing Order 181-Alleged Breach
that to constitute a breach of privilege. The Deputy Prime Minister has not alluded to that.
He has simply cited a breach of the Standing Orders, and I suggest that the case must go
somewhat further than that to bring it within the bounds of breach of privilege.
Dr WALL (Porirua): Unfortunately I have not seen the newspaper article referred to
either, but it appears from the address of the Deputy Prime Minister that the words he
considered to be offensive and to constitute a breach related to the reference to the ship of
State. It appears to me that that is a metaphorical expression referring to the Government,
as the Government is responsible for the control of the country. That reference could not be
interpreted, even metaphorically, as referring to the House. The statement implies that the
member for Mangere, having come into the House, has then become aware of a certain
situation concerning the control of the country or, in other words, the management of the
ship of State. Any reference to the ship of State is a reference not to the House but to the
Government, and the Government is not included in the Standing Order.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): We are in some difficulty, because we
are dependent upon a newspaper report, although I am not suggesting that the Christchurch
Star is inaccurate or not to be depended upon. However, I think it desirable that the member
for Mangere has an opportunity to say whether or not the report is correct; whether he did
say that he had moved from the bowels of the magistrate's court to a place like Parliament,
where the ship of State is being steered from the gutter; and whether he intended the
remarks he made to be derogatory to Parliament in comparison to the magistrate's
court that is certainly the natural inference one would draw. However, I suggest that, the
House having taken notice, it might perhaps be appropriate to leave any further discussion
until such time as the member for Mangere is present and has at least the opportunity to state
his view of the report and whether or not it is a correct report.
Mr SPEAKER: I think the course suggested is the proper one, and I propose to follow it
in future. The practice in the House of Commons is invariably to endeavour to have a
member against whom there is a complaint present when the matter is raised. The Deputy
Prime Minister very properly endeavoured to have the member here when he raised the
matter, but it seems that the member for Mangere is not available at present. The suggestion
that the matter be held over is the proper one to follow, and I shall act on it. In the past,
members have sometimes heard a complaint on the radio and have rushed in to the Chamber
half way through the complaint being presented against them. I think we are all at fault
there, including myself, in not being aware of and applying the very sound Westminster
principle that a person should hear a charge that is being levied against him.
I might say that I would reject this matter if the Standing Order referred merely to the
House. The ship of State is not the House. However, the following words are then added to
it-"or any member thereof". It can be said that the Government is not the House, but it
would be hard to say that Government does not contain any member of the House, as,
under the British system, members of the Government or Cabinet are of necessity members
of the House. However, I shall not make any determination of the matter at this stage. I
shall, as suggested, hold it over for consideration next week.

PRIVILEGE
The CHAIRMAN: Mr Speaker, Standing Order 428 states: "A member may at any time
raise a matter of privilege. If such a matter is raised in the Committee of the Whole House,


## p. 1130 (#372) ###########################################

1130
1 July
Privilege
the Chairman shall leave the Chair on an order to report progress." A matter has been raised
by the member for Porirua under Standing Order 152, which is headed, "Members having
pecuniary interest not to vote". The member for Porirua claimed that the member for Kapiti
had voted on an amendment to clause 2 of the Shop Trading Hours Bill-the amendment
being to delete the word "mall" in subclause (1)—he having assumed a directorship of a
company that the member for Porirua states would have an interest in another company that
has an interest in a mall; and, therefore, that the member for Kapiti had an uncommon or
pecuniary interest-"a direct pecuniary interest not held in common with the rest of the
subjects of the Crown". The member for Porirua therefore claimed that it was a matter of
privilege and, as he raised it immediately after the vote was cast, we are back in your hands
to allow you to adjudicate on the matter.
Mr SPEAKER: I am prepared to hear the member for Porirua.
Dr WALL (Porirua): Although the matter was summarised very well indeed by the
Chairman in his report, I presume it is necessary for me to raise again the subject on which I
think a breach of privilege has occurred. Considerable significance has been attached to the
inclusion in the Bill of the word "mall", thus allowing particular consideration of malls by
the commissioners in determining the advisability of Saturday trading. If, apart from the
present system of exempted goods, the passing of the Bill allows normal Saturday trading in
those malls, there will be financial advantage to their proprietors. That financial advantage
would accrue through a change in shopping patterns. People who now shop during the week
near their places of work would shop on Saturday mornings, and therefore the turnovers and
the incomes of the proprietors of malls would increase.
Having recently become a director, the member for Kapiti is not just in the position of a
shareholder or a member of the public who might have a financial interest in one of the
companies; he is in a position to determine the course of the policy and conduct of a
company, and so has an interest in the passage of this portion of the Bill that is not shared by
other subjects of the Crown. I had considered whether this matter of privilege should be
submerged in the provision in Standing Order 152 that the prohibition should not apply
where it is a matter of public policy. I have chosen to draw the attention of the House to the
position of the member for Kapiti, not on the subject of the short title of the Bill—which
could be a matter of public policy—but on the particular point of whether or not malls should
be included—which is a matter not of public policy, but of financial concern to the people
involved. It is for that reason that I draw your attention to the financial association of the
member for Kapiti, directly, in the company in which he has a directorship and, indirectly, in
associated companies with shared directorships.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Deputy Prime Minister): This is a gross misuse and abuse of
Standing Orders. In the point raised there is an imputation of improper motive, and I suggest
to you that it is made with malice. It is suggested that the honourable member for Kapiti has
a financial interest outside that which is mentioned in Standing Order 152. I want you to
know, Mr Speaker-and I suspect that the honourable member who raised the point already
knows it—that the honourable member for Kapiti has been appointed a director of a
company that is a broker, and has arranged finance for a company. I suggest that, in fact, he
has no financial interest outside a pecuniary interest that is held in common. I reiterate that
this point contains an implication that should be dealt with under Standing Order 184 and be
deemed to be highly disorderly. Standing Order 184 states: "All imputations of improper
motives, or unbecoming reference to a member's private affairs, and all personal reflections,
shall be deemed highly disorderly." I suggest that after you have heard the honourable
member for Kapiti you will know that what I have said is the truth.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I rise at this stage to adjust the temperature of

Privilege
no place in the discussion of the matter before the House. Neither of those was suggested by

have no means of knowing whether or not that is true, but I am sure that the member for
Kapiti will be given, and will take, the opportunity to explain the position. All you are
invited to do, Mr Speaker, is to explore a possibility inherent in some of the matters raised
during the course of debate, and to have the air cleared. If it is cleared to everybody's
satisfaction, that will be the end of it; but I am sure that there was no implication of improper
motive, and that no malice motivated the point raised by the member for Porirua.
Mr BRILL (Kapiti): The relevant Standing Order refers to a member's not being
entitled to vote on a matter in which he has a direct pecuniary interest; the direct pecuniary
interest alleged by the member for Porirua is that I have accepted an appointment to the
directorship of a mortgage broking firm. First, I point out that I am a director, not a
shareholder, and therefore the profits to the brokerage firm have no connection whatever
with my pecuniary interest, which is related only to director's fees. Secondly, I suggest that
there is no pecuniary interest whatever arising from any mortgage, in that a mortgage is in no
way related to the turnover of the operation secured, but is a fixed interest return; so a
mortgagee could not be said to have a pecuniary interest. Thirdly, I point out that, in any
event, the broking company is not a mortgagee and has no money whatsoever invested. I am
not aware even that it has ever arranged for any money to be invested with any mall owner
but, if it has done so, it was certainly well before I accepted appointment to the directorate as
from today.
The member for Porirua claimed some connection with Williams Holdings Ltd, but as
far as I am aware there is no connection between the broking company and Williams
Holdings Ltd. A "direct pecuniary interest" would require that it be established that the
broking company had money invested, which it does not; that, if it did have money invested,
the return on that money would in some way be connected with turnover, which forms no
part of the mortgage; that I was a shareholder and not a director, which I am not; and that
this Bill would increase the profits of malls, as has been suggested—and here, for the first
time in my address on this subject, I turn to opinion rather than fact-but, in my opinion, it
has certainly not been established that any pecuniary gain or increase in profits to malls will
result from the passing of the Bill.
Perhaps I should also add that, if it were said that a member cannot vote on a Bill if he
becomes a director of a company that once arranged a mortgage for another company that
once owned a mall, we would require the investigation of a breach of privilege in respect of
every member of the House-for example, of a member who is a ratepayer in a local
authority such as the Northcote Borough Council, which has an interest in a shopping centre.
We would also require to exclude from voting trustees in savings banks—because all savings
banks invest in commercial properties-and any member of the House who, directly or
indirectly, has any shareholding or debenture holding in the Fletcher companies, in
insurance companies, or in banks. We could carry this matter to the ridiculous conclusion
where any member who has any moneys invested anywhere could not vote on a Bill that has
any financial effects. If we take it to that extreme, I suggest that the point of privilege raised
by the member for Porirua is a nonsense.
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): It might assist if I read a passage from Erskine May at page
408, which amplifies a similar Standing Order in the United Kingdom Parliament: "The only
instance to be found in the Journals in which the vote of a member has been disallowed upon

a mortgage broking firm has a pecuniary interest in matters such as this, then any member

that owns or has a financial interest in a shopping centre could be said to have a pecuniary

Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I shall refer to the Standing

at the time, was mayor of a borough. Through the Audit Department, he was held
responsible for having voted on a matter in which he had a pecuniary interest. At that time
it was held that he forfeited his seat as mayor, even though the vote he cast actually reduced
the advantage to him; in other words, he voted in what he thought was the public interest.
The issue related to the way the mayoral car was to be operated-instead of a car being
purchased, the mayor was to have an allowance on a mileage basis. Even though his vote
reduced the charge the borough would have to bear, and there was no financial advantage to
him, he was held to have acted improperly in voting on an issue in which he was involved in a
way that nobody else was involved. At the time, that must have seemed an extreme case, and
I put it up simply to show that the intention is to prove the purity of motive of people who
vote.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Transport Advisory Council
1. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Transport, Has he seen the
report in the Evening Post of 8 June 1977, in which it is claimed that the Transport Advisory
Council has not met for 9 months and that the two intended meetings have been deferred,
and, if so, can he confirm that the report is correct, and, if it is, how does he reconcile this
state of affairs with the National Party's manifesto promise to "re-establish the Transport
Advisory Council as the principal adviser to Government on transport matters"?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): Yes, I have seen the report
referred to in the Evening Post of 8 June. A meeting of the Transport Advisory Council has
been scheduled and called for this month. Only one proposed meeting of the council has not
taken place, not two.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: As the Minister has confirmed that regular meetings have not
been held, can he also confirm that the Transport Advisory Council is being gagged, as many
people in the transport industry believe to be the case, and if this is not the case why have
many crucial transport matters that should have been aired before the council been handled
behind closed doors by officials committees?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: The Transport Advisory Council is meeting later this year
because of crucial matters about transport. It was the council's wish that it did not meet until
further and full information was available.
Mr Isbey: Can the Minister confirm that under the previous Labour Government the
Transport Advisory Council met almost every every 2 months?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I have no idea how often the Transport Advisory Council
met under the previous Labour Government, but if it met every 2 months the result was not
very good, and all the Government received was a green paper and a white paper from the
Minister who chaired the committee.

5. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Transport, When will a decision be

the airport runway.

6. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Statistics, What is the exact

jure married couples in New Zealand. This figure is not available, the reason being that
demographic statistics generally only relate to individuals and not to couples as a unit. The
Department of Statistics has, however, estimated that the number of de jure married persons
in the country at 31 March 1977 based on the provisional 1976 population census data would
be 1 432 000. At a quick calculation in general terms- and this is a very general assessment-
I think one could take it that there would be some 716 000 couples.

5,401, the statistics continually used by the member for Wigram, that one in three marriages
are breaking down under the National Government, must be totally erroneous?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Yes, that figure would be highly questionable, to put it at its
mildest. If we take anything like one-third of 716 000, that would be about 230 000 marriages
in general, and it would require an extraordinary turnover in marriages in any one year to
make that figure stick.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is not the question and the Minister's answer based on an
irrelevant and erroneous assumption, because is it not true that the Social Welfare Depart-
ment recognises not only de jure marriages but also de facto marriages?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: While I do not have the figures with me, those numbers
would not alter the general pattern. If we add a few more to satisfy the point, say to make the
total 800 000, it would require an enormous number of breakdowns to justify that one in
three figure.
Hon. H. J. Walker: Could the Minister confirm that the number of marriage break-
downs referred to in the report of the Domestic Purposes Review Committee relates to
marriage breaks in any one year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Yes. This is just a general assessment, the best that we can
make, about the number of married couples, and I would require notice to give anything on
the de facto side.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is not the fallacy in the proposition by the member for Raglan
that her question is based on the number of decrees absolute, which are irrelevant and do not

URGENT QUESTION
Christchurch Flood Damage
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Works and
Development, In view of the widespread damage caused by slips and floods over the weekend
to homes and property in Lyttelton, harbour bays, the hillside suburbs of Christchurch, and
the homes alongside the Heathcote and Avon rivers, would he now tell the House of the
specific measures he is taking to meet the crisis facing the residents?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The situation in regard to
the most recent flooding and erosion in Lyttelton Borough is that the local authority must
take action to assist landowners who have suffered from erosion or flooding. The North
Canterbury Catchment Board is the statutory authority set up under the Soil Conservation
and Rivers Control Act to provide technical and financial assistance for those erosion and
flood control works which are eligible under the Act. All applications for assistance must be
channelled through the North Canterbury Catchment Board in the first instance. Lyttelton
Borough and Akaroa County are not included in the North Canterbury Catchment Board's
area for soil conservation and water management works. However, I have attempted to
obtain their acceptance of the full services of the catchment board. Up until now these
efforts have been unsuccessful, but I am hopeful that agreement will be reached. The full
statutory powers and administrative expertise of the North Canterbury Catchment Board are
in effect in the Christchurch area for all soil conservation and water management matters.

STANDING ORDER 181—ALLEGED BREACH
Mr SPEAKER: This might be a convenient time to refer to a point of order raised last
week. On Friday, the Deputy Prime Minister said: "I raise a question under Standing Order
181: 'Unbecoming references to House, Judiciary, etc.-No member shall use unbecoming
words against the House or any member thereof, against any member of the Judiciary, or
against any statute unless for the purpose of moving for its repeal or in speaking to any such
motion.' I refer to a reported statement in the Christchurch Star of Thursday, 30 June. The
headline stated: 'Ship of State being steered from the gutter'. The article contains the
following statement: "The principle of ministerial responsibility is not working in New
Zealand the way it should, Mangere's Labour member of Parliament, Mr D. R. Lange,
believes.' The article states: 'It was an unusual experience to go from a law practice, from the
bowels of the magistrate's court, to a place like Parliament where the ship of State is being
steered from the gutter.' I suggest that that is an unbecoming reference to the House. I am
sorry that I was not able to talk with the honourable member before I raised the point,
because he is absent. I checked with some of his colleagues, and he is not within the precincts
at present. Otherwise, of course, I would have notified him. I suggest that this is a breach of
Standing Order 181."
The matter having been raised, I decided it would be preferable for me to allow the
member to speak before considering the merit of the complaint.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): I am grateful to you for affording me the opportunity to make
an explanation. It is as well that I was not in the House on Friday, because had I been taxed
with the matter then I would have disowned the use of the word "gutter". Certainly I did not
intend to use that word because, apart from anything else, it is a mixed metaphor that is
rather nonsensical. My belief then, and now, is that I did not actually use the word, but I
have checked over the weekend and I accept absolutely that the report is correct when it
refers to the use of the word "gutter".
The word I had in mind was "scuppers", and what I was trying to do before an audience
of students at Canterbury University was use colourful language showing that the Govern-
ment, in my view, lacked a sense of direction and purpose in the course it was taking, and
that in doing so it was overriding or ignoring Parliament itself. It has been drawn to my
attention that the use of the word "gutter" in other contexts is unacceptable in the House. It
should be accepted by me—and is that I was being too colourful, perhaps, in saying what I
did, and if I transgressed by going beyond what was acceptable and giving offence to other
members of the House, then I apologise for that.
Mr SPEAKER: Unless there is strong reason, I do not like to limit the use of colourful
language, which adds to rather than subtracts from life, but there are limits that we should all
observe, and there cannot be carte blanche in the use of colourful phrases. As honourable
members will recall, privilege relates to matters that affect the ability of individual members
to carry out their duties as members; it relates to matters that affect the ability of the House
to carry out its business as a Legislature; and it relates to matters that depress the standing of
the House in the regard of the public, and bring it into hatred or contempt. Had the matter
been one of privilege, perhaps I should have had something to consider, but I am very glad
that the question of privilege was not raised.
The question raised was whether there was a breach of Standing Order 181. The term
"gutter" normally implies revulsion, something obscene, or something of that sort, and a
real or unreal suggestion of insufficient reference to Parliament by the group of members of
Parliament that constitutes Cabinet would not be of that type. The member concerned has
already expressed his regret for any offence the use of the term may have caused, but to
avoid the overuse of the machinery of privilege, happily I think, the Acting Prime Minister
did not raise the question of privilege; and I certainly have no intention of raising it on my
own initiative.
The question remaining is solely whether there has been a breach of Standing Order
181. Here the point we should bear in mind is that the order relates to the conduct of
debates. It is in Part XXI of the Standing Orders, headed "Rules of Debate", and in my
interpretation the group of Standing Orders that follow it relate to the conduct of debates.
Therefore I read Standing Order 181 as meaning that, in the course of debate in the House,
no member shall use unbecoming words against the House or against any member thereof,


## p. 1146 (#388) ###########################################

1146
5 July

against any member of the judiciary, or against any statute unless for the purpose of moving
for its repeal or in speaking in the House to any such questions. In the circumstances,
although I find the term highly objectionable-and it has been agreed by the member
concerned that it was inappropriate as the statement was made outside the House and
Standing Order 181 relates to debate inside the House, the rule does not apply.

(1) The Governor-General may from time to time, by Order in Council, declare that goods of a
specified class are approved or special goods.

submissions from the public, and to make recommendations, on the need for all those goods that
are approved or special goods to continue to be approved or special goods, and on the need for any
other goods to become approved or special goods; and no Order in Council shall be made under

fit, and in that case shall not so recommend until it has considered all objections received by it

FISHERIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): On behalf of the
Minister of Fisheries, I move, That this Bill be now read a third time.
Bill read a third time.
NATIONAL HOUSING COMMISSION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. This is a short Bill of two effective clauses. It makes two amendments to the
National Housing Commission Act. I deal with the simplest clause first. Clause 3 makes a
purely machinery correction to an anomaly. As I explained when I introduced the Bill,
section 7 of the principal Act allows the Minister of Housing to appoint a temporary
chairman of the National Housing Commission when the chairman is absent from New
Zealand, or when, in the Minister's opinion, the chairman is unable to act. There is no
provision for a temporary chairman to be appointed if the office is vacant. Clearly that
should be possible. The chairman might resign or die in circumstances in which it would be
convenient to appoint a temporary replacement pending the appointment of a permanent
chairman. Clause 3 enables such an appointment to be made.
Clause 2 is of somewhat greater significance. It increases the membership of the
commission by two, by increasing the number of ministerial appointments from four to six.
When I moved the second reading of the principal Act in 1972, I said, "The Bill contemp-
lates the establishment of the National Housing Commission, whose functions are of an
advisory nature in relation to a wide range of housing matters", and later, on the
membership of the commission, "It is my intention to cover as wide a field as possible in the
housing area." That was 5 years ago, and it is now appropriate to review the membership of
the commission and the work the commission is called upon to do. I believe that the
commission has fulfilled the promises of its originators, and is performing a useful function
as an independent body to which the Government can look for advice, and its research
provides a second opinion. I am convinced that an increase in the commission's membership
will enhance both its advisory function and its capacity for work. It will provide the
commission with a wider range of expertise and talent, and will enable it to make an even
better contribution to housing knowledge and background research.
I have no particular persons or areas of expertise in mind, but it will enable me to fill
some gaps in the commission as they appear from time to time. I believe that a strengthening
of the financial expertise is desirable. It is also worth noting that at present there are no
13 Vol. 411


## p. 1154 (#396) ###########################################

1154
5 July
National Housing Commission Amendment Bill
women on the commission. The creation of the two new places will enable those shortcom-
ings to be remedied. I commend this short Bill, with its very restricted clauses, to the House.
I believe it will improve the commission's ability to fulfil its function as well as dealing with
what is essentially a relatively minor drafting anomaly.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): The Minister has said the Bill
has two effective clauses. How effective, of course, remains to be seen, particularly in the
light of the ineffectiveness of the commission, or its inability, so far, to convince the
Government of the right course of action. The Minister also said that the time was
appropriate to review the membership of the commission, and the work it should undertake.
One can only say that if this is the Government's answer to the housing problem and the
general chaos it has created in that area, then heaven help us, and heaven help the building
industry and prospective home owners.
The Bill changes the structure of the housing commission, which, according to its first
annual report in 1975, is an advisory body the principal functions of which are to review the
housing needs of the people of New Zealand and at appropriate intervals to undertake a
comprehensive assessment of the subsisting and prospective position relating to housing.
The role the commission has to play has been simply and succinctly summarised by a
commission member, who said: "We spend hundreds of millions a year on housing, and
therefore we ought to spend a few thousand dollars thinking about housing".
The functions of the commission are detailed in section 4, and especially in subsection
(1) (a) to (k). Five of those paragraphs—(a) to (d) and (i)—are of particular significance. I
want to remind the House of those functions, because they raise questions about the
amending Bill before us. The first function laid down in the principal Act is a general
one-to advise the Minister on all matters relating to the provision of dwellings in New
Zealand. What does the Bill do to improve the quality of that advice? If the Minister
considers that the quality of the advice will be improved by the Bill, will he give an
undertaking that that advice will be listened to more than the advice received from the
commission in the past? If the Minister considers that additional members will be some
help and he seemed to indicate that in his introductory comments-why did he decide to
stop at two additional members as provided for in clause 2?
The Minister mentioned that there are no women members of the commission. We
would all agree that women have a very important role in housing, and a great understanding
of the problem. Why not make a specific provision for the appointment of women? Why not
make a provision that would cater for Auckland, which is not at present represented on the
commission, but which clearly has the greatest housing problem in New Zealand? There is
no land development expertise, but although the Minister had an opportunity under clause 2
to remedy the deficiency, he has made no move to do so. Or is it perhaps that the
amendments are simply to provide additional personnel on the commission to reverse
decisions and recommendations that have already been handed down to the Minister? For
instance, the development of a new town at Rolleston had the approval of the present
commission, but was destroyed by the National Government, without a skerrick of an
alternative being offered.
Hon. W. L. Young: A white elephant.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: The Minister of Works and Development says that
Rolleston was a white elephant, yet the people of Canterbury, who are vitally interested in
the subject, came out only last week with a very strong commendation of the Rolleston
concept. I am interested that the Minister of Housing, who is a Canterbury member, wants
to downgrade the people who are interested. Is it intended to set aside the view of the
housing commission on that important matter?
That leads me to the commission's second function, and I turn again to the principal
Act, which states that the commission shall inquire into and keep under review the housing
needs of New Zealanders. In what way will the Bill assist the commission in such an inquiry
or review? Reports handed down by the commission reveal that already there have been
several such inquiries. One must presume that was what led the commission to state on page
6 of its 1976 report that: "The commission remains deeply concerned over the provision of
adequate mortgage finance for housing." What will the new structure provided in clause 2 do
to improve that situation? The commission has already made recommendations to the
Government, and the response was the deliberate introduction of a financial policy that
made the situation very much worse. The Minister cannot deny that. Will six voices, instead
of four, have more effect on the Minister and his colleagues? That would be a pretty fond
hope. Or will the Minister continue to tell young couples that all they have to do is put off


## p. 1155 (#397) ###########################################

5 July
1155
National Housing Commission Amendment Bill
having their families for a few years and they will be able to aspire to a home of their own?
Will he continue to let mortgagee sales go onwards and upwards?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! We must not roam, or we will have replies to this and replies to
that. Mortgagee sales have nothing to do with this. The question is whether or not the
number of members should be increased from four to six, and whether there should be a
temporary chairman on occasions.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: I make the point that the Bill alters the structure of the
housing commission, the most important advisory body that the Government has. The
Opposition, the House, and the country are entitled to know how much credence the
Government will give to the commission's advice; and what effect the changes will have on
the quality of that advice, and on the Government's response to that advice. Where does the
commission fit into the scheme of things? Will the two additional members give any muscle
to the commission's recommendations?
Resulting from its inquiry into the housing needs of the next decade, on page 5 of its
1976 report the commission stated: "As the result of its inquiry the commission believes that
planning in the housing sector should be based on the provision of between 360 000 and 380
000 additional dwelling units in the decade ending March 1986. If, as seems likely, the bulk
of these additional units will have to be provided by new construction, house building
industries will need to have the capacity of an annual production of about 35 000 units by
1981, and 40 000 units by 1986." The question I put to the Minister is: will the Government
respond to the commission's recommendations as a consequence of the change of structure,
or will it pursue the course it has followed in responding to the recommendations already
made, and do as it has done this year-reduce its housing goal to somewhere between 24 000
and 26 000 houses or, if the present trends continue, to about 22 000 houses?
Will the two new members of the commission, as provided for in clause 2, be able to
persuade the Government to recognise the seriousness of the situation, or are they being put
on the commission to persuade the existing commission members that they have it all wrong?
In what way will the new proposal expedite the third function of the commission as set out in
the principal Act: "To undertake at successive intervals of not more than 5 years nor less
than 3 years from the commencement of this Act a comprehensive assessment of the
subsisting and prospective position relating to housing in New Zealand"? According to the
Act, a survey is due by October of this year. Will the revamped commission that the Minister
is telling us about tonight persuade the Government to give the commission the necessary
resources and personnel to enable it to fulfil its statutory requirements? I believe that if we
are to alter the commission's position, we are entitled to ask whether-as it appears that the
commission is in some difficulty about fulfilling its statutory requirements-it will now be in
a position to attain that goal; or, again, is the alternative simply to censor what comes
forward to ensure that the comprehensive amendment required under the Act finally
appears in a way that will not embarrass the Government?
The fourth function of the commission, as provided in the principal Act, is a short
one-to encourage research into matters affecting housing policy. In his introduction, the
Minister said there were deficiencies in the present commission because of the number of
members. It has only four members, and I agree that it needs to be a much wider group of
people to embrace the expertise and skills required to give the necessary guidance, and I said
that in my view the commission could in fact be increased by more than two. I also wish to
question the Minister about research. Is special attention to be given to appointing someone
who can properly supervise research? My understanding is that the research vote has been
cut by $50,000, that the commission has a research staff of two, and that it has the
opportunity to use the research staff of the Housing Corporation, which in fact is understaf-
fed by three and has only five appointments of the eight provided for in the establishment.
Will the new commission continue the kind of “Mickey Mouse" operation that we have seen
over the past 12 months, or will it be able to persuade the Government that the research unit
should have the money and the people required to do the job?
When we are discussing a Bill like this, which increases the number of personnel on the
commission when the housing industry is in its present state, the question arises as to

WEDNESDAY, 6 JULY 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Blue Streak Rail Service
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Railways, In view of the most
recent press reports, which confirm that nearly 9000-I think that should be 18 000-people
have signed the petition to retain the Blue Streak rail service, can he now give his assurance
that the service will be replaced with locomotive-hauled twinsets?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways): The twinset railcars are being
converted to carriages for use on five routes selected because of difficult terrain and proven
social needs. New Plymouth-Wellington is not one of these routes. However, I have
directed the General Manager of Railways to report on the feasibility of the reintroduction
of a rail passenger service on this particular route, and further consideration will be given
when the report is made to the Government. I should emphasise that public demand will be
taken into consideration.
Mr Marshall: In view of the report that the Minister has requested from the depart-
ment, is he also prepared to receive submissions from interested parties from the West Coast
North Island area, who may help him and his department in arriving at a decision?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: Yes. The honourable gentleman will acknowledge that I
received him with a deputation.
Mr Friedlander: Can the Minister confirm that when the Labour Government was in
power it made no allowance for the replacement of the Blue Streak railcar with a rail service,
and that the Labour Government placed the orders for the buses that will be used as
replacements despite the fact that in 1972 the National Government called for tenders for
replacement railcars?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I can confirm that the previous Labour Government
placed the orders for the buses. From that I gather it intended to use the buses in the place of
railcars. As Minister of Railways I now realise the difficulty the Labour Government would
have had in obtaining replacement railcars at that time.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Is the Minister aware that an undertaking was given by the previous
Labour Government to the people of Taranaki that a rail service would be maintained and
not replaced with a bus service.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I was unaware that the previous Labour Government had
given that undertaking, but as I have explained on many occasions, I fail to see how it could
have provided the railcars or trainsets for the service.
Hon. David Thomson: When the Minister assumed office in December 1975, did he find
any evidence that the Labour Government had made any provision either for trainsets or
railcar replacements for the Blue Streak?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: All I found was a report that the railcars would not be
able to continue the run. No provision had been made for replacement of railcars, and no
thought had been given to trainsets. That eventuated some months after I became Minister.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Arising from the Minister's reply that his department is
undertaking a feasibility study into the longer-term possible replacement of a passenger rail
service, is the statement in the Evening Post of 21 June that senior departmental officials
have indicated that railcar carriages converted to locomotive-hauled twinset trains could be
used on the Wanganui and Taranaki run from Wellington premature?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I take from that question that the member wants to know
whether the statement was premature. As I told the member for Wanganui, I have asked for
a report on whether it is possible to get passenger rail services back on to that run. I cannot
comment yet because I have not had a chance to study the report, but even if it were
possible, on the reports I already have from the Railways Department it would be some time
before they could be replaced.
Mr Quigley: Has the Minister received representations on this matter from the member
for New Plymouth, and have those representations been responsible for his directing the

average ordinary-time weekly wage, making beneficiaries financially independent in their
retirement, prop-up payments introduced by the last Labour Government to subsidise
minimal pensions are, in accordance with National's election manifesto, being phased out.

a week for single people, and from $51.26 to $60.36 a week for married couples, all tax-free.

given: $3.59, from $36.22 to $39.81 a week, for single people; $5.36, from $60.36 to $65.72 a
week, for married couples where an under-age wife was included; and $7.26, from $60.36 to
$67.62 a week, for married couples where both parties were eligible. To summarise, $1.2
million of prop-up additional benefit has been replaced by $126 million of increased cash-in-
hand benefits. All superannuation will be increased twice yearly in line with increases in the
average ordinary-time wage as assessed by the Department of Labour. The next increase will
be announced shortly.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! This does seem a vast reply. Is there much more of it?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: No, Mr Speaker, about half a line. National superannuation will
reach the maximum of 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage in August 1978.

recently received recommendations from the Environmental Council suggesting procedures
that could be followed to bring this about, but in the present financial situation it will not be

already receive assistance and co-operation from Government departments. A recent

ence proceedings, and officials from a number of departments attended and presented
papers. Environmental groups can also make application through the sport and recreation
programme for financial assistance. However, this avenue is, of course, concerned with the
recreational aspects of their activities. Last year the Royal Forest and Bird Protection
Society received assistance totalling $13,240 through the national projects scheme of the
programme. No other solely environmental group applied for assistance under the national
scheme last year.

environmental groups, and one would not want to undermine the principle of voluntary
effort. I also know, of course, of the suggestion by the Environmental Council, as I
mentioned in my initial answer. However, it is not possible in the present financial situation
to introduce any new scheme at present.
Dr Shearer: Has any money been granted for outdoor and environmental education?

education in the environment last year, and made a contribution in that way. Probably the
best example of environmental education and outdoor activities would be the grant of
$97,000 towards the Otago Youth Adventure Trust for its buildings at Tautuku.
Mr Prebble: Can the inference be taken from the Minister's answer that the Govern-
ment will be giving assistance to environmental groups next year, which is election year?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The Government will continue to consider the matter, but will
make no promises about what will happen next year.
