DISCUSSION OF MOTIONS
OECD Consultations
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I move, That this House acknowledges the
success of the Prime Minister in having inserted into the communiqué, following the OECD
ministerial meeting, language that makes clear that multilateral consultations in OECD on
trade questions extend to agriculture as much as to industrial problems. Some would say that
that was stating the obvious, and that this should have been accepted as the norm. I should
have liked to think that that was true, but unfortunately it was not. What the Prime Minister
achieved in his discussions with the OECD nations in Paris was the verbal and written
recognition by the governments of those countries of the importance of agriculture to New
Zealand, and of the fairness of writing that importance into the communiqué at the end of
the session.
It was the written affirmation that New Zealand has long sought-a very important
affirmation that augurs well for this country's future exports. New Zealand understood that
this was intended in the pledge; we had hoped that agricultural as well as industrial problems
and exports were covered. History has proved us wrong, and, if agriculture was considered
before, it was considered on a very much lower level than the exports of industrial nations.
Now, as the wording states, it will be considered as much as industrial problems. I believe
that is one of the successes of the Prime Minister's recent trip overseas. He has had successes
in many other fields, but—
Hon. Members: Ha, ha!
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: I repeat, for the benefit of members opposite and particularly the
member for New Lynn, that the Prime Minister has had successes in many other fields, but
that this will be a long and enduring one. Indeed, he had one success that was supported
publicly by the Labour Party-the Gleneagles agreement. But I emphasise that this
agreement will last longer and be of more importance to New Zealand than that one. I have
no doubt that the nations who signed it will acknowledge and stand by the declaration. It is
important that the member nations of the OECD should use the existing possibilities for
consultation to find and implement multilaterally acceptable solutions to trade problems,
whether they be industrial or agricultural.
In our case, we sought the inclusion of agriculture in the communiqué, not on any
emotional ground, but on the basis of rational logic that it was fair to all nations within the
group that the major exports of the important industries of all countries should be included,
rather than nominating just one sector-namely, the industrial sector-and excluding the
agricultural sector. I believe that New Zealand's logical arguments have at last been
recognised by the OECD members. We have had problems and difficulties in marketing our
agricultural products around the world, and particularly in gaining access to some of the
industrial nations that have the economic strength to protect their own agricultural produc-
ers. We know that at this stage our own Deputy Prime Minister is overseas endeavouring to
gain or to continue access to EEC countries. We need a continuing commitment from the
industrial nations that they will not put unreasonable embargoes upon trade with nations
such as New Zealand, whose people literally live by the exports of agricultural commodities.
In this context, I can only say that, although through international forums many
countries have endeavoured to rationalise some of the trading problems that confront the
world, our problem as a trader of agricultural products has become more difficult rather than
more simple over the years. I emphasise that it has become more difficult, rather than
improving. That situation has not been helped by the fact that the OECD members
previously appeared to apply the declaration with greater assiduity to industrial products
than to agricultural products. That is why we wanted it spelt out in this instance, so that both
will stand as equal partners or as equal areas of concern.
It is understandable that some New Zealanders have found it hard in the last 3 or 4
years, when we have suffered a very severe reversal in our terms of trade and overseas


## p. 1176 (#418) ###########################################

1176
6 July
Discussion of Motions
balance of payments, to appreciate that we should honour our commitment not to impose
embargoes upon imports-that we should honour our commitment to the OECD nations
and the pledge we signed, particularly when they saw the difficulties that we as a trading
nation were having in trying to gain access for our own exports. I would be the first to admit
that it has been difficult to stand up and say that we should honour our pledge to the OECD
nations not to alter our imports or increase any embargoes while we are having such
difficulties in trading in our own products, which are so important to us.
In recent international forums it has been popular to try to place the nations of the
world into three different categories: the oil exporters, which are the new rich; the industrial
nations, which one could probably term the old rich; and the developing nations. New
Zealand does not fall into any of those three camps; none of the categories typifies New
Zealand. We are not an oil exporter; we are not an industrial nation; nor could we be
classified as a developing nation. We are a nation with a high standard of living. It may be
lower than the standard of living in some countries, but it is high measured by any rational
scale. For our standard of living we depend, as no other country depends, on the export of
our land-based products; that is where we are unique among the developed nations or the
nations with a high standard of living. We depend almost totally on the export of our land-
based products, and that is why, in the changed international scene since the hike in oil
prices in 1973, we have found it more difficult to maintain the standard of living New
Zealanders have worked for over many years.
We sell huge quantities of goods internationally when one considers our size and
population as a nation, but the prices we have received have in no way reflected the
increased costs of the imports coming into the country. We have been selling foodstuffs at
prices that have lagged behind the very rapidly escalating costs we faced in importing
industrial goods. That is why the Prime Minister, the Deputy Prime Minister, and others
have been at pains to explain at international forums the need for the world to recognise that
New Zealand could rightfully and justly claim that it should have more permanent and more
favoured access into some of the markets of the industrial nations. To date, we have had only
moderate success, but I am hopeful that, now that the OECD nations-or what, I suppose,
could be called the rich men's club of the world-accept that they should give equal
consideration to trade in agricultural commodities as to trade in industrial goods, we should
make progress in trading our agricultural products internationally, and be able to sell them at
a faster rate than has been possible in the last few years. I might add that, when I referred to
the last few years, it has been a fair number of years in this instance.
As I said earlier, we do not fit into any of the popular groups into which commentators
like to classify the nations of the world, and we have a unique economy in what it provides
for New Zealanders. However, it is important that New Zealanders understand that we have
still not achieved the ultimate. We have achieved an acceptance or an acknowledgment by
the member nations of the OECD, but we now have to impress upon them, and to try to
ensure that they accept, the commitment they made when they signed the pledge. The
pledge must not merely be put into the record; it must be honoured-and that will
undoubtedly require the continuing persuasion and the best efforts of the Government and
Ministers from the Prime Minister down. I am sure it will be given that attention.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I was surprised at the tone of
the speech made by the Minister of Fisheries. It was the quietest and probably the
unhappiest speech he has ever made, because he knows that the much vaunted intervention
in Europe achieved nothing. He knows that the Prime Minister operated from exactly the
same brief as the present Minister of Energy Resources used last year; and if the member
cares to go back even further, he will find that it was exactly the same brief that I used in
1974. The only difference between the Prime Minister's efforts and those on the two earlier
occasions is that neither the Minister of Energy Resources nor I had a battery of press staff to
emblazon the story of our alleged achievements.
I initiated the custom of a New Zealand Minister's actually going into the drafting
session. I spent hours in that drafting session, and the report of that conference makes it
clear that at that meeting New Zealand was successful in having trade in all commodities
accepted as the expression used—not just trade in industrial goods. That was in 1974, but
unfortunately, despite our efforts, it was followed by a series of OECD member decisions to
cut down on agricultural trade. I shall list them shortly.
The present Minister of Energy Resources was reported in the Dominion of 24 June
1976 as saying: "Negotiations on the pledge continued throughout Monday night before New
Zealand was satisfied with promises from its partners that the agreement to keep trade wide

open applied to agricultural as well as to industrial products." The Prime Minister had to go
back with his press corps and claim a third victory on the same barren battlefield. I wonder if
the present Minister of Energy Resources will speak in this debate. He might try to claim for
himself the same glory from the last meeting. He is reported as claiming it, but that was in

In 1974, the following statement was issued by the OECD: "That governments of
OECD member countries agree. . . (3) that unilateral trade or other current account
measures by one or more member countries to deal with the situation would aggravate the
problem of other countries and, if generalised, would be self-defeating and have a depressing
effect on the world economy; that countries have responsibilities, both as importers and
exporters, to avoid disruption of regular trade flows." It was recognised that New Zealand's
regular trade flow with Europe was significantly in agricultural produce.
Mr Falloon: It doesn't say that.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: It was recognised as regular trade, not regular industrial trade.
Mr Falloon: Not specifically.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: It was specified as regular trade of all kinds. We do not export
manufactured goods to Europe, and certainly did not in 1974, but I suppose members can
quibble and think there is something worth while in this motion. At best, the Prime Minister
was only emphasising what had been done previously. It remains to be seen if he has
achieved anything. Today's Dominion headlines the form of present developments as,
"Brussels gets tough with Japan." It is fairly clear that the whole business is an attempt
towards greater self-sufficiency by the Common Market countries, and has nothing to do
with vague promises on trade liberalisation; rather is it a selfish concern with their own
immediate prospects.
Because New Zealand is a small nation, we would be foolish to attempt to retaliate, and
extremely shortsighted if we went in, as the Prime Minister has done on other occasions,
threatening to wave a big stick. Our interest is in expanding trade in as many diverse ways as
possible, and not in making threats in any particular market. If we initiated steps to limit
trade, we would be foolish in the extreme. Members opposite know that they have taken
steps to limit imports, and have invited criticism from OECD members as well as from the
Australians in specific cases; and we have suffered the imposition of quotas and various
other forms of restraint.

Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): I move, That this House notes with great concern

The transport industry in New Zealand is in chaos and the Minister should resign forthwith,

which have been under study for 18 months. The Transport Advisory Council has not met
since last August.
The 1975 National Party manifesto states: "The prime aim of a National Government in
the transport field would be to co-ordinate all transport services and equipment to obtain full
utilisation so that the best result for the consumer could be obtained. Transport, as a service

industry, is the largest single expenditure element in our economy. As such it is vital to the
nation's well-being," Those are fine words, with which the Opposition would agree, if they
were accompanied by action. The next paragraph in the manifesto states: "A National
Government will re-establish the Transport Advisory Council as the principal advisor to
Government on transport matters. The reconstituted council will be responsible for advising
on transport co-ordination and will be given a limited decision-making role."
Regional councils were to be established, but the Government knows that the only
regional transport council was established in Canterbury by the Labour Government,
although no members were appointed. The Government has done nothing to establish such
councils in other regions, although they are needed. The Transport Advisory Council has
been ignored, while teams of officials, no doubt from the "think tank", control matters that
are the rightful province of this council.
The Labour Government reconstituted the Transport Advisory Council in the Ministry
of Transport Amendment Act 1973. I attended my first meeting of the council in December
1972, and found that it was nothing but a talking forum, with too many members all with
conflicting views. The Labour Government reduced the number of members on the council
from 20 to 8, and each had a deputy. Road, rail, sea, and air interests were represented, as
well as the Federation of Labour, the manufacturers, and Federated Farmers. During the
term of the Labour Government, that group met regularly about every 6 to 8 weeks. The
council combined the best departmental men, including the General Manager of the
Railways and the Secretary for Transport, and practical men of great ability, representing
private industry. Those men are still on the council, but this Government will not use them.
Now, perhaps as a result of this article in the Evening Post and perhaps because of this
motion, the Minister has decided to schedule a meeting for 19 July. That decision was made
last week, but one member has told me that he has not received an agenda, and another
member told me last night that he had not been told that a meeting had been called, but had
been listening to the radio yesterday and had heard the Minister say that he was calling this
meeting. The Minister has been stung into action, although it has taken him 11 months. The
Transport Advisory Council should be the principal adviser to the Government, so I do not
know what role the various bodies that come under the Transport Advisory Council are
carrying out. The council has an important role to play, and wants to fulfil it, but it has said
to the Opposition that the industry is in utter chaos- and it is a shambles. The Minister
should resign if he cannot do his job and carry out the policy on which his Government was
elected.
The Minister has said that all the council did under the Labour Government was
produce a green paper. That is quite incorrect. The green paper was prepared not by the
council, but by a Cabinet committee. It was then open for public discussion, and the council
had a number of meetings with the green paper committee. By the end of 1975, we were on
the verge of reaching full agreement on matters that this Government has been considering
for the last 18 months- and I refer particularly to the vexed question of road/rail competition
and the extension of the 40-mile limit. What progress has been made on this question? The
Cabinet considered this last year and sent it to a subcommittee. We have seen no progress,
and the transport industry can get no answers from the Government. The president of the
Road Transport Association has been quoted as saying that private enterprise would be out
of business if it worked as slowly as did the Government. The Minister referred to the green
paper as a socialist document destined for the rubbish bin, but he has already been on his
hands and knees trying to recover it, because if anything realistic is to be done some of the
recommendations made in the green paper must be carried out. The Minister of Transport
must be regretting his statement that the green paper was a socialist document that he
discarded in the rubbish tin.
The Minister of Agriculture recently said that the Transport industry was in a shambles.
Perhaps he and some of his colleagues will join the Opposition in calling for the resignation
of the Minister of Transport. The green paper suggested that the New Zealand Railways
could be reconstituted as a public corporation. In 1969, a remit to this effect was carried by
the National Party conference. What does the Minister say about that? Has that remit also
been dismissed as being socialist? The Transport Advisory Council studied thoroughly the
Wilbur Smith transport survey, which was commissioned by the previous National Govern-
ment. That survey was rejected. The 1975 National Party manifesto stated that the
recommendations made by the Wilbur Smith report would be progressively reintroduced. Is
it to be reintroduced to justify the expenditure of the $1 million the survey cost? The
transport industry does not want those recommendations carried out, so why has the

-farming. Confidence is returning after the shattering experience of 3 years of hard labour
under the Labour Government, and the shattering of the very roots of the farming economy
at that time, with a downturn in production, a build-up in costs, and so forth.
Now, half way through 1977, a new era is emerging in farming and primary production.
Encouraged by the Government, New Zealand must, and will, farm its way out of the
unreality that we had― the shattering of the economy, and the mess created between 1972
and 1975. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Overseas Trade have been successfully
involved in international negotiations, some of which have been referred to this afternoon by
the Minister of Fisheries; and at present the Minister of Overseas Trade is negotiating-we
hope successfully-the continued entry into the European Economic Community of our
major agricultural products, which the Deputy Leader of the Opposition does not seem to be
concerned about this afternoon.
The story now is one of confidence; we find confidence returning throughout the
important survey compiled by the agricultural economics research unit, a comprehensive
report that gives findings on 76 factors affecting farming right across the board. To get
farming back on the rails and to get production up again, there has to be a renewal of
investment in farming. This report shows that farm investment in the next 12 months will be
higher than it has been in the last 12 months. When we look at the intentions of farmers to
reseed and develop pastures, when we see what they are going to do in planting lucerne and
forest trees, in capital expenditure on fencing and the erection of new farm buildings- I
could go on right across the board-we see in every sector a renewal of confidence disclosed
by farmers, investing at a higher level than they have for many years.
In 1974 and 1975, up to the change of Government, there was a great fall-off in
reinvestment in farming, which is only now starting to come right; this will be reflected in the
next few years as this reinvestment is continued, with the incentives given by the National
Government. We shall find that production will increase, steadily to start off with, but
dramatically in the coming years, as the National Government's positive approach takes
effect. We see in this comprehensive survey a great and a steady swing to reinvestment in
farming right across the board, and this is important. It is the only way to get an upturn in
our production.
Let us look briefly at what the Government has been doing to make the results found in
this survey possible. The dairy beef market guarantee scheme, in which a $5 supplement was
paid on all registered calves, has been an outstanding success, with a reduction in the bobby
calf kill of more than 160 000 during the last season. This scheme was so successful that it will
be continued this year with the guarantee set at $50 a head. In the 12 months ending January
1977, sheep numbers increased by 1 500 000. The livestock incentive scheme is an outstand-
ing success, and will be more successful in the coming years. The survey shows that 9 percent
of the farmers approached have already applied, and that in the next 2 years up to another 20
percent will be applying under the present terms and conditions for the livestock incentive
scheme. In this way, we will farm ourselves out of the economic shambles created between
1972 and 1975. It is interesting that the latest figures I have on the livestock incentive

Diplomatic Post-Bahrain
Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel): I move, That this House notes with satisfaction the
announcement of the establishment of a diplomatic post in Bahrain to help open the way to
additional markets for New Zealand produce in Middle East markets but regrets that the
Opposition opposes this decision after previously advocating expansion of trade channels and
calls on the Opposition to act in the interests of New Zealand export opportunities.
In the last few weeks members opposite have opposed every Government proposal, but
it is strange to find them opposing the move to open a post in Bahrain, a positive step
towards increasing our export trade in that area. The Labour Party said in its policy: "That
New Zealand's economic and social development depends on increased overseas earnings,
and that the Labour Government is committed to continue and expand its vigorous trade
policies." I am surprised that the member for Mt. Albert has not endorsed the Government's
move. We must take every opportunity to regain the overseas trade lost while the Labour
Government was in office. In 1973, after the National Government had lost the general
election, New Zealand had a balance of payments surplus of $1,000 million. Before the
Labour Government left office, it had arranged to borrow $2,300 million. Through its
mismanagement of the economy, it had turned the credit balance into a deficit. In 1966, New
Zealand sold to the Middle East goods valued at $1.67 million. In 1975, exports to that
region totalled $42 million, and in 1976, after the change of Government, they had almost
doubled in value and amounted to $78 million.
Mr T. J. Young: That was the after effect of Joe Walding's efforts.
Mr SCHULTZ: All right. Then look at the trading posts opened in China and Russia
during the term of the Labour Minister of Overseas Trade. Exports to China reached a value
of $16 million after that post was opened-nothing when compared with exports to the
Middle East-and in 1975, the last year of the Labour Government, the figure had dropped
to $10 million. However, with the change to a National Government, exports to China now
stand at a record $25 million worth. W hen the post in Russia was opened, exports totalled
$45 million, reaching $62 million under the National Government, but nowhere near the
value of exports to the Middle East, where the trade growth is the most rapid in the world.
Surely the Opposition can see the advantage of opening up this new post in Bahrain. As a
free, independent port, it could become very much the Hong Kong of the Middle East.
Bahrain offers the greatest opportunity to consistently increase trade anywhere in that area.
New Zealand engineers will be employed in the development of the new port. The meat
exporters and the Meat Producers Board support the opening of the post in Bahrain. It will
open the way not only for exports to a rapidly developing region, but also for trans-shipment
to other countries around the gulf. New Zealand is a major partner in the construction of the
new port, and will be given berthing priority. No duty will be charged on the goods, and
better selling and buying opportunities will be available. These advantages do not exist in
any other country. I cannot understand why the Opposition is against this move, except that
it seems to oppose anything put forward by the Government.
The member for Mt. Albert has said that New Zealand might as well open up a trading
post on Norfolk Island, a little place that has not even been mentioned in trading circles.
That sums up the member's capacity for positive thinking. One of the greatest opportunities
we have ever had is now open to us, and I believe the House should recognise that
opportunity and get behind the people who are helping to develop the port. The Minister of
Fisheries mentioned recently the opening up of opportunities for primary produce exports
through the OECD. In the last few months the Government has made two major break-
throughs.
Press reports suggest that this is one of the best chances New Zealand has had. I quote
from the Trans-Tasman: "The most likely prospective service centred on Bahrain and
feeding some smaller ports. A new shipping line, Lauretzen Peninsular Reefers, will be
operating in September. It will provide a three-vessel service between New Zealand and the
Middle East-something we have never had before." The encouragement given to the
shipping lines by the construction of the new port is a very positive step. The House should
stand behind the resolution and endorse it.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): I make it perfectly clear at the outset that I do not

agree with one word the member for Coromandel has said; and very few people in the
commercial community would support him. He quoted from the Trans-Tasman, but when
the Prime Minister made his announcement on 6 April the New Zealand Herald carried a
statement on its front page that leading meat industry officials had said the Prime Minister's
statement was ludicrous, and a load of political claptrap. That is just what we have had from
the member for the last 10 minutes. He said it was important to open up new markets in the
Middle East. No one would question that, but do we want to open up a market of 265 000
people, which is smaller than Auckland, and claim that as a great victory? All produce that is
shipped there must be trans-shipped somewhere else, and I ask, where is the great
achievement in that?
The member for Coromandel talked about the importance of the Middle East, but he
forgot to tell the House that in the 9 months to March of this year our exports to the Middle
East totalled $68 million, with only $2.7 million going to Bahrain. In November last year the
Minister of Foreign Affairs said that the Government saw Cairo as the centre of the Arab
world, and that was where the first post would be established. The Opposition endorsed
that, and was committed to it as the Government. It is significant that the Minister of
Foreign Affairs made that statement while he was in Cairo, but has not repeated it. The
Opposition believes that just as we were justified in going into Iran and Iraq, the Govern-
ment should have gone into Cairo and Saudi Arabia, instead of Bahrain.
The Prime Minister said that the deal with Bahrain was a breakthrough because Bahrain
holds the key to other wealthy Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia. If Saudi Arabia is the
end target, why not go there now? Why establish a post on an island that does not have direct
connections with Saudi Arabia? The Government believes there is a free-port agreement,
but it is fooling itself. Bahrain may be a member of the Arab League, but it is not a member
of the Arab common market and, therefore, although we will have duty-free entry for our
products into Bahrain, when those products move to any other state in the Gulf they will
incur duty as well as extra handling charges. Government members who represent farmers
should be ashamed at a decision that again imposes a drain on the already dwindling funds of
farmers.
Take a close look at Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Bahrain. Egypt has a population of 40
million, and more than 100 resident diplomats. Saudi Arabia has 55 resident diplomats, and
Bahrain has 11, 6 of whom are from the other Arab states. Five Western countries are
represented in Bahrain, and then along comes little New Zealand on a crutch saying, "We
are looking for somewhere to rest. We want to move in somewhere to make a song and
dance." The talk of duty-free access to the gulf states through Bahrain is misleading. No such
access is available. Bahrain is not in the Arab common market, and New Zealand should be
trying to move directly into the market instead of through a secondary port. By the time the
causeway and other facilities have been built, the shipping companies will have accepted that
more ready access to the Gulf states is available. It is ludicrous to believe that New Zealand
will gain from this in the long term, because access will be directly into the markets
concerned and not through Bahrain.
The Prime Minister found it expedient to ignore the Government's earlier decisions to
consider the establishment of posts in Saudi Arabia and Egypt, and one can only wonder
why. Perhaps the Government is aware that it is losing contact in Saudi Arabia. It is aware
that sales of primary products to several of the Gulf states have decreased in the last 12
months, and there is a tendency towards a tightening in the attitude to New Zealand. I
suggest that the opening of a diplomatic post in Bahrain will not help to improve either
diplomatic or trade relationships between New Zealand and any of the Gulf states. The Gulf
states would prefer New Zealand's representation to be direct. If it cannot be done through
them the logical centre-as the Minister of Overseas Trade and Foreign Affairs has said—is
Cairo.
For centuries Cairo has been the centre of the Arab world, and most nations still view it
as the most important diplomatic area of influence. Our post should have been put there
rather than Bahrain. What are the assurances of the Minister of Foreign Affairs worth? If,
while he is visiting a very important country in the Middle East—a country with a population
of 40 000 000, which consume large and increasing quantities of New Zealand's primary
products he says the New Zealand Government places Egypt above any other country,
how can he expect to retain the respect of that administration when on his return to New
Zealand he turns his back on it and puts New Zealand's post in one of the smallest Arab
communities?
The Government should urgently reassess its approach to representation, not only in

LAND VALUATION PROCEEDINGS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. Honourable members will recall that this Bill was introduced last year, and
referred to the Statutes Revision Committee for recess study. The Bill has its origins in a
recommendation of the Supreme Court Procedure Revision Committee, which is at present
revising the code of civil procedure. This committee proposed that the procedures governing
land valuation proceedings be amended because of existing complexities and anomalies.
At present, land valuation committees have no independent office or existence, and are
in effect extensions of the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court. An appeal from a
committee is, therefore, an appeal from the court's subsidiary. Very complex rules have
been required to regulate procedures before the Administrative Division and the committees
themselves. The Supreme Court Procedure Revision Committee recommended, and this Bill
provides, that land valuation committees be given independent status as tribunals. This
would mean that appeals from the committees to the court could be assimilated into the
general appeal procedure at present provided in the Supreme Court (Adminstrative Divi-
sion) Rules 1969. This rationalisation of jurisdiction has the support of the Government
agencies involved with land valuation, and is also supported by the New Zealand Institute of
Valuers and the New Zealand Law Society.
Clause 2 of the Bill re-enacts in an amended form section 19 of the principal Act. This
clause, containing 14 subclauses, embodies the structural changes to the existing committees.
The first subclause renames the committees land valuation tribunals, but is otherwise the
same as subsection (1) of section 19 of the Act. Subclause (2) makes changes in the
membership of the tribunals. Three persons will be appointed-a magistrate as chairman,
and two other members, one or both of whom shall be registered valuers. The requirement
for the appointment of a valuer to each tribunal is innovative, and will strengthen the
knowledge and experience of tribunals in valuation matters. Subclauses (3), (4), (5), and (6)
are procedural in nature, and make no substantial changes. Subclause (7) is a new provision,
and qualifies the quorum provision in subclause (5). It allows the magistrate to sit alone to
determine certain matters of a legal or interlocutory nature, or where both parties agree to a
hearing before the magistrate as chairman. This subclause will promote a more efficient use
of the tribunals'- and the parties'-time. The remaining subclauses closely follow the
wording of the original section 19, and, apart from consequential amendments, leave the law
unchanged.
Clause 3 changes the office for the filing of documents from the Supreme Court to the
office of the magistrate's court in a Supreme Court centre. Subclause (1) provides for filing
in the appropriate office of the magistrate's court. The appropriate office is defined in an
amendment to section 2 of the principal Act, which appears in Part I of the schedule to the
Bill. This change is largely administrative. Because the tribunals will function at a magisterial
level, it is appropriate that proceedings be filed in magistrates' courts offices.
Clause 4 establishes hearing procedures and re-enacts the existing section of the
principal Act with minor amendments. Changes to subclauses (2) and (4) have been made by
the Statutes Revision Committee. Subclause (2) can be invoked by parties wishing to have a
matter heard in the first instance by the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court. This
provision saves time and costs, and will allow important or complex proceedings to be
referred to the court at the outset. The possibility of a party refusing on capricious grounds
to consent to a referral has been excluded by the amended wording introduced by the
Statutes Revision Committee. Subclause (4) as it originally appeared in the Bill has been
struck out and a new subclause has been substituted. This provision gives the Supreme Court
the final say on whether an application is to be heard by a tribunal or the Supreme Court at
first instance. The earlier wording intended to confer the same power on the courts, but its
application was not clear.


## p. 1194 (#436) ###########################################

1194
6 July
Land Valuation Proceedings Amendment Bill
Clause 5 amends section 31(1) of the principal Act, which provides that a local authority
may appoint an additional member to a land valuation tribunal. The local authority
appointee acts as a member when objections to the valuations of property situated in the
district of the local authority are being heard and determined. This clause makes it clear that
a member so appointed may act as a member of a tribunal only in the case of objections to
valuations made under the Valuation of Land Act 1951 or under Part II of the Rating Act
1967, which relates to annual values as well as objections to special rateable values under
Part VI of the Rating Act. Clause 6 provides for consequential amendments, repeals, and
savings provisions. Many minor amendments have been made to the Acts listed in the
schedule to the Bill. In Part VI of the schedule an amendment to the Public Works Act 1928
has been added by the Statutės Revision Committee.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): Although the Bill orginates from a recommenda-
tion of an independent committee that is engaged on a long-standing review of the code of
civil procedure, it is essentially a departmental Bill designed to improve administrative or
quasi-judicial procedure, and, as such, I do not think it need give rise to a great deal of
discussion. It is certainly not opposed on this side of the House. Essentially, its purpose is to
place the work of the land valuation committees, now to be called tribunals, in the realm
where it has always been thought of as being appropriate, namely within the magistrates'
courts, instead of its being an extension of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. I see no
objection to the Bill, and indeed, as the Minister says, it has been carefully considered by the
Statutes Revision Committee, which made a number of minor amendments.

EVIDENCE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The key clause of the Bill is clause 2, which inserts a new section 23A into the
Evidence Act to ensure that only relevant evidence is admitted in a prosecution for a rape
offence. As honourable members are aware, the Bill began as a private member's Bill
standing in the name of the member for Birkenhead. In his maiden speech to the House the
member referred to rules of evidence that allow a complainant in a rape trial to be cross-
examined about her sexual behaviour and reputation to the extent that it sometimes appears
that it is she, and not the accused, who is on trial. The new section will remedy this anomaly
by introducing a procedural safeguard, and by changing the substantive rules of evidence.
Defence counsel will no longer be able to advert to largely irrelevant but highly
prejudicial aspects of the complainant's character and behaviour solely for the purpose of
intimidating her or moving the thrust of the trial away from his client. This practice, which
has been widely criticised, particularly by the New Zealand Law Society, will now be
expunged by the presiding judicial officer whose control is strengthened by more precise
evidentiary guidelines than the common law provides. This reform will also reduce the
likelihood of acquittals in rape trials, more because the jury disapproves of the complainant's
behaviour or reputation than anything else.
I stress, however, that the proper rights of the accused nonetheless remain undi-
minished. He may still defend himself to the fullest extent, only now his efforts must be
directed to the allegation made against him, and not to muddying the waters by impugning
the complainant undeservedly. The Bill as introduced by the member for Birkenhead
followed closely on the recommendation of the United Kingdom advisory group on rape
chaired by Mrs Justice Heilbron. Since then the Statutes Revision Committee has given
careful consideration-I might even say exhaustive consideration-to the Bill and to the
numerous submissions made upon it, which, I might add, almost unanimously supported the
intent of the member for Birkenhead's proposal.
Similar legislation passed recently in other jurisdictions was also given close study by the
select committee. As Minister of Justice and a member of the Statutes Revision Committee,
I congratulate the member for Birkenhead on his effort to remedy a law that is no longer
appropriate, and for his perseverance with a reform that has tantalised us with difficulties
shown up by its wording. Thanks are also due to the other members of the Statutes Revision
Committee, particularly the lawyer members who grappled successfully with the thorny
technicalities of the Bill.
Mr Hunt: And the lay members.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: And the member for New Lynn and myself, and one or two
other lay members, as well. The Bill as reported back has three clauses. The purpose and


## p. 1195 (#437) ###########################################

6 July
1195
Evidence Amendment Bill
method of the original section 23A are retained, but more appropriate guidelines have been
formulated to enable the courts to exclude evidence that is remote, peripheral, of little
probative value, or otherwise unnecessary to a determination that accords with the interests
of justice. As introduced, the Bill went on to insert a new section 23B that would have
restricted admission of evidence to the bad character or previous convictions of the
accused. The likely effect of this section was closely examined by the Criminal Law Reform
Committee in its submissions, and it concluded that it did not merit enactment in the New
Zealand context.
The accused is already protected by other provisions contained in the Evidence Act and
by the court's wide discretion to exclude prejudicial evidence. The committee submitted that
it was undesirable to make a further and highly complex rule applicable only in rape cases,
and the Statutes Revision Committee accepted that recommendation. Significantly, a similar
proposal in England was also dropped. As I said, clause 2 inserts a new section 23A into the
principal Act to make important substantive as well as procedural changes in every case
where the accused is being prosecuted for a rape offence. "Rape offence" is a new term and
it includes not only rape, attempted rape, and assault with intent to commit rape, but also
aiding, abetting, inciting, counselling, procuring, or conspiring with any person to commit
these offences.
Procedurally, section 23A requires that before the court may hear evidence or questions
relating to the complainant's sexual experience with persons other than the accused, or her
reputation in sexual matters, the leave of the trial judge must be granted. An application for
leave may be made before or during the proceeding and, if made in the course of a
proceeding, is to be dealt with in the absence of the jury. Subclause (4) sets out two
situations in which leave is not required before bringing evidence about what would
otherwise be restricted matters. These are, first, where the purpose is to rebut or contradict
evidence of that nature already before the court; and, secondly, where the accused is
charged as a party to a rape offence and cannot be convicted unless it is disclosed to the court
that some other person has committed a rape offence against the complainant. These
exceptions do not weaken the main principle, but simply ensure that it does not have unfair
or capricious results.
Before the judge may grant leave he must be satisfied that the evidence to be given or
the question to be put is of such direct relevance to the facts in issue in the proceedings or the
issue of appropriate sentence that to exclude it would be contrary to the interests of justice.
The phrase "interests of justice" is, of course, familiar to a judge, whose oath requires him
to uphold justice. It means more than merely the interests of the accused and his right to a
fair trial. As well as those things, it encompasses the interests of society and the complainant
that there should be a just determination of all issues raised, and not an unjustified acquittal.
The present concept of relevance is qualified by the unambiguous statement that evidence
shall not be regarded as being of sufficient relevance to warrant its admission by reason only
of any inference it may raise as to the general disposition or propensity of the complainant in
sexual matters. This provision is necessary to prevent arguments that permission to bring
evidence may be granted on the basis of categories that have been laid down by the courts in
rape cases over the past 100 years, and which are of little significance against a background
of contemporary social mores. In this regard, the Bill changes and improves the substantive
law.
Clause 3 contains consequential amendments to section 15 of the principal Act, and
ensures that no evidence which the court has disallowed will be published by the media.
Publication of the details of evidence or questioning disallowed under section 23A is
punishable as contempt of court. Finally, clause 3 provides that nothing in the Bill shall
affect proceedings commenced or in progress at the date of commencement of the Act. This
is a sensible transitional provision designed to avoid confusion and uncertainty.
I am confident that this measure does not infringe the basic principle that all evidence
that is sufficiently relevant to an issue before the court is admissible. To coin a phrase from a
distinguished English lawyer, Professor J. C. Smith, it does no more than deprive the
accused of an advantage which the law in theory never allowed him, but which the ingenuity
of counsel and the human imperfections of judge and jury inevitably gave him. At the same
time, it means that those unfortunate women who have already suffered the ordeal of being
raped will be much better protected from having the intimate details of their private lives laid
open to public scrutiny. As the House knows, it is an unusual step for the Government to
take over a private member's Bill. It is a step that gives me particular pleasure, typifying as it
does fruitful co-operation in the advancement of law reform. The House, and the women of

I shall quote from the first paragraph of the report of the Department of Justice on the

members of the committee. The paragraph reads: "The department's starting point in
considering this Bill is the need to secure a just result in a rape trial, as in any other trial. The

guilty person is not in the public interest. In neither case is justice done. It follows that we
agree with those who have asserted that reform must not be at the expense of a fair trial for
the accused. At the same time, anything in the trial procedure that might lead to an
undeserved acquittal needs to be examined." The sentence to which I wish to draw particular
attention is this one: "It follows that we agree with those who have asserted that reform must
not be at the expense of a fair trial for the accused."
After close questioning of the New Zealand Council for Civil Liberties in particular, I
was satisfied that the Bill as redrafted does not—and I emphasise, does not-provide a "let-
out" for the woman. I believe the position of the New Zealand Council for Civil Liberties
could be summed up by saying that it thought that if one had all the evidence, no matter how
distasteful it was, at least nothing would be hidden from view. On the other hand, I think the
Department of Justice put it in better perspective when it said that reform, provided it is not
at the expense of a fair trial for the accused, is something that can be supported.
The Bill was totally redrafted, except for the short title. While the spirit of the
Bill- namely, to forbid evidence about a rape victim's past sexual experience or reputation
which has no direct relevance to the case-remains the same, the manner of accomplishing
this in legislative form has been radically altered. I say again that the result is a reasonably
simple Bill, which inserts one new section-section 23A-into the Evidence Act. Let us
consider what the Bill says. First, it defines "complainant", "rape", and "rape offence".
Secondly, it forbids the giving of evidence or the questioning of a witness about, first, the
sexual experience of the complainant with any person other than the accused, and secondly,
the reputation of the complainant in sexual matters, except by leave of the judge.
Thirdly, leave of the judge may be given only when the evidence is of such direct


## p. 1197 (#439) ###########################################

6 July
1197
Evidence Amendment Bill
relevance to the facts in issue or to the issuing of the appropriate sentence that to exclude it
would be contrary to the interests of justice. In that way, I believe the Bill meets the point
made by the New Zealand Council for Civil Liberties. The judge is directed not to give leave
if the evidence or question would tend merely to raise an inference concerning the
complainant's "general disposition or propensity" in sexual matters. Fourthly: (a) if
evidence is allowed about the complainant's sexual experience or reputation, this may be
rebutted; (b) if the accused is one of a party-for example, in a situation such as we heard a
lot of evidence about, namely, gang rape-evidence may be given concerning the complain-
ant's alleged actions with another member of that party; (c) the Bill gives the procedure for
applying to the judge for leave under subsection (2) of the proposed new section.
In summary, then, the Bill not only forbids, without prior consent of the judge, the
production in a rape case of evidence concerning the complainant's previous sexual experi-
ence, but it also lays down fairly precise guidelines as to when the judge may or may not give
leave. Committee members spent a long time trying to determine a balance between the
present law, which gives the judge the discretion he has tended to use in a rather
conservative way-namely, he has tended to allow the evidence to flow fairly freely in a
trial-against the point that evidence should not be used. In fact, I think the balance we
finally decided upon reflected the wishes of most if not all the committee members. Any
legal wrangling that is likely to occur will presumably be over the terms of "direct relevance"
and "contrary to the interests of justice" mentioned in subsection 3- and that, of course, will
be a matter for the courts to decide.
The Bill is sensibly designed to redress the balance in the evidence given at rape trials.
The existing law excludes evidence of the previous record and conduct of the accused, but
allows such information to be produced about the complainant. This has led to the allegation
that rape trials tend to treat the victim as the accused, with her sexual experience and
reputation put on trial. It is in the public interest that offenders be brought to justice, and
that women should not be inhibited from reporting incidents of alleged rape by the fear of
having intimate details of their sexual life brought up in public for no better purpose than to
colour the jury's attitude towards their credibility.
We heard a great deal of evidence from people who supported the Bill in the form of
examples of trials indicating that women have been cowed into a position of virtually being
unable to go any further in the trial because of questions asked by over-eager lawyers that in
fact excessively helped the man as opposed to the woman. In the words of the submission of
the Department of Justice, this "reform will do no more than deprive the accused of an
advantage he should not have anyway". I stress that point again. The Bill will do more than
deprive the accused of an advantage he should not have anyway. It is also in the public
interest, and indeed it goes without saying, that justice must be done. The provision in the
Bill for the judge to give leave for material of direct relevance to be admitted in certain
defined circumstances should ensure that the accused is not deprived of a fair trial.
The key to the reform is the relevance of the evidence and relevant evidence is
protected in the Bill. Irrelevant evidence designed to bring a slur upon the complainant's
reputation and credibility will not be so protected, and is specifically excluded. The measure
makes a needed reform in the law pertaining to rape, and indeed the level of support shown
for it in the submissions received by the Statutes Revision Committee indicates the
importance attached to the subject by the public.
Many of the submissions, particularly from feminists and women's groups, spoke of the
Bill as a good "first step", and I believe that is the case. There was, however, a call for the
repeal of section 128(3) of the Crimes Act, which makes it legally impossible for a man to
rape his wife. In effect, that means that the law regards a man's wife as his sexual property,
and directs the offence of rape towards preserving that sexual property rather than towards
protecting women against the violation of their sexual privacy. By excluding the husband-
wife situation from the law on rape, the law discriminates against those who are legally
married, compared to those living in de facto situations and others—and, like it or not as we
in this House might, we cannot escape the fact that an increasing number of people in New
Zealand live in de facto relationships.
Section 193 of the Crimes Act deals with the crime of assault. A man may not legally
assult his wife; if he does, he is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 3 years. I ask
members to consider carefully my final point. As the law stands, a man may rape his wife. To
me, rape is sexual assault. The law stands aside at present-even when this Bill is
passed- affording the woman no protection whatsoever. In my view, this must be the next
step the House has to tackle. The present law allows a husband to rape his wife. If he assaults

I first adverted to what I saw as a very serious anomaly in the practice of the law when I
delivered my maiden speech in the House last year. I suggested then that there was a strong
relationship between social change and changes in the law. I put forward the proposition that
we, as legislators, must respond to social problems as they arise, and that, because society
depends for its very survival on respect for the rule of law, we should concern ourselves with
any matter that might jeopardise public attitudes and public respect towards particular laws.
I suggested, to some extent then by way of example but also because I firmly believed it was
an area of law that required change, that we could well look at the law relating to rape, a
crime regarded by many states as so serious that, even in the twentieth century, the death
penalty is still provided for those convicted of it.
I pointed out that it was widely believed that many crimes of violence against women,
particularly rape and wife beating, are not reported to the authorities. I suggested that this
resulted, at least in part-and I emphasise those words "at least in part"-from the way in
which our courts are obliged to deal with complaints of rape. Too often the complainant
becomes the person on trial. Too often has defence counsel been required, and permitted, to
introduce irrelevant evidence of the complainant's previous sexual relationship with another
person who had nothing whatever to do with the case before the court. A situation has
developed whereby the admission of previous sexual experience is likely to favour the
accused rather than the victim.
Changing social mores dictate, I believe, that a complainant should not have to prove
she is a virgin to avoid being labelled by a court of law as a provocative or promiscuous
victim. A victim of rape should not be forced to defend her reputation in a courtroom any
more than an accused person should be obliged to prove his innocence rather than have the
Crown prove his guilt. I suggested on a previous occasion that if, without diminishing the
rights of an accused to a fair trial-and, as the member for New Lynn said, that was one of
the factors at the forefront of our minds- we could remove the legal factors that gave rise to
irrelevant attacks upon the character of the complainant, then we, as legislators, had a
responsibility to make such a change in the law.
Most members of the House will have no direct experience of cases such as those
affected by the Bill. Only those lawyers who have acted as counsel, former journalists with
court reporting experience, those who have acted as jurors, or those who have been
unfortunate enough to be called as witnesses in such cases, will have witnessed the harrowing
experience to which women can be subjected. I think I can best illustrate the situation that
this Bill is designed to control by reading from the transcripts of two recent rape trials in New

1199

Zealand. These transcripts are the official records of cross-examinations of young female

only to change the names and circumstances sufficiently to prevent the people from being
identified.
Let us take the first case. I ask the House to picture a 16-year-old schoolgirl standing in
the witness box giving evidence against members of a motorcycle gang who she claimed had
raped her and had subjected her to a number of other sexual indignities. She had, in the
company of friends, gone to a party at a beach. From there she had been taken to another
party, and it was there that the incidents complained of occurred. In order to establish the
elements of the allegation of rape—that is, as defined in the Crimes Act, sexual intercourse
without her consent-she has already had to relate in the most intimate and embarrassing
detail the relevant events of that evening.
Because there were six accused, each of the six defence counsel was entitled to cross-
examine her in turn. The first, an experienced trial lawyer, started by asking her a series of
apparently innocuous questions about the evening: who was at the party, who had invited
her, and the like. Suddenly his whole approach changed and he asked her: "Do you know a
man named Geoffrey J.?" She answered, "Yes". The next question was: "Did you make
love to him the week before?" Answer- "Yes." Question- "How many times did you make
love to Geoffrey J.?" Answer-"Once." The lawyer then proceeded to ask her questions on
other issues relevant to the trial. The whole exchange took, probably, less than 30 seconds
but in that time defence counsel laid the basis of an attack upon the complainant's sexual
character that was to be sustained by the six defence lawyers throughout the trial.
As the member for New Lynn has so rightly pointed out, all this occurs during the quick
flow of evidence during the trial. There is little opportunity for the judge to intervene to
prevent such questions being asked even if the law permitted him so to do. Most important
of all, however, the man referred to as Geoffrey J. was not one of the accused and his name
was never mentioned again during the whole trial. Members of the House might well ask
what possible relevance to an allegation of gang rape could be the fact that, a week before,
this girl complainant had had intercourse with another man in no way remotely involved with
the case.
66
The second trial involved a 19-year-old separated woman who had, perhaps somewhat
foolishly, gone with a gang of young men to a riverside shack; there she, too, had been the
victim of a gang rape. The question was asked of her, "Is it correct that the only men you
have had intercourse with in your life are your husband, Barry R., Christopher N., and
Andrew P.?" The answer was, "Yes, that is correct." Then a few moments later she was
asked, "Do you feel that you have a good reputation in . . . " and he named a district. The
answer was, "Yes, I think so. I shouldn't have a bad one. I have done nothing wrong."
Question-"Do you know John C.?" Answer-"Yes." Then, "Have you ever had inter-
course with him?" Answer-"Yes I have; I am sorry, but that was over a year ago. I forgot."
Question- “Did you forget about him in the list you gave us before?" Answer- “Yes.”
Question-"Would you like to think very carefully if there are any others you have
omitted?" Answer-"That is all I can remember." Question- "Do I take it that there could
be some others as well?" Answer-"No, not really." Question-"Do you know Edward
J.?" Answer-"Yes, I know him." Question- "Have you had intercourse with him?”
Answer- "No."
Again, none of the men whose names were mentioned had anything to do with the trial.
Their names were not mentioned before or again. The fact that she might have consented
with any or all of them on a previous occasion does not make it any more, or less, likely that
she would have consented to a gang rape on the occasion of the alleged incident. I have read
from these two transcripts not simply to illustrate to the House the harsh and brutal manner
of this line of questioning, but also to demonstrate two important points. The first is that
although the rules of evidence require that any statement made in evidence, or any question
asked in cross-examination must be strictly relevant to matters in issue in the hearing there is
no procedure that can prevent irrelevant questions being asked, although the judge can
direct that such questions be not answered or that they be struck from the record; this very
rarely happens in cases of rape.
The Evidence Amendment Bill sets up a statutory bar to questions such as this being
asked without the permission of the trial judge. That alone is an important and significant
advance on the previous situation. Second, although the law says that only relevant
questions can be asked, there has developed a substantial body of legal practice and case law
that permits questions to be asked of a woman relating to her sexual relationship with


## p. 1200 (#442) ###########################################

1200
6 July
Evidence Amendment Bill
persons other than the accused. Members will quickly appreciate that the fact that a woman
might have had intercourse with another man at another time and in another place does not
mean that she would necessarily have consented to have intercourse with the man against
whom she is now alleging rape. The law that we are changing today presupposes that a
sexually immoral complainant is less likely to tell the truth, and she is treated accordingly
when she enters the witness box.
In a trial where the charge is other than rape one could expect a jury to apply some
measure of common sense and ignore matters such as I have read out, which have no real
bearing on the issues before the court. The danger in rape cases arises from the very nature
of the charge and the fact that it involves the highly emotional allegation that sexual
intercourse took place. The danger is that the jury may well regard evidence of general
immorality as being relevant to the issue of consent as it arises in the trial. In those
circumstances I believe that we are justified in creating a special set of rules specifically for
the hearing of rape offences, for without those rules a woman will still be subjected to a line
of questioning that is not only irrelevant but also effectively places her own character on
trial.
The Evidence Amendment Bill provides that evidence and questions relating to the
sexual experience of the complainant with any person other than the accused, or the
reputation of the complainant in sexual matters, shall not be placed before the jury except
with the judge's permission. The judge can grant that permission only if he is satisfied that
the evidence is of such direct relevance to the facts in issue in the proceeding that to exclude
it would be contrary to the interests of justice, thus providing a reasonable protection not
only to ensure that the accused gets a fair trial, and is able to place all relevant matters before
the court, but also to ensure that the complainant, who has already been through a
harrowing experience, is treated with dignity and compassion.
Finally, I should like to make one or two general comments about the role that can be
played by a private member's Bill, as the Evidence Amendment Bill originally was. I
understand that the office of the Clerk of the House of Representatives can find no
precedent since 1930 of the Government's adopting a private member's measure pursuant to
Standing Order 73. I am grateful to the Minister of Justice for taking this unprecedented
step, not only because it promotes a law reform in which I have a personal and active
interest, but also because the adoption of this measure enhances the role and status of
private members of the House. A private member's Bill can have several important
functions. It can, as this measure will, result in a change in the law. It can involve a
conscience issue, such as the Bill introduced by the Minister for the Environment and the
member for Porirua during the term of the last Parliament. It can focus attention on
important legal issues that might require Government attention, such as the Crimes
Amendment Bill introduced by my colleague the member for Tauranga following the
Morgan decision in 1975.
A private member's Bill can provoke a tardy Government into action, as did the Small
Claims Tribunals Bill introduced by my colleague the member for Pakuranga, again during
the term of the last Labour Government. Finally, a private member's Bill, simply by being
on the Order Paper and being debated by the House, can promote public discussion on
matters of topical importance, as did the Bill recently introduced by the member for
Auckland Central. In short, the adoption of this Bill by the Government is an important
event for the private member in the New Zealand House of Representatives, and I hope it
will be recognised as such.

than that by saying a complaint for rape is easy to fabricate and difficult to rebut. It is often
made less to inculpate the accused person than it is to exculpate the accuser. It is often made
to extricate her from a situation which calls for an explanation, and in which the truth would
prove to be very embarrassing. As a result the tendency to fabricate is very strong indeed.
Some such instances would be where there was an unwarranted or a feared pregnancy, which
would be hard to explain away, whether at the hands of the accused or some other person,
which leads the complainant to make an allegation against an individual. The charge of rape
is often made against that person, whether or not there has been sexual intercourse, to
explain a dishevelled and untoward appearance. It is also sometimes invoked to explain a
young girl's late arrival home, especially when her family is very strict and a departure from
the normal routine calls for an explanation. Perhaps, in a state of confusion, the girl is led
into making an unpremeditated accusation of rape to explain her tardy appearance.

It is not unusual for a sexual fantasy without any physical foundation to lead to such an

This Bill seeks to preserve a balance between the accuser and the accused, and seeks to
confine the evidence to that which is truly relevant. It does that by limiting the opportunity
for the defence to embark on what can only be described as a scandalising expedition. People
have often said to me that politics is a dirty game. I do not believe it is, apart from the

face, convictions were entered in all six cases— and that was the only satisfying feature of the

As the law stands at present there is virtually an obligation on counsel to follow every
possible avenue of defence open to his client. Often in those cases you look at your client and
you look at the complainant, and weigh up their moral worth, and you know what you are
doing will do more harm to the girl, who may or may not be innocent. You feel she is not
deserving of as much censure as is your client, but you do the best you can for your client by
doing the worst you possibly can for her. When people tell me that politics is a dirty game my
mind turns to that kind of case, and I am satisfied that some aspects of the law are much
dirtier and grubbier, and I am glad to think that this Bill will change some of that.
The Bill permits the cross-examination of a witness on her previous sexual history only
within strictly relevant circumscribed limits and only with the consent of the judge. The
question might be asked why such evidence and cross-examination should be admitted at all.
The answer is that it is sometimes necessary to throw light on the vital issue of consent, which
has been gone into by previous speakers. Secondly, it cannot always be excluded on the issue
of credibility.
Amongst the numerous documents the Statutes Revision Committee studied was a
report on rape prosecutions compiled by the Law Reform Commissioner of Victoria, a Mr
Smith, an individual. In that I found the most succinct and persuasive expression of the
principle upon which examination as to credit is acceptable, and the limits that should


## p. 1202 (#444) ###########################################

surround an examination of that nature: "In general, and subject to a controlling discretion
exercisable by the court, a party, when cross-examining as to general credibility, is entitled
to seek admissions of any really discreditable behaviour; and this principle is supported by
the consideration that if a witness has, for his own purposes, chosen to do things which he
must have been aware were serious breaches of accepted codes of proper behaviour in the
community, then the court or jury may reasonably feel a doubt as to how far it can rely on his
having refrained, in his evidence, from committing, for his own purposes, breaches of the
accepted code against giving false evidence." I suppose purists or philosophers could argue
about that, but I think it is acceptable that once a person's activities and conduct depart from
the normal accepted standards of community living, then that calls in question his willingness
to conform to another part of the accepted code-namely, telling the truth. To me that quote
is as persuasive and succinct a statement of the justification for cross-examining as to
credibility that I have ever read.
When the member for Birkenhead introduced his Bill I was inclined to view it with
disfavour, and to believe there was already sufficient discretion vested in a judge to control
the proceedings before him and to restrict offensive and injurious cross-examination.
However, on reflection I persuaded myself—I did not take much convincing when I thought
about it and thought back to my own practical experience- that difficulties do arise about
when to invoke this discretion and to stop a line of questioning that has been embarked
upon. To do so once it has been started may very well do more to harm the prosecutrix than
preventing it. If one brings it to an untimely halt leaving suspicion hanging in the air, then
she faces the situation that hints have been dropped, suggestions have been made, but for
some reason unknown to those in court-and particularly the jury-the judge has intervened
to say "Do not go any further." Generally, people will imagine from that that there are
secrets to hide that he has been concerned about, and has prevented from being brought out.
I satisfied myself that the better course is not just to rely on this wide discretion.
The Bill aims to cut through a large body of case law. I hope we will make a clean cut

MARILYN WARING (Raglan): I sincerely thank the member for Birkenhead for taking
the initiative in introducing the Bill. I welcome its return to the House for a second reading,
sponsored by the Government. I hope the member will not take offence if I say that I believe
we are debating a tighter measure than that originally introduced; and that, in time, many
rape victims will report the crimes perpetrated against them, and will feel more justly and
more humanely treated by the courts.
Rape, as it must be proved in a New Zealand court of law, is defined in section 128 of
the Crimes Act. From the evidence heard, the jury and the court determine the question of
whether or not a crime has been committed. Unlike cases of murder where the presence of a
body may be evidence of a crime, unlike cases of robbery, where the physical goods, if they
are recovered, are marked and tagged, and unlike cases of aggravated assault, where overt
signs of physical damage are the main evidentiary proof, in a rape case proof is often
intangible. The act of a male person having sexual intercourse with a woman or girl without
her consent leaves no corpus delicti, no recoverable physical goods, and may leave no sign of
physical damage.
What then does the court start off with? It has the oath of a woman who says she was
raped and the oath of a man who denies it. In many criminal cases the court and jury must
weigh an oath against an oath, and courts and juries have convicted and acquitted on the
basis of the trust they decide to place in an oath. Rape is the only crime in which the victim is
always female and the offender is always male. In a court of law, where the victim becomes
the complainant and the offender becomes the defendant, oath against oath at all times
means the word of a woman against the word of a man. Because of the male against female
nature of rape, and because rape is a deliberate distortion of the primal act of sexual
intercourse, man's law has sought to measure such relative qualitative and interrelated
concepts as moral character, force, fear, consent, will, and resistance, to satisfy the


## p. 1203 (#445) ###########################################

6 July
1203
Evidence Amendment Bill
overriding male concern that beyond the female's oath, her word, and her testimony, there
was not mutual intercourse, and subsequent vindictiveness and wrath, but an objective
tangible crime.
Lord Chief Justice Matthew Hale, the famous seventeenth century jurist, assured
himself of immortality when he wrote, "Rape is an accusation easily to be made and hard to
be proven, and harder to be defined by the party accused though never so innocent." Hale's
great homily has poorly stood the test of time despite its popularity, since four out of five
rape cases go unreported. It is fair to say that women do not find an accusation of rape easy
to make. Those who do report their rape find it is a hard accusation to prove. One safeguard
embodied in the law for the protection of defendants is the chastity standard appended to the
statutory rape provisions governing assault against females below the age of consent. The
principle of statutory rape holds that the resistance is immaterial in the case of a child below
a certain age, since, as the saying goes, the law resists for her. The law does not resist for a
wife in respect of rape by her husband. It is my sincere hope that this Legislature will one day
be sufficiently enlightened to remedy that situation.
Research on rape and evidence in rape cases in New Zealand is limited. More study has
been done overseas. In a University of Chicago law school study conducted by Professors
Kalvin and Zeisel the authors reported, "The law recognises only one issue in rape cases
other than the fact of intercourse; whether there was consent at the moment of intercourse.
The jury does not limit itself to this one issue." The study weighs the woman's conduct in the
previous history of the affair. It closely, and often harshly, scrutinises the female complain-
ant and is moved to be lenient with the defendant when there are situations of contributory
behaviour on her part. I suspect that in many cases, such as the second case quoted by the
member for Birkenhead, juries would see the mere presence of the girl at the shack as
contributory behaviour.
Today, although evidentiary requirements on force and resistance may appear reason-
able on paper, the courts and juries are influenced hardly at all by bruises, and have the
poorest understanding that the threat of violence may be sufficient to terrorise a woman into
submission. Of course, in the English case that the Court of Appeal has recently decided, if
the woman had not resisted and did not have some marks she would probably have been
lucky to get a conviction because she did not have any physical damage done to her.
While some defendants in rape cases claim that some other guy did it, the standard
defence is that there was no force and no resistance because the woman freely consented to
the act. The court's concept of consent is based almost exclusively on its interpretation of the
evidence leading up to the rape, and its judgment of the victim's moral character. I have
recently read the latest feminist text on the subject by Susan Brownmiller, called Against our
Will, and I commend it to all members of the House. I should like to relate the testimony of
one of the victims as recorded in that book. She said, "I don't understand it. It was like I was
the defendant and he was the plaintiff. I was not on trial. I do not see why I did anything
wrong. I struggled. How could they have decided he was innocent, that I did not resist?"
As the law stands, although a woman's sexual history may be trotted out for a jury's
appraisal, a man's relevant sexual history, including previous charges and convictions for
rape, may not be introduced in evidence if he does not take the witness stand, and then he
can be cross-examined only with the leave of the judge. So a jury might see before it a
sexually active woman, and be told her sexual activity reacts on her character and credibility,
but the man may not be similarly examined and charged. In particular, the new subsection
(2) of section 23A will go a long way towards rectifying this anomaly. This subsection states
that "in any criminal proceeding in which a person is charged with a rape offence or is to be
sentenced for a rape offence no evidence shall be given and no question shall be put to the
witness relating to the sexual experience of the complainant with any person other than the
accused, or the reputation of the complainant in sexual matters, except by leave of the
judge".
Subsection (3) states that "the judge shall not grant leave unless he is satisfied that the
evidence to be given or the question to be put is of such direct relevance to the facts in issue
in the proceedings, or the issue of the appropriate sentence, that to exclude it would be
contrary to the interests of justice". There is a further proviso that any such evidential
question shall not be regarded as being of such direct relevance by reason only of any
inference it may raise as to the general disposition or propensity of the complainant in sexual
matters.
I was privileged to sit several times on the Statutes Revision Committee when it
considered this Bill. All members of the committee are in complete sympathy with the Bill's

intent. I should like to congratulate the members of the committee and the House, and thank
all members for their willingness to grapple with this law, under which only 50 percent of the
population can ever be a victim.

Some evidence was received from a group of women in my electorate, but unfortunately
