alarmingly high figure, as is admitted in the report. But when New York initiated a special
sex crime analysis squad and put a policewoman in charge of interviewing complainants, the
number of false accusations dropped to 2 percent, the same as for all other unfounded
felonies. The conclusion was that obviously women believe other women, while men do not
believe women.
I suspect that one of the reasons why women do not lay complaints of rape is that even
though the New Zealand police attempt, I know, to have a woman present when a complaint
is made, the complaint is invariably made to a man in the first instance. Also, for a
prosecution to be successful the victim must not wash herself-which is, of course, the first
impulse- until she has been examined by police doctors, and it is police practice that even if
a victim is examined by her own doctor she must also be examined by a police surgeon. The
reason for this is that the police want a prosecution, and prefer to have a police surgeon who
can be called in evidence. There is no doubt in my mind, having read the testimonies of
women who have taken prosecutions and those who have declined to do so, that the
procedure which women are put through when they complain of rape is probably one of the
greatest inhibitions.
The other inhibition, for which the proposed amendment makes no allowance, is that
when the offence is denied completely the intimate details of the rape will be given in court,
and a woman will be forced to tell many times in great detail exactly what happened. This is
clearly distasteful to her, and I am convinced that in many cases a woman's experience of
having to tell what happened at the time of the rape turns out, in retrospect, to be just as
damaging to her as was the rape. This is invariably done in the Supreme Court, and often the
depositions are taken orally, which means that twice she has to tell what happened. Before
that, she has to go through the evidence with the police. While the Bill remedies one aspect
of the present law that is totally unnecessary-which allows a defence counsel to talk about
the irrelevant sexual history of a complainant- many women will decide against laying a
complaint of rape for the reason that the experience of the rape will be relived twice, first in
the magistrate's court and then in the Supreme Court, with the attendant publicity. They
would also have to go through the present police routines.
I have been of the view for some time, and find it interesting that a group of women in

my electorate have arrived at the same view, that the basic problem with the law of rape is
the actual law itself. Rape as an offence is a Victorian or perhaps even a mediaeval

Bill read a second time.
INSURANCE LAW REFORM BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill implements the first report of the Contract and Commercial Law
Reform Committee on aspects of insurance law, and deals with five specific matters. These
can be summarised as immaterial misstatements, compulsory arbitration, time limits for
claims, agency of salesmen, and non-causative exemptions-topics which the law reform
committee felt warranted immediate action by the Legislature.
Introduced last year, the Bill was referred to the Statutes Revision Committee, which
received 10 submissions from insurance interests, as well as submissions from the Consumers
Institute, Federated Farmers, and the AMP Policyholders Protection Association. While
these last three groups supported the Bill in principle, several submissions from the
insurance interests strongly opposed certain provisions. As a result, the select committee
spent some time deliberating, and was assisted by discussions with members of the law
reform committee.
Clause 4 was opposed by all the life insurance offices that made submissions to the select
committee. It prevents the avoidance of a life policy on the ground that the policyholder
made a misstatement when taking out the policy that was immaterial as far as the insurer was
concerned for the purpose of assessing the risk. This will apply irrespective of whether the
statement was made fraudulently or innocently. As far as I am aware, we are breaking new
ground here, because in other countries, such as Australia, a fraudulent misstatement
permits the avoidance of a policy, regardless of whether or not the fraud was relevant to the
assessment of the risk. Not surprisingly, the life offices opposed the clause, because they felt
it weakened the utmost good faith principle of insurance law which, amongst other things,
requires all statements made by a prospective policyholder to be accurate.
The life offices argued that any element of fraud on the part of a policyholder, whether
material or not, should entitle the insurer to avoid the contract. Members of the law reform
committee were equally divided on the question, and the select committee gave the whole
matter careful consideration. The essential test is that of materiality as defined in clause 6
and, on balance, the select committee favoured the approach contained in the clause that a
fraudulent misstatement should be allowed to avoid a life policy only if it was material to the
assessment of the risk. Where a fraudulent misstatement is material to the assessment of the
risk the policy may be avoided at any time. As a result of confusion amongst insurers as to
what is meant by the term "fraudulently", the select committee has included a definition of
the term in the clause. If a misstatement is material and is made innocently, the right to avoid
the policy is restricted. Such a misstatement must have been made within 3 years of the death
of the insured or the date on which the policy is avoided by the insurer, whichever is the
earlier.
Clause 5 deals with misstatements in insurance policies other than life policies, and
clause 6 defines incorrectness and materiality. The select committee strengthened this clause
to make it clear that these definitions could not be altered by contractual agreements. Clause
9 deals with provisions in insurance policies which require a notice of claim to be given within
a certain time. The effect of this clause is that claims under life policies may be brought at
any time within 6 years of the dates of the cause of action arising. Time limits in other
policies will bind the policyholder only if failure to observe the time limit has prejudiced the
insurance company to such an extent that it would be inequitable if the policyholder was not
bound by the time limit.
Clause 10 deals with the question of agency of salesmen. The law reform committee
found that it is a common practice for insurance companies to provide in their policies that
their salesman is the policyholder's agent for the purpose of filling out the proposal form.
This means that if the agent makes a mistake in filling in your proposal, it is at present legally
your error, and not that of the insurance company. Clause 10 reverses this practice, and
makes the salesman the agent of the insurance company in such cases. As a result of
representations from the insurance interests, the select committee redrafted subclause (1) to
restrict the effect of the clause to those instances in which the salesman is acting within the
scope of his actual or apparent authority. As originally drafted, the clause could have been
wide enough to render an insurance company liable when an employee acted completely
without authority.


## p. 1207 (#449) ###########################################

6 July
1207
Insurance Law Reform Bill
The question of whether independent insurance brokers should be salesmen for the
purposes of the clause gave the select committee considerable trouble. The committee
recognised in part the validity of the insurance companies' argument that insurance brokers
are agents of the policyholder, rather than of the insurer, and wished to exclude the true
broker. However, it had difficulty in finding a satisfactory definition of a broker that would
exclude the true broker while leaving agents and the like bound by the courts. The Chief
Parliamentary Counsel prepared a number of draft definitions for the select committee's
consideration, and the views of the law reform committee were also sought. However, the
select committee was deterred from including a definition of broker in the clause because of
drafting difficulties, and recognised that the problem could be simply overcome if insurers
declined to pay true brokers a commission as is at present the case, and offered reduced
premiums for policies negotiated by brokers, leaving it to them to recover a fee from their
clients.
Clause 11 deals with what are called non-causative exemptions. Insurance policies
commonly exclude liability in certain instances. For example, a motor vehicle policy may
exclude liability while the vehicle is being driven in an unsafe condition. If the vehicle is hit
while stopped at traffic lights the insurer would be able to avoid liability even though the
unsafe condition had nothing to do with the accident. The clause confines the right to avoid
the policy to those instances where the circumstances specified in the exemption contributed
to the accident. The effect of clause 12 is that legal actions between an insurer and an insured
will be dealt with by a judge alone rather than a judge and jury as at present. This clause was
recommended by the law reform committee as a balance to clause 8, which restricts an
insurer's right to require disputes to be settled by arbitration.
Clause 13 provides for the retrospective application of the Bill to life policies. While not
generally in favour of retrospective legislation, both the select committee and I accepted that
the reforms contained in the Bill would not have full effect for many years if this
retrospective provision was not retained in the Bill. This is because life policies are normally
single contracts, which can run for many years. Unless the Bill was made to apply
retrospectively, a life policy taken out today by an 18-year-old could run for 40 years without
the protection contained in the Bill.
Clause 13A is new and makes the relationship of the Bill to the Marine Insurance Act
quite clear by providing that the latter Act is to be read subject to the Bill. This measure
represents the first real attempt by this Legislature to regulate the terms of insurance
contracts. While it is clear that some insurance interests have doubts as to the effect of the
Bill, I believe that it is a useful measure balancing the interests of the insuring public and the
insurance companies, and I recommend it to the House for favourable recommendation.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): The basic principles behind the Insurance Law
Reform Bill have the support of Labour members. The Bill is based on a report of the
Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee, which reported while the third Labour
Government was in office. The aim of the Bill is to give increased protection to people taking
out insurance policies. In particular, when mistakes are made by one of the salesmen or
clerks of an insurance company, those mistakes will be the responsibility of that company,
which in future will not be able to use them to avoid paying out on a policy. Secondly,
insurance companies will no longer be able to insist that, in the event of a dispute, arbitration
clauses are binding. In future people will be able to bring insurance claims in open court.
However, Opposition members cannot give the Bill their complete support, because it is
clear from the evidence received in the committee, and particularly that received from the
Consumer Council, that the Bill does not go far enough. In passing, I bring the attention of
members to the disturbing evidence received that many New Zealanders relinquish life
insurance policies shortly after signing them-an indication of high pressure insurance
salesmanship being exercised, with undue influence upon the people concerned. I believe
that this evidence indicates a need for an insurance commissioner to exercise an
Ombudsman-like role throughout the whole insurance industry. However, my principal
objection, which I feel very strongly, is to clause 12 of the Bill, which will remove from the
ordinary citizen the right for a trial by jury if he brings a claim against an insurance company
in respect of his insurance policy. This is the removal of a right the citizen has enjoyed-to
use the words of the Chief Justice of New Zealand-for over 800 years. Today the National
Government is proposing in clause 12 to remove one of the basic cornerstones of British
justice—that is, that any man or woman is entitled to have a case judged on the facts, by his
peers, neighbours, colleagues, and fellow citizens. The National Government, which has an
appalling record in civil rights, now intends to remove that 800-year-old principle without

any justification whatever. This has serious constitutional implications, which appear to have
escaped the Minister of Justice. I believe the House should examine the proposal very
carefully indeed.
Let us consider a statement made by the Contract and Commercial Law Reform
Committee in paragraph 20 on page 11 of its report: "Many insurers believe disputes
between an insurer and the insured will not be fairly resolved if determined by a jury.
Although some members"—that is, some members of the law reform committee-"do not
fully endorse this view, we consider that it will be reasonable for a provision in the draft Bill
that an arbitration clause shall not bind the insured to be amended to provide that the
resultant claims between the insured and the insurer be heard before a magistrate, or, if in
the Supreme Court, before a judge alone." This suggestion was made by the Non-Tariff
Insurance Association.
What does it mean? First, it means that the committee itself was divided on the
proposal, and that it brought it forward as a result of suggestions from national and multi-
national insurance companies that jury trials be done away with in insurance cases. In the
select committee, Labour members voted for the right to have jury trials retained, and
Government members put forward two arguments against this measure. The first-the one
mentioned by the Minister-was that it was a type of quid pro quo to the insurance
companies. I reject that argument completely. If something is wrong-and the law reform
committee determined that compulsory arbitration clauses in life insurance policies are
wrong-then there is no obligation upon Parliament or the Government to give the
insurance companies something in return for rectifying the situation. Simply, insurance
companies do not deserve, a quid pro quo, because their insistence on compulsory arbitration
in the past has been wrong.
Secondly, the argument was made that juries are biased against insurance companies.
There is no evidence of this, but it was suggested that the reason juries are biased against
insurance companies is the fact that lawyers cannot say in motor accident cases that their
client, or perhaps the other party in the case, is insured. There is no parallel between the
present proposal and the fact that a lawyer cannot suggest that a jury can safely award high
damages in favour of his client because the other party is insured. At the moment one can
bring a case in the Supreme Court against an insurance company and have a right to a jury
trial. Indeed, if a car belonging to an insurance company is in collision with your car, you can
bring an action against that insurance company, but you cannot suggest to a jury that it can
safely award damages because the other party is insured. I emphasise that there is no parallel
between that and the present situation. Therefore, the second argument raised by Govern-
ment members is based on a false premise.
I and other Opposition lawyers on the select committee have challenged the notion that
juries cannot handle civil cases, and did so because of our own experience. Unfortunately in
New Zealand there has been very little research into the efficiency of jury trials. However,
there has been extensive research overseas, and I refer members to research carried out in
America, where jury trials are the norm. In fact, 80 percent of all criminal jury trials in the
world are held in the United States. I refer members to an article that appeared in the April
1967 issue of the New Zealand Law Journal, which contains the report on a major study
carried out into American juries. A lawyer and a social scientist at the University of Chicago
Law School, with the aid of a substantial grant from the Ford Foundation, recently
concluded an inquiry into American juries. Their method was to invite 3500 judges
throughout the United States to answer in writing, during and immediately after jury trials, a
carefully prepared questionnaire. The report states: "The jury emerges as an institution
which any democratic society should be slow to tamper with or abolish. . . . Neither the
judge nor the jury displayed different habits of mind or different criteria. in evaluating
credibility... Contrary to the often voiced suspicion, the jury does by and large understand
the facts and gets the case straight. Its decision by and large moves with the weight and
direction of the evidence."
...
New Zealand juries are probably better than United States juries, not because New
Zealanders are better at judging issues than Americans, but because judges in our system of
law, unlike American judges, are able to give the jury much greater direction. New Zealand
judges are able to indicate to the jury the weight of value they believe particular evidence
has, and are able to indicate their own views-something an American judge cannot do. It
appears to me that we in New Zealand are disposed to condemn a jury on considerably less
evidence than we would require a jury to condemn an accused on. My reason for strongly
supporting the right of jury trials is that I believe from my own experience that not only has

In passing, I refer to the comments of the Prime Minister, who often says that he is the

go to the Supreme Court the question will not be one of technical law but of what the
salesman said. I believe that 12 ordinary New Zealanders, with their experience of living, are
far more likely to be able to determine the issue of credibility in such cases than a judge
sitting alone. I have no doubt at all that a complainant bringing a case before the courts and
seeking justice will accept a decision far more readily if it is given by a jury.

back, all members will have received an earnest and concerned submission from the Life

The second matter to which I would briefly refer is the suggestion by the Opposition

contracts of insurance should be tried before a judge alone or, in the case of an action in the

proposition that either party that wishes to sue on any type of contract other than the

determined by a judge and jury of 12 persons. Members opposite ignore the fact that,
equally so, the same parties to any contract other than a contract of insurance are entitled to
write an arbitration clause into the contract that they negotiate, and that clause will be
binding on both parties.
Clause 8 specifically provides that arbitration clauses in insurance contracts will not be
binding on the insured; in other words, the only people who in future will not be able to avail
themselves of arbitration clauses contained in a contract are insurance companies. Just as the
member for Auckland Central said we should not lightly interfere with the right of trial by
jury, so, too, should we not lightly interfere with the right of individuals to enter into a
contract and to write whatever terms they would like into that particular contract; yet that is
what we do in this Bill in saying-unanimously, because this has the support of both the
Opposition and the Government-that an insurance company cannot avail itself of the
arbitration clause contained in any contract of insurance.
For this reason, the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee, on whose
report the Bill is based, considered it would be reasonable for claims between insured and
insurer to be heard by a judge alone. This was seen by both the law reform committee and
the select committee as a reasonable compromise between what I might loosely describe as
the two extremes-arbitration on the one hand, and jury trials on the other hand. To test the
logic of the argument advanced by the Opposition, I simply ask the next Labour

if the Opposition is determined to seek removal of this bar against trial by jury on the ground
that it is unfair to the insured, is it equally prepared to remove the bar to arbitration on the
ground that it is unfair to the insurer?
Members opposite know, of course, that they cannot do it, because the proposal to deny
both trial by jury and arbitration was a carefully considered compromise between the two
extremes of arbitration on the one hand, and trial by jury on the other. In other words, if
they remove the protection of clause 12 without removing clause 8, they would create an

10, which reverses the usual practice whereby whoever fills in the writing on a proposal form

made by a clerk filling in a form is not the responsibility of the person taking out the policy.
There was some interesting evidence on this. The member for Birkenhead said that one
of his colleagues had a letter to the effect that some insurance companies were seeking to
take advantage of unreasonable mistakes made by the person filling the form out on behalf
of the person wanting to take out insurance. The example was given to the committee of
someone knocking at the door and asking the occupier if he would like to take insurance.
When he replied that he would, the occupier was asked to answer certain questions, such as
what his name, address, and age were, and if he had had any serious illnesses. In good faith
the occupier said, "No, I have not." Of course, the word "serious" has not been defined. In
terms of the present law, which fortunately will be reformed by clause 10, that person's
policy could be voided. Now it will not be able to be voided, and that is a step in the right
direction for consumer protection.
The third provision I want to discuss is in clause 12, which has been so ably commented
on by my friend and colleague, the member for Auckland Central, who, since he has come
into the House, has set out to protect the interests of the consumer in many ways. Clause 12
states that disputes related to contracts of insurance will be heard before a magistrate or a
judge alone, and that a jury will not be used in such cases. Then there is the astonishing
argument put forward by the member for Birkenhead, who said that on the one hand there
was arbitration, on the other trial by jury, and that his party was striking down the middle to
have a case heard by a judge on his own. This is like saying that, on the one hand one has an
excessively bad situation, on the other a good situation, so one should strike in the middle in
order to have something which is just bad. This logic put forward by the member for
Birkenhead is nonsense. What we propose is once again to promote the interests of
government by the people in the widest sense, instead of allowing a small clique to control
things. The Government is in favour of centralised decision making, centralised power, and
of breaking every promise it made at the last election.

But in clause 8 we have done exactly that. Under the present law, any company or person
has the right to put an arbitration clause in a contract. We are about to change it and apply a
serious restriction. Insurance companies will be allowed to put arbitration clauses in their
contracts, but they will not be enforceable by the insurance companies. Further, they will be
enforceable by the insured. There is therefore a situation in which a two-way contract,
entered into by two parties, will be enforceable by the insured but not enforceable by the
insurer a fairly stringent restriction on the normal freedoms allowed by law.
However, it was considered advisable to do away with the arbitration provision, more or
less for the reasons that have been outlined: that these provisions allow the cases to be heard
in private, no publicity is given to the outcome, and that it is in the public interest that what is
happening in claims against insurance companies should be observed. The difficulty then is
that any reform will restrict the right of freedom of the insurance company. To what extent
should this right be restricted? I suggest that it should be to no greater extent than necessary.
Freedom has been restricted to the extent that insurance companies have been required to
come out from behind the closed doors of the arbitrator and into the open court, to have
their cases heard there. The Opposition is asking clearly and simply that they have their
freedoms reduced further, and that they not only come out from behind closed doors, which
they, and any other person in New Zealand, are entitled to contract for, but that they also go
before a jury against their will. The injustice of that apparently appeals sufficiently to the
members of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee.

This is the extent of the concern that has been expressed. The Consumers Institute saw

Two other matters ought to be mentioned, because they have been of concern to the
insurance industry, which has contacted various members of the House to express that
concern. One is the provision that a misstatement or an error in a proposal will not invalidate
an insurance policy after 3 years have passed since the proposal was completed, unless fraud
is proved. The industry has expressed the view that this will encourage people fraudulently
to fill out insurance proposals, and not be concerned about the ancient and respected
doctrine of "utmost good faith". This, I believe, is based on a misunderstanding of the
meaning of the word "fraud”. Insurance interests say that it will lead at least to recklessness.
If they can prove fraud, of course, they are all right, but their argument is that fraud is
very difficult to prove. In some cases, particularly in the case of criminal fraud, it is difficult
to prove; but in this case the Statutes Revision Committee has expressly defined fraud and
given it a special meaning. The meaning that it now has for the purposes of the Bill is that a
statement is made fraudulently if the person making it, first, knows it is incorrect, or,
secondly, is without belief in its correctness, or, thirdly, makes it recklessly without caring if
it is correct or not. There is no element of intent or motive to defraud, simply if a person
completes a proposal knowing it is incorrect, or completes it recklessly without caring
whether it is right or not. When the insurance company challenges the validity of the
contract, perhaps following the death of the life insured, it will be on the ground that the
person had perhaps seen a doctor, but had not said so in the proposal. It would take very
little to establish that a person who had seen a doctor and had been advised that he suffered
from a serious illness or an illness of some significance, and had not said so in the proposal
form, would be taken to have been acting recklessly without caring if it were true or not.
Probably the conclusion would be even more readily drawn that the proposal was completed
knowing it was incorrect. The point to be borne in mind is that fraud usually carries a heavy
onus of proving that ill will or bad faith was involved; that there was an intent to extort or
defraud in some way. It does not exist in this Bill, and is merely a requirement that would
normally be an inference from the facts.
I believe that the insurance industry is overly concerned about the requirements set out
in clause 4. The other matter that has caused concern is the proposal set out in clause 10 that
the agent should be taken to be the agent of the insurer. I am certain that the law reform
committee is quite correct in saying that the agent must be taken to be the agent of the
insurer, regardless of the wording of the proposal. He receives his payment and commission
from the insurance company, and the insured-the person who fills out the proposal-has no
control over the operation, the training, or the way the proposal is completed. If loss is to fall
on one party or another as a result of a mistake made by an agent, or even as a result of
calculated mis-advice given by an agent, then clearly the loss should fall on the insurance
company and not on the person who innocently fills out the proposal form.
The major concern expressed has been that the Bill extends to the insurance brokers.
The brokers have pointed out that when a cover is compiled the insurance is regularly
spread. One instance was given of a major company with 22 insurance companies, with its
insurances spread over marine cover and public indemnity cover, perhaps written by the

quite different situation from the case of a life insurance agent selling a single policy. I have
spoken to the Corporation of Insurance Brokers, and I have been assured that in New
Zealand there are no persons or companies operating correctly with the name of “broker”

Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The member for Kapiti protested somewhat
petulantly that the provisions of the Bill should have been enacted some years ago. Of
course, the Bill is based on the report of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform
Committee, and if the member looks at the copy I am sure he has in his possession he will see
that it is dated 1 July 1975. The Parliament sitting at that time was prorogued in September
or October in order that an interesting event might take place in November, and I am sure
that if legislation had been rushed through the House and enacted before that Parliament
was prorogued he would have been the first to protest.
I consider that the Bill is admirably timed, and that no criticism can be levelled against
either delay or hasty legislation. Clause 4 has the side note “misstatements” and deals with
those. It goes on to refer to them in terms of whether they are incorrect, material,
fraudulent, or made more than 4 years earlier. The part of the report that sets out to give
effect to that takes the opposite approach. The heading of the portion concerned is
"Immaterial misstatements", and it points out that liability, as the present law stands, can be
rejected for errors both innocent and irrelevant. That, of course, is based on the principle of
uberrimae fidei or utmost faith, which originated in the practice of marine insurers, marine
insurance law being the parent of virtually all insurance law. This type of insurance was
often, and in fact usually, concerned with vessels not within the sight of the would-be insurer
and often many thousands of miles away and not capable of being seen by the insurer, who
was entirely dependent on the owner or proposer for the facts submitted to him as the basis
of the policy.
This has been carried over to other forms of insurance and extended to what I believe
are absurd lengths, especially when applied to circumstances where the risk is within the
knowledge of, or at least visible to, the would-be insurer. Examples are given in the report,
and I think it would be instructive to read them, particularly as the member for Kapiti
charged the member for New Lynn with making a totally unfounded attack on the insurance
industry. In response to that, it is appropriate to read some of the circumstances that exist in
the present law and that have been invoked by insurance companies.
The first is an English Court of Appeal judgment, which goes back to 1908. The
material facts, as recited in the report, appear thus: "Insurers are thus in the highly
favourable position that they are entitled not only to bona fides, but also to full disclosure of
all knowledge possessed by the applicant that is material to the risk. And in my opinion they
would have been wise if they had contented themselves with this. Unfortunately, the desire
to make themselves doubly secure has made them depart widely from this position, by
requiring the assured to agree that the accuracy, and not only the bona fides of his answers to
various questions put to him by them or on their behalf, shall be a condition of the validity of
the policy. This might be reasonable in some matters, such as the age and parentage of the
applicant, or information as to matters connected with his family history, which he must
know as facts. Or it might be justifiable that these conditions should obtain for a reasonable
time-say, during 2 years during which the company might verify the accuracy of state-

6 July

ments which by hypothesis have been made bona fide by the applicant. But insurance
companies have pushed the practice far beyond these limits, and have made the correctness
of statements of matters wholly beyond his knowledge and which can at best be only
statements of opinion or belief, conditions of the validity of the policy. For instance, one of
the commonest of such questions is, 'Have you any disease?' Not even the most skilled
doctor, after the most prolonged scientific examination, could answer such a question with

many companies are wholly invalid unless this and many other like questions are
correctly-not merely truthfully-answered, though the insurers are well aware that it is
impossible for anyone to arrive at anything more certain than an opinion about them.”
Another case is a little more up to date, in 1935, and again an English case. The
judgment said, "I am extremely sorry for the plaintiff in this case. I think he has been very
badly treated-shockingly badly treated. They have taken his premium. They have not been
in the least bit misled by the answers which he has made. They would never have refused to
give him his policy if they had known everything which they now know. But they have seized
upon this opportunity in order to turn him down and leave him without any indemnity for the
liability which he incurred. But I cannot help the position. Sorry as I am for him, there is
nothing that I can do to help him. The law is quite plain."
Coming a little nearer to the present, there is this New Zealand case in 1972, where the
Court of Appeal said: "Thus, there is no unspoken argument here for the strained and
technical defences which have been put up against her claim. They depend entirely upon the
apparent commercial advantages which seem to arise from the insurance company's
construction of its legal rights under the policy. It is an attitude unlikely to command much
sympathy." Those cases go back some distance, although the last I mentioned was in 1972.
We were told, however, that these practices are outdated and that we can forget all those
kinds of things because reputable insurance companies do not rely on such vagaries and
vague statements at present. However, amongst the exhibits produced, I have two from
companies which I am sure would call themselves extremely reputable insurance companies.
The first, from the T. and G. Insurance Company, asks the proposer: "Have you any
defective sight, hearing, or speech, or any other physical infirmity?" That is a question a
layman could not possibly answer with complete accuracy, yet he is required to answer it and
he could be held to his answer. Here is another one from another equally reputable
company, the AMP Society, whose policyholders appeared before the Statutes Revision
Committee: "Have you any intention or is it likely that you may be required to engage in a
hazardous pursuit?"-whatever that might mean. "Have you ever had any of the follow-
ing?" and after listing epilepsy, high blood pressure, and so on it states "any other disability,
serious illness or serious accident".
So long as insurance companies persist in asking self-defeating questions such as these,
we are entitled to say that the law is in need of change, and that we are obliged to trim their
sails at least to a degree, to ensure that they do not derive undue advantage from this
position of privilege by asking people unanswerable questions, and then relying on the
doctrine of utmost faith. Far from being an unfounded attack on the insurance industry,
what I and my colleague the member for New Lynn have been doing is simply reciting the
evidence presented to us and documented by references to decided cases and to proposals
still in current use.
I do not want to go on any longer with that. The member for Kapiti referred to broking,
which was a point dealt with by the committee in paragraphs 26 and 27. I shall not take up
the time of the House by referring to them, but some indecision on the part of the committee
was evident. Whereas we were inclined to include some reference to broking in the
provisions of the Bill, we found the same difficulties encountered by the committee—namely
the difficulty of arriving at a definition of a broker. The question is, by whom is he paid? The
member for Kapiti has said that his researches failed to disclose any cases where a person
who acts in a broking capacity is paid by the insurance company. This is probably true, but in
fact he is paid by a deduction from the premium paid to an insurer so that in the end he is in
fact being paid a commission by a deduction from the money which would otherwise go to
the insurance company. This is a device or artifice whereby what appears to be a payment by
an insured person is really carried out by way of a deduction from money that would
otherwise go to an insurance company, and should properly be regarded as a payment
ultimately made by the insurance company.
I turn finally to the question of whether issues between insurer and insured should be
dealt with by arbitration, or, if dealt with by the courts, by what mode of trial? We have


## p. 1219 (#461) ###########################################

6 July
1219
Insurance Law Reform Bill
opted for jury trial on the ordinary principle that they may seek a jury trial. The member for
Birkenhead claimed that we were depriving insurance companies of an opportunity available
to any party entering into a contract to make it a term of the contract that they wanted an
arbitration clause. I should like to be present the day the member for Birkenhead goes into
an insurance company and says he would like to take out an insurance policy. The answer
would probably be yes, but when the member for Birkenhead said he did not want an
arbitration clause there would probably be silence behind the desk, or perhaps he would be
referred to the managing director and a security guard would probably be called in to boot
him out. I am prepared to challenge the member for Birkenhead to disclose the name of an
insurance company that normally includes an arbitration clause in its policy, but which has
been persuaded to make an exception.
Mr McLay: That's not the issue.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: I thought it was the very issue he was making. I conclude by
saying that I believe the dislike for juries is based on a misconception. Insurance companies
have been right in thinking that they did not get a fair deal in personal accident cases where
they stood behind the defendant, because a rule of practice has grown up that it should not
be mentioned to the jury that the defendant was insured, because that would mean he would
not get a fair trial. This does not mean that where an insurance company itself is facing an
issue with a claimant it is in any way disadvantaged by the presence of the jury. For this
reason, we believe that such trials should, as in other civil claims, go before a jury if the
amount involved is sufficient to warrant that, and if the circumstances otherwise would
support an application for a jury trial.

5. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Transport, Are there any proposals to

that it was available to meet the considerable passenger growth forecasts at the time of
purchase. However, a slowing down of the economy reduced passenger growth rates, thus
making it more profitable to lease the aircraft overseas than use it in New Zealand. NAC
experienced little growth during the period of the lease, and the market overseas was such
that it was preferable to sell the aircraft rather than enter into a further lease arrangement.

BASTION POINT (VESTING AND EMPOWERING) BILL
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Bastion
Point (Vesting and Empowering) Bill. I earnestly hope that Parliament will urge the National
Government to recognise the need for an honourable and lasting solution to what is perhaps
one of the longest outstanding grievances. Unfortunately, judged by the latest move today,
that appears to be a forlorn hope, but I sincerely trust it is not. This issue, basically, has been
and will continue to be between the Crown and the Ngati Whatua of Tamaki Makaurau
people. The ramifications of any decision and the effect on the wider public interest cannot


## p. 1229 (#471) ###########################################

7 July
1229
Bastion Point (Vesting and Empowering) Bill
be ignored.
The reasons for introducing the Bill are founded upon the historical treatment of these
people and the injustice they have endured for many years. They are the only group of Maori
people that can be described as landless. The action taken by the Crown was reported as long
ago as 1939. These people have been-certainly for much of the time of the present
generation-tenants of the State; not that they themselves have objected to their families'
being housed in State rental accommodation, but their livelihood is very much allied to the
Crown. The mana and prestige of these people are involved, and the actions of the
Government have brought matters to a head.
The refusal of the Minister of Maori Affairs to give the people an opportunity to place
their grievance before a court of law to be dealt with judicially and impartially indicates a
lack of confidence on the part of the Government. We had hoped that the claimants' case
would be dealt with by a court experienced in Maori land claims, thus protecting the interests
of all parties, including the general public. The Crown could have put its case before such a
court in the same way. Differing views are held by the people involved, who comprise,
primarily, the elders committee, an action committee, and, of course the Orakei Marae
Trust Board, as well as the general public. All these interested groups are determined that
the Government's proposal to subdivide Bastion Point should cease, and that the Govern-
ment should have an open door policy in negotiating with the Ngati Whatua people. My
colleagues will be referring to the historical details of this important question.
The Bill provides that Crown land known as Bastion Point or Takaparawha in the city of
Auckland is to be vested in the Ngati Whatua of Tamaki Makaurau people and their
descendants. The preamble provides overdue recognition for the historical, cultural, and
emotional significance of the land to the Ngati Whatua people. It further recognises the
environmental significance of the land for all New Zealand. Clause 1 is the short title, and
clause 2 is the interpretation clause. Clause 3 provides for the establishment of a board to
be known as the Ngati Whatua of Tamaki Makaurau Trust Board in the terms of the Maori
Trust Boards Act 1955. Subclause (3) states that the beneficiaries of the board are declared
to be members of the Ngati Whatua people of Tamaki Makarau. Clause 4(1) empowers the
board to administer, manage, develop, protect, and care for the Bastion Point land vested in
it. Subclause (2) is important, and empowers the board to enter into such arrangements as it
sees fit with the Auckland Regional Authority, the Auckland City Council, and any other
municipal corporation to provide for the management, development, protection, and care of
all or part of the Bastion Point land as a reserve for recreational purposes.
Clauses 5 and 6 provide for the vesting of various lands in the board. Clause 7 provides
that land vested in the board is to be declared inalienable by the Crown or any other person
in any manner whatsoever, except with the explicit sanction of parliament acting on a
request from the board. Members may know the history of the people the Bill is concerned
with. Their land was originally inalienable, but legislation destroyed the trusteeship of the
last remnants of land at Bastion Point. Future alienation, which is very doubtful, could be
done only by Parliament at the request of the board itself. Clause 8 binds the Crown, while
clause 9 provides for the making of regulations to carry out the functions and purposes stated
in the Bill. The schedule sets out the legal description of the land concerned, which is, of
course, subject to survey. It is given as an area of 24.192 hectares, or just over 80 acres, all in
all. The Ngati Whatua people have long deserved better treatment than they have received
to date.
Hon. H. R. Lapwood: Why didn't you do something about it in your day?
Hon. M. RATA: I did, to the tune of $63,192 in grants to the marae. If Government
members feel that we might not have done enough then, the Labour Opposition will join
with the Government in any further action to bring about a lasting and honourable solution.
Hon. J. B. Bolger: Why didn't you bring a Bill in?
Mr D. M. J. Jones: You didn't do much.
Hon. M. RATA: I suggest to those members opposite who are trying to interject,
particularly the newer member, that when he has been here long enough he will probably
recognise the problem. I shall not go into the history of the third Labour Government, of
which I can be justly proud. If members opposite are as enthusiastic to correct a wrongdoing
and as keen to add to the proud record of that Government, then we as a Parliament will
achieve that end, which is absolutely essential. That need should be recognised, otherwise
this generation and this Parliament will be equally guilty of perpetuating the shameful and
sad actions of the past. Anyone who knows anything of land transactions would wonder how
on earth it was possible for a proud tribe, which was the owner of an isthmus the size of the
Auckland area northwards, to be landless and tenants of the State by 1977. The Ngati

concern not only for themselves but for others. That can be seen from their history. The

physical link with their past, and also represents their only physical link with their future.
Moreover, this land represents the spiritual and physical prestige of a proud people. We as a

In 1908, the activities of the Government were described by Sir Robert Stout, then
Chief Justice, as wrong when he declared that the order approving the alienation was illegal
and void. In 1930, Judge Aitcheson condemned the conduct of the Crown counsel who
refused to produce the documents so that the court might decide whether the transactions
were conducted validly. In 1950, we saw the most shameful eviction, which was either the
second or third of the many evictions that have taken place. The people were evicted from
what should still be their own land. Auckland could have benefited from the Crown's taking
over the land, but the Mayor of Auckland said that the city council would have no part in it
because it had examined the document; he recommended that anyone who was concerned
should review the sad and shameful history of the association of those people with the
Crown.
Many New Zealanders, and some members of the House, are prepared to talk about the
injustice to the Maori people as a sad blot on our history, and think about this matter as
some unfortunate event of last century. Many people think that events like this could not
happen in the enlightened days in which we live, but they are happening now. The people
who regret the lack of foresight and the injustice of our forefathers in their dealings with the
Maori people should think about what is happening now, and what has happened since 1950.
None of the Government's proposals indicate that it has shifted its position from one of
power and strength in dealing with these people, whose only claim is justice. These people
are poor and have no strength behind them, but they have moral support and the moral
rightness of the case on their side. They are asking—and this measure provides for it—that
the Crown abandon its position of power and present its case to a dispassionate inquiry by
the courts that are set up to deal with these matters, and that have been dealing with such
problems since their inception. The Crown should not dictate its terms, but should say,
"Right; we shall accept the fact that every authority that has looked into these dealings has
proclaimed on the injustice. We shall accept that, and we shall try to remedy it now by
keeping out of the argument ourselves except in presenting the case. We shall allow the court
to judge the rightness or wrongness of our actions and decide what should be done in the
future about this land."
The Minister should be prepared to do that, not just with selected bits of the land, but
with the bits that have been taken over the years for defence-defence of whom? Certainly it
was not for the defence of the Maoris. The Minister should be prepared to review the whole
position in the light of the attitude of this very noble people, who endowed so much to the
charitable work of Auckland by their grants to the churches in the early days, and who made
the establishment of Auckland possible by extremely generous sales of land—indeed, their
actions in land dealings with the people of Auckland and with the Government have been
consistently generous.
With that background, the Government should approach the court and say, “We shall
sit on one side. All we ask you to do is decide the rightness or wrongness of the matter, and
the Government will abide by your decision, no matter how far-reaching it may be." The
Minister should have said that some days ago, instead of saying that, for the third time in the
history of this sad people, the Government would evict them from the land that is properly
theirs. If the Minister had adopted that approach, this Bill would not have been necessary
and there would not be such concern. If the Minister's sole concern was to associate a lot of
socially unattractive groups with the member for Northern Maori, why did he not pick on the
Auckland City Council, which has declined to do the Minister's dirty work?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The honourable member's time has expired, but, in addition, he

Council.
Dr Wall: With respect, Mr Speaker, that was not what I said. I said that the Auckland

The Crown purchased part of Bastion Point in 1887-quite a long time ago-when 13 acres
were taken for defence purposes. During 1917, purchases of most of the Orakei area were
negotiated, and further purchases were made during the 1920s and into the 1930s. The
purchases were part of the policy of the Government of the time to acquire undeveloped
land for housing and associated reserves. That is the reason it was acquired, and it is no use
the member for Northern Maori shaking his head. Subdivision was made in 1927 and the
Orakei Domain was classified as a reserve in 1939—those actions were taken by a Labour
Government, by the way. The Crown reserved additional land to establish the Michael
Joseph Savage Memorial Park and the Tahaparawha Park, under the control of the
Auckland City Council. A further area of Bastion Point was taken for housing in the early
1950s, and the 24 hectares now under consideration are the last remaining area of Crown
land there.

Committee, which claims that all the land at Bastion Point should be vested in Ngati Whatua
tribal ownership; or the elders of the Ngati Whatua people, who are seeking the land on
behalf of the former beneficial owners, and whose spokesman is Professor Kawharu, a
member of that tribe. The latter group wants to establish a Ngati Whatua trust board, the

the member for Northern Maori now speaks. It is the tradition and custom according to

procedure.

Human Rights Commission Bill
HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION BILL
Mr HARRISON (Hawke's Bay): I am directed by the Human Rights Commission Bill
Committee to present the report of the committee on the Human Rights Commission Bill.
The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That
the report do lie upon the table. The attached Supplementary Order Paper refers to the
proposed amendments to the Estate Duty Act, the Income Tax Act, and the Land Tax Act.
The committee considered that since there had been no Governor-General's message the
amendment should be referred to the Government by way of a Supplementary Order Paper.
Between 23 February and 8 June the committee held 13 meetings, including 2 in
Auckland and 1 in Christchurch, taking a total of 45 hours to hear 55 oral submissions. There
were also 72 written submissions to be considered. In addition, the committee has met 10
times for nearly 22 hours to consider the submissions, and to deliberate on the Bill. This has
resulted in 18 pages of amendments.
Several people wanted a more explicit definition of the objects of the Bill, and some
thought it should be more properly called the equal opportunity or anti-discrimination Bill.
Those people apparently did not understand that it simply proposes the establishment of a
commission to promote equality of opportunity that is consistent with certain basic human
rights, and to set up a tribunal to deal with cases where the commission's attempts at
conciliation have failed. The Bill, together with the Race Relations Act 1971, aims to
promote tolerance on the grounds of sex, marital status, race, colour, ethnic or national
origins, and religious or ethical belief. Many submissions sought to extend the list to include
political belief, age, sexual orientation, and several others; but the committee thought that
the list in the Bill was enough to start with and that it should be left to the commission to
recommend additions to the Act. It therefore extended, in an amended clause 5, the
functions of the commission to include that of receiving and inviting representations on any
matter affecting human rights.
The committee added some definitions to clause 2 to make clearer such expressions as
“ethical belief", "relative", and "superannuation scheme", but omitted the term "marital
status". Some members considered it inappropriate and contradictory to put a de facto
marriage on all fours with a legal marriage; so the term "marital status" will retain its long
established meaning of being married or single. Several submissions asked for "she", "her",
and "hers" to be added to the words "he", him”, and “his” wherever they occurred, and for
such good English words as "chairman" to become "chairperson". [Time extended.] It is an
important Bill, and the extension of time will give me, as chairman of the committee, an
opportunity to give a reasonable report. Under the Acts Interpretation Act the male gender
embraces the female, and the committee felt that that was sufficient, and did not feel
inclined to rewrite the English dictionary.
Likewise, some people wanted the Bill to absorb the Race Relations Act, or to have
transferred to that Act those clauses that deal with discrimination on the grounds of race,
colour, national origin, and so on. However, it was felt that as the Race Relations Act is
working pretty well it should be allowed to continue in the meantime. Parliament may decide
in the future to consolidate the two Acts. There were some differences of opinion about the
powers and requirements of the commission to issue reports and statements. The commis-
sion must report annually to the Minister of Justice, and that report must be tabled in
Parliament. The committee has amended clause 5, omitted clause 74, and inserted a new
clause 5A to make clearer the responsibilities of the commission for making reports,
including those to the Prime Minister, and for publishing its findings.
The committee received many submissions on the composition of the commission,
mainly suggesting that it must contain at least one woman and a representative of a minority
racial group. The committee saw dangers in this. Unless the commission is to be greatly
enlarged such direct representation of all interests would be impossible. There are obvious
difficulties in trying to fit into that small commission all the possible interests the Bill sets out
to protect, such as men and women, married and single, European and Polynesian, Christian
and humanist. The committee decided against any form of tokenism and plumped for
allowing the best and most suitable people to be appointed as commissioners, regardless of
sex, race, religion, origin, or colour.
The committee had some difficulty with the concept of linking a new human rights
commission with the office of the Ombudsman, and finally decided to allow for the fullest


## p. 1246 (#488) ###########################################

1246
7 July
Human Rights Commission Bill
possible co-operation between the two by having an ombudsman appointed as a commis-
sioner. He would bring to the new commission something of the status that the office of the
Ombudsman has deservedly acquired in its 15 years of experience with comparable prob-
lems. Several submissions expressed confusion at the meaning of the various words used in
clause 14 to allow for some exceptions based on common sense or practice, such as
hairdressing, domestic work, separate accommodation, and public decency. The committee
hopes its amendments will have removed any confusion. Many people made submissions on
partnerships. Some said that all partnerships should be permitted to refuse to take on new
partners for any reason, including colour, race, sex, religion, and so on, while others said
that none should. In between were those who wanted the cut-off number raised as high as 25
or lowered down to two. The committee suggests leaving it at six.

Hon. J. B. GORDON (Acting Leader of the House): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I
seek the leave of the House for the House to continue with the reporting back of the Human
Rights Commission Bill, which was interrupted by the suspension of the sitting at 5.30 p.m.
Mr SPEAKER: Is it the pleasure of the House that this course be followed? There
appears to be no objection.
Mr HARRISON: I am reminded that the late Sir Winston Churchill once said, "If you
want me to speak immediately, I can speak for 2 hours; if you want me to speak for 5
minutes, give me some notice." I had some notice, and I worked on this until 1 a.m., so it
will be a little shorter than it otherwise would have been.
Before the adjournment I was reporting on the Human Rights Commission Bill, and the
work the committee had done on it. Several people drew the committee's attention to the
possibility of discrimination on unsound actuarial grounds against women taking out life
insurance policies or joining superannuation schemes. The former were dealt with in clause
22(6), which the committee has amended to allow distinctions to be made when there are
actuarial or statistical data upon which it is reasonable to rely relating to life expectancy,
accidents, or sickness. Superannuation caused the committee even greater difficulty than life
insurance policies. Most people would accept in principle the need for equality in superannu-
ation schemes, but there is the need to protect those in existing schemes from changes that
would be to their disadvantage. Changes that help some people could harm others, and there
is a need for a generous period to allow for adjustments. The committee has attempted to
reconcile the conflicting interests in such a way that those offering superannuation schemes
will not be forced into withdrawing them or deleting some of their beneficial provisions.
The committee spent a lot of time on clause 22, particularly subclause (7). We got over
this by inserting a new subclause, leaving it to the commission to deal with the female jockey
controversy, and satisfied ourselves by protecting the rights of single-sex clubs and of
organisers of sporting events such as the men's hurdles or the ladies' golf tournament. I am
sure members will be happy about that. Clause 23(5) would have permitted a landlord to
refuse accommodation on the ground that a couple were living in a de facto relationship. The
committee has deleted this subclause. Indeed, as I said earlier, by omitting the definition of
"marital status" from clause 2 the committee has omitted all reference to "de facto" from
the Bill. Some witnesses took exception to the so-called busybody clause, clause 32(1)(c),
and the discretion conferred on the commission by clause 32(2) not to disclose its reasons for
not proceeding with an investigation into a complaint. I am sure members and the public
generally will be pleased to hear that the committee has changed the Bill to meet both these
objections.
In answer to questions about representation by legal counsel and about legal aid, the
Department of Justice advised the committee that in the absence of provisions to the
contrary a person may appear before the tribunal either in person or represented by
somebody else, which would be counsel if you felt so inclined or could afford it. Similarly,
legal aid would be available under section 15(1)(h) of the Legal Aid Act 1969 to an applicant
who could satisfy the financial and other requirements of a grant. So both of those matters
are dealt with.
Part IV establishes an equal opportunities tribunal to consider and adjudicate on
matters referred to it by or from a human rights commission. Some people saw the tribunal
as being an unnecessary bureaucratic development; others were concerned at the constitu-
tional implications in setting up yet another quasi-judicial body to do what the courts should
be asked to do. The committee had some sympathy with these views, and in order to tie the
tribunal into the court system we have proposed amendments, first, to limit the jurisdiction
of the tribunal over claims for damages to that of a magistrate's court, which is at present

restricted to $3,000; and, secondly, to allow appeals to the Supreme Court on matters of fact

Part V, dealing with the functions of the commission in relation to privacy, evoked a
fairly favourable response, although some people felt the commission should be able to

It would be fair to say that most submissions were critical of Part VI, which deals with
the commission's functions regarding complaints against industrial unions and professional

The truth is that neither we nor anyone else can legislate against prejudice at its worst,
when it takes the form of blind prejudice. You know the kind of thing, Mr Speaker: a couple
of people are walking along a street, and one says to the other, "You see that man over
there? I hate him", and his companion says, "But you don't even know him”, and the other
says, "Of course, that's the reason. I don't know him. That's why I hate him." That is what I
would call blind prejudice at its worst. But there is also something less than that which I
believe is innate in all of us, and that is a kind of instinctive prejudice. All of us just do not
"take to" some people, and I am sure there is nothing that anyone can do to legislate that
feeling out of existence. There is no way of outlawing feelings of that kind, and it would be
unwise to try to do so, but I also think it is realistic to accept their existence. Although I

7 July
Human Rights Commission Bill
mentioned this once or twice during the committee's deliberations, and wondered if we
could include in the Bill some words that might take heed of this very human
emotion-perhaps I should call it a failing-I was also fearful of any real attempt to do so.
What we have before us is dubbed a Human Rights Commission Bill, and it is significant
that on one or two occasions, when we moved out of Wellington to hear evidence, the notice
board directing people where they were to go referred to the "Human Rights Bill", and
many people have thought of it as such a Bill. Of course, it is not. There is no definition of
“human rights” in the Bill; at best it might be called an equal opportunities Bill, because a
tribunal of that name—an equal opportunities tribunal-is set up within the framework of it.
It is true that it provides equal opportunities for some, but it excludes a provision that some
of us tried to have included—some protection against political discrimination. Various areas
of discrimination are outlawed, but not, much to our regret, political discrimination; so I
think at best one might call it an “equal opportunities for some" Bill, and really no more
than that.
That prompts me to ask the question: should we have a human rights Bill, or it might
be called a Bill of rights? That implies something of the nature of a written constitution,
about which there have been divergent opinions that I do not want to go into at this stage.
But at all events, whether or not we should have a human rights Bill or a Bill of rights, I
believe this Bill should acknowledge, however faintly, the concept of human rights as such,
and, at the urging of the Opposition members on the committee, the long title was altered to
give such an indication. I should like to read to the House the new long title of the Bill. It is
described as "An Act to establish a Human Rights Commission and to promote the
advancement of human rights in New Zealand in general accordance with the United
Nations International Covenants on Human Rights".
I moved, and my colleagues supported me, that we might consider incorporating the
United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 as a schedule, not with the
thought that it would be binding-of course, it could never be binding without formal
enactment-but as a kind of guide to the commission that it should have regard to what I
think are the very profound truths contained in that declaration. There are, we found, some
technical obstacles to that, because the 1948 declaration has been overtaken by subsequent
covenants, which is why the phrase "international covenants" is used in the long title; it
might have been misleading to have incorporated a declaration subscribed to by most
members of the United Nations, and have cast eyes back on to something rather than that
which has supplanted it, and which is, it appears, of much greater length than can possibly be
accommodated as a schedule.
I still believe it would have been valuable to tie what many people will still regard as
human rights legislation—although that is not the case-to the Declaration of Human Rights
or the various stages by which the United Nations has affirmed its attachment to the notion
of human rights. This, of course, is particularly important at present, when President Carter
is making such an issue of this in American foreign policy.
I pass to another point, on which we had a great deal of evidence and, I think it is not
putting it too high to say, a good deal of pressure, and that was to include the phrase “sexual
orientation" as a ground for non-discrimination, along with the other characteristics such as
racial origin, ethnic origin, and so on. The purpose of that was designed to meet the case of
the confirmed homosexual, but that phrase "sexual orientation" in my judgment goes too
far. It is a sad fact, but nevertheless a fact, that some people are sexually oriented towards
others of tender years, whether they are of the same or opposite sex. I would not
countenance that, and I do not believe any member of the House would countenance it or
want to give respectability to a situation of that kind. I believe that the real solution to
homosexual problems-and they are very real indeed-is an open and direct change of the
law, which I support now as I supported it when the Bill promoted by the member for
Egmont was before the last Parliament. I think that is the real way to go about meeting that
problem, with all its gravity, which I acknowledge.
I pass over with the barest of mention Parts V and VI of the Bill, which deal respectively
with privacy and industrial relations. In my judgment they are excrescences on what has
otherwise been made into a tolerable Bill, although it is still misleading in some respects. I
say no more about them at this stage, but I have no doubt that during the passage of the Bill
through the House there will be a great deal of discussion on those two parts. We will do our
best to see that the part dealing with industrial relations is deleted, and, if the one dealing
with privacy is to remain, that it is considerably altered. The Government's original plan as
set out in its manifesto-in fact, in both manifestoes on this occasion, including the one that

1249
Human Rights Commission Bill
has been resiled from-was to enlarge and enormously extend the jurisdiction of the
Ombudsman. That was totally misconceived, and betrayed a fundamental misunderstanding
of the role of the Ombudsman or the Ombudsmen, and it is a matter of some satisfaction, to
me at least, that the Government has gradually been put on the right track—but I suppose it
is too much to expect gratitude from the Government for the assistance we have given it in
this direction.
I turn now to one or two changes that appear in the Bill. We have added a phrase
dealing with ethical belief, which I think is a step forward. We have defined it, with some
difficulty, but I think it will turn out to be a workable definition, and we have made two
complementary changes. One is to omit the definition of “marital status", which originally
encompassed a de facto situation; but a kind of compensating factor for that, one by which
the Government members appeared to assuage their consciences, was to delete clause 23(5),
which omitted a de facto relationship from a tenancy situation. Again, I believe we will hear
a good deal more discussion on that, so I will say no more about it now. The provision
requiring reports to be made by the commission to the Prime Minister has been significantly,
and, I believe, substantially, altered for the better. As it originally stood, the right and power
of the Prime Minister to call upon what I would like to think is a totally independent body to
make reports to him has been substantially cut down. That is, I have no doubt, a very
considerable improvement.
Another matter which is possibly of less appeal to the public generally than to us—and I
suppose this encompasses lawyers especially-is a drafting technique new to New Zealand,
and which I think in this case is very advantageous. I cite the change in clause 14(3)(b),
which appears also in the new clause: "In the case of a position such as that of attendant in a
public lavatory or as a person responsible for the fitting of clothes to customers or others".
The point to which I direct attention is exemplification. I do not think it has ever happened
in our legislation before, and I have the word of the Chief Parliamentary Counsel that it is an
innovation that we should try to give to the courts an illustration of the kind of activity we
mean by exemplifying certain areas in which it could apply. The technique has been adopted
elsewhere in this kind of legislation. I think it is very apt here, because it proves extraordi-
narily difficult to define different kinds of occupation, different kinds of approaches, and
different kinds of victimisation, and as a guide to the courts we have set out in a number of
clauses exemplification of this by using the phrase "such as" and going on to say so and so,
and so and so. I will wait, of course necessarily, to see just how the courts or the commission
regard this. It is a development and a novelty in our way of drafting statutes, but, I think, at
any rate in this field, it has a great deal to commend it.
We had considerable difficulty with insurance policies. A good deal of evidence
presented to us indicated discrimination between male and female in the benefits open to
them when taking out life insurance policies particularly. However, on actuarial figures there
seems to be some justification for this. The figures seem to demonstrate that women have a
greater longevity than men, and as long as that is the case, naturally insurance companies
will want to adjust their premiums and the benefits derivable from their policies in relation to
the expected length of life of the individual insured. We have therefore added a clause which
enables that to be done so long as it is based on actuarial or statistical data upon which it is
reasonable to rely relating to life expectancy, accidents, or sickness.
I have already mentioned that in clause 23(5) the tenancy provision has been dropped as
a quid pro quo for the elimination of the definition of marital status. I come now to clause 25,
which was the object of a good deal of representation, because, quite honestly, it was very
difficult to understand. That clause has been replaced by a substitute which is sufficiently
summed up by its side note, "Discrimination by subterfuge". We considered that the Bill
should have—and it now has a provision enabling the commission to look behind the words
or the appearance of some situation, and penetrate to the actuality of it. If there is some
subterfuge of what is really a means of discrimination but appears not to be, the commission
can go to the heart of the matter and rule on it in accordance with the reality of the situation
rather than its description in words.
We did face up to, with, I must confess, some hesitation and not total unanimity, the use
of words that have a gender associated with them. We have added to one clause, “being a
term such as carpenter, engineer, telephonist, seaman, or typist." The word "seaman", of
course, does import masculine gender, but I would find it very hard to adopt the word
"seapeople". I do not think that "seaman" excludes the possibility that a woman may
undertake a seagoing career. I do not think she would really feel denigrated if in those
circumstances she was described as a seaman. I would certainly see her described as that

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): As Minister in charge of the Bill, it gives
me great pleasure to see it brought back to the House after a very long and detailed study by
the special select committee. I thank those who served on the committee, and join with the
member for Henderson in paying tribute to the chairman, the member for Hawke's Bay,
who did a magnificent job. I thank also those officers who assisted the committee-Miss
Bowden of the Clerk's office, and as Minister of Justice I must mention Mrs Lowe and Miss
Margaret Nixon of the Department of Justice.
The Bill is of particular pleasure to me because it is within the family of legislation
dealing with the rights of the individual. I relate back to the first of the Ombudsman Acts of
the late Ralph Hanan in the early 1960s; then through the Race Relations Act, in which I had
a part to play with the late Dan Riddiford in guiding it through the House in 1971; the matter
of women's rights in the Equal Pay Act when I was Minister of Labour in 1972; and the
private Bills brought down in 1973, 1974, and 1975 by the Minister of Works and Develop-
ment and myself concerning the rights of women. The National Government had the issue of
human rights as the first of its policy planks, so it is a pleasure to me to see that what was a
good Bill when it was introduced and referred to the special committee has now come back a
better Bill.
Indeed, in the introduction to his evidence the retired Chief Ombudsman, Sir Guy
Powles, said: “This is a good Bill, a very good Bill, and I think the Government is to be
congratulated upon introducing it. It is a marked step forward in the social field, and could
have profound beneficial effects on New Zealand society." I am sure Sir Guy would agree
with members of the committee that it is an even better Bill because of his assistance and that
of others, and because of the attention that we, and the officers assisting us, have given to it.
I do not propose to speak at length at this stage, but I want to deal with one or two
logistic matters, if I may call them that. Members will want to know when the Bill as
amended will be available in printed form. I am told that there is a good prospect of having it
tomorrow, and that would be an advantage for its distribution and study before we come to
the second reading, which, of course, will be after the recess. Miss Bowden of the Clerk's
office has prepared a record of the principal amendments made by the committee, and it has
been circulated to members and will be of considerable help to them. I have distributed a
press statement that I hope will lead to a better understanding of the effects of the amended
Bill.
Over recent weeks some people have come to believe that the Bill is a charter for sexual
disorientation, I suppose is the word for homosexuality, and that it is a charter for de facto
marriages. I have had to sign many letters correcting that impression, and saying that the
Human Rights Commission Bill contains no reference to homosexuals, and that certainly the
Government had no intention of adding any reference to the Bill; and that we had also
removed the definition of marital status, and hence the reference to de facto marriages. But
that has already been adverted to.
The member for Henderson said that this is not a human rights Bill, but more an equal
opportunities Bill. The fact is that it is what it says it is—a Human Rights Commission Bill. It
sets up a commission and gives it certain functions, particularly including the promotion of
human rights, and a better understanding of human rights and of the international covenants
dealing with them. It does not pretend to cover the whole realm of human rights, nor to
codify them. It is wise to take this first step and make quite sure-in fact it is not the first
step, because our Race Relations Bill in 1971 was. Too many people stumble by taking too
big a step at the beginning. It will be all the better because there is no attempt at the
beginning to codify every human right.
I draw attention to the amendments we have made to the Race Relations Act. It has
been amended by the schedules to this Bill to align its provisions with the Human Rights
Commission Bill. We do not propose to amalgamate the two. Each stands on its own. The
Race Relations Conciliator's office continues on its own, although he becomes a member of
the commission. I propose to have the amended Race Relations Act reprinted; that will be
necessary because of the substantial changes made. As recommended to the select commit-

That is a new offence that needs to be brought to everybody's attention, because in this
