where reference is made to an unease at the expansion of governmental and administrative
power that became apparent during the term of the socialist Labour Government, between
1973 and 1975. I believe it was as a consequence of that growing concern that the National
Party's policy was devised to introduce this type of legislation.
The Bill will help to prevent the expansion of governmental and administrative power,
and will place a new emphasis and focus new attention on the rights of the individual. Of
course, there is nothing new about this. The National Government has a long history of
promoting legislation to protect the rights of the individual, particularly during the past 15
years. During that time it has introduced legislation setting up the office of Ombudsman, and
the Race Relations Conciliator. Further progressive legislation protecting women's rights
has been introduced by our present Minister of Justice. This legislation was designed to focus
attention on and to provide a legislative answer in outlawing discrimination, but it was also
aimed at promoting the advancement of human rights, in general sympathy with the
principles of the United Nations and international covenants and other overseas legislation
enacted in the same field.
I believe the Bill provides for the proper formation of a Human Rights Commission
whose function will be to promote respect for individual people, irrespective of race, colour,
sex or creed. It offers hope for a great number of people who in the past have felt that they,
as individuals, have suffered from discrimination. This forward, far-reaching type of


## p. 1253 (#495) ###########################################

7 July
1253
Human Rights Commission Bill
legislation will have an impact on our future social life.
In the first instance, it is designed to set up a commission to look at the woes, worries,
concerns, and complaints of individuals; to offer a charter of hope to those without great
private means; to offer hope to those people who are timid and who in the past would not
have exposed their individual affairs to such scrutiny; and it charges the tribunal with the
very delicate but important job of always trying to reach conciliation between the aggrieved
party and the other parties involved in their claims. This really is the key, and is certainly the
paramount purpose of the tribunal-to conciliate between the parties-because the area
involves very human issues which cannot always be properly measured scientifically. This
legislation deals with the emotions, thoughts, and aspirations of individuals, and surely
conciliation should be not only the answer to many problems but also a guide for the future,
giving the direction to be followed by those interested in the same area.
Following on from the establishment of the commission, the Bill proposes the establish-
ment of a tribunal to deal with those difficult cases where agreement cannot be reached
through conciliation. The functions of the tribunal will play an important part in instilling
confidence in the people, who would soon lose faith in a tribunal or a commission without
teeth. It might be said that the tribunal is the instrument through which people will see that
justice is being done.
I very much enjoyed working on this select committee. This is the first real piece of
legislation I have personally been involved in on a select committee, and it is good to see it
coming to fruition. I was impressed with the variety and the large number of sources from
which submissions came to the committee. They were not just from protesting, busybody
groups or eager legal beagles, religious quarters or disenchanted racial groups. They came
from individuals and groups representing every section of the community, and this wide
cross-section that gave evidence indicates the general interest in the Bill, and the recognition
of its importance as a major part in all future social legislation.
It is pertinent to comment on the harmonious composition of the committee. It was a
pleasure to work with members of the Opposition alongside my own party colleagues. The
information drawn from many sources has added greatly to the changes, and the nature of
those changes, made to the Bill. Each member on the select committee made an important
contribution to its findings. We were, of course, well served by officers from various
Government departments and of this House, who were there to advise the committee. The
work proved to be a worth-while experience, and I look forward to the passing of this Bill
through all stages. I personally compliment the chairman of the committee, who steered us
wisely and well, and I also pay tribute to the Minister of Justice, who had the forethought to
institute the original Bill. In time it will lead to further social legislation of which New
Zealand can be proud. It takes its place properly alongside the legislation of those nations
who have embraced the spirit of race relations in the best sense.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): As a member of the select committee for some period, I echo

I reflect with interest on the submissions made while I was sitting on the committee. It

challenge which is at the root of legislation on individual rights, because those who were
professedly ultra-right-and I do not suggest they had any connection with the

I confess I do not share the confidence of the member for Awarua, who described this
Bill as a charter of hope, because the response to the balances which must be examined in
legislating for rights, as set out in this measure, is cautious—a testing of the water in specific
areas of human rights, instead of going to the issue of whether we, as a Parliament, will stop
people overtly displaying prejudice or bias. This legislation ventures into stopping that bias
being demonstrated when it comes to matters of employment and the access to goods and

services. Tests or targets of bias are limited to such matters as religion, ethical belief, race,
and marital status.
When this House eventually accepts the challenge of determining what human rights
consist of, there will be a lot of other criteria. Where in this legislation is there a charter of
hope for children, for the disabled, or for the aged? Where is there a charter of hope for
those people who hold a variety of political opinions but who are not urban guerrillas, and

I accept and welcome those provisions which allow for positive discrimination to be
exercised where to do so would enable a particular group to achieve some measure of

being implemented by this commission.
I am pleased that during the hearings of the committee the question of penalties was
grappled with. As the Bill started out the penalties were paltry, but they have now soared to
the level of penalties allowed in a magistrate's court, on a matter of human rights. From a
resumé of the legislation I am pleased to see that there might possibly even be the power for
the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court to venture into so critical an area, and to
have a measure of control in the awarding of what will approximate to damages.
During the hearings submissions were given which sought assurances on the access

this is a cautious first step.
The Bill as amended provides that until 1982 an employer may discriminate on the
grounds of sex where there are no separate sanitary facilities. I should have thought that, in a
matter which required the intervention of the Legislature in something as fundamental to the
National Party as this legislation has been stated to be, 5 years might seem a sufficiently
generous time to allow someone to procure another lavatory. Is this House really going to
stand back and allow discrimination on the grounds of sex to persist for 5 years on such a
puny matter as this? I hope that in later sittings the House will do something about amending
this.
I now want to deal with two provisions in the Bill which are quite inadequate and out of
keeping. The first is clause 58 which deals with privacy. We cannot pretend that this is any
acceptable subsitute for the privacy legislation which has been promised. It has no teeth; it is
a matter of recommendation, and gives no relief to any individual person and does nothing
to enhance privacy. I turn as well to clause 59, which begins Part VI. This clause is so
different from anything which goes before that one wonders how it was conceived in the
same thought. The clause allows a dissident person who believes that there has been some
form of victimisation or wrongful inducement to go to the commission, which may thereaf-
ter, if conciliation cannot be effected, refer the matter to the Industrial Court.
I suggest that the provisions of clause 59 are there because of political policy which is
completely unrelated to human rights. In fact, all those matters in clause 59 are covered by
the existing criminal law. Quite simply, what is proposed here is to invite people to engage in
a procedure which will result in conciliation and in reference to the Industrial Court when
what has been complained of is extortion, which is covered in the Crimes Act and punishable
by 14 years' imprisonment. What an extraordinary turn of events! If, in fact, by the offer of
violence, someone is induced to carry out a different course of conduct, then that is simply
extortion. If the argument being advanced is that people who are being threatened are more
likely to have recourse to the commission than to the police, then I invite the House to
consider what protection the commission is able to afford, day and night, that the police
cannot. I consider Part VI quite misconceived. We support this first step into considering
how Parliament can protect human rights.

Human Rights Commission Bill
The member for Avon gave her reaction to much of the detail of the Bill. When first
looking at the Bill one sees "human rights”, and we all know what they are, but when one
starts analysing human rights it is not easy to put the definition down in a few words. The
United Nations tried to do that several years ago, and I think there have been two
conventions since then when the original concept of human rights has been substantially
amended. At one stage it was suggested that the United Nations declaration should be
included as a schedule to the Bill, but the original declaration would have been inappropriate
because it has been amended, and the conventions would take many pages of presumably
legal jargon, which not many people would understand. It is simple to say that one should
not discriminate against a person because of his race, ethnic origin, or colour, and to say that
that is dealt with under the Race Relations Act. It is also simple to say that one should not
discriminate against a person because of his or her religion, or religious or ethical belief, or
sex or marital status, and that we are all equal and should be treated accordingly. However,
we then come to the fine print and recognise that we quite happily accept differences in some
areas. Earlier I mentioned the ladies golf club. Perhaps I should now mention the men's
hurdles. They are quite legitimate exercises performed at the Olympic Games, the Common-
wealth Games, and on various sports fields.
Much of the time of the committee was devoted, necessarily, to drawing the line
between what was a reasonable differentiation between people, and what was unreasonable
discrimination. The committee had to define the fine line between protecting the rights of
people and their being able to behave differently, and at the same time to protect people
from unreasonable, unreasoning discrimination. Therein lay the committee's difficulties.
What we have seen in the Bill may be expressed in the words of Isaiah: "The wolf and the
lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock, and the dust shall be
the serpent's meat; they shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, saith the Lord." I
do not know whether we will reach as far as that, because that is the idea of Utopia, if not
Eden.

sectors. Friction over the split shift was at the root of the recent tramways dispute, and in

consequences of not having the words "the 8-hour day" in clause 19(6)(h) could well be that
shop workers will be forced to work their daily 8 hours over more than an 8-hour day, which
is what some bus drivers have to do now. Accordingly, the Opposition moved to amend
clause 19(6)(h) by inserting after the words "40-hour week" the words "and the 8-hour day".
The last amendment moved by the Opposition concerned clause 23(1), and the
Opposition felt that the removal of this provision was the most important single way in which
the Government could keep faith with the public. The Government made frequent claims,
both in the House and outside, that nothing in the Bill would interfere with the present
contractual relationship between worker and employer. As it stands, clause 23(1) contradicts
that claim. The Government has consistently said that the underlying purpose of the Bill is
merely to rationalise the shop trading position, and that it does not want to erode the union's
normal prerogative; but here we have enshrined in one single clause what appears to be an
underlying movement' against the union concerned. The Opposition is of the opinion that,
whatever the inadequacies and inconsistencies in New Zealand's shop trading situation,
none of them arises from the fact that New Zealand's shop trading hours are matters for
award and negotiation. Therefore, the Opposition sees no need for clause 23(1), and
accordingly moved to delete that subclause.
The Opposition has opposed the Bill for the reasons that I have given. It has listened to
what the Government had to say, and has asked those questions that were in need of
answers, if the reason for the introduction of the Bill into our statute book was to be made
clear. The Opposition has continuously asked, "Who wants the Bill?", but has received no
answer, and, indeed, it would be hard to find an answer when one considers the number of
submissions against its introduction, and the very few submissions in its favour. The
Opposition believes that the House and the country have a right to answers to the questions
it has asked, and, until they are heard, it will continue to oppose this unwanted legislation.

This is the review committee's recommendation to the former Minister of Labour, and it
was on this recommendation that the National Government thought that it should act. This
recommendation is not the only answer to "Who asked for this legislation?" There is also the
fact that a public demand throughout New Zealand has developed as a result of practices
that have built up over a period. Last year between 600 and 700 offences were reported, and
a far greater number of people have been breaking the law for some time.
Many amendments were moved in the Committee stage. The Opposition moved an
amendment to clause 4A on the Shop Trading Hours Commission. The Opposition consi-
dered that the new commission should have one representative from the Federation of
Labour and one from the Retailers Federation. Government members felt that the commis-

During the Committee stage, the Opposition moved several amendments to clause 6,
which relates to a greater flexibility during the week between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. After the
discussion in the House, members will know that the awards will affect the amount of time
and length of the day, and that these awards will govern to a great extent, as they have
governed in the past, the working hours between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. from Monday to Friday.
Nine retail awards cover sections of the industry and allow for different opening and closing
hours. It was generally agreed that the new provisions would be more fitting and, after
considering the amendments that were moved, there is no doubt that it was better that the
House left the Bill as it came from the select committee.
There was much discussion on clause 19, and again the Opposition moved amendments.
Government members pointed out that the clause was not likely to bring about an extension
of shopping hours during the weekend, as was suggested by many Opposition members. The
criteria that must be taken into account were spelt out time and time again, and there could
be no doubt that they would not extend weekend shopping.
As has already been mentioned, the Opposition tried hard to have clause 17 altered.
This clause provides an opportunity for the occupiers of most shops in an area to apply for an
order for all shops in the area to open at specified times, and on specified days. The
Opposition tried to add as an amendment, "provided that where two or more shops in such
an area are occupied by one person he shall, for the purpose of this section, be deemed to be
the occupier of a single shop". The Minister was sympathetic to this proposal and it was
studied at some length, but it was generally felt that, under clause 19, the commission could
take it into account. The parties seeking an order would draw the matter to the attention of
the commission, which would have regard to it and other matters.
This is a good Bill. It will legalise many present practices. It will extend the number of
approved goods, especially those sold by garden centres, and handyman's suppliers which
have been acting outside the law. It will give a greater choice of shopping hours from 7 a.m.
to 9 p.m., Monday to Friday, and those hours will be controlled by the awards, which will

Clause 4A deals with the shop trading hours commission and the membership thereof,

the Retailers Federation-two groups with a vested interest in the Bill.
Clause 19 is the key to the whole process and clearly protects the New Zealand life style
against the pressures of the 1970s. Once again, in the irrational way they have debated this

previous legislation no longer applies to the 1970s. The member for Mangere wanted the
shop trading hours commission to be bound by the special eight criteria laid down,
demonstrating that he is not prepared to allow a three-man commission of this nature to have
the flexibility it needs to solve these problems and to provide a fair degree of justice in
special cases, such as that of the Parnell markets, without allowing across-the-board

fish that blows itself up. Perhaps he might reflect on that. In the second reading debate we
expressed our revulsion to the Bill with some vigour and at some length, although, I must
say, not at the same length as Government members. They continued on after we had given
them, with the gentlest of hints, the suggestion that we thought that everything that might be
said had already been said, if not once, then perhaps twice or three times. However, they
took no notice and carried on. Ultimately we came to the Committee stage, and there
fulfilled our duty as a good and loyal Opposition by doing the best we could to make what we
thought was a very bad Bill just a little better.
I should like to sum up the amendments we moved in the Committee stage, as briefly as
I can. The first amendment was to clause 4A(2), in which we sought to change the
membership of the commission by acceding to the desire expressed by the Minister of
Tourism that there should be a reasonably balanced tribunal. We offered the eminently
sensible proposal that instead of having two lay members at large there should be one
nominated by the Retailers Federation and another by the Federation of Labour, the result
of which would have been a reasonably balanced tribunal. Now that the Minister of Tourism
is here, after being unfortunately away on public business when I spoke before, I should like
to take this opportunity of saying that he would have been an eminently acceptable
representative of the Retailers Federation, with his long and honourable history in the
retailing trade.
On clause 4B we suggested that the tribunal as a whole should participate in any
significant exercise of its jurisdiction. We acknowledged, of course, that in any peripheral
matters of procedure it was appropriate that the chairman should make the ruling without
the participation of the other two parties, but in any substantial application, at least at the
outset until the new procedure had settled down, we thought it better that the whole tribunal
should participate. We moved an amendment to that effect, but again, unfortunately,
without success.
Clause 6(1) refers to specific statutory holidays. We sought to add a provision that no
shop shall open other than between the hours of 7 a.m. and 6 p.m. on four days a week
except if otherwise provided for in an award or an agreement. Once again that was rejected.
Then we come to one which the Government was on the verge of accepting, one which I had
the honour of moving. We were dealing with the situation of multiple occupancy of shops in
shopping malls or in other areas where there were a number of shops, which were called
upon or had the opportunity to vote as to whether there should be extended shopping hours.
We thought it was appropriate that where one person had a multiple interest by occupying
more than one shop his vote should not be counted merely by the number of shops he
occupied, and that there should be just one vote along with those of the other shop owners in
the mall. As I have said, the Government came very close to accepting this, but in the end, I
think with some reluctance, it felt it could not accede to it, and thus it was set aside.
Clause 19 was the subject of a number of amendments, the first being to delete from the
criteria to which the tribunal should have regard in determining the issues put before it the
matter of public demand. This amendment was put forward on the basis that that was a very
elusive concept, hard to define and even harder to grasp. The Opposition believed that
because the main criterion to which the tribunal shall have regard is the public interest,
public demand should be dropped as one of the aspects to be taken into account. The

INSURANCE LAW REFORM BILL
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Not many members were involved in
this debate on a Bill introduced by the Government to give effect to a report of the Contracts
and Commercial Law Reform Committee presented to my predecessor in the Labour
Government on 1 July, 2 years ago. The committee made recommendations on a limited
number of specific problems in our insurance law, and confined itself to five particular
>roblems while indicating that it proposed to continue its study into other matters. There is
eneral agreement that this was a good thing-that the most urgent problems and the
esolution of them should come first to the Government's attention. I am glad that we were
able to give effect to the good work of these learned gentlemen on the law reform
committee.
Although there was only minimal reference to clause 12 by witnesses before the select
committee, for reasons best known to themselves members opposite decided to find fault
with clause 12. It might be as well if I recapitulate what clause 12 provides. It provides that
legal actions between an insurer and an insured will be dealt with by a judge alone, rather
than a judge and jury as at present. This clause was recommended unanimously by the
learned gentlemen on the law reform committee. They recommended it, as they indicated in
their report, as a balance to clause 8 of the Bill, which restricts an insurer's right to require
disputes to be settled by arbitration.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: It wasn't unanimous. There was some reservation.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Yes, it was indeed unanimous; It was quite unanimous, and I
must emphasise that because I have checked it with the secretary of the committee. The
report makes that quite clear, if it is read as it should be read, and not in the way that the
member for Auckland Central wants to read it. The learned gentlemen in the committee
were unanimous. I can assure the honourable members of this, because I have checked that
fact with the secretary of the committee.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Well, read it.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I will read it, and, quoting from paragraph 20 of the report, I
want to deal with the compulsory arbitration part of the report and indicate that: "The
committee remains of the view that it is desirable for there to be a degree of uniformity
concerning arbitration clauses, but recognises that many insurers believe disputes between
an insurer and an insured will not fairly be resolved if determined by a jury. Although some
members"-that is members of the law reform committee-"do not fully endorse this
view"- the view that disputes will not be fairly resolved if determined by a jury is the one on
which they were not unanimous "nevertheless, we consider . . ."-the word "neverthe-
less" is not theirs, but this is how it is read—“. . . we consider that it would be reasonable for
the provision in the draft Bill that arbitration clauses shall not bind the insured to be
amended to provide that resultant claims between the insured and the insurer are to be heard
before a magistrate or, if in the Supreme Court, before a judge alone." This follows the
principle of arbitration that has always applied in the past. There is virtually no appeal from
arbitration.


## p. 1269 (#511) ###########################################

7 July
1269
Insurance Law Reform Bill
Members opposite no doubt have their own reasons for wanting to make a mountain out
of this, and a lot of absurd extravagances have been advocated in their argument. The law
reform committee made it quite plain that it is common for insurance policies to provide
under the present practice that any disputes between an insured and the insurer must be
arbitrated, and they go on to say: "Arbitration as a means of determining disputes can
undoubtedly have its merits. Matters in issue can be resolved relatively informally, and,
where issues are technical, there are advantages in selecting an arbitrator with experience in
the relevant field. But motives for insisting on arbitration can be less worthy, they observe,
and they say that an insurer, by insisting on arbitration, can defeat claims, because it is more
expensive to pay an arbitrator-or two arbitrators and an umpire-than to employ the
services of judges or magistrates who are, of course, paid by the State, because the process of
appointing arbitrators and settling references can lead to delay, and because legal aid is not
available for arbitrations”, and so on.
The reasons for the determination of these learned gentlemen are clearly set out, and
are in the public interest, as they are concerned with the ability of the ordinary people who
take out insurance policies with insurance companies to pay, where any dispute arises over
their entitlements in claiming. I submit that, with the Bill, we are carrying out the unanimous
opinion of these gentlemen, who were chaired by a distinguished Wellington lawyer, Mr
Patterson, having as members of the committee Mr Cameron, the Deputy Secretary of
Justice; Professor Coote; Mr D. F. Dugdale, a well known Auckland lawyer; Professor
Ellinger; Mr J. R. Fox; Mr J. S. Henry; Mr W. Iles, the Chief Parliamentary Counsel; and
Mr J. H. Wallace, Q.C., of Auckland. The Secretary, Mr Wright, of the Department of
Justice, has assured me that the opinion was unanimous. I have no doubt that members
opposite, having been told what they should have known if they had read the report
carefully, will have reason to reconsider their attitude to clause 12.
It is very reasonable to make this provision in the interests of the ordinary people of
New Zealand who want their justice dealt with simply and speedily. The abolishment of
arbitration in clause 8 and the inclusion of clause 12 as unanimously recommended by the
law reform committee does just that. The member for Auckland Central gave notice during
his second reading speech that he will move an amendment in the Committee stage.
However, I can tell him now that I will not be drawn to the course he proposes to follow. I
commend the Bill.
Bill read a second time.

HEALTH AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That the Health Amendment Bill be
introduced. The purpose of the Bill is to restrict the classes of persons who may perform
acupuncture to medical practitioners, dental practitioners, physiotherapists, and persons
approved by the Director-General of Health and acting under the direction and supervision
of a doctor, dentist, or physiotherapist. The Bill prohibits an acupuncturist from advertising
himself as performing, or being qualified to perform, acupuncture.
Although there is growing interest in acupuncture, it is not generally realised that when
performed by unqualified or unskilled persons it can be dangerous. However, acupuncture
does have a useful and legitimate place in medical treatment. A scientific basis for
acupuncture has not yet been established, and research on this is continuing. No doubt the
use of acupuncture could develop further, but only on a scientific and controlled basis. It is
important that, before acupuncture is used, proper diagnosis of any medical condition
should be undertaken by a qualified person. In some cases acupuncture, although relieving
pain, can also mask disease. Complications such as the transmission of infection can arise
from the improper or unskilled use of acupuncture.
The New Zealand Medical Association, the New Zealand Dental Association, the
Medical Council of New Zealand, The Physiotherapists Board, and the New Zealand
Society of Physiotherapists, have been consulted about the need to control the practice of
acupuncture, and all support the principles of the Bill. It has not been possible to obtain a
consensus of opinion from persons at present practising acupuncture, because acupuncturists
do not have a national organisation from which such views could be sought.
Squadron Leader DRAYTON (St. Albans): I have just one question for the Minister. Is
one of the purposes of the acupuncture Bill to prick the balloon of inflation?
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The Bill—
Hon. Allan McCready: The wong Bill.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: I will try to say the wight words-raises a number of legal as
well as medical questions. There has always been uncertainty about what liability, if any,
attaches to a doctor who invades the bodily integrity of a person in extremis in rendering first
aid, and so on. It is generally covered by the convention that medical attention is applied for
the good of the individual concerned. Acupuncture is a novel discipline in this country, and I
would imagine that the same convention applies.
However, I do not know exactly where acupuncture begins and ends—perhaps when the
prick goes in, I do not know, but there is no definition, of course. I wonder if the enterprise
is capable of definition. Just what is understood to be acupuncture? Is it the use of needles in
a particular case, or is it to be compared with the ordinary insertion of a hypodermic syringe,
and so on? I am sure a number of these questions will require consideration. Therefore, the
Bill should at least go to a committee so that some of them could be ventilated.
What qualifications are recognised? Are there any accepted schools of training for
acupuncturists, and, if so, do we recognise any or all of them? Are they all in China, or are
there some outside China? Is there any mode of training here, such as an apprenticeship?
Again, these are aspects which ought not to be passed over lightly. I suggest the matter ought
to go to a committee.
Mr DOWNIE ( Pakuranga): The acupuncture Bill raises a number of very interesting

acupuncture? Reports of what can be achieved by acupuncture have been very interesting,

but it is evident that acupuncture performed by unskilled people could conceal conditions

Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I thank the members who have so far contributed
to the debate. I do not want to go into too much detail, because this is not a party Bill or a
political move. We want it to be seen as a measure introduced by the House. I am certain
that the member for Porirua is well informed and will want to contribute. He, better than
anybody on the floor of the House, will be able to give the details that the member for
Pakuranga has called for.
The member for Henderson said that the Bill contained no definition. I realise that he
had had the Bill in his hand for only about half a minute, but it is an amendment to the
principal Act, and the proposed new section 126C(1) states that: "For the purposes of this
section a person performs acupuncture if, by means of a needle (whether with or without
mechanical, electrical, or other stimulation of the needle or of the body) he punctures any
part of the body of any other living person for the purpose of diagnosing or treating any
disease from which that other person is or is suspected to be suffering, or for any other
therapeutic, anaesthetic, or analgesic purpose: Provided that neither the administering of an
injection to any person nor the puncture of any part of the body of any person for the
purpose of removing any matter constitutes the performance of acupuncture for the
purposes of this section." If that definition does not satisfy the member for Henderson he
can speak later in the debate.
When we talk about “removing any matter", we do not want the Bill to stop a mother
from removing a splinter from a child's finger. The experts have examined the Bill and I
know that the member for Porirua will want to explain it in greater detail to the member for
Henderson. The experts thought that the definition was satisfactory for the purpose. In the
first instance, the Director-General of Health will decide who is to be registered and, at this
stage, I think that is an appropriate way to go about it. A certain amount of knowledge and
experience will be brought in; people will come forward for registration, and will produce
their records and experience. In that way, the Director-General of Health will, through the
establishment of precedents, build up a code that will be understood. I do not know how
many years it will take, but eventually, no doubt, we will have an acupuncturists board to
administer affairs, as physiotherapists have a board, and as last year, for instance, the Health
Amendment Bill took away registration of plumbers and drainlayers from the Department
of Health and gave it to a board.
Unfortunately there are dangers; that is why we want to establish the minimum
necessary controls at an early stage. Indeed, potential dangers are great, and as there is no
other control machinery legislative control is needed. Because of the lack of any control at
present, no information is supplied to the department, the Government, or any association
on the type of things that might have gone wrong. Registration is a measure of control, and it
will enable us to determine how the practice is developing and whether the potential dangers
are being realised. If any fears are realised, it may be that the dangerous practices can be
stopped by wise administration and further sensible control. Again, I believe that the
member for Porirua is in a better position than I am to explain the dangers inherent in the

practice and to say how they might be avoided.
Dr WALL (Porirua): I thank the Minister for his reply and for the remarks he made
about me. I assure him that we on this side of the House will raise no objection to the passing
of this measure. I believe it to be a very timely measure, but it raises one or two matters of
concern. I confirm the statements made by the Minister about the need for control and the
potential dangers of the acupuncture procedure. The more obvious one, and the one which
can be controlled effectively by this type of legislation, is the need to ensure that proper
standards of hygiene are adopted. Because of the obvious dangers of superficial infection,
the danger of hepatitis also exists following the unskilful sterilisation of equipment. That
problem is encountered in hospitals, wherever intravenous or subcutaneous equipment is
used, and some measure of control is vitally necessary. That is probably the greatest hazard.
In this and other fields of unconventional medical practice we have seen in the past what
can regretfully only be called scientific bigotry on the part of established professionals when
those practices have been growing in parallel with conventional practices. We are now
trying, properly, to bring that under control, but we are left with a dilemma in that, although
doctors may know and practise good and proper control from the point of view of
conventional medicine, they may be very largely or almost totally unskilled in the unconven-
tional areas. One thinks here of the field of manipulative therapy.
I hope that the restrictions imposed will not be too tight and that the machinery
followed will ensure good medical practices and will not destroy good acupuncture by
practitioners and prevent them from carrying out their craft effectively. That problem could
easily arise, in that some of the best acupuncturists may be the most unsatisfactory people
medically because they are acutely aware of the range of relief they can provide, and the
more skilled they are in acupuncture the greater relief they can give. Therefore, although in
some ways they may have the greatest amount to contribute because of the skills they have,
they are limited solely to the field of acupuncture and become less and less concerned about
diagnostic and hygiene problems and other difficulties associated with that form of treat-
ment. I hope the Minister, in ensuring control, will make provision for acupuncturists to
commence working in conditions that are as near as possible to those they want, but that at
the same time the problems created by misdiagnoses and infections, particularly hepatic
infection, will be safeguarded against.
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa): We on this side of the House recognise, as I am sure
members opposite do, that there is a growing demand for acupuncture in the community.
That, of course, poses obvious difficulties for the Department of Health, and especially for
the Minister. It is interesting to look at the Health Act of 1956, which contains no provision
whereby the practice of acupuncture can be controlled. The Bill the Minister has now
brought forward provides for such control.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: We need a gramophone needle for you.
Mr WELLINGTON: I should have thought that the Leader of the Opposition would
have some interest in a matter that is of such importance to the community, but it is clear
that he has no interest in it whatever. I remind him that restrictions are essential if the public
is to be adequately protected. The practice of acupuncture must be limited to registered
medical practitioners, dentists, or physiotherapists, or people working under their direction
or supervision. That is a very natural and proper provision to make. It is also important and
relevant to consider what is happening in comparable Western societies, and perhaps
particularly in the United States where acupuncture is practised by licensed physicians,
primarily for the purpose of relieving pain.
The problem discovered in America in the early 1970s, and the period 1972-73 in
particular, was that a growing number of patients were being treated by unlicensed
acupuncturists. That tendency developed rapidly and had to be controlled. The interest of
countries such as New Zealand, the United States, Australia, and countries in Western
Europe followed the West's recognition of and growing contact with the Republic of China.
About 5 or 6 years ago it was seen in the United States that acupuncture was rapidly being
taken almost as seriously as any new advance in Western medicine-and I think of such
things as organ transplants and the search for a remedy or cure for cancer. Consequently, the
National Institute of Health approved a recommendation to study acupuncture not just as an
anaesthetic but also for the possible management of chronic pain caused by illnesses such as
cancer, neuralgia, and arthritis.
About 5 years ago the number of non-professional and unlicensed acupuncturists in the
United States was about 100, and New Zealand is probably in a relatively similar situation
today in proportion to its population. I am speaking of the traditional oriental folk medicine,

As far as we are aware, probably the main benefit of acupuncture is in the general field
of anaesthetics. It is estimated that 1 in 5000 administrations of general surgical anaesthesia
in the United States prove fatal. There is also some slight risk of kidney and liver damage
through the administration of conventional anaesthesia, but acupuncture is relatively safe in
that it does not reduce blood pressure or depress breathing as does general anesthesia.
Also, there is no nausea or post-operative hangover with the use of acupuncture. The
purpose of the Bill is to recognise that acupuncture has a place in medicine and that there is a
community demand for it, so the House must be very careful to ensure that this new advance
in medical technology—in the Western sense-is carefully and sensibly controlled.

Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I should like to answer, to the best of my ability,
the questions that have been asked. The member for Hamilton East asked about the use of
acupuncture in drug abuse. I would not want to quote Dr Fraser McDonald, primarily

acupuncture, believing that it could make a contribution in drug abuse. The member for
Raglan and the member for Hamilton East both raised a point about the uses of acupuncture
mentioned in the Bill. These are the only uses of acupuncture that I know of. I do not know

satisfactorily.
I agree with the member for Hamilton East that it might be desirable to preclude the
giving of an injection by one person to another, except by special people or under
supervision. Nurses give injections now, and not always under direct supervision, where the
situation demands it; and, of course, anyone can give an injection in extreme circumstances.
Anybody who has been in a war would know of the absolute need for people in certain
circumstances to inject morphine, for example. The controls should not be so great that
legitimate practices are stopped, and it would be fairly difficult to define what was legitimate
and what was not. The honourable member also asked about the letters that would be put
after the practitioner's name. If you could afford it, and if your brass plate were big enough,
I suppose what you would put would be "ACUPUNCTURER”, which would be a costly
operation and the sort of operation we want to avoid.

question of whether the Bill should go to a select committee, and the Opposition spokesman
also discussed this with me before the Bill was introduced. I accept the members' recommen-

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Maintenance Payments—Audits at Main Centres
1. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Social Welfare, What is the
length of time between audits of maintenance at offices of the Department of Social Welfare
in (a) Auckland, (b) Hamilton, (c) Lower Hutt, (d) Wellington, (e) Christchurch, and (f)
Dunedin?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of
the Minister of Social Welfare. The department's inspectors carry out an audit of mainte-
nance in each district office at least once a year. Auditors from the Controller and Auditor-
General's office also examine this aspect of the department's work from time to time. In
addition, in every office maintenance records are required to be perused weekly to ensure
that adequate action is being taken for enforcement. These procedures apply in respect of all
social welfare offices, including those referred to by the honourable member for Raglan.
Marilyn Waring: I understand that in Hamilton the audit is carried out approximately
every 3 months, and has to be undertaken manually, with the result that the arrears for many
recipients of maintenance can reach incredible sums. Does the Government intend to alter
the manual system of audit?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I do not know the details about the Hamilton office,
except that the supplementary information I have been given by my colleague is that
manual instructions require maintenance officers to peruse the maintenance records each
week to ensure that adequate action is taken for enforcement. The Minister is at present
working on proposals to introduce a new system, and submissions will be made to the
appropriate Cabinet committee in due course.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
National Superannuation-Cost
2. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to ask the Minister of Finance, Has he seen the
report in the Wairarapa Times-Age of 29 June in which the member for Hamilton West is
quoted as doubting that the country could long sustain paying superannuation benefits to
those who were still working, and, if so, does he agree with this point of view, and, if not,
how does he see the increasing cost of the Government's superannuation scheme being met?
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I draw your
attention to this question, and in particular to the phrase "if so, does he agree with this point
of view". I refer you to Standing Order 87(2)(a), which states, "Questions addressed to
Ministers shall not seek an expression of opinion". I suggest that this does just that. The
question refers to an observation made by a Government member, and then asks the
Minister to say if that is his opinion. I suggest that the question is contrary to the Standing
Order, and perhaps you might care to give your view on that, Mr Speaker. The balance of
the question, "how does he see the increasing cost of the Government's superannuation
scheme being met", could stand, but I think that the first part should be ruled out of order
for the reasons given.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): An opinion is being sought from the Minister
because the Minister to whom the question is being directed is responsible for the adminis-
tration of the scheme.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): Speaking to the point of order, the argument submitted by the
member for Mt. Albert is completely unacceptable. The fact that the Minister may be
responsible in this area of administration in itself is not a reason why he should be asked to
express an opinion, because, as the member for Wellington Central has already explained,
Standing Order 87(2) clearly states that questions addressed to Ministers shall not seek an
expression of opinion, which is an unqualified exclusion. The Standing Order does not state
that the question shall not seek an expression of opinion in certain circumstances, but states
categorically that it shall not seek an expression of opinion. I believe that the relevant part of
question 2 is clearly outside the Standing Orders.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Speaking to the point of order, the
member for Mt. Albert could have overcome the problem of the breach of Standing Order
87(2)(a), which is undoubtedly raised by the words "does he agree with this point of view", if
he had asked, "and if so, is there evidence to support this point of view". However, as he put
it-and it is his responsibility to draft his own question-it clearly does offend Standing
Order 87(2)(a). The position might be met if the member for Mt. Albert were willing to
amend his question to ask the Minister whether there is evidence to support the point of view
of the member for Hamilton West. The matter then becomes one of fact and not of opinion.

Wellington Airport-Navigational Aids
4. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Civil Aviation and
Meteorological Services, Why is it that during the 21 months in which it has not been possible
to determine the cause of the intermittent malfunctioning of the Newlands beacon, other
navigational aids at Wellington Airport have been permitted to become or remain unservice-
able with the result that the Airline Pilots Association has placed restrictions on the airport's
use?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services. The honourable member will be aware that it is
unrealistic to expect the navigational aids at Wellington Airport, or anywhere else for that
matter, to be 100 percent serviceable. The level of serviceability over the period to which he
refers has been satisfactory. When failures do occur they are dealt with promptly, and
facilities are not allowed to remain unserviceable any longer than is practicable. The Airline
Pilots Association is putting no restrictions on Wellington. The Newlands beacon is being
used by some pilots. Whether or not the beacon is used does not affect the services of either
NAC or Air New Zealand.
Mr Friedlander: How many flights have actually been cancelled as a result of deficient
navigational aids in Wellington?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY: I am not aware of that. Numerous checks made of the
beacon during civil aviation calibration flights have all been faultless. The civil aviation
division is equipping a helicopter with which to make further checks. Such checks are being
carried out to the best of the division's ability.

Oral Answers to Questions
Houpapa Shooting Grounds for Refusing Inquiry
10. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Police, On what grounds
did he base his decision, conveyed by him to the member for Northern Maori in his letter of 5
January 1977, that a public inquiry into the shooting of Daniel Houpapa was neither
necessary nor desirable?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): The decision of Cabinet that a public
inquiry into the shooting of Daniel Houpapa was neither necessary nor desirable was based
on the following: first, the opinion of the Solicitor-General, who conducted an independent
and extensive review of the Police file and concluded that the policeman who fired the fatal
shot was justified in terms of sections of the Crimes Act. In regard to section 41, the
Solicitor-General's opinion stated that "the circumstances were such that the officer who
fired the fatal shot did so to prevent an act which he had reasonable grounds for believing
would, if done, amount to the commission of an offence which would be likely to cause
immediate and serious injury to others." The opinion also stated that the officer was justified
in using such force as was reasonably necessary to prevent Daniel Houpapa from shooting
again, and the only practicable means of force available was a firearm. Secondly, the verdict
of the coroner included the finding that Daniel Houpapa's death was caused by a gunshot
wound "which was received from a firearm fired by a member of the police engaged in the
course of measures being taken for the prevention of likelihood of serious injury to a
member of the police".
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Cerebral Angiography
11. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Health, Can he tell the House
the number of occasions on which cerebral angiography was used in New Zealand in the
years 1974, 1975, and 1976?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I hope my answer will be helpful to the House. I
should like to say, first that angiography involves the injection of a dye into the blood vessels
in the neck and the taking of X-rays to establish the blood circulation. It involves some risk
to the patient and it is painful. It costs between $400 and $700 per patient, depending on
whether only one side of the brain is examined or both. An earlier question was asked on
pneumography. That involves the injection of air into the brain cavity and the taking of X-
rays to detect an abnormality. That too is risky and painful, and it costs about $300 per
patient. Fifty percent of angiography and 70 percent of pneumography would be unnecessary
if we had a scanner and, as opposed to the cost of $400 to $700 per patient in one case and
$300 in the other, the cost with a scanner would be $45. The figures for angiography are as
follows: 1974, 1114; 1975, 1281; and 1976, 1385.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

ADJOURNMENT-CONSUMER PRICE INDEX INCREASE
Mr SPEAKER: I have to tell the House that I have received from the Leader of the
Opposition notice of his desire to move the adjournment of the House in order to debate the
increase in the consumer price index. The notice is dated yesterday. It was handed to me last
night, and reads: "Pursuant to Standing Order 89, I give notice that I propose to move, on
Friday 8 July, that the House do now adjourn for the purpose of discussing a definite matter
of urgent public importance. This is the increase in the consumer price index for the quarter
ended 30 June 1977 by the figure of 4.8 percent above that for the March 1977 quarter. This
information is contained in a release by the Government Statistician, dated 5 July but subject
to an embargo expiring at 8 p.m. on Thursday 7 July, and is attributable to a series of fiscal,
economic, and other measures taken by the Government prior to and during the quarter
referred to, such measures including, but by no means limited to, the following, and which, if
they remain unremedied, are likely to result in another record increase in the index for the
next quarter; (1) removal of subsidies; (2) increases in most Government charges, especially
for bulk electricity, postal, and rail charges; (3) increases in taxation on petrol; (4) increases
in interest rates to new record rates, at least partly due to Government policy. The increase
of 4.8 percent in the consumer price index has not been matched or exceeded in any quarter
since the index was compiled, and constitutes an extremely grave threat to the stability of the
economy and, as such, requires the immediate attention of the House and the Government."
The question of whether I should accept the motion is one of the most difficult I have
had to consider under Standing Orders 89 and 90. I have to consider whether the matter that
it is proposed to discuss complies with three criteria, as laid down in Standing Order 90. The
first is whether the matter that it is desired to discuss is a particular case of recent occurrence,
which requires certain things. The term "case" gives me some difficulty. If a tunnel falls in
and miners are trapped-and people naturally ask what the Government is going to do about
it-that is clearly a case or happening. "Case" comes from the Latin "cado-casum",
something that befalls or happens, something that occurs. If a ship is sinking in mid-Pacific,
it can urgently be asked what the Government is going to do about calling in the air force or
the navy to deal with that specific event, or case. When there is a continuing problem, the
area is not so clearly defined; but I shall come back to that.
Another criterion is that the matter involves the administration or ministerial responsi-
bility of the Government. Rising prices are, in part, due to factors that in part are, and in
part are not, under the influence of a Government, but I have no doubt that that criterion is
complied with. Lastly, the matter must require the immediate attention of the House and the
Government. Again, "immediate" is a strong word—not "early attention", but
"immediate", in the sense, I take it, of action forthwith, as opposed to action in the next
week or two or action by the time of the Budget.
Our Standing Orders 89 and 90 correspond to the House of Commons Standing Order
9, except that in 1967 the House of Commons changed its wording, and provided for
discussion of a specific and important matter that should have urgent consideration. We
might well look at rewording our Standing Orders in this matter. Unlike the provisions or the
custom in New Zealand, there must in the House of Commons be ordinarily about 27 hours'
notice to the Government before the debate commences, or, in very urgent cases, some


## p. 1289 (#531) ###########################################

8 July
1289
Adjournment-Consumer Price Index Increase
hours from the end of questions, when the matter can be raised, until the evening, before
which it is not debated. That is also a matter we should look at.
There is a precedent in the House of Commons that is very close to the present matter.
In October 1975, the unemployment level passed 1 000 000, and a member gave notice of his
desire to move the adjournment of the House to discuss that. Mr Speaker said, "Standing
Order 9 was not intended to cover a continuing problem such as unemployment." The
Speaker was Mr Speaker Selwyn Lloyd, who then said, "My decision must not be construed
by anyone as implying that I do not realise the importance of the problem. As a Merseyside
member I know it full well, but it is a continuing problem and one which should certainly be
debated in this House on repeated occasions, but not one for which Standing Order 9 was
drafted or intended." He then added—and I sympathise with him-"Speakers' decisions
were not so easy to make as I thought when serving on the Procedure Committee”. That
corresponds to our Standing Orders Committees that are set up from time to time. I feel I
really ought to decline to accept the motion, because of the very close analogy between
unemployment as a continuing problem passing a certain point in Great Britain in the case I
have cited, and inflation here, which is a continuing problem passing a certain point. Also, it
does not require immediate action—that is, action today as opposed to next week or the
week after.
However, after looking at the wording of the House of Commons Standing Order 9 and
at the spirit of our unhappy Standing Orders 89 and 90, I feel otherwise. Certain considera-
tions have been given weight in New Zealand. If an Address in Reply debate or a Budget
debate were in progress, I should have no hesitation in rejecting the desired motion.
Likewise, if an Imprest Supply Bill was coming up for debate in the near future, I would not
accept the motion. But we have none of those three ways of providing for a general wide-
ranging debate at present.
The more appropriate procedure would be to give notice of a motion, but the defect
there is that between two and four are debated each week, and even if the notice were put at
the top of the Order Paper we should have just two speakers from each side of the House.
The matter desired to be discussed is a major subject that I do not think would be adequately
provided for under that provision. Therefore, bending my legal conscience a bit and bending
the meaning of the word "case" and of the word "immediate" a bit, I propose to give the
Leader of the Opposition the benefit of an enormous doubt and let him move his motion. I
think this will be in accordance with the feelings of most non-lawyer members on both sides
of the House, and of the public, which will probably feel that democracy is functioning better
if I allow a brief slogging match on this subject. My decision to accept the motion is, I
believe, right in instinct, though probably wrong at law, and I should not like it to be treated
as a precedent.

The low figures for the December and March quarters indicate the effectiveness of the price

I take this opportunity to analyse the items covered by the index. Of the 532 items
subject to the study, 107 recorded no price movement. Admittedly, 34 of them traditionally
are not measured in the June quarter, but that still leaves 73.
Mr Marshall: Ha, ha!
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The member may laugh if he likes, but I am stating
the facts, and I am stating them fairly, which is more than his party would do if it were in
office. Some items reduced in price, and several items are at a lower price today than when
Labour was in office. Twenty-two percent of the items rose by between 1 percent and 5
percent, 11 rose by between 6 percent and 10 percent, and 76 rose by 11 percent or more.
One of the reasons, although it is not the main reason, for the increases in the June quarter is
the effect of the progressive lifting of the price freeze for manufactured goods from 1 January
to 15 May, with the main impact in the June quarter. The price freeze helped to give us a
good start-2.6 percent in the March quarter, compared with 4.8 percent in the June
quarter.
The main reason for the figure of 4.8 percent is the effect of an increase in wage rates of
about 15 percent, mostly during the 10 1/2-month period when manufacturers' prices were
frozen and category B prices were held. It is therefore understandable that when the freeze
was lifted there were increases in category B items. This is one of the main arguments against
restricting price adjustments to an annual basis-something that has been seriously consi-
dered by some consumer groups. I do not support such a concept, because the pent-up
demand at the end of the year would make the consumers' position very difficult indeed.
Another major reason is the effect of a 17 percent increase in the prices of imports for
the year ended March 1977. Wages and salaries constitute about 40 percent of the market
price of consumer goods as measured by the consumer price index, and import prices
constitute another 25 percent. The export pull from the effect of dairy and other pastoral
products provides another sizable chunk of the consumer price index. Another component is
the result of the Government's energy pricing policy.
I shall comment very briefly on the seven subgroups that made the most contribution to
the June figure. First, there is private transport, in which there was a 5.5 percent increase.
This derives from increased petrol prices and the price of motor vehicles and spare parts. It is
a fact of economic life that the Labour Government in its 3 years in office faced similar
problems, with similar results. The Labour Government regularly increased the price of
petrol, and the motorist faced increased costs as a result of changes in sales tax and increases
in the prices of cars and spare parts.
Second, there is home ownership, in which the increase was a moderate 2.7 percent,
lower than the increase in many other areas, and certainly lower than the doubling of house
and section prices during the term of the Labour Government. However, housing has a very
large weighting, and there are difficulties in obtaining the information, which mean that the
Government Statistician must use lagged data. Accordingly, the rise for this subgroup
reflects building costs in the March quarter, and house and section prices in the last quarter
of 1976.
In groceries, there has been a 6.1 percent increase. Members know that a considerable
part of that increase was caused by increased costs of imports, including coffee, tea, and
cocoa. I am sure that even the Opposition understands that the New Zealand Government
can have no control over import prices. At least, that was the often-repeated claim of the
Labour Government when it was defending its miserable record in the cost of living.

This morning I want to make certain crucial points about just what is causing the present
run-away spiral in the cost of living, and what action can be taken to stabilise that and,
eventually, to control it. First, we have to stop thinking that the cost of living is represented
simply by the price of goods in shops. It is not only the dollars and cents that count, it is the

of a jar of coffee that counts, it is whether the people can afford it at all. Until we get hold of

There has never been such a savage attack on the living standards of ordinary people as

campaign that if everyone tightened their belts for a while things would come right. Well,

all-time record increase in the cost of living.

if there is to be long-term prosperity and stability in this country, there has to be something

having to resort to long hours of overtime; it has to be possible for people to get ahead
through their own efforts, without being squashed back by taxation and crippling increases in
costs.
In order to do this, I believe that three major areas have to be sorted out. The first is
taxation, which I regard as the single biggest factor in pushing up the cost of living. The
reason for that is simple: for every increase of 1 percent in the rate of inflation, a worker has
to raise his income by at least $2 just to stand still. There is no point in continuing the
argument about wages and prices and which comes first, when we ignore this most important
fact of the impact of taxation. We all know only too well that there is little point in working
exhausting overtime in an effort to get ahead, when more than half of what is earned is taken
away in taxation.
Let us look at the impact of taxation on the ordinary people in the last 18 months.

ago, his standard of living has fallen; and, in fact, it has fallen by $11.53 a week. The tragedy
of this is that if the rate of inflation next year continues to be around 15 percent that same
wage earner, who over the past 18 months has had to increase his income by $34 to stand
still, will have to increase his income by a further $34 in 12 months if he is not going to fall
further behind. The likely effect is that he will fall behind by another $15 to $20.

drain by $1 or more. The pensioners have been misled. It is a disgrace. It is a total breach of

pensioners.

The bulk tariff supply charges had not been changed from 1 October 1967 until 1 October
1976, and there was a growing accumulation of losses. In fact the law itself governing
electricity generation required some contribution up to a maximum of 50 percent from
revenue towards the cost of new generation, but during the time of the third Labour

For a time that Labour Government was asking the New Zealand taxpayer to pay
money to encourage people to conserve electricity, while at the same time charging the same
taxpayers money to subsidise an artificially low price for electricity. The bulk tariff charge
was increased by 60 percent on 1 April 1976, which had the effect at the retail level of
increasing the price by 40 percent. The matter was considered again, and in April 1977 we
had a further 40 percent increase in the bulk tariff to give a modest contribution to capital.
The 40 percent increase at the retail level reflected a move designed to enable the supply
authorities to begin financing some of their capital works from revenue.
This is one of the basic facts from which no responsible Government can run away,
although the former Labour Government sought to do so. Between 1966-67 on the one hand
and 1975-76 on the other, the output of electricity increased by 80 percent, while the cost of
producing electricity increased by 210 percent. In fact, had the increase of 40 percent not

this financial year of $60 million, and that deficit would have had to be met by the taxpayers.

The responsible course the Government should follow would be to say that it was wrong
and that it will not increase the payment of superannuation to 80 percent for people who do
not need it—the over-60s who are earning adequate incomes—and to review the eligibility of
that group for national superannuation. This would make the greatest single contribution to
reducing the pressure on the Government's Budget, the level of Government charges, and
the consumer price index.
In case some members opposite do not come from the Waikato, I refer them to an
article published in the Waikato Times 2 days ago. The Hamilton Young Nationals publicity
officer, Peter Wynn-Jones claimed that the National Party was full of dead wood. He called
upon the party's hierarchy to "sweep through the stables, put the old hacks out into well-
earned pastures, and put in the new colts and fillies". Will the marginal seat holders push for
that policy? The member for Hamilton East probably put his pal up to make that statement,
and he is applauding now. The reason for this is that "unfortunate financial restraints have
been taken, with little or no thought for the quality of life in the country". I wonder where
the member for Hamilton West stands on this matter. He said the country could not afford
the National Government's superannuation scheme. Did he put Mr Wynn-Jones up to push
this? How many members will subscribe to the last item in the newspaper article: "The
National Party is in almost as bad a state now as it was before the 1972 disaster; something
has to be done."
The solution is to throw out the failures of 1972, who were returned in 1975 on a
confidence trick. They pretended that they had the answers, but the only answers they had
were to put up the price of everything. If they could not put up the price they took away the
provision of that service. The National Government has only two policies, prices up, services
down, with the consumer price index at record levels. Ministers opposite try to wriggle away,
and the king of the cockabullies, the Minister of Fisheries, talks about his achievements as a
Minister. He does not have a fillet of fish that he can present at the old price. All he can do is
make groaning noises. I wonder if any Minister will have the courage to tell the hacks on the
front benches, described in the article, to get out to pasture.

Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): With the leave of the House, I wish to

ORAL ANSWERS to QUESTIONS
Inflation-Control
1. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) asked the Minister of
Finance: Is the control of inflation still the Government's main priority; and, if so, what
additional steps does it propose to reverse the present trend?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): Inflation was one of the four major
problem areas which the Government inherited when it took office and further reducing
inflation remains one of the Government's main priorities. Quarterly movements in the
consumer price index have reflected in recent quarters price increases which were deferred
during last year's price freeze, as well as the timing of various Government charge increases
and pricing decisions deferred for up to 3 years by the Labour Government. Quarterly
movements are not currently indicative of the underlying trend of inflation. Annual figures,
which are therefore more indicative of the underlying trend, show that price increases over
the last year have clearly been slower than in the previous 2 years. The Government is not
planning to reverse this trend.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: The Minister of Finance said that inflation was one of the four
problem areas. Does the use of the term "was" indicate that he has rejected both elements of
the National Party's manifesto which stated, "National regards the fight against increases in
the cost of living as the most important single issue in economic management."?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No. I was just reminding the honourable member of the
mess in which he left the country when he was thrown out as Minister of Finance. He needs
reminding from time to time. That was my only reason for referring to four major problems.
If he likes, I will remind him of the other three. Inflation is still the most important of the
four-certainly in my mind, although I doubt whether it was in the mind of the honourable
gentleman, who allowed the rate of inflation to rise from 5.5 percent to 15.7 percent during
the term of the Labour Government.
Mr Wellington: Bearing in mind that when the Labour Government took office in 1972
inflation was running at 5 percent, that in 3 years that figure was trebled by the socialists

opposite, and that for the year ended June 1977 the rate was lowered by the National
Government to 14 percent, would the Minister of Finance not agree that the trend referred

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: That is correct. Of course, the increase during the term of

Paraplegics Resulting from Traffic Accidents
4. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Health: How many
paraplegics have been recorded as a result of traffic accidents in the years 1972, 1973, 1974,
1975, and 1976?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): As the diagnosis of paraplegia is not finally
determined until the patient is ready for discharge the following figures refer to discharged
patients from public hospitals as provided by the National Health Statistic Centre: 1972, 18;
1973, 14; and 1974, 28. The figures are not at present available from that source for 1975 or
1976. However, Middlemore and Christchurch Hospitals treat the majority of these cases,
and the numbers recorded at those two hospitals were: 1975, 18; and 1976, 30.
Mr Lithgow: In the light of those figures, can the Minister confirm that the compulsory
wearing of seat belts has had some effect in reducing the number of accidents resulting in
persons becoming paraplegics?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot confirm that specificially from the figures I have quoted, but
taking those figures in conjunction with others and from advice I have received I am led to
the conclusion that the wearing of seat belts has had a very marked effect and has helped
greatly to reduce the number of serious injuries suffered in motor accidents.

Consumer Price Index-Percentage Increases
7. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of Statistics: What
are the three quarters with the greatest percentage increase in the consumer price index since
1965?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): Since 1965 the three quarters with the
greatest percentage increase in the consumer price index have been the March 1976 quarter
increase of 4.4 percent, the June 1976 quarter increase of 4.5 percent, and the June 1977
quarter increase of 4.8 percent. This group of higher quarters was balanced by the three
lowest quarters since June 1975, the September 1976 quarter of 3.2 percent, the December
1976 quarter of 2.8 percent, and the March 1977 quarter of 2.6 percent. This suggests that
any quarterly movement should be related to annual figures-this year running at 13 to 14
percent to show the underlying trends.

are assembled now in 15 assembly plants, can he confirm that those assembly plants are

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The companies are given approval for licences, if
required, or else they operate in the exempt area, and it is their responsibility to stock
adequate parts. Generally speaking, I find this to be so. Occasionally, complaints are
received, and these are investigated by my department.
Squadron Leader Drayton: How many, if any, of these plants are presently working at
full productivity?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I would require a separate question for that as I
cannot give the honourable member the exact information. Several of these plants are
working virtually at full capacity, although several are not working overtime at present.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Can the Minister give an assurance that there is no intention of
increasing the number of assembly plants, or the number of marques on the New Zealand
market?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: No proposal is at present before me to increase the
number of assembly plants although, if another marque was introduced for trade policy
reasons, an existing assembly plant not operating to full capacity would be encouraged to
take up the job.

OECD Agricultural Products
10. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Prime Minister: What progress was he
able to make on his recent visit to Paris regarding the inclusion of agricultural products in the
OECD trade pledge?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): After deciding to renew the trade pledge
for a further year, the OECD Council went on to agree that in the words of the
communique: "Full use should be made of the existing possibilities for consultation in order
to find and implement multilaterally acceptable solutions to trade problems, whether
industrial or agricultural, in a manner which would take into account the interests of all
concerned." The wording "whether industrial or agricultural" was inserted at New
Zealand's initiative. It provides for the first time explicit recognition that the pledge covers
agricultural as well as industrial trade, though I must make it clear that at no time has the
pledge ever been regarded by New Zealand as excluding agriculture.
Marilyn Waring: Is the Prime Minister aware of any representations about the inclusion
of agricultural products being made by Labour Ministers visiting Paris during their term in
office, and is he aware of the success or failure of their endeavours?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I am not aware of any such initiatives. If there were any
they were certainly not successful.
Mr Falloon: Will this pledge enable New Zealand to improve its negotiating power
overseas with countries which signed the communique?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The trade pledge is regarded seriously. It is looked upon as
a major commitment in terms of the necessity to keep world trade flowing, and that point
was confirmed as recently as this morning in my discussions with the Economics Minister of
the Federal Republic of Germany, when we covered that ground along with a number of
other topics.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Have these words about which the Prime Minister expressed pride
had any practical result in the advice given or the result achieved by his deputy in the present
round of discussions with the Common Market countries?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: It really is rather close to the event to give a firm answer on
that. The trade pledge was renewed just a few weeks ago, but we have very specific
information that for whatever reason the representations made by the Deputy Prime
Minister in recent days have had a favourable effect on the negotiations that are now
proceeding. That advice comes from Mr Gundelach, the Agricultural Commissioner of the
Community, who said specifically to the Deputy Prime Minister that his approach to the two
specific issues that will be under consideration in the immediate future had been affected by
the Deputy Prime Minister's representations, and the proposals for New Zealand improved
accordingly.
Mr Wellington: What has been the reaction to the trade pledge from other nations
whose economy, like New Zealand's, is based primarily upon agriculture?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I have not had any indication from other nations, but there
is no doubt that when I covered similar ground at the Heads of Government meeting in
London to the ground that I covered at the OECD meeting in Paris, my views were very
warmly received by the poorer Commonwealth nations because we found ourselves, as we
have in the past, very much in their camp selling agricultural products at prices which are not
increasing as rápidly as the prices of the industrial products we import.
