International Lending-Treble A Credit Rating
14. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Finance: In which interna-
tional lending market does New Zealand have a triple A credit rating?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The United States domestic capital


## p. 1312 (#554) ###########################################

1312
19 July
Oral Answers to Questions
market is the only major capital market which requires that a formal credit rating be made
before a borrower can enter that market. In this market New Zealand enjoys treble A status.
The other major international capital markets do not have such a formal rating system,
leaving it to the particular market to signal the attractiveness of a borrower by the response
to the loan terms and conditions offered. As evidence of that fact, in 1974 the Labour
Government borrowed in Germany at 9.25 percent, and this year the National Government
borrowed in the same currency at 6.25 percent.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Does the attaining of this rating, after an invitation to Moody's to
come to New Zealand, indicate the Government's intention to borrow from the American
market, which has not been resorted to since 1962-63.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: It is rather the other way round. Without such a credit
rating we could not borrow on the American domestic market. I believe that the Labour
Government was not prepared to take a chance with a Moody's rating, because it would not
have been treble A. The National Government took such a chance, and it is now competent
for us to borrow on that market. A few weeks ago the European Commission launched a
bond issue on the American domestic market at a treble A rating, so New Zealand's credit
rating is exactly the same as that of the European Economic Community.
Mr Malcolm: Could the Minister of Finance confirm that some of New Zealand's
present borrowing is roll-over borrowing aimed at repaying old loans with money that is
borrowed for longer terms. at lower interest rates?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I am not sure if that is quite right, but I can confirm that the
Government has just made a private placement in Swiss francs at 5.5 percent-which would
be good money even in New Zealand at present-to repay early a Labour Government loan,
which was either 8.5 or 9 percent. The National Government has repaid that loan early and
borrowed at 5.5 percent. The Government is cleaning up the Labour Government's messes
in all kinds of fields.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Could the Minister of Finance explain the table published in the 18
March issue of Far Eastern Economic Review, which revealed that Nikkei Business of Japan
rated New Zealand as a single A investment risk, which is one place above Italy, and one
place below Britain.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I have no knowledge of that table, but would point out that
Moody's is the most prestigious financial rating organisation in the world. Last December
New Zealand was given a similar treble A rating from Standard and Poor's, which is another
prestigious credit rating agency. I think I told the House that when I was in Manila attending
the IMF meeting last October the bankers I spoke to, including bankers from Japan, rated
New Zealand-under the direction of the present Government-on the top line at treble A.

COUNTIES AMENDMENT BILL
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to
present the report of the committee on the Counties Amendment Bill. The committee
recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie
upon the table. Section 191F of the principal Act, which is amended by clause 2 of the Bill,
provides that a council may, after it has stopped, diverted, or diminished a road, sell any part
of the land that is no longer required to the adjoining owner or owners, or sell or lease it to
any other person. However, where any stopped road abuts a river, lake, or sea, subsection
(3) provides that the whole of the land must become a public reserve for esplanade purposes.
This restriction is more sweeping than was originally envisaged, because a road that, over its
range of, say, 5 kilometres, merely crosses a small stream at right angles and at no other
point even approaches another body of water could be said to be caught under these
provisions. I am sure that was not the intention of the original legislation.
The stopping of a road must be in accordance with the eighth schedule, and no road may
be stopped unless the consent of the Minister of Lands has been obtained. It is appropriate
to quote from town and country planning legislation; but more specifically I refer to
paragraph 8 of the schedule, which provides that the board or the court, as the case may be,
shall not confirm the decision of the council unless satisfied that adequate access to the lands
in the vicinity of the road remains or is provided.
Clause 3 repeals section 29 of the Counties Amendment Act 1961 and substitutes a new
section, which introduces more flexibility into a section that was too rigid to deal with real
situations. Provision is already made to waive reserve requirements in subdivisions where, in


## p. 1313 (#555) ###########################################

19 July
1313
Counties Amendment Bill
the case of commercial or industrial land, access to the sea is essential for the use of
adjoining land. The Surveyor-General produced examples of subdivisions where, if the
present reserve requirements had been enforced, injustices would have been suffered by the
subdividers. Parts of the New Zealand coast have an irregular shoreline, and the proposed
amendment will allow the reserve requirements to be applied equitably. The Government
will ensure that the public interest is protected at all times, and at the same time it will ensure
that the flexibility that is obviously required is maintained. The county councils' powers of
waiver, which require the consent of the Minister of Lands, will afford the protection the
committee believes is essential.
Motion agreed to.
SOUTHLAND HARBOUR BOARD RECLAMATION AND EMPOWERING BILL
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee tc
present the report of the committee on the Southland Harbour Board Reclamation and
Empowering Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as
amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. The Bill sought to authorise the
Southland Harbour Board to reclaim areas of foreshore and seabed adjacent to Ocean
Beach, Bluff Harbour, and empowered the board to develop and lease the land reclaimed
for commercial, industrial, and other purposes. The total area involved was 26.6 ha, or about
67 acres, as described in the schedule.
The proposed reclamation of an area of 6.41 ha, about 16 acres, would have made land
available to the Ocean Beach Freezing Company, the works of which are immediately
opposite the area described in the schedule. Less than 10 percent of that area is intertidal
mudflat, most of it being rock formations and partly reclaimed areas. During the delibera-
tions, and when the committee heard submissions in Bluff last week, no objection of any
substance was heard to the proposed reclamation of the 6.4 ha. The committee heard
substantial objection to the proposal to reclaim the additional 20.19 ha, or 51 acres, and after
deliberation it was decided to strike that portion out of the Bill. It was felt that the board was
seeking authority to reclaim a much larger area than it had demonstrated a need for.
I should like here to express personal observations about this empowering legislation.
The Southland Harbour Board can come back to Parliament at some future date to seek
authority for the reclamation of this land. This will be subject to debate, but the need for the
reclamation was not demonstrated to the committee. One of the uses of the reclaimed land
would have been to provide on-shore facilities for Hunt Petroleum. I think I speak on
behalf of the House and the country when I express the hope that Hunt Petroleum
exploration will be successful. If it is so, the land may then need to be reclaimed.
I should like to make some observations about what I heard during the hearing of
submissions in Bluff and I speak as the Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of
Local Government. It is sad to hear the misunderstandings expressed by territorial local
government and special purpose authorities about matters on which they represent their
people. I should like to think that misunderstandings about the interpretation or the
intention of legislation would be resolved by those parties before these matters come before
Parliament and the select committee. I hope that will happen in the future.
After most careful consideration, the committee has decided not to allow the reclama-
tion of about 51 acres. I repeat that the Southland Harbour Board is not barred from coming
back to Parliament and requesting that reclamation in the future. I am sure that the Local
Bills Committee would then give that matter the consideration required in the prevailing
circumstances.
Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua): This local empowering Bill has gone forward bearing my
name, and it is appropriate that I comment on behalf of the Southland Harbour Board. The
6.4 ha reclamation that has been approved is needed because of the new hygiene regulations
imposed by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries and which require the Ocean Beach
freezing works to update its present processing complex. That is the only suitable site for an
assembly area. On behalf of the local authority, I record my disappointment at the
committee's finding on the remaining 20 ha. In reporting back, the committee did not refer,
for instance, to the 2.14 ha for which an application was made to establish a wool scour. I am
unconvinced about the suitability of the alternative land offered by the borough on the
foreshore of Bluff Harbour. The proposal also included 1.62 ha for the establishment of a
storage building for the Southland Phosphate Company. I consider that this is a very
necessary facility, which should be adjacent to the harbour and would remove the rather

GOVERNMENT LIFE INSURANCE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister in Charge of the Government Life Insurance Office): I
move, That this Bill be now read a second time. At the end of 1976 the Government Life
Insurance Office held more than $67 million in first mortgages on houses and flats. During
1976, it invested over $14 million in properties of this nature, which represents more than 16
percent of total assets. Practically all of this amount is invested in freehold titles, as the
Government Life Insurance Act 1953 permits loans only on freehold titles and certain types
of Crown leasehold. The current interest rate of 9 percent on residential loans is among the


## p. 1315 (#557) ###########################################

19 July
1315
Government Life Insurance Amendment Bill
lowest being charged by institutional lenders. During the last decade there has been an
increasing demand for mortgage loans on properties erected on leasehold land, and in 1972
the Unit Titles Act gave recognition to the increasing popularity of own-your-own flats and
town houses.
Clause 2(1) of the Bill permits loans on any type of leasehold land where trustees would
be authorised to make loans thereon. Subclause (2) permits loans on freehold and leasehold
land where the evidence of ownership is a unit title issued under the Unit Titles Act 1972,
and authorises mortgages of a leasehold interest in land where the mortgage is also a first
mortgage over the borrower's undivided share in the freehold title. Subclause (3) limits the
amount of any advance made under subclauses (1) and (2) to two-thirds of the valuation.
Subclause (4) enables loans to be granted to staff for residential purposes on the types of
land tenure mentioned in subclauses (1) and (2). The Government Life Insurance Office will
also be able to consider loans to policyholders, which it has previously been obliged to
decline because of the limits imposed by the 1953 Act. The types of land tenure mentioned in
the Act are regarded as suitable securities by the Housing Corporation and other life
insurance offices.
Clause 3 deals with the acquisition of land and buildings. The office has more than $46
million invested in land and buildings, not only for its own occupation, but also for leasing to
selected tenants. During the past 20 years the office has acquired a number of industrial and
commercial buildings, which are leased to substantial companies on a long-term basis. This
provides a good return on the policyholders' funds, plus capital growth. Requests are
sometimes received to grant a right of purchase to the leasing company at the expiry of the
lease, but the present Act prevents this right being granted. Although such requests are
infrequent, the inability to grant a right of purchase is sometimes a bar to a favourable
investment opportunity. It is envisaged that the right of purchase could be exercised only at
valuation or the original purchase price, whichever is the greater.
Clause 4 deals with the purchase of motor vehicles. The office does not own any motor
cars and, although a great many officers are required to use cars on business, they are
recompensed by the normal State Service mileage allowance. The object of the amendment
is to do away with the intermediary step of the office's first purchasing the car before selling
it to the officer concerned on hire purchase terms, or such other terms as the Minister of
Finance from time to time directs.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): One of the main purposes of the Bill is to enlarge
the investment area of the Government Life Insurance Office. In that, it follows an
extension of the powers of private trustees by enabling the office to take up leaseholds and
other securities of a lower order than a first mortgage on freehold land. The matter of
whether freedom of investment should be extended calls for some examination, at least, of
how the office has exercised its powers in the past. It already has some authority beyond the
traditional trustee investments, in that it has the right to take out certain shares, a right it
now enjoys in common with private trustees because of a recent amendment to the law.
The office exercised this right in relation to the Securitibank group with a good deal of
publicity, which continued until the eve of that group's unhappy collapse. Its very association
with the group, along with that of the State Insurance Office, was used as a talking point by
Securitibank, no doubt with the knowledge of both those Government agencies, to persuade
many less informed and less sophisticated individuals, including widows with their life
savings and so on, to contribute those savings to the group, which many people—including
the Prime Minister, as we have on his own confession—knew was in financial trouble as long
as a year before the crash. The Prime Minister is one who says that, during that time, he and
his professional associates were advising against investing in this outlet. However, the two
Government agencies were willingly doing so, and lending not only their funds but also their
names to support the widely advertised borrowing programme of the Securitibank organisa-
tion.
What knowledge did the Government Life Insurance Office have of the impending
crisis? What did the Minister in charge of the office know of this? What, if anything, did the
Prime Minister do to impart to the Minister in charge the knowledge that he confesses he had
of the shakiness of the enterprise? If any information was passed on by the Prime Minister to
the Minister in charge, how much of this did he absorb, digest, and act upon? The Minister
is, of course, a member of the Government Life Insurance Office Board, and could have
been a channel of communication between the Prime Minister and the management of the
institution. If that channel existed—and I believe it did—why was it not used? If we do grant
the extension of powers sought by the Bill, will all the information channels open to the
18*


## p. 1316 (#558) ###########################################

1316
19 July
Government Life Insurance Amendment Bill
office be used in the future? I ask that question, because in the Securitibank affair ministerial
channels were not the only communication channels between the investment groups solicit-
ing public funds and the Government agencies that responded to the invitation by investing
funds.
The disappointed and frustrated investors have formed a consortium, made up of those
who were either not sufficiently fortunate or perhaps not sufficiently well informed to get out

The group has pooled its resources to protect its interests, and in doing so has published a

SECURITIES TRANSFER BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill will simplify the procedure for transferring securities such as shares and


## p. 1321 (#563) ###########################################

19 July
1321
Securities Transfer Bill
debentures. It permits securities to be transferred by means of a securities transfer form
without the signature of the transferee or attestation of the transferor's signature being
required. The Bill also permits the details of the consideration and the transferee to be
supplied on a separate form, called a broker's form, when the securities are transferred
through the agency of members of a stock exchange.
Simplification of commercial procedures, such as the transfer of securities, must have
regard to the public interest. For this reason, the Bill was referred to the Commerce and
Mining Committee so that submissions could be made by interested parties on, amongst
other things, whether the simplified procedure would increase the opportunity for fraud.
Several submissions expressed concern that the opportunity would increase, and recom-
mended that the Bill include certain warranties and indemnities to afford greater protection
to an issuer of securities who incurs liability for removing the owner's name from the register
of securities as a result of a forged transfer. I think the existing requirement for signature and
attestation presents little difficulty to the dishonest person forging a transfer of securities; yet
it is difficult to recall any criminal proceedings relating to forged transfers.
Except for one minor instance some 30 years ago, none of the oral submissions made to
the committee cited any cases of fraudulent transfers of securities. I think the absence of
fraudulent transfers is due to several things. First, other types of fraud are more lucrative
and easier to perpetrate, the most common example being the forging of cheques. Second,
securities-unlike cheque books—are held in custody; and, third, the only ready market for
the sale of securities is a stock exchange, and selling securities through the agency of a
sharebroker provides too many disincentives to a dishonest person.
Although the Commerce and Mining Committee did not generally accept that the
opportunity for fraud would increase, it was concerned about private transactions for the
transfer of securities not effected through the agency of an independent person such as a
sharebroker. As a result, clause 3 has been amended so that a securities transfer form can be
used only for securities sold in an authorised transaction, and clause 2 now defines an
authorised transaction as a sale and purchase of securities in which each of the parties is, or is
acting through the agency of, a member of a stock exchange, a solicitor, a chartered
accountant, a trustee company, a trading bank, or an authorised public securities dealer.
These amendments should remove much of the concern about the opportunity for fraud
without materially limiting the purpose of the Bill.
The Bill as reported back refers in clause 2, in the definition of "authorised transaction",
to sale and purchase of securities, and in clause 3 to securities sold in an authorised
transaction. As a result, transfers by way of gift or pursuant to a bequest cannot be effected
by means of a securities transfer form. This would remove much of the benefit of the Bill for
solicitors and trustee companies. This result was not intended and is not desirable. Accord-
ingly, I propose to move amendments during the Committee stage to make it clear that a
securities transfer form may be used for securities sold, given, or otherwise disposed of in an
authorised transaction. These amendments are set out in Supplementary Order Paper 7 that
has already been distributed for the information of members.
As I mentioned earlier, several submissions recommended the inclusion of certain
warranties and indemnities at present not part of the law. The purpose of the Bill is to
simplify the procedure for transferring securities-not to alter the rights and liabilities of the
parties involved in a transfer of securities, so those recommendations fell outside the scope
of the Bill. However, the effect of the amendments to clauses 2 and 3 in relation to the use of
a securities transfer form will be to strengthen the common law right of indemnity in the
sense that the classes of persons from whom indemnity can be sought will be those specified
in the definition of authorised transaction.
Apart from the amendments to clauses 2 and 3, the only other major amendments in the
Bill as reported back are in the first and second schedules, containing the securities transfer
form and the brokers transfer form respectively. Apart from a few minor alterations, the
new forms differ from the original forms in layout only. Although the Bill makes it clear that
the rearrangement of the content of the forms or the inclusion of additional information does
not vitiate the use of the forms, it was thought that, having regard to the draft forms included
in the submissions to the Commerce and Mining Committee, the forms should be rearranged
so as to be as near as possible to those the securities industry would use. This Bill forges no
new major commercial principle, but I commend it to the House for its practical importance
in simplifying an everyday commercial procedure.
Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central): The Opposition does not oppose this measure.
Those of us who were on the select committee had the opportunity of studying the

TRUSTEE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. As I said on the introduction, this short Bill amends the Trustee Act 1956 in
accordance with the recommendations of the Property Law and Equity Reform Committee.
That committee issued a working paper, and concerned organisations have been consulted
and have commented on or expressed their concurrence with the Bill's provisions. These
organisations included the Public Trustee, trustee companies, and the New Zealand Law
Society, which comprise those mainly concerned in the work of drafting wills and administer-
ing estates.
The various financial limits imposed by the Trustee Act as long ago as 1956 and 1968
are, on present-day values, totally unrealistic, and they are dealt with in this Bill. In general,
the Property Law and Equity Reform Committee recommended the removal of these limits
so as to obviate the necessity for trustees to seek the consent of the Supreme Court to the
exercise of such powers. Clause 2(1) removes the present financial limit of $2,000 up to
which a trustee could exercise his power under section 14(2)(a) of the principal Act to
purchase adjoining land without recourse to the Supreme Court. Safeguards against the
liberal exercise of this power have been written into the Bill. A purchase under the section
must be for the better development or use of the existing land, or to facilitate or improve the
carrying on of business which the trustee is empowered to carry on.
Subclause (2) amends section 14(6) of the principal Act by removing completely the
financial limit of $15,000 on the value of land which the trustee may lease with an optional or
compulsory purchasing clause, or which he may sell or exchange without recourse to the
Supreme Court. In the exercise of this unrestricted power a trustee will not be liable for any
breach of trust by reason only of any inadequacy in the amount or value of the sale price or
other consideration provided the trustee obtains a trustee valuation under section 28 of the
principal Act and sells at not less than that price. This safeguard conforms with other
provisions of the Trustee Act, and thus a measure of uniformity is maintained.
Clause 3 repeals the proviso to section 15(1)(b) of the principal Act limiting the amount
a trustee may expend on the improvement or development of trust property without the
consent of the court to $10,000. The removal of the restriction is a sensible provision giving
the trustee, acting within the terms of his trust, a wide discretion to expend money for the
benefit of the trust property, and therefore the beneficiaries.
The present financial limits for the application of capital money or assets for the
maintenance, education, advancement, or benefit of the person entitled to the capital were
fixed in 1956. Under section 41 of the principal Act such payment or application is not to
exceed half of the presumptive or vested interest of that person where the value of that share
or interest exceeds $2,000, and in any other case is not to exceed $1,000 altogether. Clause 4
increases these limits to $15,000 and $7,500 respectively. The exercise of the trustee's power
beyond these limits would be sanctioned by the Supreme Court. However, there is power to
make future adjustment to the limits by way of Orders in Council. The revision of the
financial limits to trustees' powers under the principal Act is overdue, and I commend the
amendment to the House.
Hon. Dr. A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I have nothing to add to what I said on the
introduction of the Bill. At that time I reminded the House that the Minister had been kind
enough to supply me with a copy of the original report of the Property Law and Equity


## p. 1323 (#565) ###########################################

19 July
1323
Insurance Law Reform Bill
Reform Committee, and a subsequent memorandum that he had received. This matter has
been considered by the executive committee of the New Zealand Law Society which, not

there is little more for me to say, except that the Opposition has no objection to the Bill.

BROADCASTING AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The Bill amends Part IX, concerning finance, of the 1976 Broadcasting
Act. It is an amendment to deal with the capital structure of the Broadcasting Corporation of
New Zealand. The main purpose of the Bill is to relieve the BCNZ of its loan indebtedness
of $38.9 million and of the burden of interest on those loans of $3.67 million a year. I should
remind the House, in case the canard should again be raised from the other side of the
House, that it was the Labour Administration which raised interest rates on these loans to 10
percent on 1 April 1975. The measure is designed to ensure the financial viability of the
BCNZ and the broadcasting system, and to relieve it of a debt of $38.9 million, largely
incurred under the last Labour Administration. I believe that debt arose because of the
former Labour Government's failure to appreciate financial realities; from its scrapping of
the NZBC and that corporation's plans for a complementary second channel; and also from
the over-hasty development of a competitive second channel alongside and along with the
introduction and development of colour.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: Have you read the manifesto?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I have read the papers and I understand what was proposed.
That will be covered in the debate. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition himself will want
to rise to his feet and explain why he was responsible for the excessively costly development
of the system. If he can do that, it will be a magnificent performance that might bring him
back into the reckoning. As far as I can see, the former Labour Government simply
advanced money to the Broadcasting Council. Was that the proposal of the Leader of the
Opposition? As far as I can see, money was advanced to the Broadcasting Council for the
development of the system, without any thought being given to financial guidelines, though
even the 1973 Act would seem to have required this. Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition
would explain, because I do not believe he followed his own Act. In reviewing the situation,
I could find no clear financial guidelines. The Leader of the Opposition might care to set
them out. There were no requirements for debt repayment or for repayment of interest, as
far as I could see; no concern, in short, for the financial viability of the broadcasting system.
That is the indictment. Indeed, without a Minister of Broadcasting, the 1973 Act left the
broadcasting system in the hands of the Minister of Finance at that time, the present Leader
of the Opposition. He has some explaining to do, if he wants to, on these lines: why were
there no financial guidelines and no provision for interest repayment? Any management
expert would have thought such a situation was ridiculous, and it was, the only trouble being
that the country had to pay for it. On the change of Government at the end of 1975, I found,
as the new Minister of Broadcasting, that the then BCNZ board was deeply concerned about
its financial situation. I was told, and it was quite obvious, that the broadcasting system was
facing a financial crisis, the reasons for which became outstandingly clear in the course of a
review in 1976. The corporations established in 1973 were undercapitalised and overspent.
This problem was created by the Labour Government and the Ministers
concerned and no one else that I can see. The thoughtless failure to think the situation
through led the Labour Government to tear up the NZBC as it was, quite contrary to the
Labour Party's policy, and to set out on a new course without clear guidelines. Whatever
members opposite may say about the Adam Committee, they did not set the corporations
those clear guidelines needed in a resource situation-a shortage of resources which the
Labour Government had had to grapple with itself and therefore knew was there. They did
not make the effort. The situation that had developed stood out in stark contrast to that
which the Labour Government had inherited from the previous National Government.
This is no story; it is history, if the member for Manukau wants to know. Even he
will know that in 1972, the NZBC was virtually debt free. Throughout the 1960s the NZBC
developed television services and expanded radio facilities-as anyone who has been around
the provincial centres will know-from revenue, with very limited calls on loan money, and
with rapid repayment of any loans that were required. In 1972—and this is where the Leader
of the Opposition and I differ quite markedly-the National Government considered plans,
as the Cabinet papers clearly show. I checked them with my colleagues who were Ministers


## p. 1333 (#575) ###########################################

19 July
1333
Broadcasting Amendment Bill
at the time. I repeat that those Cabinet papers clearly show plans for the gradual expansion
of broadcasting and this notable point, the development of a second channel within income.
Those plans were thrown away although they were available for the member for Manukau, if
he had wanted them.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Will the Minister table the papers?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: How can I table a Cabinet paper? Even the member for
Manukau must know I cannot, but I am entitled to ask of my ministerial colleagues who have
control of those papers, to see them. The Labour Administration tore the structure of the
NZBC apart. I believe it was done vindictively, as will be shown when some of the history is
written. It created a new system, but without providing any rational financial base, and that
is the problem we are facing tonight. As a result of those moves, we found in 1976 that the
broadcasting system established by the Labour Government was unable to pay its way. The
Government agreed to interim relief by remitting interest payments while the financial
structure was being reviewed by the new Chairman of the BCNZ, the late great Ron Jarden.
The Government is now acting on his analysis of the financial problems, an analysis
presented to it in February 1977 just before his untimely death. I believe that Mr Jarden had
a very acute sense of the BCNZ's financial needs. He proposed major financial restructuring
to convert the repayable debt of $38.9 million to equity capital—in effect, into share capital.
He proposed thereby to remove the burden of the debt and interest charges, and to provide
the basis for financial viability and a more secure independence for the broadcasting system.
If we remove our partisan attitudes, I believe the House would want this to be
developed and accepted. The acceptance of this restructuring plan was a common-sense
approach to a difficult problem. It was also a tribute to the capacity Ron Jarden brought to
the task as chairman, to his concern for the future of broadcasting, and to the confidence he
engendered both among broadcasters and, certainly, among Cabinet Ministers on this side of
the House connected with the Cabinet committee on communications. We all came to share
his vision of a restructured BCNZ, able, broadly, to finance its own capital programme, to
stand on its own feet, and to cope with its own affairs. I hope the House will endorse that sort
of corporation. If this amendment is passed, it will be open to the corporation, on this
financial basis, to adminster broadcasting within financial guidelines, but with a wide degree
of financial as well as programming independence.
Let me cover the clauses of the Bill in detail. Clause 1 provides that the Act shall come
into force on 1 April 1977. This is appropriate and convenient, because it is at the beginning
of the financial year. It covers the first full year of the operation of the new corporation, and
the beginning of a new capital programme drawn broadly from the corporation's own
resources.
Clause 2 is concerned with the capital. The capital of $38.9 million equates the total
contributed from the National Development Loans Account by the Government in cash.
When paid out it was described as advances, but, as I have said, there was no provision for
repayment. In effect, the Government has decided to leave the whole amount invested as
proprietorship capital; that is, the capital is held in the name of the Government on behalf of
the people of New Zealand. Provision is made for future increases in capital, though I would
not expect this to be used at present. While broadcasting is expected to fund its own capital
expenditure it seems sensible to ensure flexibility in the provision of further capital. I make
this point very emphatically, because it is a matter of funding the development of a State
agency. The amendment provides that any future increase will come under the purview of
the Minister of Finance.
Clause 3 deals with reserves. Over the years public broadcasting in New Zealand has, in
general, proved profitable. I admit that this record was broken under the Labour Adminis-
tration, but, from the days of the NZBS, development was largely funded from revenue.
Until now there has been no need to categorise that investment of funds. This now becomes
necessary with the establishment of a formal capital structure. In doing this I should
emphasise also that the Government recognises that these funds previously invested are
invested in the system and are not available for the payment of dividends. Subclause (1)
therefore provides for these funds to be transferred to reserves. Again, this will be
undertaken by the corporation with the consent of the Minister of Finance, who has already
established in the 1976 Act, as in the 1973 Act-for the benefit of the member for Grey
Lynn, who is trying to interject—a supervisory role essential to a Public Service system
of broadcasting.
Since the BCNZ is expected to operate, in general, as a commercial operation,
provision is also made to cover future profits, in essence as for a company. As far ahead as I


## p. 1334 (#576) ###########################################

1334
19 July
Broadcasting Amendment Bill
can see, it will be necessary to continue to plough profits back into the system. This seems
clear while broadcasting faces such wide-ranging development needs. I remind the member
for Grey Lynn that the 1973 Act provided for just the same sort of control from his Minister
of Finance, but he does not care to read or try to understand or sympathise with the problem
of the broadcasting system that he helped to create, but which he is not prepared to assist
now. Why will he not assist broadcasting in its financial problems now? Clause 4 is concerned
with dividends, and also looks to the future. In some future situation the corporation may
wish to consider the possible disposition of profits.
Before sitting down, I give notice that I intend to introduce a Supplementary Order
Paper at the Committee stage. When the Broadcasting Act 1976 was enacted I did not
contemplate that any member of the Broadcasting Corporation would be engaged full time
upon corporation business. Accordingly, while section 44 of the Act allows for the subsidisa-
tion of contributions to a National Provident Fund superannuation scheme for employees,
there is no corresponding provision for members of the corporation. The full-time appoint-
ment of the present chairman, who was contributing to a subsidised superannuation scheme
as a corporation employee and wishes to continue in the scheme in his new capacity, requires
a minor amendment to section 44. That amendment would allow the corporation to subsidise
the superannuation of full-time members, but the provision would have to be retrospective
to 16 May 1977, the date of the present chairman's appointment. As I have said, I shall be
introducing a Supplementary Order Paper at the Committee stage to implement that
provision.
In conclusion, may I say that this amendment follows a major review of the BCNZ's
financial situation. It accepts broadly the proposal of the late Ron Jarden, the former
chairman of the BCNZ. It provides for sensible and reasonable measures for the future
financial administration of the broadcasting system.

Seddon Shield Districts Trotting Jackpot Empowering Bill
WEDNESDAY, 20 JULY 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
SEDDON SHIELD DISTRICTS TROTTING JACKPOT EMPOWERING BILL
Mr HARRISON (Hawke's Bay): I am directed by the Seddon Shield Districts Trotting
Jackpot Empowering Bill Committee to present the report of the committee on the Seddon
Shield Districts Trotting Jackpot Empowering Bill. The committee finds that the allegations
in the preamble have been proved to its satisfaction, and recommends that the Bill be
allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
I thank the members of the committee for their co-operation in considering the Bill,
which is of more than passing interest because the Seddon Shield Districts Trotting
Jackpot-involving the Greymouth, Reefton, and Marlborough Trotting Clubs' establishing
a non-terminating jackpot to pick five winners in five jackpot races-was established in
October 1971. By the time the eighth jackpot meeting, which happened to be in Greymouth,
had been held on 10 April 1972, no one had been able to pick the five winners of the five
appropriate races. The pool then stood at $24,000. Unfortunately, before the ninth jackpot
meeting could be held the Racing Act 1971 had come into force on 1 August 1972 and no
further jackpots were permitted. Neither Minister in either Government was able, or indeed
willing, to issue a permit to allow a ninth jackpot meeting to be held and the money to be
disposed of.
The trustees declined to pay out to those who had picked four winners. Clearly that was
not right, according to the rules as printed on the tickets. Some of those who had picked four
winners at the last meeting, at Greymouth, sued the trustees, but, although Mr Justice Casey
gave his opinion on how the jackpot should have been run, he made it clear in his interim
judgment that he would be forced by the Gaming Act 1908 to find against the plaintiffs, and
that he would not invoke the Illegal Practices Act to override the Gaming Act. One of the
options open was for the plaintiffs and others, regardless of their success, to demand their
money back. That would have meant refunding their investment. But that, of course, is not
now practicable, because most people do not remember how much they bet, and in any case
most of them have destroyed their tickets.
The second option was to pay out the jackpot pool to all the bettors who had picked four
winners in the final jackpot meeting at Greymouth. But not all such fortunate bettors came
forward as plaintiffs. In fact, it was known that, apart from the plaintiffs who took the case
against the trustees, there were three or four others who had picked four winners; and there
were probably others who could have come forward, but had thrown away their tickets after
realising, at the end of the first race when they missed the winner, that they were
automatically disqualified and had no chance of picking the five winners required. The third
option was to hand the jackpot pool back to the trustees, and this, in fact, is what the Bill is
about and, with certain amendments, is what the committee has recommended should
happen.
The amendments, by and large, make provision for the handing back to the trustees of
the jackpot money, less, first, the costs and disbursements in the previous court case, and,
secondly, the costs and fees incurred in promoting the Bill. One-third of the balance would
go to each club for a contributing or a non-contributing terminating jackpot, with the pool
going to those who pick the five winners; or, if nobody is fortunate enough to pick five, to
those who pick four winners; or, indeed, those who pick the most winners. A terminating-a
last-jackpot meeting would be held under the auspices of each of the three clubs. It has
been suggested by the committee that if the clubs decide to have a contributing jackpot, the
tickets should be available at 50c each. The main changes in the Bill as recommended by the
committee are, first, that there should be no refund to the plaintiffs and others who picked
four winners at the last Greymouth jackpot meeting; secondly, the trustees can claim their
costs in promoting the Bill from the pool; and, thirdly, the clubs should be able to choose
whether their jackpots are contributing or non-contributing.
Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast): Mr Speaker-
Mr SPEAKER: I am in a certain difficulty here. When our Standing Orders were last
revised, those relating to private Bills were incorporated in our general Standing Orders.

and I hope that before my term as a member of Parliament finishes at the end of next year we
will again see similar good will towards other measures that will benefit the sporting life of
New Zealanders.

LAND AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That the Land Amendment Bill be
introduced. This Bill of six clauses deals with minor matters of an administrative nature. It
will enable the Land Act 1948 to be administered more efficiently by my department. Clause
1 relates to the short title. Clause 2 inserts an additional section in the Land Act to enable me
to delegate any powers conferred on me as Minister of Lands, by any enactment, to an
officer of the Department of Lands and Survey. Current legislation, especially the Counties
Act of 1956, requires the consent of the Minister of Lands to the stopping or closing of roads
by county councils. This is a statutory requirement for what is in many instances a relatively
minor issue. The Bill will give me the authority to delegate from time to time that and other
similar responsibilities for matters not already covered by legislation.
Clause 3 is an amendment that will simplify procedures. At present the principal Act
provides for the Land Settlement Board to purchase land, but the board does not have
authority to lease land. In the past leasing has been possible only by direction of the
Governor-General. The additional provision to the Land Act will obviate that. Clause 4 is
related to the good husbandry of pastoral leases. At present, pastoral lessees may graze only
the land leased, although section 108 of the principal Act allows for limited cultivation. With
improved farming techniques there are cases where some cash cropping could be carried out
but for the restriction of existing legislation. The proposed amendment will make cash
cropping possible in these circumstances.
Clause 5 also is a tidying up clause. The present policy of Government lending
institutions is for review of interest to be carried out at 3-yearly intervals, whereas the Land


## p. 1345 (#587) ###########################################

20 July
1345
Lands Amendment Bill
Act provides for 5-yearly reviews. The proposed amendment will bring reviews under the
Land Act into line with those of other Government lending agencies. Clause 6 relates to the
general offences provisions of the Land Act, which at present stipulate that informations
must be laid within 2 years of the offence. For some specific offences no time limit for laying
informations is specified. The provisions of the Summary Proceedings Act of 1967, which
limits the time to 6 months, have been used in the past. The proposed amendment will
require information for offences under the Act to be laid within 1 year.
Under the Standing Orders the Bill will be referred automatically to the Lands and
Agriculture Committee.
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central): I am pleased that the Bill will go to the
Lands and Agriculture Committee, giving an opportunity to ask questions. One that comes
readily to mind concerns the reduction in the interest-rate review period from 5 years to 3
years. This will be of great concern to Federated Farmers and many others in the farming
industry in view of the escalation in interest rates under the present Government.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The Bill does not provide for interest rates to
be increased, but for reviews to be held at 3-yearly intervals. I would just add that the
Labour Government had proposed to include this provision in the Statutes Amendment Bill
1975. It is being included in this particular measure.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That the hearing of evidence before the

Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act 1975
1. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: What

Lyttelton Health Centre
8. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister of Health: Can he advise whether he has
received an approach from the North Canterbury Hospital Board on the subject of the
proposed health centre at Lyttelton, requesting a revision of the formula laid down for the
calculation of the annual rental?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): Yes, an approach has been made by the North
Canterbury Hospital Board suggesting that rents for health centres be based on 5 percent of
total cost instead of the 8.5 percent basis used at present. The North Canterbury Hospital
Board also sought discretionary authority to make final rental charges on an individual basis
according to merit.
Miss Dewe: Would the Minister agree that the existing formula results in rents being
uneconomic for the proposed users?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The National Government introduced the legislation on health
centres, but the regulations under which we are operating were introduced by the Labour
Government in 1973. The rental is called an economic rent, but in my opinion it does not
make sense for a doctor to pay 8.5 percent of the cost of the building because very difficult
foundation and engineering problems on the site might be involved. My interpretation of an
economic rent is that the doctor should pay to the health centre the same amount of rental he
would pay for rooms somewhere else in the community, and that would be a lot less than the
rental being charged now. This matter is being reviewed. It is not a decision I can make on
my own, but I will be making recommendations along the lines suggested by the member for
Lyttelton.
Mr Hunt: In view of the Minister's comments about the recommendations made by the
North Canterbury Hospital Board, can he indicate if the recommendations will be accepted?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I have given no indication that these recommendations will be
accepted. If the honourable member had listened he would have heard me say that the rental
should not be a percentage of the capital value of the building, so I would not be in favour of
moving from 8.5 percent to 5 percent. I would be in favour of an entirely different approach,
so I can give no indication as to when some change will be made and I can give no assurance
that I will accept or support this type of approach. I have accepted the proposition that in
districts where there is a shortage of doctors and a health centre has been built, doctors
should be encouraged, not discouraged.
Mr Hunt: In view of the apparent verbal somersaulting, can the Minister now say when
it is proposed to tell either the member for Lyttelton or the North Canterbury Hospital
Board what he or his department will be doing about the present position?
Hon. T. F. GILL: If the honourable member cannot ask a question decently, without
accusing me of an apparent verbal somersault, he will not get an answer.
Mr Hunt: Notwithstanding the fact that I cannot get an answer, would the Minister tell
the House when the member for Lyttelton and the North Canterbury Hospital Board will
receive answers to this problem?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot tell the House that, but I will be in close liaison with the
member for Lyttelton and the chairman of the North Canterbury Hospital Board, who has
also been to see me about this matter.

Billfish
10. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Fisheries: Can he indicate how
many billfish were caught by game fishermen in the last fishing season, and how many were
caught by commercial fishermen operating out of New Zealand ports?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): New Zealand commercial fishermen do
not normally catch billfish, and the Ministry does not require fishermen's returns to show
how many of these fish were taken accidentally. For the calendar year 1975 data received by
the ministry from the big-game fishing clubs showed that 842 billfish were caught by game
fishermen in New Zealand waters. This figure is composed of 18 black marlin, 17 blue
marlin, 249 striped marlin, one broadbill swordfish, and 557 mako sharks. The figures for the
1976 catches have not yet been received by the ministry.

Energy Price Rises-Flow-on Effects
11. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: What
specific actions will he take to counter the flow-on effects of the recent energy price rises as
revealed by the huge rise of 27.3 percent in the June quarter in the fuel and light subgroup of
the consumer price index?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): The increase in the June quarter for
the fuel and light subgroup of the consumer price index reflects the increase in energy prices
that took effect from 1 April 1977. These price increases bring electricity prices back to
reality after being frozen by the previous Labour Government. We are all aware that the
true situation was hidden by asking the taxpayer to subsidise electricity charges by way of the
Stabilisation vote to the tune of $18.5 million in 1974-75, and $13.1 million in 1975-76. Had
there not been a change of Government, and the introduction of new policies to remove the
subsidy by unfreezing the charges, the Stabilisation vote for electricity, as estimated by the
Treasury, would have been as high as $52 million in 1976-77. No specific actions are
contemplated as a result of this recent price adjustment. It is an essential part of energy
policy development that energy supplies are properly priced, having regard to their true
value and their true cost.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Can I take it from the Minister's reply that it is the Government's
policy to pass on in full the cost of energy increases, and that the Government has no
stabilisation policy for this part of the consumer price index?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: If the honourable member implies that the Government will be a
party to the accounting deception that was inherent in the previous situation—
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I think that term is slightly too provocative. The member may
care to substitute something different.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Then I shall say accounting camouflage that was inherent in the
previous situation whereby the electricity consumer imagined he was being charged at one
rate, and in reality as a taxpayer he was paying a considerable additional amount. If the
member imagines that the Government will be a party to such a policy I advise him that it
will not be. The last part of my earlier answer made it clear that it is an essential part of
energy policy development that energy supplies are properly priced, having regard to their
true value and their true cost.
Mr Birch: Can the Minister confirm that the price rises that he referred to are part of the
Government's comprehensive energy pricing policies aimed at the proper use, conservation,
and more rational utilisation of valuable indigenous energy resources?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I can confirm that this is an important aspect of the Government's
energy policy.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: What profit does the Electricity Department expect to make this
financial year as a result of the increased bulk electricity charges that the Minister announced
earlier this year?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The Electricity Department is not expected to record a profit this
financial year.

Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied, The Auckland Hospital Board
does not envisage an accident and emergency service at Waitakere until stage II
of the hospital is complete. Experience, both in New Zealand and overseas, has
shown that it is not feasible to have such a department without the back-up services
that only an acute general hospital can provide. An accident and emergency
department in the present hospital could provide only what is already provided
by general practitioners. The Government ensured that the Auckland Hospital
Board had extra funds to develop the maternity services at Waitakere. Naturally
it takes a little time to build up a case load of obstetric patients which will justify
splitting the resources of St. Helens Hospital, to which these patients have until
now been admitted. I am advised that the board expects to reach the stage about
the end of July or mid August when resident medical staff can justifiably be
employed. At this time a full obstetric unit will be available. There is adequate
land at Waitakere for expansion of the hospital. Stage II of Waitakere Hospital
is one of the Auckland Hospital Board's top priority projects, but, for reasons
given above, it is not practicable to establish an accident and emergency depart-
ment at an earlier date.

Glass Recycling Programme
4. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry,
In view of the importance of the glass recycling programme commenced during the
Labour Government's term of office, will he ensure that the threatened action by
the Department of Health to restrict glass collection centres to industrial areas is
not implemented, and will he state: (1) the number of collection centres at present
operating; (2) the quantity of glass collected for recycling in each of the last 3 years;
(3) the estimated value of soda ash which has been saved as a result?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied,
The Department of Health is not threatening to restrict glass collection centres to
industrial areas. That department is concerned at ensuring the centres are operated
in an efficient manner so as to avoid nuisance and minimise health risks to the
public at large. I am anxious to ensure that the centres expand, since recycling of
glass not only relieves the burden on a community's waste disposal system, but also
saves energy and imported raw materials. The answers to the member's questions
are: (1) number of centres-approximately 200; (2) quantity of glass collected in
each of the last 3 years (approximate figures)-year ended 31 March 1975, 13 000
tonnes; year ended 31 March 1976, 15 000 tonnes; year ended 31 March 1977,
15 833 tonnes (actual); and (3) savings in imported soda ash since the programme
began in 1973 are about $750,000. Depending on the price of soda ash, which
varies, on present rates of collection the savings are about $300,000 annually.

Indonesian Air Pilots-Training in New Zealand
7. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Has the
Government, either directly or through any public body, made any arrangements
with the Indonesian Government for the training of Indonesian air pilots in New
Zealand?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied, Ten Indonesians
will begin training in New Zealand shortly to commercial pilot licence standard.
The 10 trainees are to be employed as pilots in the Pioneer Air System, which was
established by the Indonesian Government in 1974 to service outlying areas of the
archipelago. The Pioneer Air System, which is operated by Merpati Nusantara
Airlines, the secondary air carrier owned by the Indonesian Government, extends
to North and South Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, the Moluccas, and the Nusa
Tenggara, a system of air services using light aircraft which was initially developed
in West Irian. The training is being funded as a Colombo Plan aid project under
the Bilateral Aid Programme, and will be conducted by the training services division
of the National Airways Corporation at Christchurch Airport.

Customs Seizures-Use of Proceeds
8. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Customs, In view
of the shortage of essential equipment for the boarding and prevention group of
the Customs Department, will he consider allowing the use of the proceeds realised
at auction from seized goods for the purchase of such equipment, bearing in mind
that these seizures are made by the preventive service?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied, The increased percent-
age
of the Customs vote allocated to equipment purchases for the current year is
a reflection of the importance placed by the Government on this aspect of the
department's operations. If any particular deficiency is noted by staff members it is,
of course, part of the officers' responsibility to bring the matter to attention. Con-
cerning the use of proceeds of auctions of customs-seized goods for equipment
purchases, I do not intend any alterations to present provisions whereby these
proceeds are applied first to the payment of all sale costs (including the appropriate
customs duty and sales tax) and any residue being paid into the Consolidated
Revenue Account. However, a proposal for a further increase in allocation for
equipment purchase is now under consideration by the Government. Finally, I
would point to an inaccurate assumption in the honourable member's question. Not
all customs seizures are made by the preventive service. All customs officers have a
preventive role to play irrespective of their occupational classification. In this regard
it is proper to note that in the year ended 31 March 1977, salable customs seizures
had a value of $441,600, and of this sum $109,764 resulted directly from the activi-
ties of the customs boarding and preventive group.

Radio Programmes to Pacific Islands
13. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Broadcasting, How many
hours of programmes does Radio New Zealand compile weekly especially for
Pacific Island audiences: (a) for direct shortwave broadcast, and (b) on tape for
them to broadcast from their local stations, if any, and in the latter case are there
any figures to show whether they are in fact used?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied, (a) No regular
programmes are compiled especially for direct short-wave transmission, although
on occasion Pacific-language broadcasts of outstanding sports events have been
included. The overseas service rebroadcasts Samoan, Cook, Niuean, Tongan, and
Tokelauan language news bulletins weekly, from both the national programme
and station 1YA, Auckland. Most of these Pacific countries relay from the New
Zealand short-wave service programmes of particular interest to their audiences,
particularly in the fields of news and sport. Special arrangements are made for
outstanding occasions and important events. (b) Taped half-hour programmes
in the local languages are sent weekly to Samoa and the Cook Islands, and similar
quarter-hour programmes for Tonga and Niue are planned from the start of
August. As the Tokelaus have no radio station, Tokelauan language information
is at times included in the Samoan language programme. All these programmes
reflect news and activities of the Pacific community living in New Zealand, and,
when the occasion arises, programmes of special Pacific interest are sent in
addition. In English, four 15-minute programmes are sent weekly to Samoa, the
Cook Islands, Niue, Tonga, Nauru, and Tuvalu, covering Pacific affairs and includ-
ing material originated by correspondents in some of the islands. It is planned to
increase this island contribution and also to air it in New Zealand areas where


## p. 1358 (#600) ###########################################

1358
20 July
Questions and Replies
there is a large Pacific population. Replies to recent inquiries indicate that in
Niue, Tonga, Samoa, and the Cook Islands all or most of the material sent is
used, and its content is satisfactory.

Radio Short-wave Services to Pacific Islands
17. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Broadcasting, Do Australia
and New Zealand each have short-wave radio services beamed to the Pacific,
and, if so: (a) what are their relative strengths and hours of broadcast, to which
countries; and (b) what co-operation exists between the ABC and Radio New
Zealand in the Pacific?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied, Both Radio
Australia and Radio New Zealand have short-wave radio services beamed to the
Pacific, which operate as follows: (a) Radio New Zealand has two 7.5 kW trans-
mitters, and broadcasts daily from 6 a.m. to 10.30 p.m., New Zealand time,
extending these hours if required to cover special events. One transmitter is
directed towards Australia from 7.30 p.m. onwards, but the primary target for


## p. 1359 (#601) ###########################################

20 July
1359
Questions and Replies
the service is the immediate Pacific Basin, embracing Tonga, Samoa, Fiji, Cook
Islands, Niue, Tokelau, Nauru, and Tuvalu. Radio Australia beams a programme
to a wider Pacific area, covering the New Zealand target but extending to such
islands as the New Hebrides, New Caledonia, Papua, and the Solomons. It oper-
ates 24 hours a day using four 100 kW transmitters, three 50 kW transmitters, and
three 10 kW transmitters at various times. There is also a 250 kW transmitter used

French, but there are no Pacific language programmes as yet. (b) There is no

close liaison is maintained where necessary with regard to the use of transmitter
frequencies.

Education-Expenditure Cuts
20. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education, How much
money did the Government save from the various cuts in educational expenditure
last year?


## p. 1362 (#604) ###########################################

1362
20 July
Questions and Replies
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, For the 1976-77 finan-
cial year the Government placed some restraints on the growth of expenditure
on existing policies. These added up to approximately $8 million. The Govern-
ment aso approved new policy developments amounting to an estimated $4 million
of additional expenditure. The net effect was that total estimated expenditure on
education was $4 million lower than it would have been if the restraints had not
been imposed. Education expenditure in 1975-76 was $631.75 million. The money
voted education for 1976-77 was $704.01 million. If there had not been the need
to curb the growth of expenditure on education this amount might have been
$708.01 million. The estimated savings were achieved in the course of the financial
year.

request "none".

Travel Tax-Statistics
25. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Customs, How many people
each month have paid travel tax since its introduction in July 1976, and how many
people each month made trips that would now be liable to travel tax during the
period July 1975 to July 1976?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied, In order to avoid a
needlessly complex administrative procedure, travel agents are required to send
in only monthly returns of tax collected, not numbers of travellers involved. The
Department of Statistics has advised that the total departures (excluding departures
to the Cook Islands, Niue, Fiji, and Western Samoa) during the months of July
1975 to July 1976 were: 1975 departures, July, 19 032; August, 27 408; September,
16 996; October, 16 548; November, 13 596; December, 30 746; 1976 departures,
January, 16 470; February, 14 010; March, 18 126; April, 21 494, May, 28 442;
June, 22 478; and July, 23 284.
The above figures include departures to certain other parts of the exempted
Pacific area, but separate statistics are not available in respect of these destinations.
It is therefore not possible to state how many departures would have been liable to
travel tax.

Education-Special Teaching Needs
28. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education, Will he
outline the kinds of special staffing aid which are available to primary schools with
a high Maori and Pacific Island enrolment, and the criteria schools have to meet
before this aid is available to them?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, The following provisions
apply in primary schools for pupils, including Maoris and Pacific Islanders, who
have special teaching needs. Thirty-nine schools, 29 in Auckland and 10 in Welling-
ton, are now staffed on a notional-roll basis to meet what are termed exceptional
needs. This scheme adds from 10 percent to 20 percent to the actual grading roll for
staffing purposes, and improves both the number of teachers and the number and
quality of the positions of responsibility on a permanent basis. Two hundred
teachers, additional to entitlement staffing, are being employed this year to give
further assistance to schools where special educational needs exist. In the majority
of cases the established need which qualifies a school for this assistance is provision
of special programmes for children who have difficulties with the English language.
The reduction of teacher-pupil ratios to 1:31 this year under the new primary
staffing scheme has given material staffing assistance to all schools with rolls above
155 pupils. This better ratio, along with the provision of part-time teachers, which
is an important part of the scheme, allows greater attention to be given to the needs
of children who have difficulties.

National Superannuitants-Concessions
29. Hon. M. A. CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Social Welfare,
When will the income limits determining eligibility for telephone and television
concessions for national superannuitants be increased?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied, The Government in
its election manifesto undertook to continue the telephone and television concessions
under the same income criteria as applied when it took office. In line with this, the
income limits were set at $3,156 a year for an unmarried person and $4,580 a year
for married couples. These limits will not be increased since, when fully implemented
in August 1978, the national superannuation scheme will provide a level of retire-
ment income which will not need to be supplemented by concessions and supple-
mentary payments.

Maputo Declaration
31. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs,
(1) When did the Cabinet consider and decide its attitude to the Maputo Declara-
tion; (2) which of its provisions does the Government regard as-(a) binding on
us; (b) binding on others; (3) which of its provisions does the Government regard
as partly binding on us, and with what reservations; (4) which of its provisions
does the Government regard as-(a) not binding us at all; (b) not binding others
at all; and (5) to which countries have these decisions been conveyed, and in what
manner?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) repied, The Maputo
Declaration was drawn up at a conference convened by the United Nations. While
such declarations are of considerable moral force, they are not considered to be
"binding" in any legal or contractual sense on those countries which support them,
and certainly not on those countries which had no part in their elaboration or
adoption. The question of whether New Zealand or any other country is bound by
the whole or part of the Maputo Declaration is therefore misconceived. Cabinet has
not formally considered the detailed content of the declaration. What the Prime
Minister has indicated on behalf of the Government is that, with some reservations,
he could support the declaration.
(29/6/77)
Dentists from Overseas
32. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Health, In view of the recent
report in the Waikato Times, of 31 May, that the New Zealand Dental Council
does not consider American dental graduates eligible to practise in New Zealand,
can he say whether this policy also extends to Singaporean graduates, what the
general policy of the council is on the registration of overseas dental graduates,
and what criteria the council adopts in determining eligibility to practise?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied, The report in the Waikato Times
is not correct. The Dental Act 1963 requires the New Zealand Dental Council to
consider the academic qualifications and professional ability of any person applying
for registration as a dentist. Applications from overseas dental graduates who
genuinely wish to practise in New Zealand would be considered in terms of the
qualifications for registration laid down in the Act. The council has registered many
overseas graduates, but no firm applications have come before the council in recent
years from either the United States or Singapore.

42. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade,

ates, and working parties of the OECD at this time?
Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) replied, The benefits of
our membership of OECD can be divided into two areas. The organisation carries
out considerable technical work in such fields as education, science, and energy,
and has become a major source of information for New Zealand departments and
organisations on international developments in these areas. The second main area
is that encompassing economic and trade policies where membership provides
New Zealand with the opportunity to share in the monitoring of world economic
trends, and forecasting, carried out by the organisation, and to enjoy the benefits
of this process and the experience of other OECD members in its own economic
planning. On the trade front the OECD provides a forum in which we can express
the New Zealand point of view on policies employed by the major industrialised
countries of the world, who are also our major markets. The OECD has a very
wide-ranging structure and, over 100 committees and working parties have been
created. The main committees are as follows: Economic Poicy Committee, Econ-
omic and Development Review Committee, Environment Committee, Development
Assistance Committee, Technical Co-operation Committee, Trade Committee, Pay-
ments Committee, Committee for Invisible Transactions, Committee on Fiscal
Affairs, Committee of Experts on Restrictive Business Practices, Tourism Commit-
tee, Maritime Transport Committee, Consumer Policies Committee, Committee on
Agriculture, Fisheries Committee, Committee for Scientific and Technological Policy,
Education Committee, Industry Committee, Committee for Energy Policy, Man-

High-Level Group on Economic Relations between member countries, Governing
Committee and Advisory Board of the OECD Fund. Autonomous and semi-
autonomous bodies: The Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA). The International Energy

Gross Income, 1975-76-1976-77
49. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Statistics, Based on average
movements in wage rates for the 1976-77 year, what gross income could be esti-
mated for persons who earned $5,200 during 1975-76?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics) replied, The movement in
the nominal weekly wage rates index for the year ended March 1977 was 13.7
percent above the index for the 1975-76 March year. Applying this percentage
movement to the 1975-76 hypothetical income figure of $5,200, the 1976-77 value
would become $5,912. This exercise in arithmetic would be appropriate as an
estimate of the change in income level only if the stated income was that of the
average adult male who was on award rates of pay set by the Industrial Commis-
sion or on rates set by other wage or salary determining authorities and who enjoyed
no source of income other than salary or wages.

Taxpayers-Dependent Allowances
50. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Statistics, In respect of the last
3 years for which figures are available, what proportion of total taxpayers were
supporting a dependent spouse and child (or children) as shown by their tax codes?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics) replied, The Government ·
Statistician informs me that he has no figures showing the number of taxpayers
claiming both spouse and child allowance. However, he does have separate figures
for those claiming spouse or housekeeper allowances and those claiming exemptions
for dependent relatives, which would include children. In 1970-71 there was a
total of 1 460 820 individual taxpayers. Of these, 368 790, or 25.2 percent, claimed
full spouse or housekeeper exemption, 38 740 (2.7 percent) claimed a partial
exemption, and 463 830 (31.8 percent) claimed a dependent relative allowance.
In 1971-72, out of a total of 1517 490 individual taxpayers, the percentages were
24.1, 2.6, and 31.6. In 1972-73, out of a total of 1 574 460, the percentages were 23,
2.6, and 30.4. From this time onwards comparable figures are not available for
the dependent relative category as by definition this category no longer includes
children for whom family benefit was paid.
