(30/6/77)
Maputo Declaration
58. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs, What
are the terms of the Maputo Declaration which was the subject of comment and
partial support at the recent Prime Ministers' Conference?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied, The terms of
the Maputo Declaration to which the honourable member refers are as follows:
The International Conference in Support of the Peoples of Zimbabwe and
Namibia, held in Maputo from 16 to 21 May 1977, was attended by 92 member
states of the United Nations, and numerous observers and non-governmental
organisations representing all regions of the world and diverse political and social
systems. The conference, which resulted from General Assembly Resolution
A/31/145 of 17 December 1976, was called to express the solidarity and support
of the world community with the freedom struggle of the oppressed peoples of
Zimbabwe and Namibia.
The fact that the conference was held in Maputo, the capital of the People's
Republic of Mozambique, symbolises the profound changes which have decisively
tipped the balance of forces in favour of the struggle for self-determination and
independence in the region with the victories of the liberation movements of
Mozambique, Angola, Guinea-Bissau, Cape Verde and Sao Tome and Principe.
The extension of the frontiers of freedom to the borders of Zimbabwe and Namibia
has given impetus to the liberation struggle in these two countries and has shaken.
the foundations of the racist minority regimes of Southern Africa.
The liberation movements in Zimbabwe and Namibia have intensified their
struggle as a consequence of the intransigence of the colonial racist regimes, which
have not only consistently thwarted attempts at arriving at a negotiated settlement,
but also have increased their brutal repression of the people's of the two countries.
The minority regimes, in their desperation, have also carried out acts of aggression


## p. 1376 (#618) ###########################################

1376
20 July
Questions and Replies
against neighbouring African states, thereby seriously threatening international
peace and security.
The development of the armed struggle, the isolation of the minority regimes
and the international support for the national liberation movements are factors
creating conditions for a negotiated settlement leading to majority rule and
genuine independence in Zimbabwe and Namibia.
The conference notes that the minority racist regimes of South Africa, in
defiance of United Nations resolutions, international public opinion, and the
advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice, gives comfort and susten-
ance to the illegal racist minority regime in Southern Rhodesia and is perpetuating
its illegal occupation and exploitation of Namibia. The conference also notes that
certain Western powers continue to encourage the racist regimes by economic,
military, and other forms of collaboration with them and by their continued refusal
to support the liberation movements in their legitimate struggle.
The conference is convinced that the national liberation struggle and the over-
whelming international support for it will overcome these negative factors and
that the peoples of Zimbabwe and Namibia are on the threshold of freedom.
Against this background, the conference adopts the Maputo Declaration in
support of the peoples of Zimbabwe and Namibia, the Programme of Action for
the Liberation of Zimbabwe and Namibia.
2. DECLARATION of the Liberation of ZIMBABWE
The conference solemnly proclaims its full support for the people of Zimbabwe
in their just struggle for independence. It reaffirms that there should be no
independence before majority rule and that any settlement relating to the future
of the territory must be worked out with the full participation of the people of
Zimbabwe represented by their National liberation movement, which includes all
the progressive forces actively engaged in the struggle, and in accordance with.
their true aspirations. The conference affirms the principle of the rights of indi-
vidual citizens, regardless of race or colour, and rejects any notion of special rights
and privileges for, or discrimination against, any ethnic group.
The conference reaffirms the primary responsibility of the United Kingdom of
Great Britain and Northern Ireland as the Administering Power for Southern
Rhodesia (Zimbabwe). The international accountability which the Administering
Power assumed under Chapter XI of the Charter of the United Nations cannot
be compromised. It is imperative that the solemn obligation accepted as a sacred
trust by the Administering Power cannot be relinquished under any circumstances
until the objectives of the Charter of the United Nations and the Declaration on
the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples have been fully
implemented.
The conference strongly condemns the illegal racist minority regime in Southern
Rhodesia. It denounces the regime's brutal and repressive measures against the
people of Zimbabwe. The illegal racist minority regime has forcibly moved
thousands of villagers into concentration camps. Numerous acts of brutality have
been committed by the illegal regime against the people of Zimbabwe and foreign
missionaries. There has been beating, torture, and killing of innocent villagers
and the application of criminal and arbitrary measures of collective punishment.
Ruthless repression has escalated into genocide as shown in the massacre of
hundreds of people in the Nyadzonya refugee camp. The illegal regime is recruiting
merceneries to carry out its brutal repression of the people of Zimbabwe. It is
clear that all the actions taken by the illegal racist minority regime are designed
to consolidate its illegal rule of the territory. Recent manoeuvres such as the
amendment of the Land Tenure Act and the appointment of puppet chiefs to
"ministerial" posts are futile attempts to perpetuate the status quo. The inter-
national community should act forthwith to put an end to the illegal racist minority
regime in Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe).
Over the years, efforts have been made to achieve a negotiated settlement in
Zimbabwe. These efforts were particularly intensified in the wake of the collapse


## p. 1377 (#619) ###########################################

20 July
1377
Questions and Replies
of Portuguese colonialism in Africa and the consequent extension of the frontiers
of freedom in Southern Africa through the emergence of the liberated Mozambique
and Angola as well as the development of the struggle in Zimbabwe and Namibia.
These efforts were undertaken by the liberation movements supported by the
frontline states and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU). This support was
clearly reflected in the Dar-es-Salaam Declaration on Southern Africa adopted
by OAU in April 1975.
Painstaking attempts were made last year to reach a negotiated settlement
culminating in the Geneva Conference on Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe). How-
ever, so far all reasonable and meaningful proposals which would have secured a
negotiated settlement for an independent Zimbabwe on the basis of majority rule
have been totally rejected by the illegal racist minority regime. Confronted with
the intransigence of the illegal minority regime, the freedom fighters have intensi-
fied the armed struggle.
Furthermore, the fighting forces have forged ahead in their drive towards unity.
Positive steps were taken towards the unity of Zimbabweans and the development
of the liberation struggle. The conference stresses the importance of the unity
of all the patriotic forces in their struggle against the illegal racist minority regime.
The development of the armed struggle and the concerted efforts of the inter-
national community are creating positive conditions for a negotiated settlement
based on majority rule.
The international community should endevour to intensify its efforts so that a
speedy end is brought to the illegal racist minority regime. In this regard, the
conference takes note of the efforts of the United Kingdom, the Administering
Power, to achieve a negotiated settlement with the objective of securing indepen-
dence for Zimbabwe under majority rule in 1978.
The conference considers that the strict enforcement of existing mandatory
sanctions against the illegal racist minority regime is an important element in the
collective effort of the international community to promote a settlement of the
conflict in Zambabwe. In this regard, the actions taken by the Governments of
Mozambique and Zambia in closing their borders with Southern Rhodesia.
(Zimbabwe), imposing total sanctions against the illegal minority regime, con-
stitute a major contribution in support of the liberation struggle of the people of
Zimbabwe and towards the maximum isolation of the illegal minority regime in
accordance with United Nations objectives.
The conference deplores that some states continue to violate sanctions with the
result that sanctions have had a limited effect on the economy of Southern
Rhodesia (Zimbabwe). The principal violator of sanctions is South Africa. In
addition, some Western and other states have not implemented the mandatory
sanctions. The need to ensure that the mandatory sanctions are scrupulously
enforced is more urgent than ever. Any breaches or evasions of obligations under
the Charter of the United Nations must not be tolerated. At the same time there
is an urgent need to widen the scope of sanctions to include all the measures
envisaged under article 41 of the Charter of the United Nations.
The conference strongly condemns South Africa for its support of the illegal
racist minority regime in Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe). It is South Africa's
support which sustains the illegal minority regime. The United Nations should
examine all possibilities to ensure South Africa's compliance with the resolutions
on Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe).
The conference strongly condemns the persistent acts of aggression committed
by the illegal racist minority regime in Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe) against
Botswana, Mozambique, and Zambia. These acts of aggression have resulted in
an enormous loss of life and in destruction of property. The international com-
munity should give the utmost assistance to these states in order to deter armed
attacks by the illegal minority regime in Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe). Through

## p. 1378 (#620) ###########################################

1378
20 July
Questions and Replies
these acts the illegal minority regime seeks to achieve a dual objective on the one
hand, to intimidate the frontline states which are acting as strategic rear bases
for the liberation struggle in Zimbabwe in accordance with the United Nations
objectives, and, on the other hand, to internationalise this conflict.
The conference solemnly declares that the natural resources of Zimbabwe are
the birthright of the people of Zimbabwe. The exploitation of these resources by
the illegal racist minority regime in association with foreign economic interests is
in violation of the principles of the charter and of all pertinent resolutions of
the United Nations. The exploitation of these resources by the illegal minority
regime brings no benefit to the people of Zimbabwe and contributes to maintaining
in power the illegal minority regime. The activities of foreign economic interests
engaged in Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe) should be the object of systematic
denunciation so that their actions which are detrimental to the people of
Zimbabwe be exposed to the full scrutiny of and condemnation by the international
community.
The conference solemnly appeals to all states members of the United Nations,
other intergovernmental and non-governmental organisations to identify their
assistance to the national liberation movement representing the people of Zimbabwe
in their struggle for independence. It commends the international community for
the invaluable moral, political, and material assistance given by it to the national
liberation movement of Zimbabwe. It further commends all non-governmental
organisations which have given their solidarity and support to the cause of the
liberation struggle in Zimbabwe. The front-line states in Africa which have taken
a firm stand against the illegal racist minority regime, in accordance with resolu-
tions of the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity, should be given
all necessary economic and other assistance by all freedom-loving countries and
peoples. The conference urges that all governments, organisations, and peoples join
in concerted international action in support of the liberation struggle of the people
of Zimbabwe in this crucial and final stage of the total emancipation of Africa.
3. DECLARATION OF THE LIBERATION OF NAMIBIA
The conference solemnly proclaims its full support for the struggle of the people
of Namibia under the leadership of their sole and authentic liberation movement,
the South West Africa Peoples Organisation (SWAPO), to achieve self-determina-
tion, freedom, and independence in a united Namibia. It recognises that the
Namibian people have been forced to resort to armed struggle after many years
of arduous attempts to achieve those objectives by peaceful means. It reaffirms the
right of the people of Namibia to decide on the means of their struggle, in the
light of the conditions in the territory. The development of the armed struggle
and continued efforts of the international community have created positive condi-
tions for a negotiated settlement. It is encouraging and inspiring to see the unity
and solidarity of the Namibian people in their efforts to fulfil their true aspira-
tions and legitimate interests under the leadership of their liberation movement.
Despite a ferocious oppressor, the determination, competence, and heroism of
Namibian patriots have gained for them the respect and admiration of the inter-
national community. It is imperative that all freedom-loving forces in the inter-
national community give maximum support to SWAPO to ensure the victory of
the people of Namibia in their struggle against the forces of colonialism and racism.
The conference strongly condemns the colonial and illegal occupation of Namibia.
by South Africa which constitutes an act of aggression against the Namibian people
and against the United Nations, in defiance of repeated demands for its with-
drawal by the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations.
The policies of the illegal South African Administration are a systematic violation
of its obligations under the Charter of the United Nations, the Universal Declara-
tion of Human Rights, and the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to
Colonial Countries and Peoples. The United Nations Council for Namibia as the
legal authority to administer that Territory until independence has the respon-


## p. 1379 (#621) ###########################################

20 July
1379
Questions and Replies
sibility to assist the Namibian people in their struggle against South African
aggression and occupation. It is therefore imperative that appropriate measures
be formulated and implemented to decisively counter South Africa's continued
defiance of the authority of the United Nations.
The conference strongly condemns the policies of apartheid and homelands
which the Pretoria regime has extended to Namibia. In order to perpetuate its
exploitation of the people and natural resources of the territory, the illegal South
African Administration in Namibia follows a policy of brutal institutionalised
terrorism against the Namibian people. Many Namibian patriots have perished
under this regime. The illegal administration in Namibia imprisons and tortures
men and women under its violently repressive racist system. It carries out massive
transfers of population causing untold suffering to thousands of innocent men,
women, and children. In this respect, the conference invites all states to implement
the Declaration and Programme of Action adopted at the Dakar Conference on
Namibia and Human Rights. The conference considers furthermore that all possible
pressures should be brought to bear upon the Pretoria regime to cease its barbaric
repression of the Namibian people in their efforts to achieve self-determination,
freedom, and independence in a united Namibia.
The conference recognises Walvis Bay as an integral part of Namibia and rejects
the attempts of South Africa to separate it from the rest of Namibia with which
it is inextricably linked by geographical, historical, economic, cultural, and ethnic
bonds. All states should endeavour to dissuade South Africa from pursuing the
separation of Walvis Bay from Namibia.
The conference strongly condemns the increasing militarisation of Namibia by
the racist Pretoria regime. In its increasingly aggressive posture, South Africa has
expanded its military apparatus in Namibia in order to give itself the capability
to attack neighbouring African countries in a policy of continuous intimidation.
It has enacted the Defence Amendment Act in 1976 in order to carry out aggression
far beyond the borders of South Africa. Therefore, the sale or supply of any arms
or military material, the transfer of technology, and the provision of the means to
produce weapons, as well as any nuclear collaboration with South Africa, ultimately
support the acts of aggression by South Africa against the Namibian people and
the United Nations. It is therefore imperative that all states cease and desist from
any form of direct or indirect military consultation, co-operation, or collaboration,
with South Africa. In order to meet the continuous threat of the minority regime
to international peace and security in South Africa, the Security Council should
be called upon to impose a mandatory arms embargo against South Africa.
The conference strongly denounces the Turnhalle tribal talks as a South African
stratagem to perpetuate its ruthless colonial and racist policies and practices under
false pretences. South Africa has brought together in the Turnhalle tribal talks
the fanatical racist promoters of apartheid and tribal puppets to prepare a so-called
charter with the purpose of misleading the international community on its true
intentions in Namibia. The so-called charter is to be the basis for a provisional
government fabricated by South Africa which would pretend to be an advance
towards a pseudo-independent Namibia. The international community, especially
all member states of the United Nations, should act to frustrate South Africa's
tactics of political deception. No recognition should be accorded to any group
which the illegal South African Administration may install as a consequence of
the current fraudulent constitutional talks or any other manoeuvres in Namibia.
Any independence talks regarding Namibia must be between the representatives
of the South West Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO) and South Africa under
the auspices of the United Nations for the sole purpose of discussing the modalities
for the transfer of power to the Namibian people.
The conference reaffirms that, in order that the people of Namibia shall be
enabled freely to determine their own future, free elections be held urgently under
the supervision and control of the United Nations in the whole of Namibia as one
political entity. However, prior to such elections, conditions for a negotiated
settlement should be created in Namibia in accordance with all relevant decisions

and resolutions of the United Nations and, in particular, Security Council Resolu-
tion 385 (1976).
The conference solemnly reaffirms the responsibility of the United Nations for
Namibia until the territory attains full independence. The General Assembly
declared Namibia to be a direct responsibility of the United Nations and entrusted
the United Nations Council for Namibia with the exercise of de jure internal and
external sovereignty over Namibia.
The council has been empowered to protect the rights and to represent the
interests of the Namibian people, with the full participation of the South West
Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO). The conference recognises the United
Nations Council for Namibia as the legal administering authority of Namibia until
independence, an indispensable role which it is fulfilling. It is imperative that the
international community strengthen its support for the council in its efforts to
promote the legitimate aspirations of the Namibian people for self-determination,
freedom, and independence in a united Namibia. The conference calls on all
member states to implement provisions contained in United Nations resolutions
granting full particpation of the United Nations Council for Namabia in all con-
ferences, United Nations specialised agencies,and other organisations of the United
Nations system.
The conference solemnly proclaims its support for the nationhood programme
for Namibia. The council for Namibia received from the General Assembly at its
thirty-first session the mandate to elaborate, inconsultation with the South West
Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO),. the guidelines and policies for such a
programme and to direct and co-ordinate the implementation of the programme.
The nationhood programme shall cover the present period of struggle for indepen-
dence and the initial years of the independence of Namibia. It is imperative that
the international community ensure the success of the nationhood programme by
taking measures to increase the programmes of concrete assistance to the people
of Namibia through their liberation movement, SWAPO.
The conference solemnly declares that the natural resources of Namibia are the
birthright of the Namibian people. The exploitation of these resources by foreign
economic interests, under the protection of the repressive racist colonial administra-
tion and in violation of all principles of the charter and of the pertinent resolutions
of the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations, is illegal
and contributes to the maintenance of the illegal ooccupation regime. The rapid
depletion of the natural resources of the territory due to the reckless plunder in
which foreign economic interests engage in collusion with the illegal South African
administration is a grave threat to the integrity and prosperity of an independent
Namibia. It is imperative that the activities of foreign economic interests engaged
in Namibia be the object of systematic denunciation so that their actions, which
are detrimental to the Namibian people, be exposed to the full scrutiny and condem-
nation of the international community.
The conference welcomes the report and recommendations of the Mission of
the United Nations Council for Namibia to the specialised agencies and other
United Nations organisations with headquarters in Europe. In this regard it urges
all specialised agencies and concrete assistance within their spheres of competence
to the Council for Namibia in the discharge of the mandate entrusted to it, so as
to speed up the implementation of the relevant United Nations Resolutions on
Namibia, in particular that on the nationhood programme for Namibia. The
conference calls upon those specialised agencies and other United Nations organisa-
tions in which South Africa still illegally purports to represent Namibia to terminate
such relationships forthwith and to grant full membership to the United Nations
Council for Namibia as the administering authority of Namibia until independence.
The conference commends the international community for the invaluable moral,
political, and material assistance it is giving to the South West Africa People's
Organisation (SWAPO). It further commends all non-governmental organisations
which are giving their solidarity and support to the cause of the liberation of
Namibia from South African illegal occupation. The conference solemnly appeals to

all member states of the United Nations, other intergovernmental and non-govern-

4. GENERAL: ZIMBABWE And Namibia
The conference notes with appreciation the programmes of the United Nations,
its specialised agencies, and institutions within the United Nations system, which
are providing educational training and humanitarian assistance to Zimbabweans
and Namibians, notably the United Nations Educational and Training Programme
for Southern Africa (UNETPSA), the United Nations Fund for Namibia, the
Institute for Namibia, the Trust Fund for South Africa, the United Nations High
Commission for Refugees (UNHCR), the United Nations Educational, Scientific,
and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO), and other intergovernmental and non-
governmental organisations. It appeals to states, organisations, and individuals to
give generous assistance to all such programmes designed to assist Zimbabweans
and Namibians.
The conference appeals to the mass media to join in the campaign in support
of the peoples of Zimbabwe and Namibia. The conference considers it necessary
for the United Nations to strengthen and intensify the dissemination of informa-
tion on the struggle for self-determination and independence in Zimbabwe and
Namibia particularly through the network of the United Nations information
centres all over the world. In this regard, the conference requests the General
Assembly to allocate the necessary resources to intensify public information action,
especially through the United Nations information centres.
5. SOUTH AFRICA
The conference recognises that the South African apartheid regime has been
the bastion of racism and colonialism in Southern Africa and the main opponent
of the efforts of the United Nations and the international community to promote
self-determination and independence in southern Africa.
While fully conscious of the need for vigorous and effective international action
to thwart the manoeuvres of the apartheid regime, the conference decided to
concentrate its programme of action on specific measures with respect to Zimbabwe
and Namibia, taking into account that further action against apartheid will be
considered at the World Conference for Action Against Apartheid to be held in
Lagos, Nigeria, from 22 to 26 August 1977.
6. PROGRAM ME FOR ACTION FOR THE LIBERATION OF Zimbabwe and Namibia
A. Measures in support of the national liberation movements:
The conference calls upon governments to:
(a) give the greatest possible political and moral support to the peoples of
Zimbabwe and Namibia and their national liberation movements in their
struggle to attain self-determination and national independence;
(b) provide and increase material and financial support to the people of
Zimbabwe and Namibia and their national liberation movements in con-
sultation and co-operation with the Organisation of African Unity
(OAU);
(c) encourage the activities of non-governmental organisations engaged in pro-
viding political and material assistance to the national liberation move-
ments of Zimbabwe and Namibia;
(d) increase their contributions to the United Nations Fund for Namibia in
order to ensure the success of the Institute for Namibia in Lusaka as well
as the formulation and implementation of additional projects in support
of the Namibian people;
(e) extend travel facilities and educational and employment opportunities to
Namibians;

20 July
Questions and Replies
(f) participate in the Week of Solidarity with the Namibian people which is
to be organised each year during the week following 27 October, the
anniversary of the ending of the mandate of South Africa over Namibia,
particularly by setting up committees of assistance for Namibia.
The conference urges all member states, specialised agencies, programmes and
other institutions within the United Nations system and other intergovernmental
as well as non-governmental organisations to extend, as a matter of priority,
material and economic assistance to the frontline states in order to enable them to
more effectively implement the United Nations resolutions supporting the libera-
tion struggle in Zimbabwe and Namibia. The conference further urges them to
render special assistance to the states bordering Zimbabwe and Namibia to enable
them to provide for the increasing number of refugees from these territories.
The conference calls upon the United Nations to:
(a) further increase its contribution to the United Nations Fund for Namibia;
(b) increase its support for the United Nations Council for Namibia in its efforts
to achieve self-determination, freedom, and national independence for
the people of Namibia;
(c) consider the possibility of establishing the University of Namibia. With regard
to this initiative, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural
Organisation (UNESCO) should be invited to assist the United Nations
Council for Namibia and the South West Africa People's Organisation
(SWAPO) in the formulation of its guiding plan.
The conference calls upon the specialised agencies and other institutions within
the United Nations system to give high priority to the formulation, with the active
co-operation of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU), of programmes and
projects of assistance to the peoples of Zimbabwe and Namibia and their national
liberation movements. In the case of Namibia, such assistance should be extended
in consultation with the United Nations Council for Namibia.
The conference appeals to all non-governmental organisations to:
(a) intensify their campaigns in support of the peoples of Zimbabwe and Namibia
and their national liberation movements in their struggle to attain self-
determination and independence;
(b) intensify their campaigns in support of the South West Africa People's
Organisation (SWAPO) to prevent any action in favour of South Africa's
policies in Namibia and to increase financial contributions to SWAPO.
The conference appeals to all solidarity organisations and groups to establish
effective national committees in their respective countries in support of the South
West Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO) and the struggle of the people of
Namibia to prevent any action in favour of South Africa's policies and practices
in the territory in contravention of the United Nations resolutions and decisions
on Namibia.
The conference calls upon all trade unions to intensify their campaign in support
of the just struggle of the people of Namibia by boycotting and otherwise refusing
to handle vessels, aircraft, or any other vehicles carrying Namibian goods, in
accordance with Decree No. 1 on the Protection of the Natural Resources of
Namibia enacted by the United Nations Council for Namibia on 27 September
1974.

The conference calls upon Governments to:
(a) refrain from any co-operation or collaboration with the illegal racist minority
regime in Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe);
(b) observe strictly the arms embargo against the illegal racist minority regime;

Energy Conservation
60. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources,
Could he give details of the "number of positive steps to encourage energy conser-
vation" which he has taken and mentions in his answer to my question on 21 June?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied, In addition to the
introduction of the new energy pricing policy and the continuation of an energy
conservation publicity campaign, there is the tax incentive scheme for capital
expenditure on energy conservation by businesses. Information about this scheme.
has already been provided to the member. Considerable information has been
published on the means of saving energy. A series of booklets on energy conserva-
tion for industrial and commercial firms has been initiated. One publication in
this series is an energy conservation guide to promote the use of energy audits.
This booklet, which has been widely distributed, has been well received and has
led to many follow-up queries. A further series, on home energy conservation, has
been started with a revised booklet on the home insulation loan scheme. A series
of Energy Research and Development Committee reports have also been published,
and discussions to examine ways in which their recommendations on energy con-
servation can be followed up have been held with particular industries. An energy
conservation officer has been appointed in the Ministry of Energy Resources, and
an energy advisory service has recently been established within the Ministry of
Works and Development.

Ohai Coalfield Development
67. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines, In view of
the serious shortages of coal available from the Ohai coalfields, will he indicate
what progress has been made with the development proposals agreed to by the
previous Government for a new mechanised mine and the opening up of Wairaki
for opencast operations?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied, There is a shortage of domestic
coal at Ohai, but other grades are in good supply. Confirmatory drilling is nearly
completed on the site of the new underground unit to replace the Linton mine.
Results to date have been good. The opening up of the Wairaki mine by opencast
methods requires a diversion of the Morley stream, which entails water rights
that are under application. An environmental assessment covering all facets of the
operation is considered necessary by the Commission for the Environment, and
arrangements for this have been finalised. With the completion of these two pre-
requisites tenders will be called for the overburden removal.

Bastion Point-Maori Claims
75. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Maori Affairs, In
view of his confirmation that a telegram was sent to him on 6 January 1977
suggesting that an application to the Maori Land Court in terms of section 60
of the Maori Affairs Amendment Act 1974 be made by him for consideration of
the claims of the Ngati-Whatua people for the lands at Bastion Point, will he
advise why this suggestion was not acceded to?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs) replied, The suggestion was
not acceded to because the Government was not, and is not, prepared to give up
the whole of the Crown land at Orakei for a Maori reservation, and to refer the
matter to the court would, in these circumstances, be a waste of time. The ques-
tioner was Minister of Lands in 1974-75 and Minister of Maori Affairs at the
same time. He proposed, and had passed, section 60 of the Maori Affairs Amend-
ment Act 1974, and did nothing to facilitate the requests of Ngati Whatua in that
period. The Government has, however, through my colleague the Minister of
Lands, made certain proposals to the accredited representatives of the appropriate
section of Ngati Whatua, which they are still considering, for the return to Ngati
Whatua control of a part of the land.

Christchurch-Pollution
76. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) asked the Minister of Energy Resources, Has he
seen the report in the Christchurch Star of 15 June that Christchurch pollution on
that date was the worst recorded since 1959 when city levels were first monitored,
and the view expressed by Dr J. McLeod, an expert on pollution problems, that
the level would aggravate the problems of people with asthma, bronchial troubles,
and heart disease, and, if so, will he give an assurance that immediate action will
be taken to provide a cheaper rate of electricity to Christchurch in an effort to
alleviate the dependence on open fires?


## p. 1390 (#632) ###########################################

1390
20 July
Questions and Replies
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied, Apart from efficient
enclosed space heaters burning solid fuel (which can readily meet clea.. require-
ments) electricity already has the lowest retail price, in relation to the useful
energy obtained, of any form of energy available for use in Christchurch homes.
No further incentive for its use, in preference to other forms of energy, is therefore
warranted. Also, the Government has, in the form of the Clean Air Act, provided
the framework for action on the type of pollution experienced in Christchurch.
The Christchurch City Council has taken advantage of this in requesting a clean
air zone to be established in its area. An Order in Council to this effect is expected
to be gazetted shortly. The philosophy behind the pricing of electricity in New
Zealand is that the whole country is treated as one. Thus, no supply authority or
region gets preferential treatment. However, there is nothing to prevent any supply
authority including such a provision in its own domestic tariff if it considers this to
be justified. At present the domestic tariff in Christchurch is one of the lower
tariffs in the country and thus would not inhibit any person wishing to convert
to electric heating. Hence, I am unable to give the assurance requested.

The above figures do not include the annual cost of maintaining borstal trainees,
for whom the respective costs for 1971 and 1976 are $2,895 and $4,411. Salaries

main reason for the small increase in the annual cost per inmate. The variation

compared with 1971 and an increase in minimum security inmates over the same
period.

Helensville Vegetable Oil Refining Plant
83. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry,
In view of his statement in the Auckland Star of 22 June to the effect that the
establishment of a vegetable oil refining plant at Helensville and the operation of
a plant already under construction at East Tamaki would create an "overkill"
situation on the local market, will he: (1) advise what were the "particular merits
which justified the Government's support" of the Helensville scheme; (2) list the
items of buildings, plant, and equipment for which import licences have been
approved or are to be approved for the Helensville plant; (3) state the value of
such licences; and (4) advise whether local manufacturers of any of this plant have
been consulted?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied,
Replies to the honourable member's four specific questions are set out below:
(1) Some attractions of the Helensville project were substantial import savings
without an increase in the price of refined oil; potential for worth-while exports of
refined oil; a capability to purchase unrefined oil at favourable prices; the involve-
ment of the New Zealand company and its partner in a Middle East joint venture
which will yield benefits to New Zealand through, inter alia, New Zealand construc-
tion of plant. (2) and (3) It is not the Government's practice to publish details of
individual import licences. In any event, while I know the full cost of imported
plant for the project, a substantial proportion is exempt from import licensing, and
the company is still working out the precise amount of licences required. (4) A
specific condition of approval of the project was that plant and equipment which
was available at reasonable prices and under reasonable conditions from New Zea-
land suppliers would be purchased locally. At the request of my department the
company obtained quotations from local suppliers.

encouraging firms to undertake energy audits as a means of identifying oppor-

give the results of their audits to the Government or to seek any approvals for

Trade Aid Incorporated—Import of Shoes
87. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry,
Has he seen the report in Zealandia of 16 January 1977 referring to comments
by Father Bernard Donnelly, a Christchurch Jesuit missionary in India, and if so,
can he confirm the statement that "bowing to pressure from Christchurch business-
men, the Government stopped the import of $3,000 worth of shoes which a volun-
tary organisation-Trade Aid Incorporated-had been selling here on behalf of
poor Indian families who made them"?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied,
I have seen the report which appeared in Zealandia, and the statement that in
response to pressure from Christchurch businessmen the Government stopped the
import of $3,000 worth of shoes from India by Trade Aid Incorporated is incorrect.
In the 1975-76 import licensing period shoes were included among the items
covered in the developing countries handicraft scheme. In that year the domestic
footwear industry suffered harm from imports of adult footwear. For 1976-77
it was decided to delete for the time being adult footwear from the list of item
codes covered by the scheme. When Trade Aid Incorporated explained to me, how-
ever, that it had been obtaining sandals from a village in India and that this was
an important source of income for the village the situation was reviewed. In the
1977-78 period a licence has been issued under the developing countries handicraft
scheme to enable Trade Aid to continue to obtain sandals from this village.

Carrington Technical Institute
90. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education, What courses
will be accommodated in the new Carrington Technical Institute building, when
was it due for completion, and what are the reasons for the delay?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, A single contract for
buildings at the new Carrington Technical Institute was let in December 1974 for
two four-storey teaching blocks, one five-storey link block, one two-storey adminis-
tration block, and one major workshop complex. Construction commenced in
February 1975 with a completion date of April 1978 for the total contract. How-
ever, the workshops were given priority with the objective of completion by June
1976. The actual handover of this complex began in February 1977, and is expected
to be completed this August. Two floors of the first teaching block are scheduled
for completion in February 1978, 2 weeks ahead of schedule, while the remainder
of the block is due for completion in May 1978. The second teaching block, link
block, and administration block are expected to be completed by September 1978.
Construction delays have been caused by difficult volcanic formations on the site,
the wet weather during the. winters of 1975 and 1976, the employment of the
contractor to provide temporary accommodation not allowed in the original project,
but required urgently until the main buildings were completed, and, because of the
length of the contract period, by some alterations to the original design to meet
changes in course curricula. The workshop block, which is already being used for
painting and decorating, signwriting, carpentry, furniture finishing, and plumbing
and gasfitting apprentice training, will also be used for cabinetmaking, joinery,
boat building, and fibre glass moulding courses. Negotiations are well advanced for
the special Maori pre-apprentice carpentry course to be transferred from Manukau
Technical Institute in 1978, and fitting and turning, motor engineering, and elec-
trical courses are also likely to be established. The following courses at present
housed in relocatable buildings will be transferred progressively to the teaching
blocks: accountancy, management, secretarial, architectural draughting, quantity
surveying, building management, and building diploma and theoretical work associ-
ated with trade and technician courses.

Foreign Aid
92. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Has he seen
a copy of Newsletter No. 5, 1977, published on 2 June 1977 by the Overseas
Development Committee, in which is stated that as far as foreign aid is concerned
"It now appears that a decision has already been made to keep the vote at last
year's $51 million. This will be another reduction in terms of gross national product,
bringing the proportion down to approximately 0.38 percent"; and, if so, is this
statement correct?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied, Yes, I have seen
the Overseas Development Committee newsletter mentioned in the question. While
the final decision on the amount to be provided for the aid programme this year
must, of course, await the Budget and Parliament's decisions on the various appro-
priations involved, it is the Government's present intention to maintain the 1977-78
allocation at the same level as that of last year, i.e., $51 million. The serious
economic situation, particularly in respect of our overseas balance of payments,
does not permit an expansion of the aid programme to be considered at this time.
It will nevertheless be possible to sustain a significant and valuable range of
projects, and indeed in the case of our South Pacific neighbours some increase on
the previous year's allocations will be provided. The Government continues to
maintain New Zealand's full commitment to the agreed international target of
0.7 percent of GNP for official development assistance. Honourable members will
have noted that in the communique issued after the Commonwealth Heads of
Government meeting in London, New Zealand and other developed Common-
wealth members reaffirmed their undertaking to work towards the 0.7 percent
target. The time-scale for achieving that target will have to depend on each coun-
try's own national economic situation. In this respect, New Zealand is in the same
position as Australia and Canada, which have also made it clear they cannot now
meet the original target date of 1980 for that objective.

Industrial Stoppages
93. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of Labour, Is it correct that he
is unable to release statistical details of individual industrial stoppages, and, if so,
which statute precludes the release of this information?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied, It is correct that I cannot
release details of industrial stoppages in individual firms, as this would effectively
constitute a breach of confidence. In 1974 the Department of Labour provided


## p. 1397 (#639) ###########################################

20 July
1397
Questions and Replies
details of stoppages in individual freezing works for the Committee of Inquiry into
the Freezing Industry. The firms involved regarded this as a breach of confidence
and threatened to withdraw their co-operation in providing the statistics. It took
some time for the department to re-establish relationships with these firms. Whilst
the department is not strictly bound by any statute to observe confidentiality, it is
a well established principle that a data-collecting agency should adhere to this
doctrine. The Department of Statistics is bound by the Statistics Act to preserve
confidentially. It is fatuous to suggest that the Department of Labour should not
adhere to this principle simply because it is not legally bound to.

Mortgage Sales
98. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Housing, is he
aware that the Minister of Justice confirmed, as reported in the Evening Post of
2 June, that mortgage sale applications registered with the Supreme Court were
already up to 131 for the first 4 months of 1977, and can he confirm that the
number of loans for refinance through the Housing Corporation fell from 368 in
the year ended 31 March 1976 to 138 in the year ended 31 March 1977?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied, I am aware of the
report and I confirm the drop in the number of loans for refinance between 1976
and 1977. The refinance policy currently being administered by the Housing Cor-
poration has not changed since it was introduced by the former Government in
1973, with its emphasis on assisting home owners suffering hardship through very
high interest rates on second or subsequent mortgages. The figures suggest to me
that the objective may well have been achieved. While the corporation does under-
take a limited amount of first mortgage refinance, it is invariably in the role of a
lender of last resort, and frequently in situations where the corporation's participa-
tion is the only means of preserving the family home. The honourable member will
be aware that it is not possible for the Housing Corporation to fund the needs of
all those whose mortgages might be in the process of being realised or overdue, and
that the private sector must be held to its responsibility in this area. The Housing
Corporation will continue to administer the Government's policy in this area against
the existing stringent criteria laid down.

North Shore Hospital-Casualty Services
107. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Health, In view of his
concern reported in the North Shore Times-Advertiser of 20 November 1975, about
the need to provide urgently for a 24-hour casualty service at the North Shore
Hospital, can he say what action the Government has taken, or proposes to take, on
this matter?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied, I am aware that for some time
the Auckland Hospital Board has had difficulty in staffing the accident and emer-
gency department at North Shore. At present, the board has in prospect two
doctors from overseas who have expressed an interest in working in this depart-
ment. To a large extent the difficulties experienced at North Shore have been due
to the lack of the back-up facilities that an acute general hospital can provide.
This is not simply a matter of beds, but rather of the other resources of a general
hospital-for example, laboratory and X-ray services, and particularly the avail-
ability of specialist staff. Experiences overseas and in New Zealand have confirmed
that it is most important to transport accident patients to a hospital that has all
these necessary facilities, rather than delay definitive treatment. Treatment at the
site of an accident or other emergency, and also during transport, is equally
important. It is for this reason that ambulance authorities consider that the double
manning of emergency ambulances is so vital. In the case of North Shore, I have
approved the acceptance of tenders for phase II, North Shore Hospital, by the
Auckland Hospital Board. The board has been so advised.
(24/6/77)
Ngati-Whatua Claims
108. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Maori Affairs,
Will he confirm that there was no formal application to him to make the applica-
tion, required by section 60 of the Maori Affairs Amendment Act 1974, for the
Maori Land Court to consider the claims of the Ngati-Whatua during 1974 and
1975, and also confirm that a telegram was sent to him on 14 December last seeking
his approval for having these claims referred to the court, and would he now
indicate why this request was refused?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs) replied, I am unaware
whether any formal request in writing was made in 1974-75 to the honourable
member, as Minister of Maori Affairs, to make an application under the section.
concerned. There is no evidence of any such request in the files of the department.
I can confirm that the honourable member telegraphed me on 14 December last
suggesting such an application. The Government was not prepared to submit to
the Maori Land Court a proposal for the setting aside of the whole of the Crown
land at Orakei as a Maori reservation. My colleague the Minister of Lands and I
concur in that decision. In the first place, the Government recognised no legal or
formal claim by the Ngati-Whatua people in respect of the land and, while it has
through my colleague the Minister of Lands made certain offers to the recognised
elders of the people concerned, it is not prepared to go further than this. But in
any case the constitution of the land as a Maori reservation would be quite in-
appropriate, and, I imagine, unacceptable to the people concerned, because of the
severe restrictions on the use of land of this status-in particular its non-availability
for residential building.

## p. 1404 (#646) ###########################################

1404
20 July
Questions and Replies
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied, I have said before in answer to
a question by the honourable member that it will probably not be until the mid
1980s that my department will be ready to begin planning the next big under-
ground coal mine north of Huntly. The reasons for this are: (1) that experience
must first be gained in operating large mechanised mines in New Zealand condi-
tions; (2) a skilled work force must be built up; and (3) the technology must be
developed to recover the greater part of the coal in the thick deep seams which
exploratory drilling has shown exists in this area. Much of the coal north of Huntly
is privately owned and there is no reason why private mines should not be
developed, but in the interest of energy conservation I would want to be satisfied
that the mining methods used would recover the greater part of the coal.

Timaru Courthouse
121. Hon. SIR BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Justice, Will

agreement is reached with the Timaru City Council?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied, The Timaru court-
house was first included in the 1975-76 works programme, with construction to
start in 1977-78. Because of the setting up of the Royal Commission on the Courts,
the project was deferred along with other major projects, but it has been brought
back into the 1977-78 5-year programme with a proposed construction start in the

any event, the overriding question is one of priorities and of allocating limited
resources among many competing and persuasive claimants. There are places that
are much less well off than Timaru in the matter of court accommodation.

Commonwealth Fund for Technical Development
122. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Prime Minister, In view of
his expressed concern, repeatedly made at the Commonwealth Conference of
Prime Ministers, about the need to assist the poorer developing countries, why
has the New Zealand Government not increased its contribution to the Common-
wealth Fund for Technical Development as have other Commonwealth nations
such as Sri Lanka (100 percent), Australia (25 percent), and Canada (50
percent)?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister) replied, New Zealand's
capacity to help the developing countries depends on the well-being of our own
economy. In a time of economic difficulties, such as we now face, it has not been
possible to increase the overall level of development assistance. Inevitably, there-
fore, decisions on priorities to be accorded to particular items within the aid vote
are more difficult to take than in a time of expansion. The level of New Zealand's
contribution to the Commonwealth Fund for Technical Co-operation for 1977-78
has not been finally determined. In making this decision the Government undoubt-
edly will have regard to the acknowledged effectiveness of this organisation and
the increased levels of contributions from other Commonwealth countries announced
in London.

from the International Labour Organisation?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied, The United States Govern-

before November this year) whether or not it would remain a member of the

colleague the Minister of Foreign Affairs, I will be considering what steps New
Zealand might take when we have had an opportunity to study the reports of the
New Zealand delegation to the conference.

Progressive Youth Movement-Leaflets
131. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Education, Has he seen the
leaflet handed out to Mt. Albert Grammar School pupils by the Progressive
Youth Movement, which openly encourages rebellion in schools and aims to
discredit teachers and our New Zealand society; and, if so, can he advise what
specific parts of the curriculum in secondary schools are designed to give students
sufficient understanding of the truth to enable them to reject such propaganda?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, I have seen the leaflet
handed out to Mt. Albert Grammar School pupils by the Progressive Youth
Movement. The secondary school curriculum gives students many opportunities
to examine objective and subjective writing and statements to enable them to
recognise bias and propaganda, and to distinguish these from rational, tenable
statements. These opportunities are provided in English and social studies in forms
III and IV, and continue through subjects such as English, history, and economics
in form V. In form VI, with the growth of school-based sixth-form certificate
courses, there is increasing scope for liberal, general, and political studies in which
controversial subjects and propaganda, and their effects, can be analysed. Schools
themselves organise liberal studies programmes for students in form VII, who may
also opt into subjects in the formal curriculum, like English and history, where
propaganda is examined through historical and literary materials.

New Poor
134. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Social Welfare, Has
he seen the report in the Evening Post of 9 June 1977 of an address by the
national president of Birthright, Mr P. T. Gifford, in which the situation of the
"new poor" in this country is likened to a ticking bomb, and, if so, can he indicate
what steps he is taking to alleviate the situation Mr Gifford describes?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied, Yes, I have seen
the article referred to by the honourable member. The origin of and the reasons
for the creation of the "new poor" as referred to by the questioner are clearly
set out in Hansard, Volume 398, at page 2232, dated 18 June 1975, when the
member for Papanui showed the relationship between their creation and the
financial policies of the Labour Government. Steps currently being taken by the
National Government to alleviate their position include: a significant amount of
tax relief for low income families with pre-school children; significantly reduced
the rate of inflation from 4.4 percent in the first quarter of 1976 to 2.6 percent in
the first quarter of 1977; reduced unemployed numbers from 5600 in December
1975 to 4500 in May 1977. National turned a trading deficit of $338 million
as at 30 April 1976 into a trading surplus of $104 million as at 30 April 1977;
it reduced the increase in net Government expenditure from an average of 26
percent per annum under the Labour Government to only 2.7 percent under the
National Government, and because of the reduced number of immigrants permit-
ted to enter New Zealand, the waiting list for State houses has been reduced
by 17 percent since National came into office. These and many others are typical
of the actions being taken by the National Government to overcome the problems
inherited from the previous Government by the "new poor".

137. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Education, Can he state
when work will be commenced on the proposed secondary school which is to be

expected to be opened?

by the Eastern Beach action group. Objections under the Town and Country
Planning Act concerning the use of the land for a secondary school must be

National Superannuitants Supplementary Benefits
138. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Social
Welfare, How many age beneficiaries, following transfer to national superannua-
tion, have had additional benefits reduced in accordance with Government policy
to phase out additional benefits, and what is the total value per week and per
annum of such reductions to date?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied, A total of 47 808
former age beneficiaries had their grants of additional benefit reduced from 9
February 1977 following their transfer to national superannuation. These grants
were reduced by a uniform amount of 50c a week, and will be phased out over a
period of 5 to 6 years. The amount of the initial deduction from additional benefit
grants was decided bearing in mind the increases in cash-in-hand payments that
superannuitants received under the new scheme while ensuring that even after
the deductions, national superannuitants would be significantly better off than if
age benefits had been retained. When national superannuation reaches 80 percent
of the average ordinary-time weekly wage it is considered the relationship between
wage earners and superannuitants will be such that an additional benefit will no
longer be justifiable.

Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied on behalf of the Min-
ister of Forests. Kahikatea in pure stands is relatively scarce, but it is often a

well represented, will be considered at a seminar being held in Hokitika this week.
The member will undoubtedly be aware that remnant stands of kahikatea can
still be found on the Hauraki Plains and in the Waikato, where it was the dom-
inant forest type on some of this country before the land was cleared for
farming.

Praziquantel
163. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) asked the Minister of Agriculture, Can he
confirm that extensive research on the drug praziquantel has been undertaken in
New Zealand, and, if so, what were the findings of this research? In view of the
very long reply given to my earlier question, could the Minister confirm that the
experimentation was carried out at the research station at Invermay?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied, The research was
carried out at the hydatids research unit at Taieri, which I assume is the same
as Invermay. As already indicated, the drug praziquantel has been the subject
of extensive research both overseas and within New Zealand. This drug has been
found to be highly effective against all species of tapeworm, which are found in
dogs in New Zealand. No evidence of toxicity or any undesirable side effects
attributable to treatment with this drug has become evident in any of the 4000
dogs included in the three field trial groups set up. These groups have been sub-
jected to 6-weekly treatment for at least 12 months. To give the member the
full facts, the only reported case of any side effects concerned a 14-year-old dog,
which was back to normal next morning. It seems more likely that the symptoms
shown by this dog were caused by a heart turn, and were not due directly to
Droncit.

Coal Miners-No-replacement Policy
166. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), on behalf of Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone),
asked the Minister of Mines, How does he justify his department operating a no-
replacement policy for underground coal miners in certain mining districts at a
time when the department is either rationing or refusing to accept new customers?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied, The only places where the Mines
Department operates a no-replacement policy for underground coal miners are in
Greymouth and the Buller. The Liverpool mine at Greymouth exists only to
supply coal to South Island gasworks, and it will have to close when these plants
go off coal and on to other feedstocks for gas making. In anticipation of this,
the Mines Department operates a no-replacement rule at both the Liverpool and
Strongman mines in the hope that, when Liverpool has to close, it will still be
possible to employ all the remaining miners at Strongman. The department is not
taking any new orders for Strongman industrial coal, but ample supplies of an
alternative coal are available from the Island Block mine at Reefton. There is no
shortage of coal from the Buller.

Minister of Agriculture, Can he advise the quantities and values of hare meat
exported from New Zealand each year since 1970, and can he further advise any
restrictions applicable to such exports?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied, According to the
statistics of external trade issued by the Department of Statistics, and based on
customs returns, the following are the exports of hare meat by volume and f.o.b.
value: 1970-71, 25.5 tonnes, $11,200; 1971-72, 10 tonnes, $6,100; 1972-73, 35.9
tonnes, $17,000; 1973-74, 23.2 tonnes, $21,400; 1974-75, 2.6 tonnes, $3,200; and
1975-76, 10.2 tonnes, $13,900. The figures for 1972-73 to 1975-76 are provisional.
Hares are "game" within the provisions of the Game Regulations 1975, and there
are no special restrictions placed on their export compared with other "game"
animals. Hares may be exported provided they are procured, inspected, and pro-
cessed in compliance with regulatory requirements. The export of uneviscerated
hares, which was permitted until the promulgation of the current regulations, is
now precluded by the requirement that all carcasses and their accompanying
viscera are inspected to comply with overseas veterinary requirements for game
exports.

School Buildings Comparative Cost of Steel and Structurally Engineered Timber
173. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Education, Can he advise
the cost of structural steel in an S68 school; the cost of the same work carried
out in structurally engineered timber; and the reason imported steel is used in
preference to locally grown and manufactured structurally engineered timber?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, This question was
referred to the Ministry of Works and Development, which designed the S68
school and was responsible for the selection of materials. I quote the answer sup-
plied by the ministry. "(1) The approximate cost of structural steel in an S68
school was $34,000 in January 1976, which is the date of the most recent S68
contract. (2) The comparative cost of structural timber at that time was estimated
to be about 1 to 2 percent dearer than structural steel. The relative cost of the
two materials fluctuates considerably. (3) The light steel construction used in
Mk II and Mk III versions of S68 design are made from New Zealand steel rolled
in New Zealand. The imported content is restricted to alloys incorporated into
the finished product, and this amounts to approximately 4 percent of the pro-
duction cost. (4) Laminated timber members use imported glue which constitutes
approximately 5 percent of the cost of the manufacture of the timber members,
and there is no significant cost difference between the imported content of the
laminated timber members used in Mk I S68 design and the light steel members
used in Mk II and Mk III S68 design."

Steel-Substitution by Structurally Engineered Timber
185. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry, Can
he advise (1) the value of items imported under tariff codes 73.11.039, 73.11.031,
73.11.021, and 73.11.139 covering steel girders, channels, and joists; (2) the build-
ing value of that material when fabricated; and (3) what steps his department is
taking to encourage the substitution of steel by locally grown and locally manu-
factured structurally engineered timber?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied,
The total value of channels, girders, beams, and joists imported under the four
tariff items was 1974-75, $13,471,760; 1975-76, $6,979,081; and 1976-77, for the
9 months to March 1977; $9,131,661. No statistics give the building value of these
materials when fabricated. As a general policy, my department encourages the
use of New Zealand's indigenous resources. However, no steps are being taken to
promote the substitution of steel by structurally engineered timber of New Zealand
origin, although from time to time the Department of Trade and Industry has
advised the professional people concerned to consider the use of alternative domestic
materials where available. Other materials used in construction also have a high
New Zealand content, for example, pre-cast reinforced concrete beams. The choice
of materials to be used is subject to the expert advice of architects and engineers
about the type of structure required, and other factors.

Livestock Incentive Scheme
186. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister in
Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation, Is it true that over 95
percent of farmers have not taken advantage of the livestock incentive scheme?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation) replied, A devious question may receive a devious answer. Over 95


## p. 1425 (#667) ###########################################

20 July
1425
Questions and Replies
percent can be read as 4 percent or less, and since more than 3000 have applied
that could represent 75 000 farmers. However, if the figure was 3 percent that
could represent 100 000 farmers. In the question the term "farmer" is not defined,
so I shall try to answer the question with that background. The scheme applies
only to farms carrying sheep, beef, or dairy cattle, and to commercial deer
farms. It also includes farmers engaged in mixed cropping and livestock enter-
prises-all other types of farming such as horticulture, poultry, pigs, etc., being
excluded from the scheme. A further requirement is that to be eligible for assis-
tance dairy farmers must increase their stocking to a minimum of 500 stock units,
and other farmers to 1000 stock units, carried at the completion of a programme.
Having regard to these factors, and as the scheme commenced in late October
1976 and the closing date for applications is 31 March 1979, the more than 3000
applications to date represent a significant proportion of those eligible farmers
the scheme was designed to attract. It was estimated that 16 000 farmers would
be eligible, and so 19 percent have applied so far.

Farm Leasehold Lands-Rent Increases
196. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of
Lands, In view of the policy pledge "National will give priority to controlling
farm costs", is it Government policy to raise rents on Crown 33-year leasehold
lands by 600 percent or more when the rents come up for renewal?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied on behalf of the
Minister of Lands. The rental value of a leasehold property is the value of the
land in the lease, and excludes the value of improvements on the land. Rent is
charged upon the rental value. The present rental rate is 4.5 percent gross and
4 percent net. The rental rate has not been altered since 1970, when it was reduced
from 5.5 percent gross and 5 percent net. The same formula used by the Labour
Government is still in use. The reason rents on 33-year leases expiring now are
showing substantial increases is only a reflection of the increased land values
that have taken place since the mid-1940s, when the lease commenced or was last
renewed. The increase in rents would have been greater had the rental rate not
been reduced.

Milk Consumption by Children
198. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central), on behalf of Mr HUNT
(New Lynn), asked the Minister of Health, Has he seen the article in Town Milk,
May 1977, which points out that the purchase of milk in households where there
are children under the age of 15 years is down 13.2 percent and, if so, is he con-
cerned at this drop, and what measures does he propose to take to ensure adequate
nutritional standards for children?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied on behalf of the
Minister of Health. "I have seen the article in Town Milk, May 1977, referred to.
I am aware of the drop in the purchase of milk where there are children under
the age of 15, but it is considered that milk intake is more important during infancy
and the pre-school years. A dietary survey of the pre-school age group made in the
early 1970s by the Department of Health and the epidemiology department of the
Wellington Hospital, before the increased milk prices, showed an average daily
consumption of 500 ml of milk per day per pre-school child. A 13 percent decrease
would represent 65 ml a day, and the effect on the nutrition of a child would be
negligible."

(6/7/77)
National Superannuation-Amount Paid
213. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Social Welfare, Has he seen
the banner headline in the Evening Post dated 24 June 1977 which states "Benefits
cut by $1 million since super", and, if so, will he state how many beneficiaries
receive a lesser amount of cash in the hand since the introduction of national
superannuation, and also what increases, if any, have been granted to superannui-
tants since the National Party took office in December 1975?


## p. 1433 (#675) ###########################################

20 July
1433
Questions and Replies
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied, Yes, I have seen the
banner headline referred to. It is grossly misleading. Far from receiving a “cut” in
benefits, all beneficiaries have received substantial net "cash in hand" increases
since the introduction of national superannuation. As the benefit soars towards its
maximum of 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage, making bene-
ficiaries financially independent in their retirement, prop-up payments introduced
by the last Labour Government to subsidise minimal pensions are, in accordance
with National's election manifesto, being phased out. Between December 1975 when
National became the Government and 9 February 1977 when national superannua-
tion was introduced, the age benefit was increased from $30.75 to $36.22 a week
for single people, and from $51.26 to $60.36 a week for married couples, all tax-
free. With the introduction of national superannuation, further cash in hand in-
creases were given: $3.59, from $36.22 to $39.81 a week, for single people; $5.36,
from $60.36 to $65.72 a week, for married couples where an under-age wife was
included, and $7.26, from $60.36 to $67.62 a week, for married couples where both
parties were eligible. To summarise, $1.2 million of prop-up additional benefit has
been replaced by $126 million of increased cash in hand benefits. All superannua-
tion will be increased twice yearly in line with increases in the average ordinary-
time wage as assessed by the Department of Labour. The next increase will be
announced shortly. National superannuation will reach the maximum of 80 percent
of the average ordinary-time weekly wage in August 1978.

by environmental groups. I have recently received recommendations from the
Environmental Council suggesting procedures that could be followed to bring this
about, but in the present financial situation it will not be possible for any new

receive assistance and co-operation from Government departments. A recent

attended and presented papers. Environmental groups can also make application
through the sport and recreation programme for financial assistance. However,
this avenue is, of course, concerned with the recreational aspects of their activities.
Last year the Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society received assistance totalling
$13,240 through the national projects scheme of the programme. No other solely
environmental group applied for assistance under the national scheme last year.

Christchurch Flood Damage
226. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) asked the Minister of
Works and Development, as an urgent question, In view of the widespread damage
caused by slips and floods over the weekend to homes and property in Lyttelton,
harbour bays, the hillside suburbs of Christchurch, and the homes alongside the
Heathcote and Avon rivers, would he now tell the House of the specific measures
he is taking to meet the crisis facing the residents?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied, The situa-
tion in regard to the most recent flooding and erosion in Lyttelton Borough is that
the local authority must take action to assist landowners who have suffered from
erosion or flooding. The North Canterbury Catchment Board is the statutory
authority set up under the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Act to provide
technical and financial assistance for those erosion and flood control works that
are eligible under the Act. All applications for assistance must be channelled
through the North Canterbury Catchment Board in the first instance. Lyttelton
Borough and Akaroa County are not included in the North Canterbury Catch-
ment Board's area for soil conservation and water management works. However,
I have attempted to obtain their acceptance of the full services of the catchment
board. Up until now these efforts have been unsuccessful, but I am hopeful that
agreement will be reached. The full statutory powers and administrative expertise
of the North Canterbury Catchment Board are in effect in the Christchurch area
for all soil conservation and water management matters, and the present situation
will be dealt with by the board when requests are received either from individual
ratepayers or the local territorial authority on their behalf.

done independently, and great credit must go to Mr Pryde for the thorough manner in which
he conducted it. It anticipates that this year there will be slightly more cows in milk than
there were last year, and slightly more cows to calve in the coming spring. This will give a
greater increase in dairy production and indicates the farmers' continuing confidence in the


## p. 1438 (#680) ###########################################

20 July

Government's efforts.
The sheep breeding figures show there has been a slight increase in the number of
breeding ewes. It is not spectacular, it is true, but there has been a steady slight increase.
There has also been an increase in the number of ewes about to lamb. This has all been
brought about by primary producers' confidence in the Government. Indeed, this quiet
confidence has come through from the meeting being held along the street yesterday, today,
and tomorrow. The Government has done a lot to encourage and and foster increased
production. Last year we announced a dairy beef market guarantee scheme that was so
successful that 160 000 fewer bobby calves were killed than in the previous season. The
farmers have asked the Government to implement the scheme for the coming year, and the
Government has agreed to do so. A livestock incentive scheme was introduced. At 21 June
last, 3320 farmers had applied for either a grant or a taxation option. This amounts to about
2 600 000 qualifying livestock units at an overall net cost of about $34.6 million—quite a
substantial incentive.
A stabilisation scheme for meat and wool returns, incorporating minimum and trigger
prices, has been introduced. This should provide greater stability of farm incomes in the
future. We introduced the farm equalisation account whereby farmers are encouraged to
even out fluctuations in their incomes. Interest will be paid on all money deposited in those
accounts. What a contrast these figures are to the position during the 3 years of the Labour
Government when there was a decline in stock numbers and a lessening of the effect of the
primary sector on the overall income of the nation. We have seen the increase in production,

projected deficit. It has already been reduced from $1,400 million to $506 million. Increased
production will go a long way towards ensuring that the country returns to the position where
primary producers receive a just reward for their efforts. The Government is doing all it can
to foster confidence.

responded to incentives and to the encouragement given to them. It is proof positive that the
assistance handed out to farmers in a mealy-mouthed fashion during the term of the previous
Government was not sufficient to provide a climate for the expanding production we have at
present and the continuing expansion we will see as the year goes on. I predict that in the
coming year we will see an overall increase in production of at least 2.5 to 3 percent, or
something like that.

Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West): I intend to speak to question 46, about geothermal
drilling, but before doing so I refer to the comments about transport made by the member
for Southern Maori. The member assumes that the Minister of Transport should have a
magic wand, at a wave of which he should be able to redress all the neglect and wrongs
perpetrated in the transport sector over many years. It was not mentioned that the railway
