## p. 1441 (#683) ###########################################

20 July
1441
Discussion of Questions-Adjournment
never been more run-down in its history. The Minister also inherited the 3 years of Labour's
indecision about ports, its production of green papers, and a threat of even greater
bureaucratisation of the whole transport industry than the country had ever faced.
Having said that, I turn to question 46, dealing with the geothermal drilling programme.
Geothermal energy is of primary importance to New Zealand, and it is very evident that it
has a considerable potential impact upon the Taupo area, which is significant from my point
of view because the Waikato River, which flows through my electorate and my city, stems
from Lake Taupo. The full potential of this resource has yet to be ascertained, and New
Zealanders should not be carried away by remarks attributed to Dr Teller, who was recently
in New Zealand, that we have a huge geothermal resource. It is right and proper that an
extensive drilling programme should be mounted and sustained. It is pleasing to note that
$1.8 million for drilling programmes in this area was approved for the 1976-77 financial year,
and that a further $2.5 million is likely to be appropriated for the 3-year period 1977-80. A
considerable resource may exist, and, if it does, it has very important implications, not only
for the Taupo area, but for all New Zealand.
I stress that the quality and quantity of the steam have yet to be fully ascertained. Such a
resource, of course, needs to be wisely used, and a high usage efficiency developed.
Unfortunately, as high wastage is associated with the use of geothermal steam for electricity
generation, its full utilisation will depend on the location of industries capable of using this
fuel close to source. Whether geothermal energy is a continuing resource has yet to be
ascertained. The bores may not deliver steam for ever because of either water or heat
depletion, and until this is known no one, not even Dr Teller, can be sure of the full extent
and likely duration of geothermal steam resources. A reasonably cautious approach based
on very astute conservation measures is needed. Another factor is the corrosive nature of
geothermal steam, and the difficulties attaching to its distribution.
It is most unlikely that in geothermal energy we will have an assured, continuing, low-
cost, large-scale source of energy for the future. People who may have got that idea from Dr
Teller's remarks would be wise to re-examine them. In addition, there are conservation
problems resulting from masses of boiling water, which is part of the wastage problem.
Unless it is reinjected in some way, the boiling water will find its way into rivers and cause
further pollution problems.
It seems then that we have a valuable resource, the exploitation of which needs to be
very carefully planned. We still have some way to go before we can be confident of the
extent and quality of that resource. This emphasises the continuing need for an approach to
the energy problem, based firmly on the principle of conservation and wise use of the limited
indigenous resources the country is known to possess. Waikato people will be very interested
indeed in the results of the drilling programme that I have referred to. They will be
concerned at the possible environmental implications of it. I sound the final caution that care
is needed.

decision. In many cases his income was only just above the level of the pension, and he did
not really know whether to retire or to remain in employment. In fact, under the Labour
Government the pension was an incentive to retire. It would have been of no advantage
whatever for many people to stay in the work force. Therefore, I repeat that the Leader of

between 60 and 65—or anyone up to 100 years of age for that matter-the incentive to
remain at work and to enjoy their wages plus their superannuation and continue to
contribute to the economy. Many people in this age group are staying on in the work force. If
they choose to retire, that, too, is their choice, and a generous superannuation scheme is
available to them.
This Government sees that senior citizens are treated fairly and equitably. Those
receiving a good wage, plus superannuation, will pay a fairly hefty amount of tax because of

up to humiliating means tests, and no longer are hardworking, frugal, and conscientious
New Zealanders punished for their efforts throughout life. That was the cry heard during the
1975 election campaign.

Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): I move, That this House calls upon the Government
to throw out its outmoded ideas which are crippling the building industry and depriving
homeseekers of a home and notes with alarm the comments as appearing in the news media
where claims are made that the industry was in a panic situation and directs the Government to
return to a policy as was operated in 1975 which provided a record number of homes that year.
Everybody in the building industry has been warning the Minister for months of the
impending collapse of the industry, but the Minister has carried on with both eyes shut, and
the only way to make him and his colleagues understand appears to be to ram it between
their eyes this afternoon. Apparently the Minister feels that builders are simply "crying
wolf" despite the fact that mortgagee sales are running at about three a day, record numbers
of bankruptcies are occurring, property values are falling and building costs are rising, and
skilled tradesmen are leaving New Zealand in droves. During the last 18 months the country
has suffered from the most ignorant and misguided policies ever seen. The Government has
apparently achieved its ambition-an achievement that will stand as a mark of its administra-
tion for years to come.
The building industry is teetering on the brink of collapse, and skilled workmen are
leaving the country after being laid off because forward orders are not coming in. Many
hardworking families face the prospect of being thrown out on to the streets and losing the
equity they have built up in their homes because they cannot get finance. Those people
believed National Party promises that finance would be available and that the private sector
would be able to operate in the mortgage market, so they put their faith in short-term
mortgages. Repossessions have been running at the rate of more than one a day in the major
centres, and a major building society has recently pulled out of the finance market, so many
more young couples are placed in danger.
I return now to the first point I made; that the building industry is teetering on the brink
of collapse. I offer some facts to support that statement. For the first 2 months of this year
commencements are down by 1200 units, or 600 units per month, or 7200 a year. Comple-
tions for the first 2 months of this year are down 1000 units, or half the maximum decline
predicted by the Minister. Permits are down by 1500 units for the first 3 months of this year,
which represents 6000 a year. This year's completions and starts will total about 22 000 units,
unless something dramatic is done in the next few days. The second point I raised was the
number of skilled workmen being exported. Look at some of the facts: for the year ended 31
March 1977, 290 bricklayers, plasterers, and construction workers arrived, and 662
departed a net loss of 382; 430 carpenters, joiners, and cabinetmakers arrived, and 1096
departed a net loss of 666; 442 electricians and related workers arrived, and 850

Fishing Industry
Miss DEWE (Lyttelton): I move, That this House note that the value of fish exports from
New Zealand increased from $26 million in 1975 to $38 million in 1976, and that in the first 3

Government for its far-sightedness in moving to protect New Zealand's fisheries in the long

control and use of a 200-mile economic management zone.
I felt that the remarkable upsurge in the fishing industry required some commendation


## p. 1452 (#694) ###########################################

1452

from the House of the industry, the men involved in the industry, and also of the
Government itself, because of its role in this. The Government's actions in this field, and its
support of and its constructive approach to the fishing industry, have, I am quite convinced,
been a direct spur to the results we now see in fishing exports. To look at some of the figures,
in the 3 months to March 1976 4.6 million kg of fish were exported, from which receipts were
$8.6 million. In the 3 months to March 1977 we exported 6.7 million kg of fish, from which
total receipts were $14 million, an increase of 2 million kg and $6 million in income. It was a

Most remarkable of all, though, were the exports of fresh fish, which were up by 52

remark how the Government's actions to extend the increased export taxation incentives
have affected the export of wet fish, because I recollect that in 1973, in the term of the last
Labour Government, fresh fish exports were removed from the export incentive scheme.
They were reinstated in April 1976, and we have seen this remarkable upsurge in the exports
of wet fresh fish since this category was reinstated in the schedule. The Labour Government
failed dismally to recognise the potential of this sector of the fishing industry. The returns for
rock lobster hearten me greatly. In the 3 months under review, exports were up in weight by
25 percent, and up in value by 73 percent, an increase of $3 million; and our earnings from
the export of rock lobsters for those 3 months of 1977 now total nearly $7.1 million.
The Government has not only seen the importance of the fishing industry but has done
something constructive to help it, by appointing a Minister of Fisheries. This appointment
emphasises the importance the Government places on this industry, its future, and its
growth. Two important Bills have been introduced, designed specifically to protect and to
encourage the fishing industry. One was the Fisheries Amendment Bill, and the other is
commonly known as the 200-mile economic zone Bill. The Fisheries Amendment Bill was
designed to control the popular and valuable species found in our in-shore waters. I recollect
that in the Chatham Islands many years ago there was a considerable rape of the rock lobster
fishing industry. Had legislation of this nature existed at that time, the rape and the downfall
of the rock lobster industry in the Chatham Islands would not have occurred. It is very
important to my electorate. The fish covered by this amendment are scallops, rock lobsters,
paua, eels, mussels, and oysters; some of those species are now in danger of overexploita-
tion. The move by the Government was timely and worthy, and has the support of the fishing
industry. A Government cannot force an industry to expand, but it can lay the foundations
on which the industry can grow. The Fisheries Amendment Bill and the Territorial Sea and
Exclusive Economic Zone Bill are the cornerstones on which this foundation is to be laid,
and the growth that will come from these Bills when they become law is assured. The
industry knows that the Government will support, in every way possible, the growth and
advancement of this industry.

INSURANCE LAW REFORM BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a third
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): The Labour Opposition generally supported the
Insurance Law Reform Bill in the Committee stage, but made it clear to the
Government-and, in fact, we divided the House-
Hon. T. F. Gill: You didn't make it clear at all.
Mr PREBBLE: We tried to make the Minister of Health understand that what he and
the Government were doing in clause 12 was wrong. We still believe that what is proposed in
that clause is wrong. When an insured brings a case against an insurance company in the
Supreme Court, he should be able to have the case heard before a jury. Clause 12 takes away
the right to a jury trial if such a case is heard in the Supreme Court. The Opposition believes
that that is wrong. For 800 years, we have had the right to a jury trial; that system of justice
has worked very well. The British system of justice has been the envy of the world. The best
of that system is that a case can be brought in the Supreme Court and 12 ordinary people, the
same as the insured, can hear the facts of the case; those 12 people decide who is telling the
truth and what the justice of the matter is. That system is accepted by the people of New
Zealand, and should not be lightly tampered with, but it will be taken away by this Bill. A
right of the citizen is being removed by the Bill, and we strongly oppose what is being done.
No arguments of any merit have been raised in favour of making this fundamental
alteration to our system of justice. Government members referred to the fact that the Bill
resulted from the report of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee. No one
on this side of the House disputes that. In the main, it is a good report; the people who made
it are worthy and well qualified academics and practising lawyers. The writers of that report
made it quite clear that the reason for taking away jury trials was that the insurance
companies felt that juries were biased against them. I think that is wrong. I do not know of
any evidence to suggest that New Zealand juries are biased. That statement is a reflection on
the fairmindedness of the ordinary New Zealander. In my experience of jury trials, New
Zealanders take juries extremely seriously, and approach the matter in an impartial and
unbiased fashion.
By removing the right to a jury trial, this Parliament is attacking the whole system of
jury trials; it is suggesting that juries are not fair and are incapable of dealing with these
questions properly. No survey has been done in New Zealand of just how well juries do carry
out their tasks, but a survey has been done overseas. The best evidence I can find is the
book, The American Jury, which made a study of 3500 jury cases in America. I believe the
conclusions of that study are worth bringing to the attention of the House yet again. The
authors of that report—which was funded by the Ford Foundation-said: “Contrary to the
often voiced suspicion, the jury does, by and large, understand the facts, gets the case
straight, and its decision, by and large, moves with the weight and direction of the
evidence." It concluded that the jury emerges as an institution that any democratic society
should be slow to tamper with or abolish.
I do not believe that the fears and prejudices of insurance companies, unsubstantiated
by any concrete evidence, should be allowed to sway the House to take away the right to a
jury trial. There are two fundamental reasons for keeping jury trials. First, the cases that will
be heard will be questions of fact-whether an insurance salesman did or did not make a
promise to the insured, or whether the salesman did or did not tell him that filling out a form
in a certain way was satisfactory. That is a question of fact, and 12 men and women who are
used to dealing with such situations are just as competent as one judge, and, I suspect, are
even better at judging the truth of the matter. But it is important that ordinary citizens not
only get justice, but are seen to be getting justice and feel that they are getting justice.
Twelve ordinary people give a decision that the man in the street accepts. By taking that
away and by giving the responsibility for the decision to a judge alone, we are instituting a
system of justice in which, although people may get justice from the judge, they will not
accept the decision as they would from a jury. For that reason, the Government is making a
grave mistake and is undermining the jury system.

Insurance Law Reform Bill
It has been argued that, because compulsory arbitration clauses have been removed
from insurance contracts, the right to jury trials should also be removed. The right to jury
trials has existed for a long time. It is the insurance companies that are taking away that right
in their contracts, not the House, but we are striking out arbitration clauses because the law
reform committee considered them wrong, and we are instituting a system of justice in secret
because they considered the procedures too lengthy and too expensive. We should ensure
that people who want a jury trial always have a right to one. Some might not always want
such a trial, but if they do want it they should be able to have it. The select committee that
considered the Bill heard evidence from lawyers and insurance companies, but who
represented the consumer, the insured? Surely we, as members of Parliament, should
represent such people, and make sure that the rights of the citizen are not undermined. I
consider that to be one of our main tasks as members of Parliament.
In the Bill before us we are taking from the citizens a right they have had for 800 years.
It is a long established right; it should not be tampered with lightly and, certainly, not merely
because one or two insurance companies do not believe they can receive justice from 12
ordinary New Zealanders. If that incredible statement of the insurance company representa-
tives is true, it is probably a reflection of their past practices, but I do not believe it is true. I
regard the jury system in New Zealand as very valuable and fundamental to our system of
justice. It is a cornerstone of our democratic way of life and of the rule of law that is the basis
of our society. For that reason, members of the Parliamentary Labour Party drew their
opposition to the attention of the Government. We divided the Committee in an attempt to
persuade the Government to delete the provisions in clause 12, and we wish to record again
our fundamental opposition to that thoroughly bad clause.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The speech of the member for Auck-
land Central was an exercise in absurdity. It was so extravagant that it diminished the
credibility of the member, but did nothing else. I have no doubt that, on similar matters in
the future, his judgment will be held less valuable because of the speech he has just made.

an exercise in absurdity. The Bill we are now reading a third time is the consequence of a
report made by the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee on aspects of
insurance law; it was brought down to my predecessor, the member for Henderson, the
Labour Minister of Justice, 2 years ago. It has been studied carefully. No action was taken on
it by the former Labour Government, but we are determined to take action on reports from
learned committees.
In presenting their report, the members of the Contracts and Commercial Law reform
Committee confined themselves to five specific present problems in insurance law, and said
of them, "There is in our view a strong case for early corrective legislation." They also said:
"We have not overlooked our obligation to consider insurance law in a more general way
and we intend to issue further reports, but it seemed to us that action in respect of the
particular matters to which we refer should not be held up by the need for a wider study."
Well, that report has been studied for 2 years, and last December I introduced the Bill to
give effect to the remedies proposed for those five problems.
One of the suggested remedies is that attacked by the member for Auckland
Central-the remedy of taking away from insurers, mainly insurance companies, the right to
insist on arbitration for the determination of disputes and of putting in its place a
determination by a judge alone. That recommendation was made by the members of the
Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee- not by Government members or any
member of Parliament, but by those whom the member for Auckland Central himself
referred to as "the eminent lawyers who are the members of that committee". I agree that
they are eminent men, and I repeat that it was they who suggested that, instead of the
insurance companies, the insurers, having the right to insist on the determination of disputes
on insurance contracts by arbitration-which, they observed, was expensive, time consum-
ing, and not simple on many occasions-those should be determined by a judge alone. And
so the Bill provides.
As a member of the Statutes Revision Committee, the member for Auckland Central
knows very well that the New Zealand Law Society, which represents all members of the
legal profession in New Zealand, did not think of looking at the Bill, knowing the report and
knowing that there was nothing untoward in the Bill. Had there been any substance to the
points raised by the member for Auckland Central, I have not the slightest doubt that not
only would the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee not have recommended
it, but the New Zealand Law Society would have been quick indeed to rise up and advise the

Under a Conservative Government, private enterprise started broadcasting in New

share capital, which will lead to financial independence and greater security of operation.

Comment has been made also about paying the chairman. I should like to make the
point that the present three-channel system is putting a tremendous amount of pressure on
the chairman. This situation did not exist previously, because under the Labour set-up there
were three chairmeņ, plus a chairman on top, which equalled four chairmen. We now have
one full-time chairman doing an onerous, far more demanding job, and it is quite reasonable
and logical that he should be paid. I do not know where this expression “executive director"
has come from. The man is a chairman. The fact that he is a full-time chairman justifies a
reasonable remuneration, but that does not make him an executive director, and it has not
been said that he was an executive director. This is another figment of the Labour Party's
imagination.
To bring this debate back on to the rails, I should like to explain logically what the Bill
seeks to do, why it seeks to do it, why it seeks to do it right now, and what effects will flow on
as a result, because that is what the public wants to hear, and I believe it is what this
Chamber should be debating. First, to see what the Bill seeks to do we have to return at least
to 1973, because at that time the single Broadcasting Corporation was about to launch a
second channel, and about to launch into colour. These were two steps of great significance,
involving great technological and potential expense, but the corporation that existed in 1973
had a long history of paying its own way, and of developing at a pace that reflected the reality
of the New Zealand communication scene. It was geared up and planning to move into
colour and a second channel, based on the philosophy on which it had always operated,
bearing in mind that New Zealand, with mountain ranges and 3 000 000 people spread over
two long islands in small decentralised communities, is a very expensive country to cover
with television channels.
In 1973, the old corporation had developed a balanced programme of growth at a
reasonable pace and within its own resources. Then the member for Manukau, the previous
Minister of Broadcasting, came into the picture. He took a crazy psychedelic trip during his
Christmas holidays and came back to produce a technicolour extravaganza dream of a
broadcasting system that would go, go, go all the way. It all seemed so exciting and so
daring, and it was all so wonderful for the Labour Government in its day. However, in
November 1975 a bucket of cold water was thrown on the Labour Government, its dreams,
and its castles in the sky. When we all woke up as a result of that cold bucket of water in
1975, we found the psychedelic dream was a nightmare of uncontrollable structures and
costs.
For the large part, that exercise was tidied up in 1976 by the National Government's
Broadcasting Bill, which was extensively debated. In the words of old Scrim, the legislation
last year was fair, logical, sensible, and very much in the public interest. I will not traverse
the ground covered in that debate. However, part of the problem not tidied up was the
financial structure of the corporation. Money had been poured into a bottomless pit. There
was no central accounting facility, a lack of adequate budgeting systems, no profitable
financial guidelines, or adequate capital funding. This was the corporation dreamed up by a
reputed accountant.
Although in 1972-73 the old NZBC had operated on about $27 million, by 1975-76 the
system required about $60 million, not all of which was necessarily revenue. About $39


## p. 1467 (#709) ###########################################

20 July
1467
Broadcasting Amendment Bill
million advanced from the National Development Loans Account, some of which, as I
mentioned before, went not into capital expenditure and equipment as it was meant to do,
but into paying next week's wages. No account had been taken of how to repay that $40
million or the cost of interest, especially bearing in mind that on 1 April 1975 the Labour
Government had raised the interest rate on that loan to 10 percent, which placed an interest
burden of $4 million a year on top of all the other financial woes of the broadcasting
structure.
An Hon. Member: What was the interest rate?
Mr MALCOLM: It was 10 percent, which meant that, on top of everything else, the
broadcasting system had to cope with interest payments of $4 million.
An Hon. Member: And members opposite talk about low interest.
Mr MALCOLM: Yes. The Bill seeks to provide the final step to tidy up that mess. In
1976 the National Government provided interim relief by remitting the interest repayments.
The Bill provides for a $38,900,000 advance from the Crown, to be declared as the capital of
the Broadcasting Corporation. The Government seeks to do that now for several reasons,
one being that it was not possible to do so earlier. The corporation's finances were such that
no one knew the exact position. The remission of interest payments to which the Govern-
ment agreed in 1976 gave the breathing space for the board, under the direction of the late
Ron Jarden, to establish its position and to advise the Government. That breathing space
having been used, and that advice having been given, the Government is now acting at an
appropriate time to tidy up the matter.
Why is the Government declaring that advances from the Crown to the corporation will
be declared as Broadcasting Corporation capital? It is doing so because it does not believe
that a public broadcasting system should, through no fault of its own, be placed in the
position of being a permanent supplicant dependent on borrowed funds and constantly at the
whim of successive Governments for its continued existence-the situation in which it was
left by the Labour Government. It was a Micawber-like policy of borrow and hope, the
same as the Labour Government's general economic policy. It poured borrowed funds into
the broadcasting structure and hoped that somehow it would be able to repay the interest,
make capital materialise, and pay that back. Why is the National Government taking this
step now? Because the timing of the Bill is logical. The legislation could not be brought down
in 1976, because of lack of information. The Act is deemed to come into effect on 1 April
1977, a logical date, because it is the start of a full financial year and the first full year of the
restructured corporation.
I now want to deal with the effects that will flow from the legislation. First, the
corporation will be permanently relieved of $4 million a year in interest repayments.
Secondly, the provision of a capital structure will encourage sensible financial planning
within reasonable resource limits-I stress, within reasonable resource limits-because a
large highly technical organisation such as broadcasting cannot just expand and expand and
expect the funds to come off a little cherry tree; it must work within reasonable resource
limits. Thirdly, the legislation will remove the need for the corporation to face heavy debt
repayments over and above the $4 million a year interest repayments of which it is relieved.
The corporation will be encouraged to plan for its own future development and growth with
a large degree of independence, because the board and the organisation's professional
officers now know where they stand. In turn, that growth will result largely from the
corporation's own resources, as has previously happened under a National Administration,
which is what I and the Government believe the people of New Zealand want. The result of
the Bill will be the independence and pride and resourcefulness of the corporation, which
will effectively have a capital structure the same as any large independent company, and no
longer be dependent on handouts and borrowing.
The Labour Opposition sees the Bill as taking away the corporation's independence.
However, the reverse will happen; the Bill will give broadcasting the independence and
dignity it deserves. I recall that last year some journalists and professional people in
broadcasting feared their jobs would be under threat of political interference or some form
of insecurity. That has not materialised. However, if the Bill is not passed, and if their
employing body remains in debt to the tune of $40 million and has to carry interest
repayments, then their job security is threatened, because no bankrupt employer in New
Zealand can continue to pay its staff wages. The situation last year was critical at times,
because borrowed money meant to be spent on capital development was spent on paying the
wages of journalists and professional people. I wonder if they realise how crucially
precarious their position was while that financial situation was allowed to continue. To recap

Let us consider the Bill, which the member seems to fear and dislike so greatly. It
retains, and in fact ensures, the autonomy of the corporation. The Broadcasting Act 1976
once again amalgamated the corporations. During the passing of that legislation the
Opposition raged and ranted and made wild accusations of political interference, saying the
measure would bring about Government control, and the destruction of the broadcasting
system. We are now hearing it all again-political interference, financial control-simply
because we are trying to assist the Broadcasting Corporation out of a financial difficulty it
should never have been in in the first place.
It is in this financial difficulty because of the Labour Government's action in breaking
up a profitable trading corporation into four separate organisations and dividing among
them the equity reposed in the NZBC; but not a cent in cash was given to them, and not a
cent was available to them. The four organisations tried to struggle on-Radio New
Zealand, the Broadcasting Council, TV1 and TV2—that poor new babe that had been born
and left without any mothering to help it on its way. What happened? They got into financial
trouble and turned to the Government of the day, borrowing two lots of money totalling in
all $30 million. They borrowed that money from the Labour Government, and the interest
charged them by that Government was 10 percent, which, on any sort of calculation, came to
roughly $3 million. That amount was the first charge on the revenue of the new corporations,
which were still struggling to establish themselves and to make a profit and to earn a living.
They were competing against each other and splitting the advertising revenue, which in New
Zealand is limited. That must have had a very adverse effect on poor struggling TV2 as it
tried to establish itself, contending with TV1, which was already well established and had a
large following and nationwide coverage.
So, not being content with breaking up a profitable corporation into three corporations
and a council, and not being concerned to encourage sound, efficient, businesslike develop-
ment by providing adequate working capital, the Labour Government lent money at 10
percent. This so concerned the corporations that they were moved to comment in their 1976
report. I quote from Radio New Zealand's report: "Despite careful budgeting and manage-
ment and financial control in planning and introducing new styles of programming, escala-
tions in costs of this labour-intensive industry, coupled with a restricted commercial revenue
... have made it a very difficult year for the public radio system." The Broadcasting Council
reported: "During the 1975-76 financial year the Government advanced $16.9 million from
the National Development Loans Account to the council for capital purposes." That was
done, I might add, before the change of Government in 1975. "This advance, together with
the existing $14 million loan liability of 1 April 1975, brought the total loan liability of the
council to $30.9 million as at 31 March 1976. The current interest rate charged to the council
in respect of cash advances is 10 percent per annum. The total amount paid by the council in
1975-76 in respect of interest on loan liability was $1,802,753. Capital development of the
publicly owned broadcasting system is forecast to amount to about $44 million over the next
5 years and present indications are that most of this development will have to be financed
from Government sources."
What is the main purpose of this Bill? It is to relieve the corporation of that onerous
burden of interest, which now amounts to about $4 million per annum. And do not forget
that the debt was incurred to provide two television channels in colour long before colour
had been planned. No undercapitalised company embarking on a rapid expansion of
expensive capital equipment can survive without running into debt, and possibly it will end in
disaster. That is what would have happened to the BCNZ. The Bill virtually changes the loan

important to broadcasting as it is to every other sector. That is why, with this public service
system, this amendment relies on the authority of the Minister of Finance to approve the
financial programme. The Government with its financial voice must oversee that develop-
ment. This is reasonable in so far as any system can be too eager in its development and too
concerned about meeting needs, which have to be related to resources. The powers of the
Minister of Finance are contained not only in the 1976 Act as they are in this amendment,
but also in the 1973 Act.
Finally, I should like to conclude the debate by suggesting very strongly that broadcast-
ing is in good hands. We have a strong well balanced corporation. I believe that members on
both sides of the House can have confidence in all the men and women on the corporation,
who are aiming to ensure the independence of broadcasting, and that it will continue without
political interference. We have a group of dedicated and very capable directors-general
following in a great tradition, and I am grateful to them all. I hope the House is grateful for
their continuing efforts in maintaining the high standard of New Zealand broadcasting. I am
particularly grateful to have someone of the capacity of Ian Cross take on what I believe is
one of the most demanding jobs in this country, that of chairman. I hope that members who
know him will say the same, because I received a very wide-ranging number of letters
complimenting me on my choice. I do not believe I deserve these compliments, but believe
that he does for taking on the task. He is an excellent choice, and will demonstrate that in the
time he is there.
In view of the pyrotechnics we have had over this it is important for me to remind the
House why he was appointed full-time chairman. The appointment is to ensure better policy
making and better management of a much bigger and more complex system than that of a
few years ago. Sir Alister McIntosh, the then chairman of the Broadcasting Council
established in 1973, told me that he worked 3 days a week, and had far fewer responsibilities
than under the unified corporation. I know personally of the pressures that were placed on
the chairman, particularly on Ron Jarden while he was chairman. I know from Mr Freeman
when he was acting chairman. It was those pressures which led me to recommend to the
Government the appointment of a full-time chairman. I do not believe there is anyone of
greater skill and integrity than Ian Cross; these qualities are manifest in the man himself and
in all his work as a great New Zealander. I believe he is acceptable to broadcasters and to the
public. I am sure that all fair-minded members of this House will acknowledge that, and I am

HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION BILL
With the leave of the House, it was agreed that the speaking time of the Minister of
Justice be extended.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The human rights policy was the first of the major planks made public by the
National Party in 1975. That is an indication of how important it is to the National
Government that we should do all we can to preserve and enhance the rights and dignity, the
worth and the value, of the individual citizen of this country. Indeed, I hope I am not too
bold when I say that one of the attractions of New Zealanders in the world abroad is their
sense of the value of individuals around the world. They can walk and talk with a duke or a
dustman without distinction or discrimination; and this, I believe, has come to us from our
beginnings. It is certainly something that is greatly valued by all of us who have been
overseas and seen how welcome we are, for that reason as well as others.
The National Government wants to preserve and enhance the dignity of the individual
in New Zealand. The Human Rights Commission Bill as reported back is the culmination of
many hours of hard work by the special parliamentary committee, and, as Minister in charge
of the Bill, I should like to thank the member for Hawke's Bay for his chairmanship, and all
members for the bipartisan spirit in which the task was carried out. The Bill attracted an
unusually large number of submissions-127 in all- and no fewer than 55 of these were
supported by personal appearances. Notwithstanding this very close scrutiny the basic
structure of the Bill has emerged intact, and it is pleasing to note this endorsement of the
soundness of the Government's original proposals.
For some years now it has been apparent that legislation to prohibit discrimination on
the grounds of sex or marital status in the crucial field of employment and in other key areas
must inevitably be passed. On 11 November 1972 the National Government agreed to
incorporate this policy in its election manifesto. Unfortunately for the progress of this
endeavour the National Government was not returned to office, and we had to wait for 3
years in Opposition while the Labour Government did nothing more than set up a committee
to look at women's rights. Speedy progress towards equal opportunity is not just a necessary
corollary to the achievement of equal pay. It is fundamental to the aims and objects of the
women's movement, and as such was strongly endorsed in the report of the select committee
on women's rights. It was after the passage of the Equal Pay Act in 1972 that I asked my
colleagues to take the further step towards outlawing discrimination against women in job
opportunities. I introduced a Bill from the Opposition benches in 1973 and again in 1974,
and my colleague the Minister of Works and Development introduced a similar Bill in 1975.
The achievement of this Bill lies in grasping the opportunity provided by these social
pressures and using it as a means of opening up the prospect of better protection for human
rights in New Zealand on a broad basis-not the whole realm, but on a broad basis-and the
new title of the Bill better reflects that objective.
Part I of the Bill establishes the Human Rights Commission and sets out its functions
and powers. The changes made by the committee are largely of a clarifying nature, though
the commission is given a new duty to report from time to time on the progress being made
towards eliminating discriminatory provisions not caught by the Bill. In addition, the
reporting provisions are rationalised in a new section 5A. Because of the broad scope of the
legislation, reports are to be made to the Prime Minister as head of the Government of the
day, rather than to the Minister of Justice, and there is ample power for the commission to
publicise its reports.
Part II of the Bill sets out the areas where discrimination is prohibited on the grounds of
sex, marital status, or religious or ethical belief, and, where it is necessary to supplement and
strengthen the Race Relations Act, on the ground of race, colour, or national or ethnic

1475
Human Rights Commission Bill
origins. I believe that the Race Relations Act, which was passed in 1971, was probably the
first clear step towards the protection of individual rights, although some people would claim
that the passage of the Ombudsman's Act in 1962 was the first step.
Part II deals first with discrimination in matters relating to employment. The drafting of
clause 14 has been clarified, particularly as regards sex as a bona fide qualification and
preferential treatment accorded on the basis of a particular religious belief. It became clear
during the submissions that the clause as originally drafted did not confer a wide enough
exemption where a person of a particular belief might be legitimately required for a task such
as selling religious books. A subclause has been added to protect restrictions on employment
of persons on work involving national security, as is done in the Race Relations Act. A
further subclause provides that an employer does not commit a breach by declining to
provide employees of a particular sex or marital status with the same accommodation as is
provided for other employees if in all the circumstances it is not reasonably practicable to do
so. An example of this would be be where a nurses' home is maintained for female nurses
only.
Two new clauses have been added. Clause 14A creates an exemption for service on ships
and aircraft of the armed forces or service in an active combat role. Second, because of the
need to cope with situations involving violence or potential violence, it will not be a breach
of the Act to recruit greater numbers of men as police officers, prison officers, or traffic
officers. Clause 14B allows a 5-year phasing-in period for employers to upgrade sanitary and
other facilities to meet the requirements of a mixed-sex work force. It should be noted,
however, that the temporary exemption applies only where it is not reasonably practicable
for an employer to meet those requirements immediately. I know that women's organisa-
tions will have reservations about this provision, but after careful consideration the Govern-
ment is satisfied that it is a necessary transitional measure. The remaining changes to the
employment section of the Bill are basically of a drafting nature, apart from the deletion of
clause 20, which I shall comment on later.
It might be as well if I comment now on the observations I made during the reporting-
back stage about the absence of any provision in the Bill dealing with the outlawing of
discrimination of a political nature. When that was suggested by one of the witnesses it was
suggested that the Bill should provide for the outlawing of discrimination against persons of
a particular political party. I objected on the ground that, as a member of the National Party
and because of my own attitudes and sense of values, I would not belong to the same political
party as a fascist, a Nazi, or a communist. I suggested to the committee and to the members
of the New Zealand Labour Party that I understood that the rules of that party would not
allow a person to be a member of the party if he was a member of the Communist Party, or
indeed any other party.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Any other party.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I thank the member for Roskill for that confirmation. It was
very obvious to the members of the committee that it would not be possible to put a
provision in the Bill outlawing discrimination on the grounds of political belief. Yet oddly
enough, on the reporting back the member for Henderson and the member for Mangere
indicated their interest in the inclusion of such a provision.
I turn now to clauses 21 to 23, which deal with discrimination in access to public places,
the provisions of goods and services, and the disposal of land, housing, and accommodation.
These clauses have survived the committee's examination without major change. Subclause
(6) of clause 22 has been expanded so that insurance companies can make use of statistics
relating to accidents and sickness as well as to life expectancy, so long as it is reasonable to
rely on the particular data. This was done in response to representations that the original
subclause was too restrictive.
Subclause (7) of clause 22 has been amended to make it clear that promotion of, for
example, a women's bowling tournament will not constitute a breach of the Act. I might add
that the problem of sporting contests proved a hard nut to crack, and because of this a new
subclause (8) has been added to clause 22. This enables the Human Rights Commission to
make a special report to the Prime Minister if it considers in a particular case that the
exclusion of men or women from sporting contests is unreasonable. I might say—and I could
almost say this on behalf of all members of the committee-how delighted I am to see that
the racing fraternity of New Zealand has decided to take the step to allow women riders to
become jockeys. That will be warmly welcomed.
The fifth subclause of clause 23 was quite contentious. It referred to persons living in a
de facto marriage, and that has now been deleted to accord with the removal of the

definition of marital status from clause 2. Following the Canadian precedent, the definition
of marital status will now be a matter for the commission, and ultimately, of course, for the
courts, having regard to legal and social considerations. Before leaving clause 22 I should
perhaps advise members that a drafting amendment will need to be made in the Committee
stage to subclause (9), which refers to the Race Relations Act. Clause 25 has been rewritten
to clarify its object of combating surreptitious discrimination-that is, the imposition of a
condition or requirement that cannot be justified, but that nevertheless operates to the
detriment of persons of a particular sex, marital status, race, or religious belief. Clause 25A
replaces clause 20. It has been expanded to permit the commission to approve special
programmes for groups who need, or may reasonably be supposed to need, assistance in
order to achieve an equal place with other members of the community, not just in the
employment sphere, but in other matters as well. If we did not have this clause giving special
approval these programmes would amount to a breach of the Act; and they are sometimes
referred to, as they were in the discussion of the Race Relations Act in 1971, as positive
discrimination—that is, discrimination to the subject's advantage. Clauses 28 to 30 relate to
victimisation, to unlawful advertising, and to the liability of employers and principals. Clause
28 is strengthened and clause 29 is clarified. Clause 30 is tightened so that an employer does
not escape liability for discriminatory acts of his employees unless he shows that he took
reasonable steps to prevent his employees from indulging in discrimination. Without this
there might be a premium upon inadequate supervision.
Part III of the Bill deals with the commission's functions in respect of unlawful
discrimination. Clause 31, as amended, highlights the fact that the commission may
investigate a possible discriminatory act or practice notwithstanding the fact that it has
received no complaint; that is, it may act on its own initiative. The deletion of paragraph (c)
of clause 32(1) is an important change pressed upon us by those who feared that special
interest groups might otherwise be debarred from taking up the cause of disadvantaged
persons. It will not now matter that the actual complainant does not have a particular
interest so long as the aggrieved person is content for an investigation to be made. Where
conciliation fails and no settlement can be reached, the commission may take a case to the
Equal Opportunities Tribunal provided for in Part V. If for some reason the aggrieved
person wishes to take the case himself, he may do so by agreement with the commission. He
may also do so where the commission declines to take proceedings, or where it is of the view
that no breach of the Act has occurred.
Clauses 35 and 36 deal with the remedies that the tribunal may grant. Four new clauses
have been added. Clause 36A limits the jurisdiction of the tribunal to that of a magistrate's
court in respect of the remedies it may grant. The result is that the monetary limits in the
Magistrates Courts Act will apply. There was some feeling that the Bill as introduced
allowed the tribunal too free a hand in the matter of remedies. Accordingly, under the new
clause 36B the tribunal must refer the granting of a remedy to the Administrative Division of
the Supreme Court if the limits previously mentioned are exceeded. However, clause 36c
permits the plaintiff to reduce his claim to damages so as to bring it within the tribunal's
jurisdiction to make an award. Finally, the parties to a proceeding before the tribunal may
by written agreement allow the tribunal to grant a remedy regardless of the financial limits
imposed by clause 36A. I am satisfied that these new clauses strike the right balance between
flexibility and control.
Part IV provides the machinery clauses for the establishment and the functions of the
Equal Opportunities Tribunal. The tribunal is to consist of a chairman, who must be an
experienced lawyer, and two members appointed for the purpose of each case from a panel
of suitable names kept by the Minister of Justice. The purpose of this is to enable cases to be
heard before persons who have some expertise in the matters in dispute. The right of appeal
from a decision of the tribunal has been considerably extended. Any party will now have an
open right of appeal to the Supreme Court instead of an appeal on a point of law only. The
new clause 53 also envisages that questions of fact may be reopened and traversed again in
the Supreme Court. This means that there will be comprehensive supervision of the
tribunal's rulings by a superior court.
Part V, which was not supported by the Labour members, retains the commission's
watchdog role over privacy matters. The object of clause 58 is to assist the Government to
take such action as may from time to time be thought necessary to give better protection to
individual privacy. Subclause (2) has been limited in two ways. First, the commission is no
longer obliged to meet a request from the Prime Minister for a special report, and, secondly,
the content of such a report is restricted to comment about the need for talking legislative or
other action. It is also made clear in the new subclause (4) that the Wanganui Computer

Centre is not within the Human Rights Commission's jurisdiction. It is of interest to me,
because, as Minister of Justice, I inherited from the Labour Government two Bills on
privacy, one of which I can remember describing on its introduction as providing for a super
snooper. This Bill contains no such provision.
Part VI, which was also disputed by the Labour members, implements the Govern-
ment's commitment to provide a simpler and less formidable avenue than the Supreme
Court for redressing the grievances of those who feel that they may have been unfairly
treated by their union or professional or trade association. I can see no good reason why a
body charged with protecting people's rights in a number of areas should not be given a
function to conciliate in this particular area. It must be remembered that the commission has
no power to impose a solution on the parties. I say that again, because Labour members are
obviously interested in this: it must be remembered that the commission has no power to
impose a solution on the parties. If its good offices fail to produce a settlement it may, in its
discretion, refer the matter to the Industrial Court. Note that the word is "may", and not
"shall". I fail to see in any of this the heavy hand that some purport to detect. The flexibility
of Part VI is also enhanced by the amendment to subclause (2) of clause 60: if the
commission considers that the provisions of any enactment provide remedies for the
complainant, it may at any time direct that those remedies be pursued.
I do not wish to dwell on Parts VII and VIII as they deal very largely with machinery
matters, and were very little altered by the select committee. I should, however, say a word
about clause 80, which deals with superannuation schemes. This clause has been completely
rewritten. It emerged from the submissions that the previous clause had two basic shortcom-
ings: first, it did not allow the managers of superannuation schemes sufficient time to bring
their schemes into compliance with the Act; and, second, it conferred no right to equal
treatment upon those who were already in a scheme at the commencement of the Act, so
that discriminatory treatment could have been perpetuated for up to 40 years or more.
Furthermore, it was rather restrictive in not permitting data on life expectancy to be taken
into account when assessing contribution or benefit rates for members of each sex. The
broad effect of the new clause 80 is to remedy these deficiencies. In particular, nothing in the
Act will apply to superannuation schemes until 1 April 1980, which is the deadline for
approval of a scheme under the Superannuation Schemes Act 1976. Moreover, where a
scheme is amended to confer non-discriminatory treatment only on those persons who
joined after 1 April 1980, anyone who joined before that date has a 12-month period in
which to opt into the non-discriminatory provisions, with such adjustments as may be
equitable. In addition, the commission is given a watching brief to recommend any changes
that may prove to be necessary in section 80 as time goes on. I am confident that these
measures will greatly speed up progress towards full equality in superannuation matters.
The last important matter I wish to mention is the amendment made to the Race
Relations Act by the insertion in that Act of a new section 9A. This amendment is set out in
the first schedule to the Bill. Under section 25 of the Race Relations Act 1971 it is a criminal
offence to use or publish words that are threatening, abusive, or insulting, and that are likely
to excite hostility against groups of persons in New Zealand, or bring them into contempt or
ridicule, on the grounds of race or colour, with the proviso that no offence is committed
unless there is an intent to bring about such a result. The need for the requirement of intent
was very carefully considered by the Statutes Revision Committee in 1971. It has since been
suggested that intent should be removed so as to facilitate prosecutions. I do not agree with
that suggestion. Section 25 was carefully drafted to strike a reasonable balance between
obligations imposed by the International Convention on Racial Discrimination on the one
hand, and the need to protect freedom of speech on the other. I do not think that this
balance should be disturbed. What the new section 9A does, therefore, is to import the
milder processes of conciliation and the civil law to deal with cases where the language used
is not sufficiently flagrant to lend itself readily to a criminal prosecution. I believe this should
be a useful additional power for the Race Relations Conciliator when combating manifesta-
tions of racial prejudice.
The Bill honours the Government's election commitment to set up a Human Rights
Commission, and confer on it specified powers in the field of human rights. The Bill is a
logical addition to previous National Party initiatives resulting in the establishment, first, of
the Ombudsman's Office, and, later, of the Race Relations Office. Though clearly linked to
the aspirations of the women's movement and the recommendations of the select committee
on women's rights, the Bill casts its net wider, and is a clear demonstration of the
Government's continuing concern to achieve equal opportunity and fair play for all indi-

Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon): I do not intend to go through the Bill clause by clause, as
the Minister has already done so in explaining the Bill. However, I do wish to comment
generally, and to refer more specifically to one or two parts of the Bill in a few moments. In
1975 the National Party promised human rights legislation. However, this Bill goes only part
of the way. Many aspects are not covered, and many others are covered only in a very
general way. Specific clauses deal with unlawful discrimination and equal opportunities, but
much of the Bill is machinery in nature. To refer to the Bill as human rights legislation tends
to mislead people into thinking it deals with human rights. It does not. The legislation is
more antidiscriminatory, and, while it is welcomed on that basis, it should be made quite
clear that it does not deal with human rights as was expected.
As a member of the select committee hearing submissions on the Bill, it seemed to me
that the principle of individual rights proved too elusive, and Government members backed
away from the problems they had created with their own legislation. Submissions presented
to the committee expressed the belief that the proposed Bill gave too much emphasis to
discrimination on the issues of sex, jobs, marital status, and religious beliefs, and therefore
made no provision for organisations other than those interested in such issues to make
comments. The intellectually and physically handicapped, as well as those with reading or
other specific difficulties, are also entitled to their human rights, but the Bill does not give
them any recognition. In submission 42 the New Zealand Society for the Intellectually
Handicapped stated: "The society is arguing for the inclusion in the Bill of clauses protecting
the right of the mentally retarded person, not only to proper medical and physical care, but
also to such education, training, rehabilitation, and guidance as will enable him to develop
his ability to the fullest possible extent, on the ground that every citizen is entitled to the
opportunity to achieve the most complete physical, mental, and emotional development
possible, irrespective of age, race, sex, or religion."
Surely that is what human rights are all about. But instead of concentrating on the true
principle of individual human rights, the Bill interferes with established rights. For instance,
it interferes with the established rights of the trade unions; and that part of the Bill is
completely out of place in legislation such as this. It is almost as if the Bill is being used as a
vehicle for the erosion of the trade union movement, and as if the high-sounding name of the
Bill is a cover for its real purpose. Speaking as a member of the select committee which
considered the Bill, and as a member of the Labour caucus manpower committee which
examines industrial matters, I urge the Government to take note of the considerable public
concern surrounding clause 59, and indeed Part VI of the Bill. A very impressive array of
national organisations came out against that clause and that part of the Bill. I mention only a
very small number of the organisations in a very long list, which included the New Zealand
Insurance Workers Union, the Public Service Association, the National Youth Council, the
New Zealand Federation of Labour, the New Zealand Employers Federation, the National
Council of Women, and many others practising and specialising in industrial law. Because of
that very considerable opposition, the Government should delete Part VI and particularly
clause 59 of the Bill entirely.
The Minister of Justice has indicated that he is prepared to listen to criticism of the Bill.
On Checkpoint last night he justified the deletion of the marital status definition in clause 2,
because at the select committee "the evidence was very strong for removing the de facto
relationships from the protection of the Bill". In fact, only about three submissions wanted
such relationships unprotected. If the Minister is prepared to delete something after only
three submissions against it, then surely he must do something about Part VI and clause 59,
in view of the very considerable opposition against those provisions. Unfortunately, there
seems to be a difference between the Government's willingness to take notice of criticism in
the justice area and its inability to listen to constructive criticism on industrial relations.
Last year, when the now notorious Industrial Relations Amendment Act was passed,
the Labour Opposition tried to point out the error of that type of approach. Tragically, that
advice was not heeded, and as a result the country has suffered a period of unparalleled
industrial disruption. The same can be said of the recently passed shop trading hours
legislation. In the face of almost universal public opposition and considerable constructive
criticism, the Government forced that legislation through. The Opposition was proved
correct when it predicted disastrous results from the Industrial Relations Amendment Act,
and confidently expects to be proved correct in other areas affecting industrial harmony.

the individual, then surely it must cover all individuals and all groups of individuals. If any
one group is left open to discrimination or victimisation, then the Bill has not lived up to its
expectations. I regret that the Bill does nothing to ensure that basic human rights and
freedoms are promoted and maintained for the enjoyment of all. After all, New Zealand has
neither a constitution nor a Bill of Rights. Nowhere do we have set out a formal declaration
of the rights and freedoms guaranteed to all New Zealanders, apart from the presently
unenforceable provisions of the United Nations Declaration and Covenant on Human
Rights. Unfortunately, this Bill does nothing at all to rectify that rather sad situation.
Mr BRILL (Kapiti): It is a significant comment on the priorities of the previous speaker—
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.

Social Welfare Beneficiaries
Concession
1. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Has he seen the
Labour Party advertisement in the Wanganui Herald dated 21 May 1977 which states,
"Those who really need the pension have lost TV, travel, telephone rebates", and, if so, has
this claim any validity?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I have seen the advertisement
referred to, and the claim has no validity whatsoever. The only national superannuitants who
lost the telephone and television concessions from 9 February 1977 were those who were
formerly receiving a reduced age benefit because their private income was in excess of the
exemption of $884 a year. On transfer to national superannuation, which is paid regardless
of financial circumstances, these people received a greater increase in cash-in-hand
payments than those who were previously receiving a full age benefit. It is therefore quite
ridiculous to claim that these particular people represented those most in need of the
concessions. The travel concession is the responsibility of the Minister of Railways, but I
understand that this concession will not be withdrawn until the rate of national superannua-
tion is increased to 80 percent of the average ordinary-time wage from 31 August 1978.
Contrary to the statement made in the advertisement, no national superannuitant has
therefore lost the travel concession.
Mr Downie: Was that Labour Party advertisement the one that says "Labour cares"?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I have a copy of the advertisement, and it does say "Labour
cares". In my view Opposition members care little; otherwise they would not give misleading
information to aged people.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that all national superannuitants have lost the
NAC air travel concession, and has the Minister not admitted in the House that thousands of
national superannuitants have lost the telephone and television concessions?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I suggest that the honourable member direct his question about
NAC to the Minister of Civil Aviation, but I can say that those whose telephone and
television concessions have been taken away have in fact received a net increase in payments
of $7.7 million.
Mr McLay: Can the Minister confirm that the National Party's policy in 1975 was that
the benefits referred to in the question would continue under national superannuation at the
same rates and subject to the same tests, and be payable to the same classes of persons as
were entitled to receive them when National became the Government in December 1975;
and can he also confirm that that policy was implemented in the Social Security Amendment
Act passed last year?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, I can say that all the points raised by the honourable
member are correct and have been implemented by the Government.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Can I take it from the Minister's original reply that many people
have lost those concessions as a result of the implementation of national superannuation?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Anyone who has lost a concession is substantially better off in the
cash-in-hand he or she receives as a result of the introduction of national superannuation.
Mr Wellington: Can the Minister confirm that the statements of Opposition members on
concessionary benefits, made both inside and outside the House, have created an unneces-
sary and unjustified climate of unease among superannuitants, which has been proved
utterly groundless as a result of the vastly improved cash-in-hand position of the elderly
under national superannuation?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: If Labour Opposition members lived up to the claims they make
in a paid advertisement and did care they would not give misleading information to aged
people, which causes those elderly folk a great deal of concern. It is time Opposition
members showed some concern for the aged.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Can I take it from the Minister's replies to supplementary

Employment Information Survey—Average Weekly Wage
4. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) asked the Minister of Labour: In view of the Department
of Labour's half-yearly employment information survey, released on 6 July, would a person
receiving the average weekly wage, including overtime, be better or worse off in after-tax
terms than in October 1975, allowing for price increases as measured by the consumer price
index up to and including the June quarter 1977 record increase?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): After tax, overall wages and salaries, but
including overtime, adjusted for price inflation, were lower in April 1977 than in October
1975. However, the terms of trade depreciated sharply in 1974, declining from a level of 113
in the March quarter of 1974 to a level of 80 in the March quarter of 1977, the most recent
figure available. The real income of New Zealand as a whole has therefore suffered a sharp
fall due to the decline in purchasing power of the goods we produce for export and real
wages and salaries have been adjusted towards this decline.
Mrs Batchelor: Would the Minister then concede that, despite recent statements to the
contrary, it is taxation rather than wage increases which is causing the pressure on inflation?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The answer is definitely no. It would depend entirely on the
fluctuation in the amount of overtime and many other factors. I point out to the member that
just 6 days ago a headline in one of her city's papers stated that the worker is still better off
than he was 20 years ago, and the article listed many of the changes.
Mr Luxton: Would the number of part-time workers have an influence on the figures
the Minister has just given?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The answer is yes, and indeed in April 1977 there were more
part-time workers in surveyed employment than was the case in October 1975.
Mrs Batchelor: Would the Minister confirm that a married person working full time,
with two children under 5 years of age and with a non-earning spouse, after deducting tax,
adding on the family benefit, and adjusting that net amount for inflation, would find that his
net wage from October 1975 to April 1977 would have declined?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: With due respect I would need notice of that question. Otherwise
I would need to take the first number I thought of and try to find an answer. I am afraid I
cannot answer the question without notice, particularly in relation to the children.

Meat and Wool Properties-Estimated Capital Expenditure
5. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Agriculture: What estimated capital
expenditure for future growth has there been on meat and wool properties over the past 12
months compared with the 3 previous years on an annual basis?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): Official figures for aggregate capital
expenditure on farm holdings are available only up until March 1975. A frequently used
proxy for investment on sheep farms is expenditure per stock unit. Because this figure
comprises some expenditure which is capital in nature, it can be used as an indicator of the
overall investment on sheep farms. It is generally accepted that about $4.40 per stock unit in
real terms-1965-66 input prices-is required for maintenance on sheep and beef farms. Last
year, real expenditure per stock unit is estimated to have equalled $5.07, a 9 percent lift over
the $4.67 per stock unit recorded in 1975-76. This in turn was 12 percent greater than the
depressed level of $4.19 for 1974-75. Recent estimates of livestock numbers suggest that the
investment levels achieved over the last 3 years are about to be reflected in a renewed
upward movement in total livestock units.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Would the Minister verify the figures that appear in the report of the
agriculture review committee, which show that the highest capital expenditure in real
terms-that is real expenditure-occurred in the year 1973-74 when the Labour Government
was in office?

Consumer Price Index-Revision
6. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn), on behalf of Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui), asked the
Minister of Statistics: In view of the recent large but unequal rises in the various subgroups of
the consumer price index and the resulting changes in the consumer expenditure pattern on
which the index is based, will he inform the House of the date on which the next revision of
that index will commence, and that on which the new weighting pattern will first be used to
compile the index?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): I am advised by the Government
Statistician that the present pattern is still reasonably representative, but that work on the
revision of the consumer price index began on 1 April 1976. The Government Statistician
expects the department to complete the revision on target by the end of the 1977 calendar
year, when he will update the expression base of the index to the December quarter 1977
equalling 1000. I would emphasise that the present revision is of a limited nature, and that
there is no intention to depart from the broad concepts and expenditure coverage inherent in
the present index which follows the recommendations of the 1971 consumer price index
revision advisory committee.
Miss Dewe: Could the Minister confirm that one of the reasons for the unequal rises in
the various subgroups of the consumer price index is that the National Government has been
much more successful in holding housing costs than was the Labour Government in the
period immediately preceding the last revision of the index in 1974?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Yes, since the last revision a considerable change has taken
place in the housing weighting. The result has been shown in the last consumer price index.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Could the Minister also confirm that had the calculations for the
last index been made on the updated basis, the increase in the cost of living would have been
5.2 percent and not 4.8 percent?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: There is no such evidence, and I am not certain what the
member is referring to. The index is at present being updated and the member should, I
think, be correct in his facts.
Richard Walls: Could the Minister tell us what efforts will be made in the revision to
correct any shortcomings?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: A revision is being undertaken at the moment to update the
weighting system for the consumer price index. This is not a major effort, and the normal 5-
yearly review will begin in 1978.

during 1974-75 and 1975-76. A survey carried out recently by my ministry, however, based

Consumer Price Index-“Other Foods" Subgroup
9. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: What

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The relatively
larger movements in the "other foods" group of the consumer price index since December
1975 compared with the movement in the index as a whole reflects in the main the relatively
large movements in the imported cost of such commodities as tea, cocoa, coffee, and dried
fruit. The pricing legislation and pricing policies in respect of these goods are no different
from those applying to other goods represented in the consumer price index, and I shall not

depending on their impact on the consumer price index movements.

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: This is a somewhat complex subject. [Interruption.] I

show a very high figure, but they do not represent the bulk of total products. It is a fair
question to ask. The honourable member will know that fruit and vegetables-goods sold at
auction are not subject to price control, and they were not under the Labour Government.
Meat, which represents a considerable proportion, is not subject to price control at retail. It
was subject to price control for a short time under the Labour Government, but it was
withdrawn. Other products have been subject to price control regulations, and they are the
same regulations that operated under the Labour Government.
Mr Fenton: Does the Minister have evidence that all the items in the food subgroup
mentioned in the original question, such as beverages, sweets, and takeaways, are essential
elements in the average family's budget?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Takeaways, and that type of product, are not
generally recognised as essential parts of a family's budget. Items that have a sugar content
are. It is significant that while the price of sugar increased substantially twice under the
Labour Government it has been stabilised under the National Government.

ROTORUA COUNTY COUNCIL EMPOWERING BILL
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I move, That leave be given to introduce
the Rotorua County Council Empowering Bill. This is a short Bill to give the Rotorua County
Council the right to renew the leases of land on the shores of Lake Rotorua that is covered
by the Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Act. The section holders have leased the land for
the past 20 years, and under the existing legislation the council can renew the leases only on
the same terms and conditions as the former leases. The value of the land has increased
considerably, and the council desires to renew the leases at the present values.
Accordingly, the Bill enables the existing legislation to be amended to substitute the words,
"on such terms and conditions as the Minister of Lands may determine". I am sure this will
meet with the approval of the section owners, and it will give them the right to renew their
leases for a further 10 years.
Motion agreed to.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
SOUTHLAND HARBOUR BOARD RECLAMATION AND EMPOWERING BILL
Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. The Bill
requests authority for the reclamation of land in the Bluff Harbour area. The application is
for a total reclamation of 26.6077 hectares, which includes 6.4177 hectares to be used by the
Ocean Beach Freezing Co., 2.43 hectares for a future wool-scouring plant, 2.83 hectares for
a wood-chipping and storage area, 1.62 hectares for a storage facility for the Southland
Phosphate Co., an estimated area for possible fish packing and processing plants, 4 hectares
for a future ocean oil terminal, 10.12 hectares for servicing in the event of an oil strike in the
Great South Basin, and the remainder for recreational and sporting purposes.
The principal motivation for the Bill was an application made by the Ocean Beach
Freezing Co. to the Southland Harbour Board for assistance in establishing an area suitable
for the assembly of container meat packaging. The company's application was centred
around two main reasons: the need to update and improve the substandard hygiene facilities
in the old freezing works at Ocean Beach, and the advent of the container era in the shipping
of meat through Port Chalmers or Bluff. The company itself is in some difficulty, because
between 25 percent and 30 percent of the present storage facilities at the works is
substandard, according to the new hygiene regulations of the Ministry of Agriculture and
Fisheries. There is no doubt that a new complex will have to be built. The application covers
what I consider to be the only suitable area. Much of the ground surrounding the present
company is unsuitable because of its structure and elevation. In the main it is high, rocky
ground, and a future building must be so placed that meat can be fed from the present
cooling facilities down to a packing area, and from there on to rail wagons.
The oil exploration being carried out by Hunt International Petroleum Ltd in the Great
South Basin has triggered off the second suggested need for the reclamation. Hunt Interna-
tional is operating the largest exploration in the deep-sea area off the coast of New Zealand,
and is conducting a programme of petroleum prospecting under petroleum prospecting
licence No. 863, which extends from Stewart Island to the Auckland and Campbell Island
areas. In addition, the company holds prospecting licences Nos. 38013, 740, and 864, all for
the same area of ocean, roughly. These well known prospecting licences have received a
great deal of publicity and public attention.

Southland Harbour Board Reclamation and Empowering Bill
In the event of an oil strike, there will be a problem in the availability of suitable land
adjacent to the harbour. The company has completed three wells, Parara 1, Toroa 1, and

products, and perhaps, ultimately, oil, if the exploration is successful. I am a little
disappointed that only 6.4 hectares have received the blessing of the committee, but I thank
the committee for its consideration.
