RODNEY COUNTY COUNCIL (GULF HARBOUR) VESTING AND EMPOWERING
BILL
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. Nowadays, we are getting abundant reminders that New Zealand's unique
coastline, particularly in its choicer sections, is a strictly finite resource. This inescapable fact
has two major implications: the first, that a lot of the still undeveloped choice coastline will
have to be protected in what is substantially its natural state-and moves have already been
made in this direction; second. which is essentially what the Bill is all about, that much more
intensive use will have to be made of the available coastline, particularly near the bigger
urban areas.
Parkdale Development Ltd, a land development subdivision of the Winstone group of
companies, has purchased about 300 acres on the Whangaparaoa Peninsula, and intends to
develop this over 12 to 15 years as a model marine suburb of Auckland. The plan is
impressive, futuristic, and imaginative, and the development will both enhance the environ-
ment of the peninsula and advance its inevitable destiny as a choice suburban part of the
Auckland metropolitan area. In contrast to most recent land developments, this subdivision
has been comprehensively planned before the development actually starts, and the develop-
ment company will be involved in the continued planning and execution of the scheme until
the project is finished.
The focal point of this marine suburb will be a major marina to be developed in the
Hobbs Bay area of the Whangaparaoa Peninsula, which will be far and away the biggest
marina in the Auckland metropolitan area, with accommodation for about 1000 boats. In
addition, all kinds of amenities and recreation areas are to be provided; there is also
provision for the quite new concept of a marine public transport terminal, which will
ultimately link the Hibiscus Coast directly to Auckland City. So the planners of this marine
suburb are looking well ahead into the later years of the century when a sizable proportion of
Auckland's commuters could well be travelling by fast water-borne craft.


## p. 1490 (#732) ###########################################

1490
Rodney County Council (Gulf Harbour) Vesting and Empowering Bill 21 July
I think every Auckland member is well aware of the explosive need for expanded
marina facilities. Figures from the Auckland Regional Authority show just how pressing this
is. At Half Moon Bay there are 500 marina berths, at Westhaven 351, plus 385 other
moorings; the present waiting lists are 485 for Half Moon Bay, and 1600 for Westhaven. Gulf
Harbour will provide 700 permanent berths for 20 to 60 ft boats, together with an extra 100
temporary berths and storage for about 200 small craft, so that about 1000 extra craft will be
accommodated at the Gulf Harbour marina and boat harbour. After 5 years of preparation,
there has, significantly, been no objection to the project from the general public. We have
had strong support from the Auckland Harbour Board, the Royal Akarana Yacht Club, and
the Royal New Zealand Yacht Club, and all the submissions from Government departments
have been substantially met. Last, but by no means least, it is heartening also to have the
concurrence of the Auckland Regional Authority, now that its requisitions have been met.
To summarise the salient points, the Bill seeks to vest in the Rodney County Council an
area of just under 40 hectares of Crown seabed, and to reclaim about 16 hectares of this area
for the project. The whole area is to be developed as a public facility. I heard somebody a
minute ago mention Ngataringa Bay. I assure the Opposition that no private individual will
profit from this reclamation, except those involved in boat servicing at the marina. I am sure
that if the member for New Lynn had been down to the Half Moon Bay project, particularly
in its early days, he would agree that there was a need to expand the servicing of small craft
in that bay. This Bill follows an earlier Bill, which was introduced when the old Waitemata
County had jurisdiction over the Whangaparaoa, but was later withdrawn when an agree-
ment was reached that further hydraulic studies be done on the water environment involved
in the development.
This Bill was introduced in 1976 under Standing Order 266, and the Local Bills
Committee inspected the site and conducted hearings in Auckland last April. Briefly, the
information delivered to the committee on that occasion proposed that the boat harbour and
marina, with adjoining reserves and various public facilities, be constructed by Parkdale
Development Ltd under licence and lease for the Rodney County Council. But I make it
abundantly clear the land is vested in the Rodney County Council, and no development can
take place other than by licence and lease from the council. The facility will cost about $6
million, which indicates its size.
The Bill contains very full safeguards dealing with public use and access, water
pollution, and other environmental factors. A leading Auckland solicitor considers that the
protections for the public interest provided in the Bill are as advanced as those in any Bill of
this kind in modern times. Under clause 5, the reclamation cannot be started until the water
and sewage reticulation on the Hibiscus Coast, particularly the Whangaparaoa Peninsula,
has advanced to the point where water and sewers can be provided for the marina and boat
harbour as soon as they come into operation. Clause 9A assures public right of access to all
the reclaimed land, but not to the buildings thereon, naturally. Someone might possibly
object and say that the general public should have the right to go in and out of every
boatshed on the marina, but we do not think this is reasonable; apparently, as there was
general agreement between the parties and at the Local Bills Committee, both sides agreed
that this would be unreasonable. The county council is obliged to make certain bylaws for
access to the pontoons within the marina. I understand that the member for Grey Lynn
raised in the committee the possibility of trafficking in moorings at the marina.
Mr Isbey: That's right.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: I assure him that the council is obliged to make bylaws about
this, and that no one will be able to traffic in moorings. In fact, I understand that if an
Occupier wants to vacate a mooring it will have to be surrendered back to the county council.
These, in essence, are the main points of the Bill, and perhaps I should stress them again.
First, it will provide a very advanced, futuristic subdivision for this attractive area of the
coast. Secondly, the fears that were dredged up at the time of the Ngataringa Bay
controversy do not apply in this case. Thirdly, the marine development provided in the Bill
represents a very major advance in marina facilities for the growing number of pleasure craft
in Auckland.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): I just want to say that the Bill has the support of
members on this side of the House. The members of the select committee visited the area
and looked at the extensive proposal, which, as the Minister said, is valued at about $6
million. The most important aspect is the preservation of the right of public access. The
concept is an excellent one, and, I am sure, would be welcomed by any authority in New
Zealand. We wish the enterprise well.

International Situation
The international economic outlook is one of continuing uncertainty.
In the short term there are no grounds for optimism. There is no sign
that international conditions will assist New Zealand's adjustment to
the difficult circumstances of recent years.
The financial surpluses of the oil exporting countries are unlikely
to diminish over the next few years and may even increase further.
The industrial countries that comprise the bulk of both our export
markets and import sources have contrived to cut back their overall
deficit, but at the expense of full employment. They have failed to
reduce inflation to the extent expected and are vulnerable to any
economic shock that could lead to its resurgence. The cost to smaller
countries such as New Zealand has been a reduced demand for their
exports and a disproportionate share of the global current account
deficit resulting from the OPEC surplus. Reflationary policies clearly
need to have regard to the risks of rekindling inflation. Unless the
action of the United States in allowing its current account to move
sharply into deficit is continued and followed by others, New Zealand's
efforts to adjust its economy towards exporting will encounter
increasing difficulties. .
The first half of this year has, however, seen some favourable
developments. The Economic Summit, which met in London in May,
has led to a stronger determination to establish the stable underlying
conditions that are necessary for economic growth. The International
Monetary Fund is to play a larger role in channelling surplus funds,
from oil exporters and industrial countries alike, to those deficit
countries willing to adopt the necessary economic discipline.
These moves are, however, insufficient to offset the generally pessi-
mistic attitude which a survey of the world scene must produce. The
political will to do what is essential is still lacking in the countries
which can most influence the course of world events.
New Zealand in the World Economy
Our balance of payments outlook, which is a major determinant of
economic policy, will depend on three things: the growth in export
production, world demand for our exports, and access to markets.
It is our job to expand export production. No one else can do that


## p. 1493 (#735) ###########################################

21 July
1493
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
for us. The other two factors, world demand and market access, are
largely beyond our power to influence.
At the recent OECD ministerial meeting I took the opportunity
to stress New Zealand's concerns about the state of world demand
and the continuing barriers to agricultural trade. In signifying New
Zealand's reluctant acquiescence in a further extension of the OECD
trade pledge, which enjoins members to avoid trade restrictions, I
reiterated our long-standing dissatisfaction with the dual standards
to which industrialised countries subscribe in preaching free trade
in manufactured goods while protecting their agricultural sectors.
It would only require policy changes at the margin in the United
States, the EEC and Japan, involving a managed relaxation of import
policies, to expand significantly the volume of international trade in
dairy products and beef. Our hopes must now be pinned on the
GATT multilateral trade negotiations to improve the position of
agricultural producers in the longer term. The inclusion of agriculture
in the OECD communique in this sense was, however, a major break-
through.
The Government has taken every opportunity to make clear to
our major trading partners the adverse effects which continuing
protectionist measures, as well as some of their general economic
policies, are having on New Zealand's economic performance. A
concrete response from Japan to our requests for more liberal and
secure access is awaited before any negotiations on fishing commence.
Ministerial visits to EEC countries have ensured that our concerns in
our largest market remain well understood and that the foundations
for a rewarding long term relationship are being laid.
Protectionist decisions have unfortunately in the past year affected
our important trade in manufactured goods with Australia. The
Government regards an expansion of the number of products which
are traded freely both ways across the Tasman as a key objective. It
will be pressing the Australian Government to resume progress in
developing NAFTA as soon as economic circumstances permit, and
acknowledges the case for equitable access to the New Zealand market
as part of this process. Trade with Australia is still nearly two to one
in Australia's favour and Australian manufacturers would be unwise to
press for action by their Government which would result in New Zealand
applying dollar for dollar quotas in total trade.
The New Zealand Economy
The last 12 months have seen some progress made towards restora-
tion of balance in the New Zealand economy. Externally, the deficit
in the current account of overseas exchange transactions in the May


## p. 1494 (#736) ###########################################

1494
21 July
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
year just ended was $550 million in round terms, an improvement of
$170 million on 1975-76 and just over half the record deficit experienced
in 1974-75. This has been achieved despite only a marginal recovery
in the terms of trade from the lowest level experienced since the great
depression of the 1930s. Since 1973 our terms of trade have deteriorated
by between 35 and 40 percent. This means that a given quantity of
exports will buy less than two thirds the volume of imports which it
would buy in 1973. Some of our export prices have weakened in recent
months, yet the deficit is still far from the level we can live with and it
may even worsen temporarily before the recovery can be resumed.
On the internal side, the deficit between Government revenue and
expenditure has been cut in half-from the record level of $1,002
million in 1975-76 to $506 million in the year ended 31 March 1977.
That deficit was still too high and a further reduction will be achieved
this year, thus aiding the fight against inflation.
Unemployment has been held down to a level which, although still
higher than any New Zealand Government would wish to see it, is
manageable. An increase in unemployment this year will still see New
Zealand with one of the lowest rates of unemployment in the world.
These achievements reflect, firstly, the sound economic policies
which this Government was pledged to implement. They also, and
perhaps more importantly, can be attributed to the degree of restraint
exhibited by most sections of the community. In my Budget statement
last year, I said that the Government sought the co-operation and
support of all New Zealanders of goodwill to combat the most
dangerous economic situation we had faced since the 1930s. I believe
that, in large measure, that co-operation has been forthcoming.
I do not, however, want to give the impression that the battle has
been won. It is far from over and it would be easy to lose the ground
which has been gained. Any relaxation of internal restraint in the
near future would be irresponsible.
The past year and a half has been a period of restoration-of
recovery from a situation where New Zealand was living far beyond
its income. We are still living beyond our income but the gap is
narrowing and we have a clear idea of what is ahead. The next
year will be one of consolidation-of ensuring that the gains which
have been made are held, and that the New Zealand economy is again
placed on a sound footing. The aim now must be to build a foundation
from which the legitimate aspirations of all sections of the community
for higher living standards can be realised, even though a further move
forward must be delayed.
Economic growth is not an end in itself. It is, however, a necessary
prerequisite to the attainment of our society's individual and collective_


## p. 1495 (#737) ###########################################

21 July
1495
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
objectives, whether they be expressed as the spending power of personal
incomes, the quality of family life, the quality and quantity of our
social services or the economic, social and physical environment in
which we and succeeding generations will live.
Traditionally, economic growth in New Zealand has been con-
strained by external factors. A small country not generously endowed
with natural resources, New Zealand is highly dependent on imports
of capital equipment and raw materials to sustain the industries in
which most of the work force is employed. The extent to which the
country can purchase these imports depends on the volume and
purchasing power of our exports.
The extent to which the deterioration in our terms of trade will
be reversed is impossible to determine. What is clear is that there
have been far reaching structural changes in the world economy which
have adversely affected our country. We cannot expect, and would
be foolish to depend upon, an upturn in the near future of sufficient
size and permanence to restore New Zealand's economic fortunes. If
we are to complete an economic recovery and achieve sustained growth
once again, we shall have to rely on our own efforts.
In particular, the fight against inflation is going to be a hard one.
Government policies were successful in substantially reducing the rate
of inflation from the high point it reached in mid 1976. The removal
of the price freeze inevitably saw an upturn in prices as cost increases
which had been held back were finally reflected in prices. There is no
magic formula for beating inflation. It requires perseverance, restraint
and even sacrifice if we are to win through.
I repeat: continued restraint is essential. The measures to be
announced in this Budget represent a package of policies aimed at
re-establishing a basis for growth. The objectives of these policies
are three-fold:
to increase the proportion of national production which is
exported;
to stimulate the development of efficient import replacement
industries;
to encourage the better utilisation of our scarce resources, and
particularly of imported capital equipment.
For many years, production policies in New Zealand have tended
to be based on the needs of industries rather than on the contribution
which they are or should be making to the national economy. Last
year's Budget represented an important change in direction with its
emphasis on the selective application of incentives based on perform-
ance, with particular regard to exporting. That emphasis is to be

continued and extended. Both businesses and individuals who make
the necessary effort will be rewarded.
Government policies can, however, only point the way. Their success
will depend ultimately on the combined efforts of all New Zealanders
and, in particular, on a willingness to accept that change is an essential
part of the progress we seek and that the ways which have served us
well in the past may not serve as well in the future.
We must continue to look to farming, forestry, and manufacturing
to produce the additional exports we so badly need. In an inter-
dependent economy, other sectors must also contribute if we are to
resolve our problems. Tonight I want to pay particular attention to
two sectors which are only indirectly involved in export production-
energy and transport.
Energy
Massive increases in oil prices in recent years have resulted in radical
changes throughout the world in attitudes towards energy. For a
country at present heavily dependent on imported oil as a primary
energy source, we must be concerned that it will become increasingly
more expensive and its supply unreliable.
New Zealand's annual import bill for oil is now approaching $550
million. By way of comparison this is about equal to our export
receipts from dairy products.
The extent of recent increases in the capital costs of energy produc-
tion and distribution are a further indication that energy costs will
continue to rise in real terms. Electricity generation and distribution
alone is expected to require a continuing annual capital outlay in the
next few years of approximately $300 million per annum-or about
$100 per head of our population.
The Government's energy strategy is directed towards reducing the
importance of imported oil in our energy requirements and the
accelerated development of indigenous energy resources. This is to be
supported by an expanded research and development programme and
the intensification of investigations into New Zealand's potential to
provide energy from indigenous sources. This strategy should help
to ensure that sufficient energy will continue to be available to meet
our economic and social needs.
We have already introduced a comprehensive energy pricing policy
and various conservation measures. A decision was taken earlier this
year to divert a substantial and increasing quantity of Maui gas from
electricity generation to industry and households.
The forthcoming merger of the three energy departments is another
step which will strengthen the Government's ability to plan, implement


## p. 1497 (#739) ###########################################

21 July
1497
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
and continually update the comprehensive energy policies the country
will need in the future. We cannot wait until the new Ministry of
Energy is firmly established and as a consequence the following very
important measures will be implemented to promote further our
energy objectives.
ENERGY RESEARCH
The New Zealand Energy Research and Development Committee
continues to be a valuable catalyst in stimulating and financing energy
research and development activities. This year additional finance will
be made available to increase these activities. The total provision for
energy research this year, including Government activities, will be
over $1.1 million which is more than double the amount spent last
year.
DEVELOPMENT OF INDIGENOUS ENERGY RESOURCES
It has become abundantly clear that we do not know enough about
the sources of energy that can be found and developed in New Zealand.
The Government is resolved to establish, as a matter of urgency, com-
prehensive programmes that will provide information on our energy
resources as quickly as possible and on a continuing basis, so that we
are much better equipped to assess the energy options that are available
to us.
Accelerated Geothermal Investigation Programme
Geothermal energy is one of New Zealand's most underdeveloped,
yet most readily available, sources of renewable energy. Its consider-
able potential for electricity generation and for use by industry has not
been properly investigated. Therefore the Government has decided to
increase the rate of investigation drilling from the present 4 to 6 wells a
year to 14 to 16 wells a year.
Accelerated Coal Exploration Programme
An intensive programme of exploration drilling is needed to establish
the real extent of New Zealand's coal reserves. Last year the Govern-
ment initiated a continuing programme for proving coal in the South
Island. This year a highly successful programme of coal exploration
in the Waikato area is nearing completion. The Government has decided
to continue this programme and extend it to the whole of the North
Island.


## p. 1498 (#740) ###########################################

1498
21 July
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
Onshore Petroleum Exploration
Over the last 2 years the Government has participated in offshore
oil exploration with a number of oil companies and this activity is
continuing. Over $30 million has been spent so far and a further $22.5
million is provided for this year.
On-shore, however, no exploration has taken place for some years. It
has therefore been decided to establish a continuing programme of on-
shore seismic work and exploration drilling by the Government itself.
The Government has also decided to bring the functions of the Offshore
Mining Company Limited and the Natural Gas Corporation of New
Zealand under the control of a new company which will have the
responsibility for carrying out the on-shore programme.
Plans have been drawn up for the first well to be spudded in near
Hastings during September and subsequent drilling will follow in North
Canterbury, the West Coast, Hawke's Bay, Manawatu, and through-
out Taranaki. Prospecting licences have been issued by the Minister of
Mines today.
In a full year the costs of this expanded energy exploration pro-
gramme will be approximately $7.5 million for geothermal exploration,
$2.5 million for coal exploration and $10 million for onshore petroleum
exploration.
Local Hydro Schemes
A substantial potential exists for the development of numerous local
hydro schemes of up to 50 megawatts each. The Government would
prefer to see these schemes proceed under the auspices of the electrical
supply authorities using local design and construction facilities. After
discussion with the Electrical Supply Authorities Association, a series of
measures have been decided upon which will provide both the incentives
and the funds needed to stimulate development in this important area.
The Minister of Energy Resources will announce full details of this
scheme.
INCENTIVES FOR ENERGY CONSERVATION IN INDUSTRY
New Zealand must improve its performance in conserving energy

Farming
Farming is our greatest single earner of overseas income. If, there-
fore, our overseas earnings are to increase at the rate required to
provide a sound basis for economic growth, agricultural production
must play a central role. The Government is determined that farmers
be given every incentive to undertake the substantial investment
required if increases in farm production are to be achieved.
Increased farm investment has already been a significant factor
in the maintenance of economic activity at a time when economic
realities have demanded restraint. This increased investment can be
attributed to the improved returns for certain of our major commodi-
ties, to the favourable climatic conditions that many areas have enjoyed
and to a recognition by the farming community of the importance the
Government attaches to the agricultural sector.
The measures which I will announce tonight are aimed specifically
at increasing production further by widening and improving the schemes
introduced last year.
The Government is also aware of the social disadvantages faced by
many of our rural communities and policies will be announced tonight
which will relieve some of these.

THE LIVESTOCK INCENTIVE SCHEME
This scheme, whose objective is to encourage permanent increases
in livestock numbers, was introduced in 1976 and has met with a good
response in its first year. As at 21 June, 2,485 applications had been
approved. It is estimated that these will result in an increase of 2.4
million stock units at a cost to the Government of $27 million. Advances
under the scheme this year are expected to exceed $12 million.
It is, however, apparent that the scheme can be further improved.
At present farmers must achieve a minimum increase equal to 2 percent
of the basic livestock units for each complete year of the programme.
To assist farmers who need a longer development period before addi-
tional stock can be carried and for whom the successive annual increase
of 2 percent was too inhibiting, the cumulative qualifying increases
will be reduced from 4 percent to 3 percent for 2 year programmes
and from 6 percent to 4 percent for 3 year programmes. The initial
minimum 2 percent increase requirement will remain unchanged.
A second modification is aimed particularly at easing the entry
requirements for smaller farms. It is proposed to reduce the minimum
stock unit increase from 100 to 50 for all farms.
Both modifications will be implemented retrospectively to apply to
programmes already approved.
In the coming year the Government will examine the possibility of
developing productivity incentives as an alternative to incentives for
increasing livestock numbers.
LAND SETTLEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT
The Government's emphasis on land settlement and development
continues. This year the Government will increase its financial support
for these activities through the Rural Banking and Finance Corpora-
tion. In 1977-78 the level of loan funds available for farming will be
increased to $163 million. This includes an increase in the amounts
provided for both the special settlement scheme for young farmers
and the Livestock Incentive Scheme. The Minister of Lands has
already announced the Government's intention to put 55 farms up for
ballot in the present financial year.
As a further inducement to those people wishing to enter farming,
the purchase of a first farm will be exempt from stamp duty after
tonight.
Production is inhibited in some areas by either lack of water or
problems of drainage and flooding. The Government is increasing its
funding for water and soil projects, including the provision of an
additional $2.9 million in the current financial year to commence new
projects with high economic potential.

FERTILISER AND LIME SUBSIDIES
As I said in last year's Budget, the Government's objective is to
ensure that the rate of fertiliser application is kept at a level which
allows for both adequate soil maintenance and development needs.
There is a continuing need to restrain the growth of Government
expenditure at the same time as maintaining, or where possible
increasing, support for production orientated incentives. Fertiliser has
a high cost, both in terms of its energy and import content and in terms
of its cost to the taxpayer-about $88 million a year if the present rate
of application and level of subsidies were to continue.
After taking full account of the level of farm incomes and of those
sections of the farming industry which have the greatest potential for
increased production, it has been decided to make certain changes to
the fertiliser subsidies.
From tonight the fertiliser price subsidy will be reduced from $25
per tonne to $22.50 per tonne. At the same time the transport subsidy
rates for fertiliser and lime will be altered to:
first 65 kilometres-4.4 cents per tonnes kilometre;
next 185 kilometres-3.7 cents per tonne kilometre;
over 250 kilometres-2.0 cents per tonne kilometre.
These changes bring the transport subsidies into line with the new
rail tariff and will benefit all farmers more than 30 kilometres from
the nearest fertiliser works. The spreading bounties will not be altered.
Although the cost of fertiliser and lime subsidies will be somewhat
reduced, this is more than compensated for by the increases announced
tonight in other items.
ASSISTANCE TO THE MEAT FREEZING INDUSTRY
There is an urgent need to up-grade buildings, plant and machinery
and operations in our freezing works to meet the strict hygiene
requirements of the countries to which our meat is exported, particu-
larly the EEC countries. The total cost of this up-grading could be as
much as $300 million.
While up-grading has commenced in most works, the size of the
expenditure involved has been a major factor inhibiting progress.
The freezing companies and co-operatives will therefore be offered
further assistance for hygiene expenditure in addition to that already
available.
This special assistance, which will be subject to certain conditions,
will be in the form of either:
a grant of 10 percent, in the year of first use, of the cost of new
plant and machinery installed for hygiene purposes; or
a grant of 7 percent, in the year of expenditure, of the cost of new
plant and machinery installed for hygiene purposes.

Fishing
In my last Budget I announced that a comprehensive study was being
undertaken to determine the most appropriate ways in which the fishing
industry could develop. I also referred to the growing importance that
marine resources would play in our economy and to the challenging
opportunities for expansion presented to the fishing industry by the
establishment of a 200 mile economic zone around New Zealand.
Although international agreement has not yet been reached on a
new Law of the Sea Treaty, several countries have already declared
economic zones around their coastlines. The Government has moved
to safeguard New Zealand's interests by introducing the Territorial
Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill. This measure, together with
policies I am about to announce, will encourage the industry more
fully to exploit the undoubted potential of our marine resources.
The Ministers concerned will announce details later.
From 1971 to the middle of 1976 there was a gradual rundown in
New Zealand's fishing capacity with losses through obsolescence, sales,
and natural wastage exceeding vessel replacements.
To reverse this trend as quickly as possible, the Government intro-
duced, from 1 September 1976, a policy of importing fishing vessels free
of duty, provided they met certain criteria. While this policy has been

Manufacturing Industry
The export sectors I have mentioned so far-agriculture, fishing,
forestry, and tourism-provide, and must continue to provide, the
largest part of our export receipts. Nevertheless, a significant part of
the increased exports required to re-establish economic growth must
come from increased production of manufactured exports.
Exports do not however form the major contribution of the manufac-
turing sector to the economy. Over 90 percent of manufacturing
output is devoted to production for the local market. Manufacturing
employs about one-quarter of the total labour force and is a major user
of resources.
Now that New Zealand's industrial infrastructure is well established
and many New Zealand manufacturers have demonstrated through
exporting that they can meet world standards, substantial benefits can
be achieved by concentrating future investment in those areas that can
make the best contribution to growth and the balance of payments.

Small Business Agency
As announced in our 1975 election policy, the Government has

of finance, management, and marketing will be tackled by the pro-

together with the successful Applied Technology Programme of the

INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENT PLANS
The industry development plan programme will remain a major
component of the Government's industrial strategy. Last year I
announced the introduction of an investment allowance of up to 40
percent on new manufacturing plant and machinery for which an
industry could be considered if it implemented a comprehensive industry
development plan meeting criteria based on the Government's broad
policy objectives. Since then, a number of industry groups have made

designed to encourage the implementation of an approved industry

Transport
Tonight I am announcing the Government's decisions on some
major issues in transport policy which have been studied over the
last 18 months. These decisions are aimed at improving the efficiency
of the country's transport system.
RESTRICTION ON ROAD TRANSPORT
First, the present restriction on the transport of goods by road in
competition with the railways is to be relaxed. Exemptions from
the existing 40 mile restriction have been available but the effect on
road haulage remains severe. It is apparent that overall transport costs
are higher than necessary because for some transport tasks rail is a less
suitable and more costly mode than road transport. This was a major
conclusion of the transport study commissioned by the Government
from the consultants, Wilbur Smith and Company.
While some relaxation of the 40 mile limit is required in the interests
of transport efficiency, the Government is adamant that the Railways
should not, as a result, become a declining force but should be an
efficient and competitive organisation. The most difficult questions that
the Government has had to resolve have, therefore, been the extent and
form of the relaxation.
After considering various alternatives, the Government has decided
that at this stage the most appropriate step is to extend the limit on
road transport from 40 miles to 93.5 miles. In metric terms, the limit


## p. 1513 (#755) ###########################################

21 July
1513
Appropriation.Bill-Financial Statement
will increase from 64 kilometres to 150 kilometres. The Government
recognises that not all road transport users will benefit from this exten-
sion. However, it does mean that for shorter trips the transport
user will have a free choice between the two transport modes. In
particular, two major transport corridors, Auckland-Hamilton and
Wellington-Palmerston North, will be open to road haulage. The new
limit will come into effect on 1 October 1977.
ROAD TRANSPORT TAXATION
While studying the extension of competition between road and rail,
the Government considered the structure of taxation of heavy road
transport vehicles. The present structure of road taxation developed
over the years in a haphazard fashion. While the total taxation revenue
accruing to the National Roads Board and the Consolidated Revenue
Account from commercial vehicles is sufficient to cover the roading and
other community costs which can be attributed to them, there are some
basic anomalies from an economic point of view. The wear and tear on
the roads and the strength which must be built into new roading
structures increases exponentially with laden axle weights. It is
apparent that very heavy vehicles are not, at the present time, paying
their due proportion of road costs, while lighter trucks are paying too
much.
With the extension of competition between road and rail, it is
clearly important to ensure that the heavier trucks, which are most
competitive with rail, are paying their share of roading costs. The
Government therefore proposes to introduce a new distance charge for
all heavy road transport vehicles, which will increase in relation to the
laden axle weight of the vehicle. This charge will be levied on all
heavy vehicles, including trailer units which are not at present subject
to road taxation. It is not, however, the intention of the Government to
increase the tax burden on the industry as a whole and, accordingly,
other taxes on heavy vehicles, such as petrol tax, mileage tax, heavy
traffic fees, and sales tax, will be either abolished or phased down.
The reduction of sales tax will take place in a series of steps. Sales tax
on all vehicles other than motor cars and motor cycles will be reduced
from 40 percent to 30 percent on 1 April 1978. Sales tax on vehicles
with a gross vehicle weight exceeding 3 tonnes will then be reduced
from 30 to 20 percent on 1 April 1979 and further reduced to 10
percent on 1 April 1980. In order to remove anomalies within the road
transport industry, trailers with a gross laden weight exceeding 31
tonnes will be charged 10 percent sales tax with effect from tonight.
The proceeds of the proposed distance charge will be paid into the
National Roads Fund, the magnitude of the charge being set by


## p. 1514 (#756) ###########################################

1514
21 July
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
agreement between the Government and the National Roads Board
in relation to a forward roading programme. This arrangement will
ensure that the National Roads Board receives the appropriate amount
of revenue from the road transport industry and will have the financial
resources needed to enable the Board to perform adequately its vital
function. As an interim measure, the Government has provided an
additional 1 cent per litre on petrol tax as from 1 April of this year
in recognition of the impact of inflation on the Roads Board's pro-
gramme of works. This will increase the Board's income this year by
a further $20 million. However, the Government believes that a major
readjustment of funding arrangements for the board is required. The
introduction of a forward roads programme and the new distance
charge will represent a considerable improvement on past procedures
and will provide a better framework for the discussion and planning
of future roading improvements.
The detailed implementation of these changes will be discussed by
the Government with the National Roads Board and the road transport
industry.
URBAN TRANSPORT
Urban transport is an area of great social and economic importance
which has become a matter of widespread concern. The Government
recognises the need for reform of the organisation and financing of
urban transport. Our approach builds on the report of the Carter
Committee, published in 1970, which identified three basic principles.
First, public transport should be evaluated in terms of its contribution
to the welfare of the urban community. Secondly, the primary respon-
sibility for the provision and financing of urban passenger services should
rest with the area receiving the benefit. Thirdly, all aspects of the urban
transport system should be planned and managed on a co-ordinated
basis and should be integrated with land use planning for each urban
region.
After wide-ranging discussions with local authorities and transport
operators in the main centres, the Government has decided to introduce
substantial reforms in the urban transport field. In order to over-
come the fragmentation of responsibility for different aspects of the
urban transport system, it has been decided that one organisation in
each major urban area should be designated the urban transport
authority. It will have responsibility for overall planning and program-
ming, for designated regional roads and for all public transport services
in its area except railways.
It is proposed to use existing organisations for this purpose wherever
possible. It is unlikely that the designation of the new urban transport


## p. 1515 (#757) ###########################################

21 July
1515
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
authorities will occur simultaneously and there will be provision for
smaller centres to apply for designation when appropriate.
In line with this new approach, which places emphasis on co-ordina-
tion, the Government has decided that changes are also needed at the
national level. The Urban Public Passenger Transport Council will be
reformed to create an institution with a wider view of the urban trans-
port system which will provide the Government with advice on national
policies for the development of urban transport. The new body will be
named the Urban Transport Council. It will be given responsibility
for co-ordinating central Government involvement in urban transport
and for central Government assistance, both financial and advisory, to
urban public transport other than railways. It will report to the Govern-
ment annually, in conjunction with the National Roads Board and Rail-
ways, on the co-ordination of national programmes for urban transport.
Until the Urban Transport Council is formed, the UPPTC will continue
to operate.
It is hoped that, with this new structure, the Government can
encourage urban transport authorities to initiate and implement their
own schemes for improved urban transport. The Minister of Transport
will be making a further statement on the new arrangements.
Concurrently with the deterioration in urban transport, investment
in new buses and railway carriages has been delayed with the result
that a large percentage of the fleet is aged and costly to maintain.
Accordingly, we are bringing in a programme designed to replace buses
over 15 years old in the four main centres. This programme is estimated
to cost $50 million over 5 years. The funds will be distributed by way of
grant, and $6.8 million is being made available for this purpose in the
current year. In later years it is expected that the bus replacement
programme will be merged with the new arrangements for urban trans-
port, whereby all Government financial assistance will be disbursed on
the basis of comprehensive and co-ordinated urban transport plans.
As the Urban Public Passenger Transport Council will no longer be
responsible for bus replacement in the four main centres, its funds for
capital assistance in the current financial year have been reduced to
$0.5 million for assistance to other centres.
The Government is conscious that the Railways' suburban
passenger rolling stock is in poor condition and that repairs are increas-
ingly uneconomic. Accordingly, the Government has decided on a
replacement programme. The cost of Stage I of this programme is
assessed at $44 million which will be spread over the next 4 years. This
will cover replacement of the carriages used on the major suburban rail
routes which are the Wellington commuter lines and the Auckland-
Papakura line.

Post Office
The Government is determined that the Post Office should maintain
profitability and efficiency and make significant contributions from its
own resources towards its increased capital needs.
The higher charges in 1976 have restored the profitability of the Post
Office but, as costs continue to rise, the Post Office will soon be making
losses again unless charges are increased. Accordingly Post Office
charges will rise again from 1 October 1977. Details will be announced
by the Postmaster-General shortly.
Building and Construction
Demand in the building and construction industry has eased over
the past 18 months consistent with the Government's policy of shifting
resources into the export sector. A reduction in activity was inevitable
given the unrealistic levels of 1974-75. The Government is concerned
to ensure that the industry's adjustment to a lower level of activity
proceeds gradually. A limited amount of support is considered desirable
now to prevent too abrupt a contraction.
As well as the measures I am announcing tonight in the housing
field, there will be a substantial relaxation of the Loans Board General
Determination to allow essential local authority works to proceed from
1 August 1977. I have already referred to the revised funding arrange-
ments for the National Roads Board.
The Government is keeping trends in building and construction
under review in close consultation with the industry and, if necessary,
will supplement the measures announced tonight to enable a reason-
able level of activity to be maintained.
Housing

houses was announced for 1977-78, reflecting the easing demand for
home building.
The measures I will announce are in line with this objective. Where

Inflation Accounting
The Report of the Committee of Inquiry into Inflation Accounting
was presented to Parliament in December 1976. At that time I called
for submissions on the committee's recommendations. In response to
this invitation 72 submissions were received. The majority of these were
in favour of showing in accounts the effects of inflation. Detailed study
of the submissions is currently under way as part of the Government's
investigation of the committee's recommendations.
This is a difficult and complex subject which has implications for
income distribution, tax, and pricing policy. The Government believes
that, as a nation which lives by trade and which is dependent on sub-
stantial amounts of overseas capital, we need to keep in step with
decisions to introduce inflation accounting in other countries. These
international developments will be taken into account when reaching a
decision on the proposals of the Committee of Inquiry.
Prices and Incomes
Two main factors are maintaining the present inflationary momen-
tum. These are import prices and wages. In the year March 1976 to
March 1977 import prices rose by 17 percent. Average ordinary time
hourly earnings, as measured by the Department of Labour's half-
yearly survey, rose by 14.9 percent in the year to April 1977. The
impact of import prices on domestic prices is something we cannot
avoid, and this is an important factor for a small country such as New
Zealand which is so dependent on international trade. Imports, wages
and salaries are costs, and co s must enter into and push up prices.
The deterioration in our terms of trade has caused a sharp reduction
in our rate of economic growth. New Zealanders must accept this
simple economic fact. Until they do there is only one inevitable result
and that is accelerating inflation with all that that means for
economic growth, the erosion of the profitability of our export
industries, and the willingness of firms and individuals to undertake
the new investment so vital to the future welfare of all our citizens.


## p. 1526 (#768) ###########################################

1526
21 July
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
While close regulatory control of wages and salaries may be neces-
sary as a short term measure, it is recognised that in the longer term
it creates distortions and dissatisfaction, and limits the flow of labour
resources to the most efficient areas. It is the Government's view that
an enduring system of wage fixing must be one which has been
negotiated with employers and unions, but which, at the same time,
recognises the economic situation which the country faces. To this
end, a number of meetings have been held between the Federation of
Labour, the Combined State Service Organisations, the Employers
Federation, and the Government on the system of wage fixing to
replace the wage freeze which expires on 14 August. It is intended
that legislation giving effect to the new system will be introduced
shortly.
Taxation
FAMILY ASSISTANCE
In last year's Budget the Government introduced the young family
rebate to assist those on low incomes with young families. It has been
decided that additional tax relief is necessary for low-income families
and families relying on only one income.
From 1 October 1977 the PAYE tax tables will include an expanded
young family rebate for the principal income earner in families with
a child under 5 years of age. Instead of the present rebate of $6 a week
on incomes up to $100 a week, the rebate will be increased to $9 a week
on incomes up to $150 a week. The increased rebate will reduce by
10 cents per dollar of income in excess of $150 a week compared to the
present reduction of 15 cents per dollar of income in excess of $100 a
week. This means there will be no rebate on incomes of $240 a week
or more. The present maximum is $140 a week.
In addition, a new rebate is to be introduced for single-income
families with a child under 10. It will also be available to widows and
other solo parents with a child under 10. The new rebate, to be claimed
by the principal income earner, will be $208 a year (equivalent to $4 a
week). It will reduce by 30 cents for every dollar of spouse's income in
excess of $20 a week.
This new rebate will considerably reduce the disadvantage suffered
by single-income families under the present personal income tax struc-
ture. In families where the youngest child has reached 10 years of age,
there is generally more scope for the wife to supplement the family
income by working full or part time.
The existing wife rebate is also to be adjusted so that a wife may
earn up to $520 a year before the rebate reduces instead of the present
level of $375.

rebates will pay no tax if their taxable incomes are less than $82.63 a
week. At present they would pay tax if their taxable incomes exceeded
$57.65 a week. If their taxable incomes are between $80 and $180, their
after-tax incomes will be increased by between 8 and 12 percent.
These tax reductions will amount to about $85 million in respect
of 1977-78.
NATIONAL SUPERANNUITANTS
Those persons whose only assessable income is National Superannua-
tion will be relieved of the obligation to file annual tax returns for the
current income year ending 31 March 1978 and subsequent years. Tax
deductions made during the year will be final unless they elect to file a
return to obtain a tax adjustment. This will be of particular benefit
to former age beneficiaries who may have been out of the tax system
for a number of years.
CHARITABLE DONATIONS AND SCHOOL FEES
The Government's activities in many areas are assisted by the
dedicated work of charitable, cultural, and educational organisations.
At present there is a special exemption from taxable income for chari-
table donations and school fees paid by individuals up to a maximum
of $200.
So as to relate the tax saving more directly to the level of payments,
this exemption is to be replaced by a flat-rate rebate on personal
income tax of 50 percent of all qualifying charitable donations and
school fees. The maximum rebate will be $175, equivalent to an
exemption of $350.
This will apply from the income year commencing 1 April 1978. The
total cost of this change will be about $3 million a year.
DEPRECIATION LIMIT ON MOTORCARS
The Government has decided to raise the limit for depreciation and
losses on business motorcars for income tax purposes from $6,000 to
$7,000. This will apply from the income year commencing 1 April 1977.
SALES TAX
Changes have been made in the application of sales tax to the motor
vehicle industry, both to eliminate existing anomalies and to ensure

a rational system applies under the restructured road taxation scheme.
Some of the changes have already been mentioned in that context.
The changes to take effect from tonight are:
the extension of sales tax to cover all motor vehicle parts and

of all parts and accessories are taxed at this rate;

DUTY ON ALCOHOL AND TOBACCO
The Government is concerned at the high level of public expendi-
ture caused directly and indirectly by the consumption of tobacco
and alcohol. The adverse effects on health of smoking and drinking
have been well publicised. Alcohol is also a major cause of many road
accidents. The cost of providing health care and treatment in public
hospitals and elsewhere for those affected is very high.
As from midnight tonight, the duty on tobacco products and
alcoholic beverages other than wine will be increased. Once old stocks
are cleared, prices to the consumer will rise by the equivalent of 1 cent
for a packet of 20 cigarettes, 1 cent for a standard glass of beer and
1 cent for a nip of spirits; there will be proportionate rises in the prices
of alcohol and tobacco products sold in other forms with the exception
of wine.
The additional revenue from this measure is estimated to be $18
million in 1977-78 and $27 million in a full year. This will help sustain
the high level of spending on health, including the extension of com-
munity health services which I mentioned earlier.
Financial Management
The Controller and Auditor-General has informed me that he
proposes to carry out a comprehensive review and inform Parliament
of the present state of the financial management and control systems of

Public Accounts
PUBLIC ACCOUNTS 1976-77
The Public Accounts for 1976-77 have already been published.
The main features were:
net Government expenditure amounted to $4,504 million, an
increase of $118 million or 2.7 percent on 1975-76;
revenue and other receipts, after deducting a statutory payment
of $41 million to the Reserve Bank to meet losses arising
out of exchange rate changes, totalled $3,998 million. This
represented an increase of 18.1 percent and left $506 million
to be financed from borrowing compared with $1,002 million
in 1975-76.
The firm control on Government expenditure and increased revenue
last year created a surplus in the Consolidated Revenue Account. Part
• ($100 million) of this surplus was used to restore the Reserve Fund
to its pre-1975-76 level and part ($100 million) was transferred to the
Loans Redemption Account for future debt repayment.
In addition the Government succeeded in preserving Parliament's
control over expenditure by keeping unauthorised expenditure well
within the statutory limit. This is in sharp contrast to the 2 previous
years when unauthorised expenditure exceeded the statutory limits
by amounts of $120 million and $176 million respectively.
GOVERNMENT FINANCES 1977-78
When the Government took office 20 months ago, it inherited a
situation where Government expenditure had grown to approximately
41 percent of GNP. Last year we succeeded in bringing expenditure
down to approximately 36 percent of GNP.
Most of the growth in Government expenditure this year is attribut-
able to necessary increases in social services expenditures and pay
increases to State servants. It has not been possible to limit expenditure
to last year's level. This year, the indications are that Government
expenditure will amount to about 38 percent of GNP which is still
consistent with the long term objective of reducing Government expen-
diture as a proportion of GNP.
Budgeted revenue and expenditure for 1977-78 are shown in the
tables. The main features are:
an increase in net expenditure over 1976-77 of $846 million or
18.8 percent to $5,350 million;


## p. 1530 (#772) ###########################################

1530
21 July
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
an expected rise in taxation and other receipts of 24.3 percent to
$4,968 million;
an estimated $382 million to be borrowed to finance net
expenditure.
The reduction of $1,000 million in the deficit before borrowing,
from a projected annual rate of $1,400 million when we took office
to less than $400 million 20 months later, is a major step towards
containing expenditure in the public sector.
Conclusion
After only 20 months in office the Government can claim that
substantial results have been achieved in turning around the alarming
situation which it inherited. The balance of payments deficit has been
substantially reduced and the Government's own deficit has been more
than cut in half. However, our terms of trade are still depressed and
the balance of payments deficit is still far too high for comfort.
While the rate of inflation has declined, it is still a serious and
urgent problem.
Like many other small countries New Zealand faces difficult times
brought about by the structural changes which have taken place in
the world trade and economic scene. Many of the things which
affect us directly we can do little about, such as our export and
import prices. Other things we can shape in a manner which helps
our eventual recovery. It is of little use blaming the world for our
problems. We are the ones who have to solve them. We can adopt
sensible and fair policies which ensure that the hardship we have to
suffer now is fairly apportioned and we can all think of tomorrow and
not try to take what we can today.
I believe New Zealanders have the resources, the strength, and the
courage to win out. The Government can only give a lead and this
will not be lacking. The real battle has to be fought by all the men and
women in this country and I have every confidence that they will carry
the day.
Debate adjourned.

Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. I think I should give an explanation, because some members seem rather
misinformed about the way these provisions are brought into effect. In fact, there are six
different methods by which this bracket of taxes will be brought into effect. The first is the
Customs Acts Amendment Bill, the second reading of which we are now proceeding with;
the second is the Excise Duty (Spirits) Order, executed by the Governor-General in Council
and signed when this Bill is passed and gazetted tonight; the third is the Sales Tax Exemption
Order 1974, Amendment No. 7; the fourth is a determination by me as Minister of Customs;
the fifth is a further determination pursuant to section 9 of the Sales Tax Act, which is done
administratively; and the sixth is a further action taken administratively under the provisions
of Part II of the Customs Tariff. These methods are in addition to the Bill before us, and, for
the benefit of the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, have been the custom for many years. It
just so happens that some of these provisions can be enacted by Order in Council, some are
legislation, and some can be done by executive act.
We are referring tonight to those items that have to be enacted by this Bill. Clause 3, the
first substantive clause, deals with the amendments to the Customs Tariff. The goods for
which the rates of import duty are increased are beer, spirits, liqueurs and other spirituous
beverages, and tobacco products. Clause 4 provides for increases in the rates of excise duty
payable on cigarettes, cigars, and other tobacco products made in New Zealand. Clause 5
increases the maximum rate of excise duty that can be imposed on cigars and snuff
containing less than 75 percent of tobacco grown in New Zealand to $9.15 per kilogram, and
provides in subclause (3) that all such cigars and snuffs shall pay excise duty at the rate of
$9.15 per kilogram.
The increases in the rates of excise duty payable on locally produced whisky, gin, and
related products are provided for in the Excise Duty (Spirits) Order 1977, which, as I said a
minute ago, is to be signed as soon as this Bill is passed. The effect of the foregoing measures
which concern alcohol and tobacco products will be to increase the prices of the goods


## p. 1544 (#786) ###########################################

1544
21 July
Customs Acts Amendment Bill
concerned by the amounts mentioned in tonight's Budget. These include 1c per 200 millilitre
glass for beer, lc a nip for spirits, and 1c for a packet of 20 cigarettes. There will be
proportionate rises in the prices of alcohol and tobacco products sold in other forms. The
duty payable on beer brewed in New Zealand is increased by clause 11 in Part III of the Bill,
and this increase will have the same effect on the price of a 200 millilitre glass of beer. It is
estimated that the annual tax gain from these measures will be $27 million or, for the balance
of this financial year, approximately $18 million.
Part II relates to sales tax, and should be read in conjunction with the Sales Tax
Exemption Order 1974. I should first explain that, under the provisions of the Sales Tax Act,
all goods are subject to sales tax unless specifically exempted by an item in the Sales Tax
Exemption Order. The rates of tax that apply to goods not so exempted are set out in the
first schedule to the Sales Tax Act. The measures now being introduced involve the
revocation and amendment of certain items in the Sales Tax Exemption Order relating to
petroleum products. The item for domestic clothes dryers is also revoked. Two new
exemption items are created to maintain the exemption of automotive gas oil-diesel fuel, as
it is more commonly known—and white spirit, which will also remain exempt.
A new provision in the Sales Tax Exemption Order states that no part of the order,
other than the item for seat belts, will apply to parts and accessories of motor vehicles. This
means that all parts and accessories for motor vehicles, apart from seat belts, become taxable
at the established rate of 20 percent. Clause 7 substitutes the new first schedule to the
principal Act to provide for the changes in the tax status of the goods covered by the Budget.
Trailers having a manufacturer's rated gross vehicle weight exceeding 3.5 tonnes, and the
trailing unit portions of articulated motor vehicles, are excluded from item 1 of Part C of the
new first schedule, and I have determined these goods under item 2 of Part F of the schedule
as being liable to tax at the rate of 10 percent. These trailers have also been excluded from a
ministerial decision, which provides that any person manufacturing trailers is not required to
be licensed. This means that persons manufacturing the trailers referred to will now be
required to license and pay tax on their sale at the rate of 10 percent. The position with other
trailers remains unchanged.
Part E of the schedule is amended by the addition of item 12, and all the air-
conditioning units referred to are now liable to tax at the rate of 30 percent. Part G is new,
and makes provision for the imposition of a sales tax of 1.5c a litre on certain petroleum
products. The major products affected are power and illuminating kerosene, heating fuels,
including home-heating fuels, marine diesel, and certain other oils such as mould and cutting
oils. Part H of the first schedule to the Act covers any goods that are not exempt and not
included elsewhere in the schedule. With the cancellation of the exemption item for
domestic clothes dryers and the amendment to the exemption order with regard to those
parts and accessories of motor vehicles previously exempt, these goods will now be liable to
tax at the rate of 20 percent.
Reference was made in the Budget to two further sales tax measures which will take
effect at later dates. First, the rate of sales tax on vehicles other than motorcars and motor
cycles will be reduced from 40 to 30 percent on 1 April 1978. Secondly, the provision
whereby persons carrying out the combined building and fitting of bodies to commercial
trucks and delivery vans do not require to be licensed under the Act will be withdrawn on 1
April 1980. At this date the combined building and fitting of bodies to these vehicles will
take the same rates as the vehicle itself. These measures do not form part of the legislation
now before the House.
Clause 8 allows for a new provision in the Act to apply tax at a specific rate rather than
on the sale value. This has been included to provide for the new tax of 1.5c a litre on certain
petroleum products. Clause 9 relates to the deduction of discount where sales tax is paid to
the department at the time of importation or clearance from bond or within 28 days after the
end of the month in which the goods are sold. The present discount rates vary from 0.75
percent to 2.5 percent according to the rate of tax involved.
Mr Hunt: Is that 2.5 percent or 2.75 percent.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: It will be amusing later on, when the member for New Lynn
asks me to explain points that I am explaining now. This clause amends subsection 31(1) of
the principal Act to provide for a single discount rate of 1 percent to replace the varying rates
I have just mentioned. [Interruption.] I often think of the behaviour of children in kindergar-
tens; when they cannot understand they become disruptive. Subsections 36(2) and 36(3)
simply repeat the provisions of the principal Act. Subsection 36(4) is new, and provides that
the discount will no longer be available to holders of limited licences. These companies,


## p. 1545 (#787) ###########################################

21 July
1545
Customs Acts Amendment Bill
paper wholesalers as they are sometimes known, were set up by motor vehicle dealers to
defer the payment of tax to the department. Special provisions were made for them under
the 1974 Act. Subclause 9(2) makes a consequential amendment to section 37 of the Act, and
makes it clear that the penalty provisions regarding the payment of tax by holders of limited
licences are unchanged. Subclause 9(3) repeals two earlier enactments. The first of these
provides for discount rates of 0.75 percent and 2.5 percent for certain classes of goods, and
the second provides for variations in discounts to be made by Order in Council. Subclause
9(4) provides that, except in the case of tax paid on goods at the time of importation or
clearance from bond, and tax paid at the new rate of 1.5c a litre on certain petroleum
products, the new discount provisions will apply to goods sold on or after 1 August. This step
has been taken to maintain equity between taxpayers having different accounting periods.
The total net sales tax gain on the next full financial year is estimated to be $17.2 million.
I come briefly now to Part III of the Bill which, as I said earlier, relates to the duty

made or distilled in New Zealand. Clause 13 aligns section 63 of the Distillation Act 1971
with the customs tariff to set the maximum excise duty rate that may be applied by Order in
Council on spirits made or distilled locally at $5.14 a proof litre. As I said earlier, the actual
rates set in the Excise Duty (Spirits) Order 1977 for locally made spirits are lower than this
maximum rate.

Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY: Speaking to the point of order, I was dealing with the
stated objectives of the Government's economic policy, and was pointing out how the Bill
works counter to them. I was about to show how the Bill would provide revenue to finance
national superannuation, and thus trigger off an increased demand for overseas funds for
travel overseas by those superannuitants, and increase demands for imports as a result of the
extra purchasing power in the hands of that section of the community, which was not in need
prior to the introduction of national superannuation. I believe I am entitled to demonstrate
how the transfer of revenue raised by this Bill to those who will expend it externally will have
an impact on the external deficit.
Mr SPEAKER: I am placed in a difficult position. To deal with the point raised I am
almost required to enter into the debate, which I do not want to do. As to the suggestion that
a tax on tobacco and spirits would increase the demand for imports, that seems so fanciful
that I find it difficult to think it is relevant. I will say no more than that. It is not increasing
the amount of money in circulation, but simply transferring some. I will not go beyond that.


## p. 1549 (#791) ###########################################

21 July
1549
Customs Acts Amendment Bill
It has been suggested that this is to finance national superannuation. There is nothing in the
Bill about national superannuation. It has also been suggested that it is to finance additional
health expenditure. The provisions in the Bill are for a trifling amount compared with the
total national superannuation, so it does seem to me that the member is seeking to roam
around the field and have a Budget debate on a Customs Acts Amendment Bill. If he has
any reasons why the Bill should not be passed we should be glad to hear them; if he has any
reasons why it should be passed, we should be glad to hear them also. One feels—and I think
everyone in the House feels-that he wants to have a good Budget-debate splurge and leave
the Bill behind, except as a tenuous hook on which to hang irrelevant arguments.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY: Thank you for your comments, Mr Speaker. I
appreciate the points you made. Nevertheless, I think it is appropriate to attempt to link the
measure with the Government's economic objectives, and that is what I was doing. I am
happy to wait for the Budget debate and deal with it then. Sufficient has been said about the
measure tonight to show that it is a very cunning instrument of Government policy, and not
all that it is represented to be. It is one of the instruments the Government is using to take
away from the people the benefits that the Government claims the Budget provides. We will
take the opportunity in the Budget debate, and in other debates following the Budget
debate, to expose the Government and show that when it had the opportunity to take action
to build the country's economic base and put it on a sound footing again-which the
Government claims is its objective—and when it had the opportunity to deal with inflation,
unemployment, and other problems, in a measure that could have been directed positively
towards that end, it dealt with the difficulties in a negative manner, which will be to the
detriment of the economy and ultimately to the detriment of the people.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): First I shall refer to one or two
comments made by the Deputy Leader of the Opposition about the effect of the proposed
new measures on spirits. He asked whether all spirits, New Zealand or otherwise, would cost
an additional 1c a nip at the bar. The answer is yes. Even though the duty rate on New
Zealand spirits is less than that on imported spirits, the increase in the consumer prices
reflected by the duty increase will be the same. In other words, the duty is sufficient to give a
1c a nip increase for a standard glass, namely the 200 ml glass. The member was a little
perplexed about the fact that we quoted only standard figures. I think he realises as much as
I do that when we are providing information for Budgets and talking about a comprehensive
field such as this we have to talk in standard terms for the sake of brevity. It may well be that
there is a marginal difference between the standard glass and others, but it is of no real
significance.
I was asked why 30 percent is being imposed on air conditioning units that contain
refrigerating equipment. I am sure no member on the other side of the House, even in his
wildest dreams, could say that would affect young families on small incomes. I just cannot
believe that they can be concerned about that. Why was it set at 30 percent? It had to be a
substantial increase because we regard this equipment as a particularly wasteful consumer of
energy, and the imposition of that tax was consistent with our basic energy policy of
conserving fuels wherever we can.
The Deputy Leader of the Opposition asked about kerosene other than aviation
kerosene. The reason for taxing that commodity is abundantly clear. It is an imported fuel,
and furthers our basic aim to conserve the use of imported fuels wherever possible. I could
not understand his statement that there are no alternatives to kerosene. It really surprised
me that he believes we should regard the average New Zealander as being so unimaginative
and so lacking in ingenuity that he cannot, with the aid of the legislation we are bringing in
tonight, find an alternative for many energy uses. If that is not so, we are just playing with
the problem, and might as well forget it. Every fuel-importing country in the world,
including the United States-and I know President Carter has many admirers on the other
side of the House-is directing a great deal of attention to energy conservation.
The Deputy Leader of the Opposition also opposed the additional tax on cigarettes. I
point out that he opposes the tax increase of 2.8 percent in this Bill, but in 1958 he supported
an increase of 109 percent. Where he gets the logic for that change of heart I do not know.
He also said he is opposed to increased revenue when it is not justified. Well, he is in a
corner there, because we have said specifically that some of the money obtained will be used
for community health. I am beginning to wonder whether, as the member for Tauranga
suggested, the Deputy Leader of the Opposition includes community health among those
things that are not justified. It has been estimated that smoking and alcohol consumption
generate health costs of about $30 million to the community each year; so it is a little


## p. 1550 (#792) ###########################################

1550
21 July
Customs Acts Amendment Bill
surprising to find Opposition members objecting to a means of lessening those activities. The
figure of $4.075 million for community health has been quoted by Opposition members on
more than one occasion. I cannot see that figure in the schedules in the Budget or in the
script.
We have been criticised because tonight, in this Bill, we have not set out the whole
rationale for the transport package. The most important part of the transport package in the
Budget, for me as Minister of Customs, is the statement that sales tax on vehicles with a
gross vehicle weight exceeding 3½ tonnes will be reduced from 30 percent to 20 percent on 1
April 1979 and further reduced to 10 percent on 1 April 1980. I know Opposition members
had representations from the transport industry when they were in power about the burden
of sales tax, particularly when it came to replacing the larger rigs. I know that they are well
acquainted with the pressure this is imposing on the transport industry, and frankly I would
be very disappointed if they were to declare their opposition to this staged-down reduction in
tax on the larger transport vehicles.
In summary, Opposition members can scarcely attack the Government for increasing
indirect taxes. Their own record in this field is far more ruthless than ours. When we refer to
the schedule we see that every one of the items in the big tax brackets-in the 60 percent tax
bracket and in the 50 percent tax bracket-had that rate of sales tax imposed by a Labour
Government. In the 40 percent tax bracket all but one item had that rate imposed by the
former Labour Government, and in the 20 percent tax bracket half the items had that rate
imposed on them by the Labour Government. I believe that is clear evidence of their
determination, which they showed clearly when in power, to ruthlessly use indirect taxes for
their own ends. No more need be said about the 1958 Budget; I did not hear very much
about it after we on this side brought up those conservative figures. Apart from an abortive
attempt to raise the superannuation issue again, the Opposition put forward a limp, half-
hearted, meandering case.
I finish on this very serious note. Throughout this second reading the Opposition made
no attempt to debate the rationale behind the reasons for the taxes being imposed by this
Bill. I shall list the most important of them: first, to co-ordinate a restructured road transport
tax system; secondly, to conserve imported fuel and avoid wasteful fuel usage; and, thirdly,
to switch resources from the socially wasteful use of alcohol and tobacco to socially
productive community help. In putting forward their case, Opposition members hardly
alluded to the basic rationale for imposing these brackets of tax. I am forced to conclude that
their attack was half-hearted because, basically, they see the sound reasons behind our
imposition of the measures in this Bill.
The House divided on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
